arxiv_record.abstract:
In this paper, we empirically reveal an invariance over images-images share a
set of one-way wave equations with latent speeds. Each image is uniquely
associated with a solution to these wave equations, allowing for its
reconstruction with high fidelity from an initial condition. We demonstrate it
using an intuitive encoder-decoder framework where each image is encoded into
its corresponding initial condition (a single vector). Subsequently, the
initial condition undergoes a specialized decoder, transforming the one-way
wave equations into a first-order norm + linear autoregressive process. This
process propagates the initial condition along the x and y directions,
generating a high-resolution feature map (up to the image resolution), followed
by a few convolutional layers to reconstruct image pixels. The revealed
invariance, rooted in the shared wave equations, offers a fresh perspective for
comprehending images, establishing a promising avenue for further exploration.

metadata.abstract: In this paper, we empirically demonstrate that natural images can be reconstructed with high fidelity from compressed representations using a simple first-order norm-plus-linear autoregressive (FINOLA) process—without relying on explicit positional information. Through systematic analysis, we observe that the learned coefficient matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) in FINOLA are typically invertible, and their product, $\mathbf{AB}^{-1}$, is diagonalizable across training runs. This structure enables a striking interpretation: FINOLA’s latent dynamics resemble a system of one-way wave equations evolving in a compressed latent space. Under this framework, each image corresponds to a unique solution of these equations. This offers a new perspective on image invariance, suggesting that the underlying structure of images may be governed by simple, invariant dynamic laws. Our findings shed light on a novel avenue for understanding and modeling visual data through the lens of latent-space dynamics and wave propagation.

C1.justification: The shared-wave invariance claim remains. However, v2 broadens the introduction and conclusion beyond hidden-wave reconstruction to claim advantages over conventional reconstruction techniques and effective self-supervised learning with lightweight networks. FINOLA and its representation-learning application become central contributions rather than the paper focusing on two extensions of earlier FINOLA.

C2.justification: v2 interprets reconstruction quality through total latent size MC, discusses the tradeoff between texture reconstruction and semantic representation under masking, and connects feature curvature to semantics. It also clarifies that wave speeds are obtained through post-training diagonalization and that diagonalizability is not guaranteed. These substantially extend v1's interpretation of path counts, wave speeds, and spatial shifts.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's architecture and reconstruction-training tables, v2 newly documents attentional pooling, the L2 objective, parallel autoregression, expanded encoder/decoder specifications, and masked-learning/probing/fine-tuning settings. Appendix A.2.3 adds training and inference hardware and timing, including eight V100 GPUs and an Apple M2 CPU. These disclosures substantially improve implementation guidance without establishing changes to every retained experiment.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ImageNet image reconstruction. v2 retains that task and adds quantized image compression on ImageNet and Kodak, masked prediction and ImageNet classification, and COCO object detection and instance segmentation (Sections 4–5, Appendix B). These substantially broaden both datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 mainly compares against single-path FINOLA and repetition; its DCT/wavelet comparison is conceptual. v2 adds quantitative comparisons with DCT, DWT/DTCWT, convolutional autoencoders, JPEG, and generative-model autoencoders (Tables 5–8 and 15). New downstream comparisons include MAE, SimMIM, MoCo variants, and DETR-based detectors.

E3.justification: v2 extends reconstruction feature resolutions from 16–128 to 8–256 and the path sweep to 16 paths. The all-one-wave comparison changes its repetition control from dimension 3072 to 4096. New protocols include bitrate evaluation, 1600-epoch masked pretraining, linear/transformer probing, and frozen versus fine-tuned COCO backbones. The original 100-epoch reconstruction schedule remains, while the 512×512 image-size experiment disappears.

E4.justification: v2 adds normalization/nonlinearity controls, encoder-size and single-vector-position ablations, embedding sampling/interpolation/PCA, masked-decoder-depth and training-duration studies, and feature-curvature analysis. Existing path-count and wave-speed analyses remain. The detailed four-path spatial-offset sweep in v1 Table 3(b) is omitted, although scattering comparisons are retained and expanded.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 21 introduces box-and-whisker summaries of feature curvature, adding distributional spread reporting absent from v1. Neither version reports benchmark seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, or confidence intervals. The new plot does not specify its box/whisker conventions, so it should not be interpreted as confidence intervals across training runs.

E6.justification: The original C=2048, M=8 reconstruction PSNR of 28.0 is retained. v2 newly reports 29.1 for M=16 and 30.0 with scattered initial positions, representing added configurations rather than same-setting improvements. It also adds substantial compression and downstream results, including 83.9 ImageNet top-1 accuracy and 49.0 COCO detection AP (Tables 9 and 28). v1's 512×512 reconstruction result of 25.1 is omitted.

M1.justification: The reconstruction framework is retained, but v2 introduces Masked FINOLA with cropped-block inputs and loss computed only on masked pixels. Its element-wise variant compresses the visible block, while its block-wise variant preserves uncompressed features and predicts assigned masked positions, with different decoder architectures (Appendix B.1). These are substantive procedural extensions.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion. It reorganizes the narrative around FINOLA before wave-equation generalization, moves special-speed and scattering discussions into Appendix A, and adds dedicated self-supervised-learning and limitations sections. The appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 redraws framework diagrams, adds single-path, parallel-execution, and masking illustrations, and removes v1's wave-quartet diagram. The reconstruction plot gains a 16-path column and latent-size contours. Existing reconstruction galleries are relocated or relabeled, while numerous comparison tables, embedding visualizations, training curves, and curvature plots are added.

R1.justification: v1 explicitly builds on Chen et al. (2023), 'Image is first-order norm+linear autoregressive.' v2 removes that citation and presents FINOLA directly. Its positioning also expands substantially into autoregressive language models, contrastive learning, and masked image modeling, including explicit distinctions from MAE's masking and prediction mechanisms.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the transformed normalization: the denominator's quadratic-form matrix changes from CI - V^-1 J V in v1 Equation 7 to V^T(CI - J)V in v2 Equation 7. Appendix D.1 supplies a stepwise derivation absent from v1. This is a localized mathematical correction; the central diagonalization, superposition argument, and special wave-speed cases remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence and reproducibility: v1's conceptual transform comparison becomes quantitative, new component controls test the FINOLA design, implementation details become more complete, and Appendix D.1 corrects and derives the normalization. These gains exceed mere expansion of scope. Tradeoffs include loss of the detailed spatial-offset sweep and earlier FINOLA attribution, plus a new 27.8 versus 27.7 inconsistency for C=1024, M=16 in Figure 5 and Table 18. Those weaknesses do not outweigh the stronger validation and mathematical documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FINOLA/one-way-wave reconstruction framework, with matching equations and retained ImageNet results despite retitling and substantial expansion. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction, compression, representation-learning, classification, detection, and segmentation results in Sections 4–5 and Appendices A–C.

before.justification: v1 Section 3 and Appendix B report original ImageNet reconstruction results, including PSNR measurements and experiments varying channels, paths, resolutions, wave speeds, and initial positions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) and interpretable machine learning methods help to build trust in model predictions and derived insights, yet also present a perverse incentive for analysts to manipulate XAI metrics to support pre-specified conclusions. This paper introduces the concept of X-hacking, a form of p-hacking applied to XAI metrics such as SHAP values. We show how easily an automated machine learning pipeline can be adapted to exploit model multiplicity at scale: searching a Rashomon set of 'defensible' models with similar predictive performance to find a desired explanation. We formulate the trade-off between explanation and accuracy as a multi-objective optimisation problem, and illustrate empirically on familiar real-world datasets that, on average, Bayesian optimisation accelerates X-hacking 3-fold for features susceptible to it, versus random sampling. We show the vulnerability of a dataset to X-hacking can be determined by information redundancy among features. Finally, we suggest possible methods for detection and prevention, and discuss ethical implications for the credibility and reproducibility of XAI.
arxiv_record.authors: Rahul Sharma, Sergey Redyuk, Sumantrak Mukherjee, Andrea \v{S}ipka, Eyke H\"ullermeier, Sebastian Vollmer, David Selby
arxiv_record.title: X Hacking: The Threat of Misguided AutoML

C1.justification: V3 elevates the custom directed-search implementation and its efficiency comparisons to principal contributions. Its abstract claims threefold acceleration over random sampling, and its introduction claims tenfold acceleration over post-hoc selection. V1 claims feasibility and proposes greater efficiency without these quantitative comparisons; the original redundancy-related claim remains.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly relates vulnerability to predictive multiplicity, interprets unsuccessful finite searches as evidence of robustness, and restricts operational defensibility to predictive performance. It adds preregistration guidance covering AutoML search spaces while removing much of v1's domain-standard and audacity discussion. The core redundancy explanation and absence of observed real-world misuse remain.

D1.justification: Appendices B and D document search-space extraction through ConfigSpace, Optuna/Ray integration, trial storage, algorithm and hyperparameter inventories, and directed-search resources of up to 292 CPUs and 1 TB RAM. The retained post-hoc resources remain 192 CPUs and 300 GB. The cited replication repository changes from Selbosh/p-hacking to datasciapps/x-hacking.

E1.justification: The same 23 binary-classification datasets appear in v1 Table 1 and v3 Table 5, and the original synthetic noise/redundancy scenarios are retained. Targeting four features per dataset in the new search experiments changes experimental settings, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds random sampling as an evaluated comparator for Bayesian directed search under matched budgets, and directly compares directed search with post-hoc cherry-picking for search time. The default random-forest reference remains. Appendix A's AutoML capability survey does not constitute additional experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The retained post-hoc study still uses a one-hour search, 100-second candidate limit and 20% test split. V3 adds 12-hour directed searches targeting four features per dataset, totaling 92 targets, with one-hour candidate limits and matched Bayesian/random budgets. Section 5.4 additionally evaluates first success within one hour.

E4.justification: V3 adds a controlled optimizer substitution—Bayesian versus random search—to assess the benefit of guidance, together with convergence-over-time and time-to-first-success analyses. It also identifies targets for which searches fail within the allotted budget. The earlier noise/redundancy sensitivity experiments and SHAP-slope diagnostics are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify random seed 42. Neither reports repeated independent runs, confidence intervals or significance tests for the experimental comparisons. V3's additional convergence curves and summaries across features do not change this uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds Bayesian/random convergence results across 92 feature targets, reports 20/92 targets without a defensible model, and supplies first-success times for 15 datasets. Table 1 includes 3 seconds for breast-w and 55 minutes 18 seconds for credit-g. These are new results under new protocols; the earlier post-hoc and simulation findings are retained.

M1.justification: V1 presents post-hoc selection, weighted-sum optimization and a small Optuna simulation. V3 adds an implemented distributed directed-search procedure combining auto-sklearn's search space, Optuna's MOTPESampler and Ray Tune to jointly maximize accuracy and minimize mean absolute SHAP. Weighted-sum scalarization remains an alternative in Appendix C.

P1.justification: The background and introduction are extensively rewritten. V3 separates the problem statement, methods and experiments, removes the standalone misconduct taxonomy and audacity subsection, moves scalarization into Appendix C, and reorganizes the experimental appendices. An impact statement is also added. These are substantial narrative changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main-text layout and substantially resizes and relocates existing displays. It adds timing, capability and implementation tables, an architecture diagram, and directed-search convergence plots. Retained simulation scatterplots gain axis labels, while the original appendix's post-hoc plot images are preserved under new numbering.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands positioning around model multiplicity, underspecification and Rashomon sets, citing works such as Black et al., Brunet et al., Fisher et al. and D'Amour et al. It claims to extend model-family studies to complete analysis pipelines and adds an extensive AutoML capability survey, replacing much of v1's broader research-misconduct background.

T1.justification: Sections 3–4 add formal definitions of the searched model sets and their confirmatory Rashomon intersection. The scalarization also changes its sign reference from the baseline model in v1 Equation 2 to the best-performing model in v3 Appendix C, and revises the weight prescription. No theorem or proof is added; the simulation-generating equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked a real-data evaluation of its directed-search proposal. V3 addresses this with matched-budget Bayesian/random comparisons across 92 feature targets and substantially fuller implementation documentation, strengthening empirical support and reproducibility. The exact speedup claims remain underqualified: the reported timing summaries do not directly establish threefold acceleration, repeated-run uncertainty is absent, and post-hoc versus directed-search resource limits differ. These limitations constrain the quantitative claims but do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence for the directed-search approach.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same X-hacking study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched reliably across the reorganization.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds original Bayesian-versus-random directed-search experiments and time-to-first-success measurements in Sections 5.2 and 5.4 and Appendix D.

before.justification: V1 reports original AutoML/SHAP experiments on 23 classification datasets and synthetic noise/redundancy experiments, with additional results in Appendices B–D.

arxiv_record.abstract: The advancement of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) has increasingly highlighted the critical issue of their tendency to hallucinate non-existing objects in the images. To address this issue, previous works focused on using specially curated datasets or powerful LLMs to rectify the outputs of LVLMs. However, these approaches require either costly training or fine-tuning, or API access to proprietary LLMs for post-generation correction. In response to these limitations, we propose Mitigating hallucinAtion via image-gRounded guIdaNcE (MARINE), a framework that is both training-free and API-free. MARINE effectively and efficiently reduces object hallucinations during inference by introducing image-grounded guidance to LVLMs. This is achieved by leveraging open-source vision models to extract object-level information, thereby enhancing the precision of LVLM-generated content. Our framework's flexibility further allows for the integration of multiple vision models, enabling more reliable and robust object-level guidance. Through comprehensive evaluations across 5 popular LVLMs with diverse evaluation metrics and benchmarks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MARINE, which even outperforms existing fine-tuning-based methods. Remarkably, it reduces hallucinations consistently in GPT-4V-assisted evaluation while maintaining the detailedness of LVLMs' generations. We release our code at https://github.com/Linxi-ZHAO/MARINE.
arxiv_record.authors: Linxi Zhao and Yihe Deng and Weitong Zhang and Quanquan Gu
arxiv_record.journal-ref: In Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025
arxiv_record.title: Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Image-Grounded Guidance

In response to these limitations, we propose Mitigating hallucinAtion via image-gRounded guIdaNcE (MARINE), a framework that is both training-free and API-free. MARINE effectively and efficiently reduces object hallucinations during inference by introducing image-grounded guidance to LVLMs. This is achieved by leveraging open-source vision models to extract object-level information, thereby enhancing the precision of LVLM-generated content. Our framework's flexibility further allows for the integration of multiple vision models, enabling more reliable and robust object-level guidance. Through comprehensive evaluations across 5 popular LVLMs with diverse evaluation metrics and benchmarks, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MARINE, which even outperforms existing fine-tuning-based methods. Remarkably, it reduces hallucinations consistently in GPT-4V-assisted evaluation while maintaining the detailedness of LVLMs' generations. We release our code at https://github.com/Linxi-ZHAO/MARINE.

C1.justification: v2 makes multi-source image-grounded aggregation a central contribution and adds explicit claims of the lowest mitigation overhead and preserved general caption/VQA quality. The abstract narrows improved detailedness to maintained detailedness. Training-free, API-free inference-time hallucination mitigation remains the central objective, but the claimed contribution and advertised benefits materially expand.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations based on detector agreement and model-dependent adaptive guidance, explicit hallucination-metric limitations, and boundaries concerning other hallucinations and inherited language-model biases. Earlier guidance-strength and noise interpretations largely remain. Some new interpretations overgeneralize: Section 5.3 claims intersection consistently beats union, although Table 7 favors union on LLaVA-v1.5; Tables 17–18 also show some text-quality declines.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-release link, A6000 hardware specifications, per-model batch sizes, generation limits, detector thresholds, baseline hyperparameters, prompt templates and NLTK-based synonym integration (Appendix A). These substantially expand implementation documentation. Conversely, v1's exact GPT-4V snapshot and January 2024 evaluation dates are omitted. Newly disclosed settings do not establish that those settings changed in previously reported experiments.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates MSCOCO captioning/object-presence tasks and LLaVA-QA90. v2 retains these and adds POPE evaluation on A-OKVQA and GQA image sets (Tables 4 and 16), substantially broadening the evaluated data. These additions concern object-presence probing rather than evaluation of the benchmarks' full native VQA tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds OPERA to the main CHAIR and POPE comparisons. VCD expands from two previously reported POPE model results to comparisons across five LVLMs and participation in CHAIR. Appendix B.1 adds direct-prompting and prompt-as-guidance controls. LURE-with-cutoff and the separate sampled Original rows are removed from the principal comparisons.

E3.justification: v1 specifies temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.9 for CHAIR; v2 makes greedy decoding the main setting. Its fixed guidance strength of 0.7 also replaces the 0.5 specified for v1's GPT-4V evaluation. LLaMA-Adapter-v2 is dropped, and GPT-4V evaluation narrows from six models to two. New protocols include random/popular POPE settings, general text-quality and ALOHa metrics, and latency/memory measurements.

E4.justification: v2 adds single-versus-combined detector and intersection-versus-union ablations, engineered-prompt controls, adaptive guidance, stochastic-decoding robustness, resource analyses and quantitative guidance/quality tradeoffs (Tables 6–7 and Appendix B). Earlier LLaVA/mPLUG-Owl2 threshold plots and the logit example are retained or relocated, while InstructBLIP sweeps and several qualitative judge examples disappear.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix A.2 reports means over seeds 42, 142 and 242 without dispersion. v2 specifies seed 242 for deterministic main evaluations, adds mean ± standard deviation for stochastic CHAIR results (Table 22), and adds ± entries to GPT-4V results (Table 3). The new run counts and meaning of the GPT-4V uncertainty entries are unspecified; increased replication cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: Main results are extensively replaced: LLaVA's CHAIR (CS, CI, Recall) changes from (24.3, 7.1, 67.8) for v1 MARINE-DETR to (17.8, 7.2, 50.8) for v2 MARINE; POPE accuracy changes from 80.6 to 66.9 (Tables 1–2). Changed guidance and decoding settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains or losses. Numerous cross-dataset, ablation, efficiency and ALOHa results are added, while several model/judge result entries are removed.

M1.justification: v1 constructs guidance from a single DETR source. v2 adds explicit aggregation of multiple guidance models in Algorithm 1, implemented using DETR and RAM++ with synonym-based intersection. Appendix B.2 also introduces a confidence-adaptive guidance variant. The underlying two-branch logit combination remains unchanged, but guidance construction and its optional weighting procedure materially expand.

P1.justification: Beyond changing the title and MARINE acronym expansion, v2 extensively rewrites the introduction, contribution statement, method exposition and results narrative. Earlier logit, fine-tuning and detector-noise discussions move into reorganized Appendices A–C. References move before the supplement, and acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. This constitutes substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout, redraws the framework around multiple guidance models, restructures main tables with average columns and a smaller GPT-4V panel, and adds radar, efficiency and ablation displays. Retained case studies and logit panels are relocated or rearranged; the GPT-4V prompt figure becomes Table 15. These are substantial visual changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix C.2 substantially expand positioning around OPERA, HALC, BRAVE and newer grounding, steering and evaluation approaches. Additional references support aggregation, benchmarks and metrics, while several diffusion-guidance references disappear. The positioning shifts from a novel multimodal classifier-free-guidance application toward a training-free, modular framework combining visual sources.

T1.justification: The autoregressive factorization, Bayesian classifier-free-guidance derivation and logit-mixture equations remain substantively unchanged. Appendix B.2 newly defines confidence-dependent guidance through gamma' = 0.4 + 0.4(s - s_min)/(s_max - s_min). This is a limited mathematical definition added for the adaptive variant, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: aggregation and prompting controls test the contribution of visual guidance, additional datasets and ALOHa reduce dependence on the original evaluation, and measured latency/memory plus implementation details make efficiency claims more assessable. Narrower model/GPT-4V coverage, incomplete uncertainty definitions and overstatements such as the interpretation of Table 7 are drawbacks. Nevertheless, the gains in experimental scrutiny and reproducibility substantially improve the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the MARINE research work despite retitling and substantial extensions. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations and additional aggregation, prompting, adaptive-guidance, robustness, latency and memory experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original CHAIR, POPE and GPT-4V evaluations across six LVLMs, plus guidance-strength, detector-threshold and qualitative analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Despite the success in specific scenarios, existing foundation agents still
struggle to generalize across various virtual scenarios, mainly due to the
dramatically different encapsulations of environments with manually designed
observation and action spaces. To handle this issue, we propose the General
Computer Control (GCC) setting to restrict foundation agents to interact with
software through the most unified and standardized interface, i.e., using
screenshots as input and keyboard and mouse actions as output. We introduce
Cradle, a modular and flexible LMM-powered framework, as a preliminary attempt
towards GCC. Enhanced by six key modules, Cradle can understand input
screenshots and output executable code for low-level keyboard and mouse control
after high-level planning, so that Cradle can interact with any software and
complete long-horizon complex tasks without relying on any built-in APIs.
Experimental results show that Cradle exhibits remarkable generalizability and
impressive performance across four previously unexplored commercial video
games, five software applications, and a comprehensive benchmark, OSWorld.
Cradle is the first to enable foundation agents to follow the main storyline
and complete 40-minute-long real missions in the complex AAA game Red Dead
Redemption 2 (RDR2). Cradle can also create a city of a thousand people in
Cities: Skylines, farm and harvest parsnips in Stardew Valley, and trade and
bargain with a maximal weekly total profit of 87% in Dealer's Life 2. Cradle
can not only operate daily software, like Chrome, Outlook, and Feishu, but also
edit images and videos using Meitu and CapCut. Cradle greatly extends the reach
of foundation agents by enabling the easy conversion of any software,
especially complex games, into benchmarks to evaluate agents' various abilities
and facilitate further data collection, thus paving the way for generalist
agents.

metadata.abstract: Despite their success in specific scenarios, existing foundation agents still struggle to generalize across various virtual scenarios, mainly due to the dramatically different encapsulations of environments with manually designed observation and action spaces. To handle this issue, we propose the General Computer Control (GCC) setting to restrict foundation agents to interact with software through the most unified and standardized interface, i.e., using screenshots as input and keyboard and mouse actions as output. We introduce Cradle, a modular and flexible LMM-powered framework, as a preliminary attempt towards GCC. Enhanced by six key modules, Information Gathering, Self-Reflection, Task Inference, Skill Curation, Action Planning, and Memory, Cradle is able to understand input screenshots and output executable code for low-level keyboard and mouse control after high-level planning and information retrieval, so that Cradle can interact with any software and complete long-horizon complex tasks without relying on any built-in APIs. Experimental results show that Cradle exhibits remarkable generalizability and impressive performance across four previously unexplored commercial video games (Red Dead Redemption 2, Cities:Skylines, Stardew Valley and Dealer's Life 2), five software applications (Chrome, Outlook, Feishu, Meitu and CapCut), and a comprehensive benchmark, OSWorld. With a unified interface to interact with any software, Cradle greatly extends the reach of foundation agents thus paving the way for generalist agents.

C1.justification: v1 presents a preliminary RDR2 case study demonstrating potential for GCC. v3 claims demonstrated applicability across diverse games and software, and emphasizes converting commercial software into benchmarks and collecting unified interaction data. The abstract and conclusion consequently broaden the claimed contribution substantially.

C2.justification: v3 extends the RDR2-focused discussion with interpretations of pixel-art perception failures, GUI context and noise, negotiation behavior, and infrastructure failures in city building. It distinguishes assisted from autonomous city outcomes and adds limitations concerning repeated LMM-call costs, limited task coverage, and environment-specific support.

D1.justification: v1 already provides implementation details, prompts, and code-access information. v3 substantially extends these with exact software/game versions, hardware, temperature, reset/load resources, cross-platform control details, environment-specific skills, and an expanded prompt appendix. Previously unspecified RDR2 parameters, such as the three-interaction task horizon, are also documented.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates RDR2 alone. v3 retains that coverage and adds Stardew Valley, Dealer's Life 2, Cities: Skylines, 25 tasks across Chrome, Outlook, CapCut, Meitu, and Feishu, and 369 OSWorld tasks. This introduces farming, negotiation, city planning, media editing, and broader computer-operation requirements.

E2.justification: v1 compares CRADLE with variants lacking self-reflection or task inference. v3 instead reports adapted ReAct-like, Reflexion-like, and Voyager-like agents, plus a Claude 3 Opus backbone comparison in Table 6. OSWorld additionally compares against GPT-4o and GPT-4o+SoM in Tables 4 and 16.

E3.justification: RDR2 evaluation changes from selected tasks with a ten-minute limit and termination on mission failure to checkpoint-based tasks with 500-step limits and permitted retries. The default backbone changes from gpt-4-vision-preview to gpt-4o-2024-05-13. Added evaluations introduce distinct step budgets, financial and efficiency metrics, and city-building measurements with and without bounded human assistance.

E4.justification: The isolated RDR2 module-removal study is replaced by broader baseline and backbone comparisons, including cultivation-progress analysis. New appendix analyses compare GPT-4V/GPT-4o perception, examine negotiation and GUI failures, and diagnose city-building errors through human repairs. Existing RDR2 case studies are largely retained in Appendix B.

E5.justification: v1 reports success percentages from five trials without dispersion estimates. v3 adds mean-and-standard-deviation reporting and explicit success fractions, while retaining five trials for the main game/application evaluations. Appendix G.6 separately discloses one OSWorld run; this does not establish increased replication of existing experiments.

E6.justification: v3 replaces and expands the reported RDR2 outcomes under changed experimental conditions and adds substantial new results. Examples include 4/5 cultivation successes, city populations of 450 ± 224 without assistance and 850 ± 142 with assistance, and OSWorld success of 7.81% versus 5.03% for GPT-4o and 4.59% for GPT-4o+SoM. These are not evidence of a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: The six-module architecture remains, but v3 adds SAM2SOM grounding with label-based mouse actions, toolbar exploration for skill generation, visual-grid prompting, and video-analysis skills. These adaptations change perception, skill acquisition, and execution procedures beyond simply applying the unchanged RDR2 agent elsewhere (Appendices C, E, and F).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusions are extensively rewritten around the broader study. The standalone GCC discussion is integrated into the introduction, framework subsections are reordered, and much RDR2-specific material moves into a reorganized appendix with environment-specific sections and a contents list.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the framework overview and adds task maps, cross-environment workflow diagrams, benchmark plots, comparison tables, and grounding illustrations. Retained displays are also relocated: for example, v1's Figure 5 self-reflection case becomes v3's Figure 17. These are substantial visual and organizational changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Related work expands into separate discussions of computer-control environments and foundation agents, adding substantial coverage of embodied simulators and software benchmarks. New positioning against Universe, SIMA, and OSWorld emphasizes unified interfaces and contrasts CRADLE's approach with API-dependent environments and demonstration-trained agents.

T1.justification: Appendix D.6 adds explicit mathematical definitions for the newly introduced financial evaluation quantities, including valuation deviation and buying/selling-price-to-valuation ratios. This is a limited formal addition; neither version develops theoretical guarantees, theorems, or proofs for CRADLE.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence connecting GCC's broad ambitions to demonstrated applicability: v1 offers one game study, whereas v3 tests diverse environments with explicit comparators, richer failure analysis, and detailed implementation documentation. Tradeoffs remain: bundled baseline comparisons isolate module effects less clearly, OSWorld is evaluated once, and the headline thousand-person city requires human assistance. Despite these qualifications, the broader validation and improved transparency provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the GCC setting and CRADLE framework, retaining the RDR2 study despite substantial expansion and a changed title. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original results across four games, five software applications, and OSWorld, alongside baseline comparisons and extensive appendix case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original RDR2 gameplay cases and five-trial success rates for seven tasks, including module-removal comparisons in Figure 8.

arxiv_record.abstract: Temporal Graph Neural Networks (TGNNs) are widely used to model dynamic systems where relationships and features evolve over time. Although TGNNs demonstrate strong predictive capabilities in these domains, their complex architectures pose significant challenges for explainability. Counterfactual explanation methods provide a promising solution by illustrating how modifications to input graphs can influence model predictions. To address this challenge, we present CoDy, Counterfactual Explainer for Dynamic Graphs, a model-agnostic, instance-level explanation approach that identifies counterfactual subgraphs to interpret TGNN predictions. CoDy employs a search algorithm that combines Monte Carlo Tree Search with heuristic selection policies, efficiently exploring a vast search space of potential explanatory subgraphs by leveraging spatial, temporal, and local event impact information. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art factual and counterfactual baselines demonstrate CoDy's effectiveness, with improvements of 16% in AUFSC+ over the strongest baseline.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhan Qu, Daniel Gomm, Michael F\"arber

C1.justification: The abstract replaces the claim of up to 59% higher counterfactual-discovery success with 16% improvement in AUFSC+ over the strongest baseline. This changes the headline performance claim to a sparsity-aware criterion while retaining the central contribution of counterfactual explanations for TGNNs.

C2.justification: v2 adds practical guidance on choosing spatio-temporal policies without ground-truth labels, proposes possible early-stopping and hybrid-search options, and identifies user studies as future validation. Its TGAT and sensitivity discussions connect weaker results to search configuration. The original limitation to removal-based explanations remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies detailed CoDy subroutines, node attributes, and score updates in Appendix B, specifies the neighborhood-depth rule and characterization weights, and newly reports CPU, GPU, and memory specifications. It replaces the anonymous code location with a named GitHub repository. However, v1's explicit 30-epoch training and early-stopping description is omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate future-link explanations on UCI-Messages, UCI-Forums, and Wikipedia, separating correct and incorrect predictions. Publishing previously omitted TGAT results adds model-specific evidence, not another dataset, task, or population.

E2.justification: PGExplainer is newly evaluated in the TGN comparisons in v2 Tables 1 and 4; v1 explicitly excluded it. T-GNNExplainer and the GreeDy variants remain. TempME remains unevaluated, and the newly discussed GRACIE is not an experimental comparator.

E3.justification: v2 makes AUFSC+ and AUFSC- primary metrics, integrating fidelity with explanation sparsity. It also corrects the reported fidelity- definition from one minus prediction agreement to agreement. Added protocols include PGExplainer at fixed sparsity 0.2 and controlled sensitivity settings for alpha and candidate-set size; the main CoDy search budget remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a focused sensitivity study on TGAT/UCI-Messages, varying the exploration–exploitation balance and candidate-set size. The earlier runtime, search-iteration, and Jaccard-similarity analyses are largely retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable empirical uncertainty estimates. The added results retain descriptive reporting without introducing an uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds AUFSC results, PGExplainer scores, complete TGAT results, and sensitivity findings. For example, TGAT/UCI-Messages correct-prediction fidelity+ is 0.38 for GreeDy-spatio-temporal versus 0.32 for CoDy-spatio-temporal. All 216 existing TGN values in v1 Table 2 are retained in v2 Table 4; the new metrics do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The greedy and MCTS procedures, four selection policies, and fallback strategy are retained. Event-impact renames local-gradient. Normalizing the default search weights from (2,1) to (2/3,1/3) preserves their relative weighting. Expanded pseudocode documents existing components without establishing a procedural redesign.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 separates the evaluation framework, adds practical considerations, and reorganizes appendices around algorithm details, target models, and sensitivity analysis. Terminology changes include local-gradient becoming event-impact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a factual-versus-counterfactual illustration, redraws the CoDy framework, retypesets algorithms, and introduces a differently structured main AUFSC table. The original results table moves to the appendix; TGAT and sensitivity displays are added, while the fidelity+/fidelity- scatter display is removed. Several existing plots are resized or redisplayed.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of GRACIE and explains why its discrete-time formulation does not transfer directly to continuous-time graphs. It also adds generative-explainer and MCTS references while trimming broader background citations. The central positioning around counterfactual explanations for CTDG-based TGNNs remains.

T1.justification: Appendix D corrects the mathematical definition of fidelity-, resolving its conflict with the stated sufficiency interpretation. Appendix F.2 adds a model-call complexity argument: O(itmax), or O(itmax + N) for event-impact with N candidates. No substantial theorem or proof development is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the paper's evidential support and reproducibility through previously omitted TGAT results, detailed CoDy procedures, controlled sensitivity evidence, and correction of the sufficiency definition. These address important gaps in v1. Reporting remains imperfect: TGAT Table 3 includes char=0.03 for fidelity values 0.19 and 0.50, inconsistent with its formula, and explicit training-duration details disappear. These defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoDy/GreeDy research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and renamed policies and relocated results can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original TGN experiments and additionally reports TGAT results, PGExplainer comparisons, and parameter sensitivity experiments in its main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original TGN explanation experiments, including fidelity, sparsity, runtime, search-iteration effects, and explanation similarities in Section 5 and Appendices C–G.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to jailbreaking attacks that lead to generation of inappropriate or harmful content. Manual red-teaming requires a time-consuming search for adversarial prompts, whereas automatic adversarial prompt generation often leads to semantically meaningless attacks that do not scale well. In this paper, we present a novel method that uses another LLM, called AdvPrompter, to generate human-readable adversarial prompts in seconds. AdvPrompter, which is trained using an alternating optimization algorithm, generates suffixes that veil the input instruction without changing its meaning, such that the TargetLLM is lured to give a harmful response. Experimental results on popular open source TargetLLMs show highly competitive results on the AdvBench and HarmBench datasets, that also transfer to closed-source black-box LLMs. We also show that training on adversarial suffixes generated by AdvPrompter is a promising strategy for improving the robustness of LLMs to jailbreaking attacks.
arxiv_record.authors: Anselm Paulus, Arman Zharmagambetov, Chuan Guo, Brandon Amos, Yuandong Tian
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted to ICML 2025. Code is available at http://github.com/facebookresearch/advprompter

C1.justification: The core contribution remains fast, conditional adversarial generation through alternating training. v2 removes the approximately 800-fold headline speed claim and qualifies the introduction's performance-superiority claim. It also explicitly extends the claimed safety benefit from resistance to AdvPrompter to resistance against other attacks.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about AdvBench's semantic overlap and generalization evidence. It explains transfer performance through source-model difficulty and interprets weaker defense gains against GCG as a consequence of its high-perplexity attacks. These materially expand the paper's explanations and boundaries of defensive applicability.

D1.justification: v2 identifies HarmBench baseline implementations but shortens the warm-start recipe and omits v1's explicit greedy TargetLLM-generation disclosure. Core hyperparameters, hardware, PPO settings and code access remain. Its new 'around 10 hours' training-time statement conflicts with the retained 16-hour-12-minute and 20-hour-4-minute figures in Appendix C.1.

E1.justification: v2 adds HarmBench's distinct harmful-behavior collection for attack and robustness evaluation, extending coverage beyond AdvBench. It also adds MT-bench conversational-utility evaluation after safety fine-tuning; AdvBench and MMLU remain.

E2.justification: Alongside retained GCG, AutoDAN and PPO comparisons, v2 evaluates PAIR, TAP, TAP-T and PAP-top5 in its HarmBench experiments. Appendix C.7.1 also compares BEAST against AdvPrompter on two Vicuna models. These are reported comparisons, not merely added citations.

E3.justification: v2 introduces training on HarmBench's 80 validation behaviors and testing on 320 test behaviors, its LLM evaluator, BEAST budgets of 10/60 seconds, and additional target configurations including Llama3.1-8b. The original AdvBench split and evaluators remain. The retained model-transfer comparison is labeled validation in v1 Figure 3 but test in v2 Table 5; this reported setting revision does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds source-model sensitivity analysis for transfer attacks (Table 9), tests whether safety fine-tuning transfers to GCG and AutoDAN on HarmBench (Table 8), and examines conversational utility. The original trial-count, decoding, amortized-AutoDAN and PPO analyses are retained, largely relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: Three-independent-run averaging for the original AdvBench comparison is retained in v2 Table 3 and Figure 3, as are the existing shaded plots. No new seed-count, confidence-interval, significance-testing or uncertainty-reporting practice is specified.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial HarmBench, MT-bench, BEAST and source-model results. For example, Table 8 reports Mistral's GCG ASR falling from 63.4 to 57.8 and AutoDAN ASR from 71.0 to 35.0 after safety fine-tuning. Original whitebox and StrongREJECT numbers are retained. The Vicuna-7b, Llama2-7b and Mistral-7b transfer entries from v1 Figure 3 are omitted.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes the specified expansion from k candidates per beam to k/b candidates per beam, while both versions report k=48 and b=4. This is a limited revision to the stated search procedure; the alternating training framework, model architecture, replay buffer and gradient-free scoring remain.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and condenses the abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative. Related work, implementation details and most ablations move into reorganized appendices; experiments are framed explicitly around direct, data-transfer and model-transfer settings. An impact statement is added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main paper, adds multiple experimental tables, and redisplays selected original results in compact tables. The transfer bar chart is replaced by Table 5, the runtime chart gains baselines, and many retained figures and tables move to the appendices.

R1.justification: Mostly retained related-work text gains focused comparisons with LoFT, BEAST and AmpleGCG, plus references for TAP and HarmBench. These clarify distinctions involving proxy training, amortization and query budgets. Some broad application and amortized-optimization references are removed, without replacing the central research positioning.

T1.justification: The formal q-step changes from minimizing L plus the AdvPrompter likelihood penalty in v1 Equation (6) to minimizing L in v2 Equation (5). Appendix B.2 retains the penalized derivation but explains bypassing that penalty through candidate sampling. The remaining mathematical framework is substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1's generalization evidence relied on AdvBench, and its defense evaluation principally used AdvPrompter itself. v2 adds HarmBench, broader baseline comparisons, cross-attack robustness tests and conversational-utility measurements, addressing important validation gaps. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including inconsistent training times and Table 11's claim of five targets despite displaying only two.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdvPrompter research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds HarmBench evaluations, additional baseline comparisons, cross-attack robustness tests and MT-bench measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack evaluations, safety fine-tuning experiments, sampling ablations and PPO experiments in the main text and appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: While numerous frameworks have been developed to enhance the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), there is a scarcity of methods that effectively balance the trade-off between cost and quality. In this paper, we introduce Fleet of Agents (FoA), a novel and intuitive yet principled framework utilizing LLMs as agents to navigate through dynamic tree searches, employing a genetic-type particle filtering approach. FoA spawns a multitude of agents, each exploring the search space autonomously, followed by a selection phase where resampling based on a heuristic value function optimizes the balance between exploration and exploitation. This mechanism enables dynamic branching, adapting the exploration strategy based on discovered solutions. We conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark tasks, ``Game of 24'', ``Mini-Crosswords'', and ``WebShop'', utilizing four different LLMs, ``GPT-3.5'', ``GPT-4'', ``LLaMA3.2-11B'', and ``LLaMA3.2-90B''. On average across all tasks and LLMs, FoA obtains a quality improvement of ~5% while requiring only ~40% of the cost of previous SOTA methods. Notably, our analyses reveal that (1) FoA achieves the best cost-quality trade-off among all benchmarked methods and (2) FoA + LLaMA3.2-11B surpasses the Llama3.2-90B model. FoA is publicly available at https://github.com/au-clan/FoA.
arxiv_record.authors: Lars Klein, Nearchos Potamitis, Roland Aydin, Robert West, Caglar Gulcehre, Akhil Arora
arxiv_record.title: Fleet of Agents: Coordinated Problem Solving with Large Language Models

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes efficiency and accuracy relative to ToT on two puzzles. v2 broadens the central claims to superiority over multiple SOTA methods, approximately 5% better quality at 40% of their cost, the best trade-off at all price points, and FoA enabling Llama-11B to surpass the standalone 90B model. These materially expand the claimed scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving fleet diversity, noisy historical value estimates, and inconsistent repeated evaluations, plus a fixed-fleet-size limitation and the qualification that ToT might catch up at higher budgets. It removes v1's warning about failing to reproduce published GPT-4 Crossword results and its explicit caveat about backtracking through irreversible actions.

D1.justification: v1 mainly identifies reused ToT prompts and broad hyperparameter categories. v2 supplies seven prompt templates, model checkpoints, API providers, token prices, generation settings, tuning plots and selected configurations, and caching/batching details in Appendix C. It also supplies a FoA code-access URL. These substantially improve implementation and reproduction documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds WebShop alongside the retained Game of 24 and Mini Crosswords datasets. This substantially extends evaluation from self-contained puzzles to sequential decision-making in a simulated shopping environment, requiring navigation, product selection, and purchase.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares against ToT, with literature-sourced IO and CoT reference scores for GPT-4 Game of 24. v2 adds evaluated CoT-SC, AoT, GoT, and RAFA comparisons for Game of 24, and IO, CoT, CoT-SC, and GoT for Crosswords. WebShop adds Act, ReAct, Reflexion, LASER, and LATS. RAFA is evaluated with GPT-3.5 and Llama-11B, not the configurations marked DNR.

E3.justification: The original puzzle splits and metrics are retained. v2 adds Llama3.2-11B/90B evaluation settings, a WebShop design with 50 test and 15 validation tasks, and a new budget-controlled experiment in Section 5 that allocates $5 per method and measures success across multiple trials. These extend the evaluation design substantially.

E4.justification: v1 describes hyperparameter searches and reports selected configurations but has no component ablations. v2 adds removal or alteration studies for selection, resampling, backtracking, caching, and batching across tasks (Figures 6, 11, and 12), explicit hyperparameter sensitivity plots (Figures 8-10), and model-size and budget analyses.

E5.justification: v1 displays benchmark confidence intervals, specifies bootstrap intervals for GPT-4 Game of 24, and qualifies its nonsignificant accuracy advantage. v2 removes those intervals and qualifications. It retains the stated one-run GPT-4/five-run GPT-3.5 practice and extends five-run reporting to other models, but the promised standard errors are absent from Tables 6-8. New sensitivity plots contain error bars whose meaning is not specified.

E6.justification: Many original FoA values remain unchanged, including GPT-4 Game of 24 at 76% and $62.93 and Crosswords at 46% and $12.938. arxiv_record.abstract: Driven by steady progress in deep generative modeling, simulation-based inference (SBI) has emerged as the workhorse for inferring the parameters of stochastic simulators. However, recent work has demonstrated that model misspecification can compromise the reliability of SBI, preventing its adoption in important applications where only misspecified simulators are available. This work introduces robust posterior estimation~(RoPE), a framework that overcomes model misspecification with a small real-world calibration set of ground-truth parameter measurements. We formalize the misspecification gap as the solution of an optimal transport~(OT) problem between learned representations of real-world and simulated observations, allowing RoPE to learn a model of the misspecification without placing additional assumptions on its nature. RoPE demonstrates how OT and a calibration set provide a controllable balance between calibrated uncertainty and informative inference, even under severely misspecified simulators. Results on four synthetic tasks and two real-world problems with ground-truth labels demonstrate that RoPE outperforms baselines and consistently returns informative and calibrated credible intervals.
arxiv_record.authors: Antoine Wehenkel, Juan L. Gamella, Ozan Sener, Jens Behrmann, Guillermo Sapiro, J\"orn-Henrik Jacobsen, Marco Cuturi

V2 broadens the contribution to addressing and investigating prior misspecification while retaining the central calibration-set/OT approach. C2.justification: V2 replaces prior misspecification as merely a future-work limitation with an implemented mechanism and interpretation of tau. It adds substantive discussion of biased calibration sets, overlapping versus disjoint support, the assumed prior covering the true distribution, and ACAUC's inability to assess joint calibration (Section 6 and Appendices E/L).

E1.justification: The six original tasks remain, but v2 substantially expands assumption-violation scenarios: prior-mismatched pendulum populations, newly collected light-tunnel data with betabinomial parameter distributions, and calibration/test distribution mismatch (Appendices C and L). The existing vertically flipped light-tunnel scenario is retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated NPE-RS comparisons across the six tasks and extends NNPE from tasks A–B to tasks C–F (Figures 1–2). V1 cited the NPE-RS source but did not evaluate that comparator and explicitly excluded NNPE from C–F. Existing principal baselines remain.

E3.justification: The original LPP/ACAUC metrics, 2,000-example test sets, and core training settings largely remain. Added protocols include tau sweeps from 0.1 to 1, controlled prior-mixture weights, and error-versus-distance evaluation using normalized-color MAE. NPE-RS additionally uses the 2,000 test observations for its regularization.

E4.justification: V2 adds prior-mismatch and tau sensitivity experiments, biased-calibration robustness tests, error analysis by distance from the calibration distribution, and corresponding posterior examples (Figure 3 and Appendices C/L). V1's component ablations, entropy sensitivity, and image-flip robustness analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both main comparison captions report means and plus/minus one standard deviation over three random draws and additional randomness. The appendices retain the fixed real-data split descriptions. No changed repeated-run counts, seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures are documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for RoPE*, NPE-RS, expanded NNPE comparisons, and the new robustness scenarios. Figure 3 shows benefits from relaxing transport balance under prior mismatch. Appendix L reports increasing prediction error away from the calibration distribution despite near-zero marginal calibration scores for larger calibration sets. These are additional findings under new conditions.

M1.justification: V1 fixes both marginals in balanced optimal transport. V2 introduces RoPE*, replacing the simulated-data marginal constraint with a KL penalty controlled by rho/tau, permitting simulations to be down-weighted under prior mismatch (Section 2.3 and Algorithm 1). The original NPE and calibration fine-tuning stages remain.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction and motivation, gives misspecification a dedicated background subsection, expands the OT-benefits discussion, introduces Related Work, and reorganizes the appendices. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main text and redraws the six-task comparison as Figures 1–2 with direct method labels. It adds robustness displays and relocates the workflow and posterior illustrations to appendices. Existing corner/calibration plots are retained and renumbered. New Figure 15 reverses the SBI/prior reference labels relative to the main comparison.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantial Related Work section positioning RoPE against simulation-to-reality transfer, domain adaptation, semi-supervised/few-shot learning, generalized Bayesian inference, and robust SBI. Numerous newly cited works support these distinctions, substantially expanding v1's limited positioning.

T1.justification: V2 formalizes semi-balanced transport, adds a Gaussian-offset counterexample and posterior derivation distinguishing misspecification definitions (Appendix A.2), and develops coupling/prior-support reasoning (Appendix E). The original self-calibration proof is retained for balanced RoPE. The new counterexample's final bias expression is incorrect: its preceding posterior mean implies lambda*n/(n+1).

improvement.justification: V1 identifies prior misspecification as potentially severely damaging and leaves unbalanced transport as future work. arxiv_record.abstract: Dense depth prediction deep neural networks (DNN) have achieved impressive results for both monocular and binocular data, but still they are limited by high computational complexity, restricting their use on low-end devices. For better on-device efficiency and hardware utilization, weights and activations of the DNN should be converted to low-bit precision. However, this precision is not sufficient to represent high dynamic range depth. In this paper, we aim to overcome this limitation and restore high-precision depth from low-bit precision predictions. To achieve this, we propose to represent high dynamic range depth as two low dynamic range components of a Hilbert curve, and to train the full-precision DNN to directly predict the latter. For on-device deployment, we use standard quantization methods and add a post-processing step that reconstructs depth from the Hilbert curve components predicted in low-bit precision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method increases the bit precision of predicted depth by up to three bits with little computational overhead. We also observed a positive side effect of quantization error reduction by up to 4.6 times. Our method enables effective and accurate depth prediction with DNN weights and activations quantized to eight-bit precision.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large autoregressive models like Transformers can solve tasks through in-context learning (ICL) without learning new weights, suggesting avenues for efficiently solving new tasks. For many tasks, e.g., linear regression, the data factorizes: examples are independent given a task latent that generates the data, e.g., linear coefficients. While an optimal predictor leverages this factorization by inferring task latents, it is unclear if Transformers implicitly do so or if they instead exploit heuristics and statistical shortcuts enabled by attention layers. Both scenarios have inspired active ongoing work. In this paper, we systematically investigate the effect of explicitly inferring task latents. We minimally modify the Transformer architecture with a bottleneck designed to prevent shortcuts in favor of more structured solutions, and then compare performance against standard Transformers across various ICL tasks. Contrary to intuition and some recent works, we find little discernible difference between the two; biasing towards task-relevant latent variables does not lead to better out-of-distribution performance, in general. Curiously, we find that while the bottleneck effectively learns to extract latent task variables from context, downstream processing struggles to utilize them for robust prediction. Our study highlights the intrinsic limitations of Transformers in achieving structured ICL solutions that generalize, and shows that while inferring the right latents aids interpretability, it is not sufficient to alleviate this problem.
arxiv_record.authors: Sarthak Mittal, Eric Elmoznino, Leo Gagnon, Sangnie Bhardwaj, Tom Marty, Dhanya Sridhar and Guillaume Lajoie
arxiv_record.title: Does learning the right latent variables necessarily improve in-context learning?

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Large autoregressive models like Transformers can solve tasks through in-context learning (ICL) without learning new weights, suggesting avenues for efficiently solving new tasks. For many tasks, e.g., linear regression, the data factorizes: examples are independent given a task latent that generates the data, e.g., linear coefficients. While an optimal predictor leverages this factorization by inferring task latents, it is unclear if Transformers implicitly do so or if they instead exploit heuristics and statistical shortcuts enabled by attention layers. Both scenarios have inspired active ongoing work. In this paper, we systematically investigate the effect of explicitly inferring task latents. We minimally modify the Transformer architecture with a bottleneck designed to prevent shortcuts in favor of more structured solutions, and then compare performance against standard Transformers across various ICL tasks. Contrary to intuition and some recent works, we find little discernible difference between the two; biasing towards task-relevant latent variables does not lead to better out-of-distribution performance, in general. Curiously, we find that while the bottleneck effectively learns to extract latent task variables from context, downstream processing struggles to utilize them for robust prediction. Our study highlights the intrinsic limitations of Transformers in achieving structured ICL solutions that generalize, and shows that while inferring the right latents aids interpretability, it is not sufficient to alleviate this problem.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims: explicit latent recovery aids interpretability but generally does not improve generalization, because downstream prediction remains inadequate. The new contribution bullets organize claims already present in v1.

C2.justification: The shortcut-injection discussion introduces an important boundary: explicit models can generalize better when training strongly encourages nearest-neighbor shortcuts. Appendix D adds explanations for classification-versus-regression behavior and interprets the proxy results as separating latent recovery from predictive generalization.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the modular task's five tanh experts, five stages, and four-dimensional inputs/outputs, and provides layer configurations and parameter counts in Tables 1–8. Existing optimizer, training-budget, hardware, and timing disclosures remain. However, v1's code-access footnote is omitted; this does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 adds reusable five-stage mixture-of-experts composition as an evaluated task. It also expands generalization scenarios with near-context training followed by far-context queries and OOD-latent evaluations for linear regression and classification (Figure 7; Tables 1–2). The original task suite is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds the implicit-proxy comparator in Figure 11 and the direct-versus-decoded auxiliary-supervision comparison in Figure 8. The existing auxiliary-supervised model also gains entries in Figure 4(a)'s latent-decoding comparison. The original comparator families remain.

E3.justification: New protocols vary the fraction of expert compositions observed during training, independently sweep context/prediction depths over 4, 6, and 8 layers, and match context-aggregator capacity. Additional tests vary output dimensionality and evaluate linear-regression interventions using counterfactual MSE. Original default training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial tests of alternative explanations: direct latent supervision, query access through the implicit proxy, aggregator capacity, parameter allocation, and injected shortcuts. It also adds linear-regression counterfactual interventions, output-dimensionality analysis, and sinusoid prediction visualizations. The original scaling analysis is retained as Figure 6.

E5.justification: Both versions show error bars or shaded bands without specifying repeated-run counts or their statistical construction. v2 introduces no documented seed-reporting, uncertainty-estimation, or significance-testing procedure; additional plots and point-estimate tables do not establish such a change.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results, including an explicit-model advantage under injected shortcuts and better prediction but worse latent recovery for the implicit proxy. New Table 3 reports sinusoid OOD-query losses of 0.002 for four-layer Explicit-Known, 0.179 for 4+4-layer Explicit-Tsf, and 0.153 for eight-layer Implicit. These are additional reported results, not demonstrated improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The core bottleneck architecture remains unchanged. v2 adds focused procedural variants: an implicit proxy whose bottleneck also receives the query, and direct bottleneck supervision instead of supervision through a linear readout (Figures 8 and 11).

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction, adds contribution bullets and a Notation section, moves the main related-work discussion into Appendix A, and introduces analysis and formalism appendices. It also shortens the conclusion and removes the dedicated limitations paragraph, substantially changing the document's organization.

P2.justification: The main text switches to a two-column conference layout, with retained figures resized and relocated. v2 adds experimental plots, proxy and dependency diagrams, eight numerical tables, and auxiliary-supervision bars in Figure 4. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds recent positioning references, including Song et al. on shortcuts, Lampinen et al. on ICL's scope, and Yang et al. on task vectors. It removes several references associated with v1's shortened future-work discussion. The underlying positioning relative to neural processes, shortcuts, and meta-learning remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds the formal query-conditioned proxy definition p_gamma(y|x,z_psi(D,x)) and its dependency structure. Its descriptions of the original implicit and explicit models largely restate existing mathematics. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 left important capacity and representation confounds insufficiently tested. v2's aggregator-capacity controls, layer-allocation sweeps, direct supervision, and matched-architecture proxy substantially strengthen the evidence distinguishing latent recovery from downstream prediction. Shortcut injection also reveals a meaningful applicability boundary. These gains outweigh the removed code link and the conclusion's insufficient qualification of its broad no-improvement wording.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same explicit-versus-implicit in-context learning study. Their complete main texts, figures, equations, references, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained content across restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds modular-composition experiments, architectural controls, shortcut tests, and extensive appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on regression, classification, compositional reasoning, and gene targeting, including latent decoding, counterfactual interventions, and scaling analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graph neural networks use relational information as an inductive bias to enhance prediction performance. Not rarely, task-relevant relations are unknown and graph structure learning approaches have been proposed to learn them from data. Given their latent nature, no graph observations are available to provide a direct training signal to the learnable relations. Therefore, graph topologies are typically learned on the prediction task alongside the other graph neural network parameters. In this paper, we demonstrate that minimizing point-prediction losses does not guarantee proper learning of the latent relational information and its associated uncertainty. Conversely, we prove that suitable loss functions on the stochastic model outputs simultaneously grant solving two tasks: (i) learning the unknown distribution of the latent graph and (ii) achieving optimal predictions of the target variable. Finally, we propose a sampling-based method that solves this joint learning task. Empirical results validate our theoretical claims and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
arxiv_record.authors: Alessandro Manenti, Daniele Zambon, Cesare Alippi
arxiv_record.title: Learning Latent Graph Structures and their Uncertainty
