C1.justification: The central claim favoring Gaussian-based flows with a final tail transformation remains. However, the conclusion changes materially: v1 identifies TTFfix as best overall and generally favors two-stage methods, whereas v2 recommends joint tail learning for density estimation while retaining the benefit of fixed parameters for VI. This changes the principal practical recommendation.

C2.justification: V2 explains learned tail parameters as compensating for preceding flow layers, links joint learning's benefits to flexibility such as tail asymmetry, and identifies substantial preliminary tail-estimation costs. It revises the CDF transformation's applicability and develops a mechanism-based proposal for differential-equation generative models. The explicit warning about dependence on arbitrary coordinate parameterization is removed from the limitations.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies spline bounds [-2.5, 2.5] with five bins, full-batch synthetic training, real-data batch size 512, and additional optimization and dataset information (Appendices G and I). Much of the expanded implementation appendix relocates existing initialization, sampling and numerical-stability details. These disclosures do not establish changed settings for retained experiments, and code-access information is effectively unchanged.

E1.justification: Real-data evaluation expands from S&P 500 returns to include Insurance medical claims, Fama 5 financial returns and CLIMDEX meteorological data (v2 Section 4.2 and Appendix I). V2 also adds the heavier-than-Cauchy ν = 0.5 VI scenario, which v1 explicitly excluded. The original regression and synthetic density-estimation tasks remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds normal and COMET comparators to the retained S&P 500 experiment, includes COMET at synthetic dimension d = 50 where v1 omitted it, and adds TTF_tBase to the synthetic comparisons. These extend the existing comparator suite; the VI comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The added CLIMDEX evaluation uses five RQS layers alternating with LU layers and a different optimization schedule, including cosine annealing and more steps. The new ν = 0.5 VI experiment uses gradient-norm clipping at 5. S&P evaluation contracts from 100/200/300 dimensions to 300 and reports total rather than per-dimension NLL. Synthetic-table failure markers change from Inf/NaN outcomes to final loss above 1e5. These are distinct from newly disclosed settings for retained experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix J adds an architectural ablation combining heavy-tailed inputs with TTF and a learned-tail-parameter analysis comparing fitted parameters against fixed theoretical values. Appendix D adds a qualitative exploratory comparison with the CDF transformation, and VI receives a stronger tail-severity test. The sigmoid/ReLU regression analysis is retained in Appendix F, while the S&P dimensionality comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Real-data uncertainty reporting changes from ten-repeat boxplots in v1 Figure 2 to means and standard deviations, with within-one-standard-deviation highlighting, in v2 Table 2. Synthetic density-estimation standard errors and the stated ten density-estimation/five VI repeats remain unchanged; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds results for three real datasets, ν = 0.5 VI, TTF_tBase and higher-dimensional COMET comparisons. CLIMDEX NLL is -2214.28 for TTF versus -2090.91 for TTFfix. S&P results are replaced: gTAF now scores 321.81 versus mTAF's 322.98, reversing their earlier ranking. The 100/200-stock results disappear. Shared synthetic density-estimation and ν ≥ 1 VI table entries are retained, so the additions do not establish improvements in those unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The main TTF transformation in Equation (3) and the TTF/TTFfix procedures remain unchanged. V2 adds the experimental TTF_tBase architecture, combining TTF with a Student's T base whose degrees of freedom are trained. Appendix D also describes a two-stage application of the previously discussed Student's T CDF transformation.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: regression moves to Appendix F, initialization to Appendix G, and dataset descriptions to Appendix I. Theory receives separate subsections, references move before the appendices, and experimental summaries and conclusions are rewritten. These changes reorganize existing material as well as accommodating additions.

P2.justification: The S&P boxplots are replaced by a broader real-data table, and a new Figure 2 displays learned tail parameters. The synthetic table becomes a main-text subset plus an expanded appendix table; the regression table moves to the appendix, VI gains columns, and hyperparameter and dataset tables are added. The document also adopts a denser layout without the earlier running headers.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused positioning around universality, citing Huang, Jaini, Draxler, Teshima and Van der Vaart, and connects future applications to Lipman's flow-matching work. The established positioning relative to TAF, COMET and extreme-value methods remains. Publication updates for existing references are bibliographic changes rather than newly cited research.

T1.justification: V2 adds a proof that finite Gaussian mixtures are light tailed (Appendix A), a formal weak-convergence definition of universality, and a continuous-mapping proof that adding TTF preserves a universal flow family's universality (Appendix E). The proposed extension to coupling-flow results is explicitly left incomplete. Existing TTF and COMET asymptotic results are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited to one real dataset and lacked high-dimensional COMET comparisons. The expanded evaluation reveals where TTFfix performs poorly, producing better-supported guidance on learning versus fixing tail parameters. New ablations, parameter analysis and the universality proof improve understanding of the method. Although removing the smaller S&P comparisons loses one sensitivity analysis, the gains in empirical support and theoretical characterization outweigh that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Flexible Tails for Normalizing Flows by the same authors. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds real-data evaluations, experimental variants and parameter analyses. Some CLIMDEX baseline scores are explicitly attributed to prior work, but the paper also reports its own results.

before.justification: V1 reports original neural-network regression experiments, synthetic density estimation, S&P 500 density estimation and synthetic variational-inference results.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper introduces a family of learning-augmented algorithms for online knapsack problems that achieve near Pareto-optimal consistency-robustness trade-offs through a simple combination of trusted learning-augmented and worst-case algorithms. C2.justification: v2 more explicitly distinguishes assumptions needed for trusted fractional algorithms, robust MIX and integral conversion, and states that learning the predictor is outside scope. It adds interpretations of the synthetic error parameter and suggests that workload-value distributions explain Sentinel's poorer Google-trace performance.

D1.justification: Appendix A.7.1 newly documents uniformly generated prediction intervals for MIX and IPA. It also specifies Google instance construction through duration scaling, resource factors, item counts and weights. The code-access information is unchanged, and neither version supplies hardware or seed details.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on Google cluster traces, introducing workload-derived inputs beyond synthetic and financial data. Its reported Bitcoin coverage also expands from 2017–2018 to 2017–2019 (Appendix A.7.1).

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain their comparator sets: the Sentinel synthetic comparison includes PP-a, Fr2Int-PP-a, Sentinel and ZCL; Bitcoin includes the first three. Google extends that existing three-method comparison without introducing a new baseline.

E3.justification: For 10,000 Bitcoin items, the reported item weight changes from 0.0001 to 0.001, increasing total offered weight from 1 to 10 against unit capacity. v2 also introduces a Google-trace instance-construction protocol. These materially change evaluation conditions, although the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The new Google experiment tests sensitivity to prediction error across several delta values (Figure A4), extending robustness evidence to workload-derived inputs. Existing studies of value range, critical-item weight, interval width, prediction correctness and trust parameter are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use CDFs and notched boxplots. v2 introduces no seed reporting, repeated-run counts, significance tests or new uncertainty-estimation procedure; changed boxplot values retain the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Google results show plotted median competitive ratios around 1.15–1.19 for PP-a and Fr2Int-PP-a versus approximately 1.53–1.62 for Sentinel at delta values 0.5–2 (Figure A4). Synthetic and Bitcoin boxplot distributions also change between v1 Figures 3–4 and v2 Figures A2–A3. Bitcoin results use revised conditions, so they do not establish same-setting gains.

M1.justification: PP-b, PP-a, IPA, MIX and Fr2Int retain their decision rules. Indexed state notation in PP-a, expanded explanations and relocation of IPA pseudocode do not change the algorithms.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around near-optimal trade-offs. Assumptions receive dedicated discussion, proofs are reorganized and rewritten, and most Sentinel and real-data experimental discussion moves from Section 6 into Appendix A.7.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, adds a contribution-summary table, and moves IPA pseudocode into the main text. Existing Sentinel comparisons move to the appendix and are redrawn alongside a new Google plot. Retained supplementary plots are redistributed and regrouped, rather than constituting entirely new figures.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands positioning against frequency predictions, advice complexity and Pareto-optimal algorithms for simplified knapsack variants, explaining why their guarantees do not transfer. Appendix A.1 adds stochastic and unit-profit knapsack coverage, with new references including Vondrak and Zenklusen and Boyar et al.

T1.justification: v2 adds the matching interval-prediction lower bound (Theorem 3.6) and integral-knapsack impossibility results (Theorems A.1–A.2). It corrects the point lower-bound proof to use min{1, omega}, substantially rewrites PP-a and Fr2Int proofs, and explicitly conditions Theorem 5.2 on maximum item weight. It also specifies an adaptive adversary and restricts Theorem 4.2 to deterministic algorithms.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses concrete weaknesses in the theoretical account: capped critical-weight reasoning is corrected, PP-a receives explicit feasibility and profit invariants, and Fr2Int's weight condition becomes precise. Added interval and integral lower-bound analyses substantially improve completeness, while Google-trace experiments broaden validation. These gains support a substantial improvement independently of higher reported performance; the changed Bitcoin setup limits direct score comparisons.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same knapsack algorithms, predictions and theoretical framework despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, Bitcoin and Google-cluster-trace experiments, including comparative performance and sensitivity results in Section 6 and Appendix A.7.

arxiv_record.abstract: In recent years, generative artificial intelligence has achieved significant advancements in the field of image generation, spawning a variety of applications. However, video generation still faces considerable challenges in various aspects, such as controllability, video length, and richness of details, which hinder the application and popularization of this technology. In this work, we propose a controllable video generation framework, dubbed MimicMotion, which can generate high-quality videos of arbitrary length mimicking specific motion guidance. Compared with previous methods, our approach has several highlights. Firstly, we introduce confidence-aware pose guidance that ensures high frame quality and temporal smoothness. Secondly, we introduce regional loss amplification based on pose confidence, which significantly reduces image distortion. Lastly, for generating long and smooth videos, we propose a progressive latent fusion strategy. By this means, we can produce videos of arbitrary length with acceptable resource consumption. With extensive experiments and user studies, MimicMotion demonstrates significant improvements over previous approaches in various aspects. Detailed results and comparisons are available on our project page: https://tencent.github.io/MimicMotion .

Conversely, v1's explicit SVD 1.1 checkpoint designation, 40GB GPU specification and executable Merge listing are omitted.

E1.justification: Appendix D adds evaluation on four cartoon and four animal dancing videos, extending coverage beyond human subjects to different visual styles and body proportions. E4.justification: v1 supports its three components with qualitative ablations. v2 retains those examples and adds Table 2, measuring configurations that progressively enable fusion, confidence guidance and hand enhancement across four metrics. after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds quantitative component ablations, additional comparison metrics and cartoon/animal generation examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Advances in large models, reinforcement learning, and open-endedness have accelerated progress toward autonomous agents that can learn and interact in the real world. To achieve this, flexible tools are needed to create rich, yet computationally efficient, environments. While scalable 2D environments fail to address key real-world challenges like 3D navigation and spatial reasoning, more complex 3D environments are computationally expensive and lack features like customizability and multi-agent support. This paper introduces Craftium, a highly customizable and easy-to-use platform for building rich 3D single- and multi-agent environments. We showcase environments of different complexity and nature: from single- and multi-agent tasks to vast worlds with many creatures and biomes, and customizable procedural task generators. Benchmarking shows that Craftium significantly reduces the computational cost of alternatives of similar richness, achieving +2K steps per second more than Minecraft-based frameworks.

C1.justification: V2 expands the main contribution from a customizable RL environment framework to an efficient platform for single-agent, multi-agent, embodied and continual-learning research. It adds quantitative efficiency claims and claims novelty in combining vast 3D open worlds with multi-agent support. The original five environments, presented partly as benchmarks in v1, are explicitly reframed as illustrative examples.

C2.justification: V2 adds proposed explanations for throughput differences, interprets selected continual-learning gains as forward transfer, and discusses richness–efficiency tradeoffs. It newly states that agent count is limited by CPU-core count and qualifies the learning demonstrations as untuned examples whose performance may improve with longer training (Appendices E and G).

D1.justification: Beyond v1's basic mod and Gymnasium examples, v2 documents engine modifications, action mappings, API functions and PettingZoo usage (Appendices A–D). It adds benchmark hardware, CleanRL implementation and commit references, preprocessing, budgets, prompts, generator parameters and an environment-creation tutorial (Appendices E, G and I). The project repository link is retained.

E1.justification: The five original single-agent task types are retained. V2 additionally evaluates one-versus-one combat, an open world with resource-gathering, hunting and defense objectives, and a ten-task continual-learning dungeon sequence (Section 3.5 and Appendix G). These substantially expand the evaluated task requirements and interaction settings.

E2.justification: V1 discusses alternatives without evaluating comparators. V2 benchmarks Craftium against MineDojo and VizDoom for single-environment throughput and against VizDoom for parallel throughput. Its demonstrations also compare PPO+LSTM with LLaVa-Agent and from-scratch PPO (FS) with continual fine-tuning using L2 regularization (FT-L2).

E3.justification: Reported episode limits change substantially: ChopTree and Room increase from 500 to 2,000 steps, SmallRoom from 200 to 1,000, Speleo from 500 to 3,000, and SpidersAttack from 2,000 to 4,000 (v1 Section 3.4; v2 Appendix G.1). V2 also introduces throughput-testing and learning protocols, including million-step PPO training and open-world comparisons with different observation formats and time/step budgets.

E4.justification: V1 contains no corresponding analyses. V2 tests throughput sensitivity to parallel environment count, frame skipping, observation resolution, world complexity and agent count (Appendix E, Figure 13). It also compares four LLaVa-Agent prompts to select the demonstration prompt (Appendix G.3, Figure 17).

E5.justification: V2 introduces repeated-run and uncertainty reporting absent from v1: five-run throughput measurements with means and standard deviations in Table 4, five-run learning curves with standard errors in Figures 8 and 15, ten random seeds for the open-world comparison, and five repetitions per prompt. These are newly reported experiments, not increased repetitions of v1 results.

E6.justification: V1 reports no measured performance. V2 adds throughput means of 2,746.69, 2,091.91 and 71.87 steps/s for Craftium, VizDoom and MineDojo respectively (Table 4), plus over 12,000 steps/s in a parallel configuration (Figure 13a). It also adds learning curves, open-world achievements and task-dependent FS/FT-L2 results. These are new findings, not same-setting improvements over v1 measurements.

M1.justification: V1 leaves multi-agent interaction and PettingZoo integration as future work. V2 implements them through per-agent communication channels and clients coordinated by the engine server (Section 3, Figure 2 and Appendix D). It also introduces a parameterized dungeon-generation algorithm (Appendix G.4). These are substantive procedural additions, independent of the engine terminology change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, background, related work and conclusion are substantially rewritten around flexibility, efficiency and broader autonomous-agent applications. Section 3 gains dedicated performance and illustrative-example sections. The original task descriptions move to Appendix G.1 within a new, extensive appendix structure.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text to a two-column layout and redraws Figure 2 for the multi-agent architecture. It adds performance and learning plots, maps, a skills tree, comparison/API/prompt tables and tutorial screenshots. The original five-task image panel is retained and reordered as Figure 14, rather than being removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning toward embodied AI, continual learning, open-endedness and multi-agent research, adding discussion of works such as Habitat 3.0, Craftax, OMNI-EPIC and JaxMARL. Table 1 introduces a structured framework comparison, while Appendices F and H expand the arguments concerning VizDoom's dimensional limitations and MineDojo's customization restrictions.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical results, formal assumptions or proofs. V2's additional action-space notation explains existing controls, while its new generator descriptions concern implementation rather than substantive mathematical analysis.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves v1's central evidential gap: a largely descriptive framework proposal gains measured performance comparisons, learning demonstrations and sensitivity analyses (Sections 3.4–3.5; Appendices E and G). Its implementation and usage documentation also becomes substantially more complete. Different benchmark tasks/resolutions and unequal open-world budgets limit broad superiority conclusions, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and practical assessability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Craftium framework by the same authors. All text, figures and tables are readable, including v2's Appendices A–I. V1 has no appendices. The substantial expansion supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original throughput and memory measurements, learning curves, multi-agent self-play, open-world agent comparisons, prompt experiments and continual-learning results in Sections 3.4–3.5 and Appendices E and G.

before.justification: V1 presents framework and task descriptions, code examples and illustrative screenshots, but reports no original experimental measurements or evaluation outcomes.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present Gradient Boosting Reinforcement Learning (GBRL), a framework that adapts the strengths of gradient boosting trees (GBT) to reinforcement learning (RL) tasks. While neural networks (NNs) have become the de facto choice for RL, they face significant challenges with structured and categorical features and tend to generalize poorly to out-of-distribution samples. These are challenges for which GBTs have traditionally excelled in supervised learning. However, GBT's application in RL has been limited. The design of traditional GBT libraries is optimized for static datasets with fixed labels, making them incompatible with RL's dynamic nature, where both state distributions and reward signals evolve during training. GBRL overcomes this limitation by continuously interleaving tree construction with environment interaction. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that GBRL outperforms NNs in domains with structured observations and categorical features while maintaining competitive performance on standard continuous control benchmarks. Like its supervised learning counterpart, GBRL demonstrates superior robustness to out-of-distribution samples and better handles irregular state-action relationships.

C1.justification: v1 primarily claims viable GBT-based actor-critic learning, structured-data advantages and an efficient shared architecture, motivated partly by interpretability and edge deployment. v2 retains the framework claims but makes superior OOD robustness, resistance to spurious correlations and handling of state perturbations an explicit central contribution. The earlier interpretability and low-compute deployment emphasis is substantially reduced.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations linking tree partitions to preservation of rare reward signals, SHAP feature reliance to resistance against misleading cues, and threshold-based predictions to noise robustness. It also develops explanations of convergence/runtime tradeoffs and algorithm-dependent update frequency. The principal limitations concerning ensemble growth and nondifferentiable Q-functions are retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the NN's two 64-unit tanh layers and separate output heads, GAE and critic-loss details, the depth-4 choice, and actor/critic split-scoring alternatives. Appendix C and Table 2 document the new variable-isolation environment and its hyperparameters. These materially expand reproducibility information, although v1's Algorithm 1 and some traditional-library setup details disappear. Hardware disclosures and repository access remain.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark coverage and adds three linear-equation variable-isolation tasks. Section 5.2 also introduces distinct MiniGrid correlation and distractor scenarios, noisy control observations, and Football scenarios with missing opponents, substantially expanding task and input-environment coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated external comparators remain NN implementations of PPO, A2C and AWR, plus CatBoost and XGBoost. A2C/AWR comparisons remain in the appendices despite the main text's PPO focus. The new experiments extend existing comparator families rather than introduce additional baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds cross-condition training/testing, 100-episode noisy evaluations with variance from 0 to 0.2, asymmetric training budgets for variable isolation and distractors, controlled CartPole parameter sweeps, and a synthetic incremental-learning timing protocol. Original benchmark budgets and tabulated hyperparameters are retained. For the aggregate plot, v2 Section 5.1 substitutes the earlier per-environment difference formula for v1 Figure 1's ratio normalization, leaving the plotted normalization ambiguous.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained shared-versus-separate architecture experiment, v2 adds tests of spurious correlations, distractors, observation noise and missing opponents, with a SHAP case study examining feature reliance. Section 6 and Appendices A–B add sensitivity analyses for actor/critic learning rates, tree depth, batch size, split scoring and updates per rollout.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds and means with standard deviations. v2 makes this more explicit in retained table and learning-curve captions and extends the practice to new experiments, without reporting increased run counts, confidence intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 2–5 and v2 Tables 3–6 contain identical benchmark values, and the four appendix learning-curve images are retained. New results nevertheless substantially expand the evidence: Figures 5–15 report variable-isolation performance, robustness, feature attribution and sensitivity findings. New Table 1 reports incremental-learning times of 5.47 seconds for GBRL, 36.17 for CatBoost and 67.11 for XGBoost under its specified workload.

M1.justification: Both versions grow ensembles from actor-critic gradients, share actor/critic tree structures and use distinct output learning rates with PPO, A2C and AWR. v2 documents and compares gradient-normalization and cosine split-scoring options, but does not establish a revision to the underlying procedure; these additions concern implementation disclosure and ablation evidence.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. Standard experiments are consolidated, library and shared-architecture comparisons move into Section 4.3, and A2C/AWR explanations move to the appendix. The standard/challenge experiment structure and reordered conclusion and limitations substantially change the presentation beyond simply adding scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. The framework diagram and overview plots are redrawn, v1's per-environment comparison Figures 3–5 disappear while their underlying results remain, and v2 adds a timing table plus extensive robustness, SHAP and ablation graphics. Retained appendix tables and curves are resized, relocated and recaptioned.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around tabular inductive biases and OOD behavior, adding works such as Jeffares et al., Beyazit et al. and Xu et al., while removing the dedicated interpretability discussion and several associated references. It also explicitly positions GBRL as extending NPPG beyond discrete Gibbs policies to general actor-critic objectives, replacing the earlier broader functional-policy-search discussion.

T1.justification: The gradient-fitting target changes from -epsilon times the gradient in v1 Equation (2) to the unscaled negative gradient in v2 Equation (1), while learning-rate scaling remains in the ensemble update. This removes an extra scaling factor from the mathematical presentation. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 mainly established benchmark viability and inferred advantages from structured-data performance. v2 directly probes robustness through controlled changes to correlations, noise and opponent availability, and adds sensitivity/runtime studies that substantially improve evidence about when GBRL works and how to configure it. The implementation disclosures further improve reproducibility. Removal of pseudocode and ambiguity in Figure 4's normalization are drawbacks, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GBRL work by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds variable-isolation experiments, distribution-shift evaluations, feature-attribution analyses and hyperparameter ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original GBRL-versus-NN experiments across control, Football, Atari RAM and MiniGrid environments, together with library-throughput and shared-architecture experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse engineer the computation performed by a neural network in terms of its internal components. Although there is a growing body of research on mechanistic interpretation of neural networks, the notion of a mechanistic interpretation itself is often ad-hoc. Inspired by the notion of abstract interpretation from the program analysis literature that aims to develop approximate semantics for programs, we give a set of axioms that formally characterize a mechanistic interpretation as a description that approximately captures the semantics of the neural network under analysis in a compositional manner. We demonstrate the applicability of these axioms for validating mechanistic interpretations on an existing, well-known interpretability study as well as on a new case study involving a Transformer-based model trained to solve the well-known 2-SAT problem.
arxiv_record.authors: Nils Palumbo, Ravi Mangal, Zifan Wang, Saranya Vijayakumar, Corina S. Pasareanu, Somesh Jha
arxiv_record.title: Validating Mechanistic Interpretations: An Axiomatic Approach

C1.justification: V2 broadens the contribution from an axioms-guided 2-SAT interpretation to a framework for validating both existing and newly derived interpretations. Its claimed applicability also expands to circuit/subgraph analyses, which v1 explicitly excludes in its related work and limitations. The underlying claim that the 2-SAT model parses clauses and enumerates assignments remains unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive qualifications about discretization weakening internal-fidelity checks, unrestricted abstraction/concretization hiding computation, and redundant circuit computations masking interventions. It explains why IOI is not fully evaluated and why worst-case compositional bounds can be misleading. V1's blanket circuit exclusion is revised, while its explicit warning that the 2-SAT interpretation techniques require human effort and cannot be applied automatically is omitted.

D1.justification: V2 supplements the existing 2-SAT implementation descriptions with abstraction/concretization pseudocode in Listings 1–4. Appendix H and Listings 8–9 document modular-addition decomposition, mapping fitting, and the equivalence test. The implementation pointer changes from sat-mi to axiomatic-validation. The original 2-SAT hardware, data-generation instructions, and training hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: V1 empirically studies only 2-SAT; v2 also evaluates the interpretation of a Transformer performing addition modulo 113. This adds a distinct task beyond Boolean satisfiability. The original 2-SAT coverage is retained. Appendix I explicitly leaves IOI unevaluated, so it does not constitute added empirical task coverage.

E2.justification: The decision-tree and disjunction-only interpretations remain the compared alternatives in the 2-SAT study. Nanda et al.'s model becomes an additional object of validation, not a competing baseline. The expanded discussions of causal abstraction and causal scrubbing do not add an empirical baseline comparison.

E3.justification: The original 2-SAT training and evaluation settings remain unchanged. New protocols include independently replacing each parsed clause with a random clause with 1% probability and evaluating propagation through all three components (Appendix F). Modular-addition evaluation introduces learned mappings using the original train/test split and tests rounding and downstream-equivalence discretizations (Section 5, Appendix H).

E4.justification: Appendix F adds a controlled error-injection analysis testing whether componentwise checks miss propagated interpretation errors. Section 5 and Appendix H add discretization sensitivity analyses showing that apparent internal agreement depends strongly on the equivalence criterion. The earlier attention analyses, decision-tree-size comparisons, and activation-amplification analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report epsilon using upper bounds from one-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals. V2 clarifies that error estimation counts equality violations, but does not report a different uncertainty estimator, confidence level, repeated-run count, or seed-reporting scheme.

E6.justification: The original 2-SAT accuracy, axiom-error values, and neuron interpretation tables are retained. V2 adds modular-addition validation with epsilon 0.000335 under the selected discretization, versus epsilon 1 for second-component equivalence with one-decimal rounding. Its new Table 1 reports final-component prefix-equivalence error 0.0315 under injected noise versus 0.0128 without noise. These are new conditional results, not improvements to the original model.

M1.justification: The 2-SAT model and interpretation procedure are retained, but the validation method is substantially extended. Appendix B.1 introduces graph-based interventions, a parallel-intervention formulation, and circuit linearization. Section 5 and Appendix H add an adaptation for continuous intermediate representations using discretization, downstream-equivalence classes, and learned linear abstraction/concretization maps.

P1.justification: The title and narrative are reframed around validation. Existing data/model and interpretation sections are consolidated into a 2-SAT case study, previously separated axiom checks are grouped together, and probing/attention related work moves to Appendix A. Terminology is systematically refined from layers to Transformer blocks and from embeddings to representations, alongside expanded explanations and appendix reorganization.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and substantially rearranges existing displays, including moving v1 Figures 2–3 into the appendix. It adds an error-comparison table and diagrams for extensional equivalence, the 2-SAT decomposition, and IOI circuits. Existing plots are reformatted, while the two original neuron tables are retained as Tables 2–3.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands its positioning against causal abstraction and causal scrubbing, discussing their mappings, interventions, and treatment of internal representations. It adds works including Chan et al. on causal scrubbing, Scheurer et al. on its pitfalls, and additional Geiger papers. Appendix C develops this comparison through an extensional-equivalence example, beyond v1's brief related-work discussion.

T1.justification: Beyond the retained original axioms, v2 adds graph formulations and Axioms 7–11, a circuit-linearization construction, and an extensional-equivalence argument concerning restrictions on abstraction/concretization (Appendices B–C). Appendix E derives depth-dependent equivalence bounds and a replaceability bound under invertibility assumptions. Section 3 also explicitly requires discrete values for its equality tests.

improvement.justification: V1 supports its framework chiefly through intuitive motivation and one 2-SAT study. V2 substantially strengthens the central justification with compositional-error derivations, a controlled experiment showing what componentwise checks miss, and validation on an independently developed modular-addition interpretation. It also makes important applicability limits explicit. Modular-addition success depends on a discretization that weakens internal-fidelity checks, and IOI remains only a sketch; nevertheless, the stronger theoretical and empirical support provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same axiomatic interpretation framework and retain the same 2-SAT study despite the changed title. The complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds its own modular-addition interpretation validation and synthetic-error experiments. These new evaluations are distinct from the underlying models and interpretations attributed to prior work.

before.justification: V1 reports original Transformer training results, including 99.76% 2-SAT test accuracy, attention and neuron analyses, and empirical validation of mechanistic interpretations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Early exits enable the network's forward pass to terminate early by attaching trainable internal classifiers to the backbone network. Existing early-exit methods typically adopt either a joint training approach, where the backbone and exit heads are trained simultaneously, or a disjoint approach, where the heads are trained separately. However, the implications of this choice are often overlooked, with studies typically adopting one approach without adequate justification. This choice influences training dynamics and its impact remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a set of metrics to analyze early-exit training dynamics and guide the choice of training strategy. We demonstrate that conventionally used joint and disjoint regimes yield suboptimal performance. To address these limitations, we propose a mixed training strategy: the backbone is trained first, followed by the training of the entire multi-exit network. Through comprehensive evaluations of training strategies across various architectures, datasets, and early-exit methods, we present the strengths and weaknesses of the early exit training strategies. In particular, we show consistent improvements in performance and efficiency using the proposed mixed strategy.
arxiv_record.authors: Piotr Kubaty, Bartosz W\'ojcik, Bart{\l}omiej Krzepkowski, Monika Michaluk, Tomasz Trzci\'nski, Jary Pomponi, Kamil Adamczewski
arxiv_record.title: How to Train Your Multi-Exit Model? Analyzing the Impact of Training Strategies

C1.justification: V2 elevates the diagnostic framework to a central contribution and explicitly claims generalization across modalities, classification, regression, and exit criteria. Its conclusion strengthens the gradient-scaling finding into a claim that scaling is unnecessary with mixed training. It also recommends mixed training particularly for medium/high budgets, replacing v1's contradictory concluding recommendation for easy inputs and early exits.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations linking deeper-classifier gradient dominance and mode connectivity to mixed training's behavior, and interprets classifier capacity as dependent on the training regime. It reconciles the concluding budget recommendations with the earlier mutual-information discussion and identifies shared-backbone circumstances favoring disjoint training. However, the explicit warning about mixed training failing with an undertrained backbone is removed.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 and Appendix E newly document optimizer, scheduler, batch sizes, learning rates, weight decay, patience, augmentations, model dimensions, exit positions, sequence lengths, and ImageNet hardware. These substantially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to previously undocumented settings. The code repository remains the same; v1's explicit 100-threshold sweep and best-checkpoint restoration description are no longer supplied.

E1.justification: V2 expands beyond vision classification to 20-Newsgroups text classification and STS-B regression, and adds TinyImageNet evaluation. It also reports direct ImageNet-1k classification experiments. Imagenette remains in Table 20, while CIFAR-10 remains in the mode-connectivity and loss-landscape analyses; neither should be treated as removed.

E2.justification: Appendix C adds evaluated branch-wise, separate, and alternating training comparators. V2 also evaluates PBEE and entropy-based exiting, and adds SDN and increasing/decreasing loss-weighting comparisons alongside gradient equilibrium. The retained Imagenette head-size experiment gains disjoint-regime rows in Table 20, absent from v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: V2 adds MSDNet, ResNet-50, BERT, and ViT-S configurations and no longer reports the EfficientNetV2-s experiment. Placement controls change from ViT every-1/2/3 and first/last-four arrangements to ResNet-50 every-1 through every-5 and asymmetric arrangements. Regression introduces MSE evaluation. One setting remains ambiguous: identical ResNet-50 results are labeled 25% budget in Table 1 but 35% in Table 11.

E4.justification: V2 adds gradient-dominance and mode-connectivity analyses, convergence-time comparisons, and expanded loss-weighting and classifier-size/placement studies. V1's learning-rate and undertrained-backbone analysis in Section 5.3 and Figure 11 is not retained. The loss-landscape analysis survives in Appendix B, so its relocation is not a removal.

E5.justification: The reported replication changes from four different seeds in v1 to three runs in v2 Section 4.1. Mean and standard-deviation reporting continues in Appendix C, although the new TinyImageNet ablations in Tables 6–7 lack corresponding uncertainty tables. V2 also discloses Monte Carlo estimation of mutual information. These statements do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E6.justification: V2 supplies extensive new benchmark, comparator, and diagnostic results. For example, Table 1 reports ImageNet-1k ViT-T accuracy at 100% budget of 71.20% mixed, 68.39% joint, and 71.61% disjoint. Conversely, all 30 mean/standard-deviation pairs from v1 Table 2 remain unchanged in v2 Table 20. EfficientNet and undertrained-backbone results disappear; results under new configurations are not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The original two-phase mixed procedure remains, but Appendix A introduces mixed-gradual training. It progressively optimizes the last i classifiers across multiple phases, keeps weights unfrozen, and uses early stopping to advance. This adds a substantive training procedure beyond the original joint, disjoint, and mixed regimes.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, updates the author block, and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. Related work moves after the experiments, the analytical framework is separated from its empirical evaluation, and supporting material is organized into Appendices A–E. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Budget tables become the principal performance presentation, with additional curves grouped in Appendix D. New gradient-dominance and mode-connectivity figures are added, the loss landscapes are redrawn and relocated, and v1's two-panel numerical-rank figure is reduced to the retained backbone-versus-mixed panel.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around conditional computation, classifier cascades, distillation, ensembling, and training–inference mismatch. Section 5 acknowledges SDN's consideration of both joint and disjoint training and a concurrent comparison by Bae et al., qualifying the novelty as broad systematic analysis. Appendix A additionally relates alternative regimes to BERxiT and LayerSkip.

T1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.2 add a formal gradient-dominance definition and a permutation-alignment optimization with an interpolated parameter path for mode connectivity. These materially expand the mathematical analysis beyond v1. The loss-landscape equation is retained in Appendix B, while v1's explicit gradient-rescaling equation is omitted. No formal theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens generalizability and reproducibility through NLP/regression tests, broader regime comparisons, diagnostic analyses, and concrete training specifications in Appendix E. It also fixes v1's conflicting concluding guidance. These gains outweigh losing the undertraining study and reducing the stated run count. Qualifications remain necessary: Appendix A's blanket mixed-gradual advantage is contradicted by its worse 20-Newsgroups results in Table 13.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe the same research work despite the changed title. All supplied pages are readable, but v1 ends after its references without the appendices cited in Sections 4–5, limiting verification of those supplementary analyses. V2 includes Appendices A–E.

after.justification: V2 reports original vision and NLP experiments, diagnostic analyses, ablations, and convergence measurements, with additional results in its appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original training-regime experiments, accuracy–computation curves, representation analyses, and classifier-size and placement studies in Figures 1–12 and Tables 1–2.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large repositories of image-caption pairs are essential for the development of vision-language models. However, these datasets are often extracted from noisy data scraped from the web, and contain many mislabeled instances. In order to improve the reliability of downstream models, it is important to identify and filter images with incorrect captions. However, beyond filtering based on image-caption embedding similarity, no prior works have proposed other methods to filter noisy multimodal data, or concretely assessed the impact of noisy captioning data on downstream training. In this work, we propose, theoretically justify, and empirically validate LEMoN, a method to identify label errors in image-caption datasets. Our method leverages the multimodal neighborhood of image-caption pairs in the latent space of contrastively pretrained multimodal models to automatically identify label errors. Through empirical evaluations across eight datasets and twelve baselines, we find that LEMoN outperforms the baselines by over 3% in label error detection, and that training on datasets filtered using our method improves downstream captioning performance by more than 2 BLEU points over noisy training.
arxiv_record.authors: Haoran Zhang, Aparna Balagopalan, Nassim Oufattole, Hyewon Jeong, Yan Wu, Jiacheng Zhu, Marzyeh Ghassemi
arxiv_record.title: LEMoN: Label Error Detection using Multimodal Neighbors

C1.justification: The central claims of multimodal-neighbor error detection and improved downstream training remain. The introduction replaces earlier F1-based superiority claims with more qualified AUROC advantages on three of four classification and three of four captioning datasets. The abstract also explicitly foregrounds theoretical justification and quantifies downstream captioning improvements.

C2.justification: v2 hypothesizes that noisy CC3M captions retain useful word associations, explaining why filtering can underperform using the full corpus. Its new impact statement discusses disproportionate removal of rare or minority examples and recommends expert review. It also expands component-importance and captioning-headroom interpretations, while removing v1's explicit limitation concerning untested instance-dependent noise.

D1.justification: v2 adds selected hyperparameters for individual datasets and methods, baseline reference-set and checkpoint details, VDC model/prompt adaptations, and web-corpus preprocessing and training instructions. These materially extend v1's search-space and hardware disclosures. Reproducibility remains limited by conflicting split descriptions for the added classification datasets in Table 1, Section 5.1, and Appendix D.1.

E1.justification: v2 adds miniImageNet and StanfordCars with real annotation noise, CC3M and DataComp filtering/pretraining experiments, VTAB transfer evaluation, and CIFAR-10C corruption testing. These substantially expand coverage beyond v1's six datasets to web-scale training and shifted evaluation conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds Discrepancy to classification and captioning comparisons, adapted VDC to captioning, and additional Thomas–Kovashka scores and combinations in Table I.13. Captioning Datamap's documented score changes from a ratio to a product of loss statistics. Downstream Figure 3 adds Discrepancy and removes AUM and Datamap from that comparison.

E3.justification: Reported downstream captioning settings change from five to ten maximum epochs, learning rate 1e-5 to 1e-4, and top-k sampling to four-beam search (v1 Appendix F.2; v2 H.2). Classification changes from at most 15 epochs and averaging across learning rates to at most 30 epochs with learning-rate selection and early stopping. Added experiments introduce transfer, validation-subsampling, and corruption-evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds score-component combinations, validation-set-size sensitivity, empirical checks of theoretical assumptions, checkpoint-selection controls, runtime comparisons, and corruption robustness. Conversely, v1 Figures G.3–G.4, examining detection metrics versus downstream accuracy and caption-filtering thresholds, are removed. The scope of supplementary analysis changes substantially.

E5.justification: The three-run mean/standard-deviation reporting and manual study's binomial confidence intervals remain. Appendix A.2 newly applies Shapiro–Wilk normality tests, including subsampling classification distances and testing caption-distance distributions. There is no reported increase in the main experiments' repeat count.

E6.justification: Many existing numerical entries change: for example, Table 2 reports CIFAR-10 LEMoNOPT F1 as 93.1 in v1 and 92.0 in v2. Extensive new results include CC3M average zero-shot accuracy of 10.83% for LEMoNFIX, 10.34% for CLIP filtering, and 14.08% without filtering (Table I.15). Revised downstream captioning scores use changed training and decoding settings, so they do not establish same-setting gains across versions.

M1.justification: The three-term score, neighbor weighting, LEMoNOPT/LEMoNFIX variants, and hyperparameter-search procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure; the corrected weighting subscript in Equation (3) matches the parameter already described in v1.

P1.justification: The seven-section main structure and much of the existing method and experimental prose remain. Editing refines wording and definitions, converts the contribution summary into bullets, adds a plain-language algorithm explanation and notation glossary, and adjusts appendix organization. Most expansion accompanies the substantive additions assessed separately.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. Tables 2–3 are reorganized across datasets, with fuller results including AUPRC placed in the appendix; Figure 3 is redrawn with different comparators. New histograms, sensitivity and robustness plots, algorithm/notation displays, and experimental tables substantially change presentation, alongside removal of Figures G.3–G.4.

R1.justification: A new multimodal-neighborhood subsection and Appendix B position LEMoN against Thomas and Kovashka (2022), distinguishing semantic diversity from label-error detection and relating their scores to LEMoN's components. Additional neighborhood, data-cleaning, and benchmark literature substantially expands the research positioning beyond citation updates.

T1.justification: v2 introduces paraphrase-set and Gaussian-distance assumptions, a neighborhood-score AUROC theorem, and a better-than-random-signal lemma with proofs. v1's CLIP-loss robustness proposition is removed, while its noisy-label separation proposition is substantially reformulated as a Lipschitz perturbation bound in Appendix A.3. These are substantive mathematical revisions, not relocation alone.

arxiv_record.abstract: In the field of Image Quality Assessment (IQA), the adversarial robustness of the metrics poses a critical concern. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmarking study of various defense mechanisms in response to the rise in adversarial attacks on IQA. We systematically evaluate 25 defense strategies, including adversarial purification, adversarial training, and certified robustness methods. We applied 14 adversarial attack algorithms of various types in both non-adaptive and adaptive settings and tested these defenses against them. We analyze the differences between defenses and their applicability to IQA tasks, considering that they should preserve IQA scores and image quality. The proposed benchmark aims to guide future developments and accepts submissions of new methods, with the latest results available online: https://videoprocessing.ai/benchmarks/iqa-defenses.html.

C1.justification: The claimed contribution expands from a defense benchmark and adversarial-image collection to include large-scale subjective evaluation and MOS-labeled data for training and attack detection. The conclusion now foregrounds compression-based defenses, limitations of diffusion purification for IQA, and randomness, beyond v1's general recommendations about scenario-dependent effectiveness.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations involving frequency structure, model architecture, training-domain bias, and discrepancies between objective and perceived quality. The single-dataset limitation disappears following expanded coverage; limitations concerning multiple attack parameters, transferability, and ranking remain and are elaborated in Appendix A.1.

D1.justification: The supplied v2 documents parameter grids, fixed defense settings, model bounds and preprocessing, 30-epoch training with a 1:1 clean/adversarial ratio, smoothing parameters, and the subjective-study procedure. Reported compute rises from approximately 5,000 to 25,000 GPU-hours. Much of this information was deferred to unavailable supplementary material in v1, so added disclosure does not establish changed implementations.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from KonIQ-10k images to include KADID-10k artificial distortions, NIPS 2017 images, and AGIQA-3K generated images. v2 also adds human assessment of attacked and purified images and reports a 5,200-image collection with subjective scores.

E2.justification: v2 adds Liu et al.'s gradient-norm regularization method, NT, to the evaluated training defenses in Table 3. The 17 purification methods and six certified methods remain, and the six SSIM/LPIPS-by-budget training configurations were already described in v1. The headline increase from 25 to 30 therefore does not establish five new algorithms.

E3.justification: v2 adds CLIP-IQA+ and TOPIQ as evaluation targets, introduces Rscore and PLCC reporting, and replaces the combined Qscore with separate image-quality measures. The human study introduces pairwise comparisons, verification filtering, and Bradley–Terry scoring. Certified-defense sample sizes remain ambiguous: Section 3.4 says 50 images, while Table 3 and Appendix A.3.1 specify ten.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's attack-strength and defense-parameter analyses, v2 reports cross-dataset behavior, architectural comparisons, sampling sensitivity, and objective-versus-human quality comparisons. Figures 4–6 and Appendix A.5 provide substantial additional diagnostic evidence, including examples of defense-induced artifacts.

E5.justification: v1 mainly reports intervals reflecting variation across experimental conditions. v2 adds ten resampled 50-image subsets with variance estimates and Kruskal–Wallis tests, plus paired one-sided Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction. Main result tables omit v1's intervals, although several appendix tables retain them.

E6.justification: Aggregate results are substantially revised: JPEG and DiffJPEG have non-adaptive SROCCadv values of 0.718 and 0.703 in v1 Table 4, versus 0.605 and 0.608 in v2 Table 2. These use different model/data coverage and are not same-setting performance changes. New results include NT comparisons and human judgments favoring Real-ESRGAN over the undefended attacked images.

M1.justification: The described purification procedures, SSIM/LPIPS-adjusted APGD training, and smoothing adaptations remain substantially unchanged, including ten in-range quality classes plus two overflow classes. Gradient-norm regularization is added as an existing comparison method, rather than a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, related work, results discussion, and conclusion receive extensive rewriting. Results are reorganized around mechanisms, datasets, architectures, computational cost, and perception. Limitations move into an integrated appendix containing detailed methodological and experimental subsections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, merges defense inventories, redesigns the polar summaries, and adds a benchmark schematic, statistical displays, and qualitative image panels. R1.justification: v2 adds IQA-specific training work by Chistyakova et al. and Liu et al., Yang et al.'s black-box attack, and references supporting newer models and datasets. arxiv_record.abstract: Modern code completion engines, powered by large language models (LLMs), assist millions of developers with their strong capabilities to generate functionally correct code. Due to this popularity, it is crucial to investigate the security implications of relying on LLM-based code completion. In this work, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art black-box LLM-based code completion engines can be stealthily biased by adversaries to significantly increase their rate of insecure code generation. We present the first attack, named INSEC, that achieves this goal. INSEC works by injecting an attack string as a short comment in the completion input. The attack string is crafted through a query-based optimization procedure starting from a set of carefully designed initialization schemes. We demonstrate INSEC's broad applicability and effectiveness by evaluating it on various state-of-the-art open-source models and black-box commercial services (e.g., OpenAI API and GitHub Copilot). On a diverse set of security-critical test cases, covering 16 CWEs across 5 programming languages, INSEC increases the rate of generated insecure code by more than 50%, while maintaining the functional correctness of generated code. We consider INSEC practical -- it requires low resources and costs less than 10 US dollars to develop on commodity hardware. Moreover, we showcase the attack's real-world deployability, by developing an IDE plug-in that stealthily injects INSEC into the GitHub Copilot extension.
arxiv_record.authors: Slobodan Jenko, Niels M\"undler, Jingxuan He, Mark Vero, Martin Vechev
arxiv_record.title: Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on LLM-Based Code Completion

C1.justification: The central claim of practical black-box attacks that increase insecure completions while largely preserving functionality remains. V2 adds implemented IDE deployment as an explicit abstract contribution and changes the introduction's cross-engine increase from over 50 percentage points to around 50.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretations of composability, transferability, attack-token patterns, and defenses' security–utility tradeoffs. Appendix F explains why accurate assessment of known CWEs does not establish static analysis as a general defense. The targeted-only limitation is superseded by composition experiments, while v1's explicit caveat about larger, more complex vulnerabilities is no longer retained.

D1.justification: V2 announces a public code and dataset release and adds model-version information, approximate GPU optimization time, rule-based vulnerability classifiers used during optimization, excluded mutation tokens, and VSCode deployment details with a code listing. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures, not evidence that every newly documented implementation choice changed.

E1.justification: The original 16-CWE, five-language coverage is retained. V2 adds repository-context completion using RepoBench, human-written C++ and JavaScript reference solutions from HumanEval-X, and simultaneous targeting of multiple CWEs, substantially extending the evaluated data and scenarios.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates unattacked engines and internal attack variants but only discusses potential defenses. V2 Appendix F adds quantitative comparisons involving security-inducing comments, comment scrubbing, and Jain et al.'s perplexity filtering. This introduces a substantial defensive comparison component; it does not add a competing attack algorithm.

E3.justification: V2 adds StarCoder2 models at three sizes, a 333-instance RepoBench protocol using EM, ES and CodeBLEU ratios, sampled multi-CWE combinations, and defense-testing procedures. Reported attack lengths also change: v1 describes five tokens for StarCoder-3B and ten for the other engines, whereas v2 Appendix A specifies five generally, with Copilot-specific exceptions of ten or fifteen. This reporting revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds attack-composition and cross-model transfer analyses, a manual CodeQL precision audit, validation against human-written reference solutions, and experiments on security comments, comment removal, ASCII-only optimization, and perplexity defenses. The original position, initialization, tokenizer, length, temperature, and case-study analyses remain, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report aggregate point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run and seed summaries. V2's additional sampled tasks and CWE combinations expand experimental design; they do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original four-engine results match between v1 Figure 2 and v2 Figure 3. V2 adds StarCoder2-3B/7B/15B results, with clean versus attacked vulnerability rates of 13%/62%, 21%/67%, and 29%/73%, respectively. Substantial additional results cover composition, transfer, RepoBench, HumanEval-X validation, 98% CodeQL precision on 50 audited instances, and defenses.

M1.justification: The five initialization schemes and mutation–selection optimizer remain substantially unchanged. V2 Section 4.4 adds a composite attack that inserts separately optimized CWE strings on separate lines, extending v1's single-CWE procedure without redesigning its optimizer.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, threat model and method are consolidated into Section 3, and detailed algorithms, initialization explanations, experiments, and case studies move into appendices. Metrics are renamed, discussion and related work are reordered, and the title and author information change.

P2.justification: V2 adds an attack-flow diagram, deployment screenshots, and new experimental displays; expands the main results figure; and redraws initialization distributions from grouped bars into pie charts. It also merges temperature plots, changes plot scales and styling, relocates existing figures and algorithms, and adopts a different main-text and appendix layout.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against random-search jailbreaks, semantic-preserving code attacks, and concurrent RAG-context attacks, alongside additional defense and deployment literature. Section 6 now distinguishes these approaches through access requirements, per-query optimization, stealth, and preservation of functionality; these are substantive additions beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The vulnerability-rate, pass@k, and relative-functional-correctness definitions remain mathematically equivalent despite renaming and reordering. The adversarial-engine composition is restated, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs. V2's added low-overhead requirement is qualitative.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical credibility and practical substantiation. Where v1 asserted CodeQL reliability and proposed IDE deployment, v2 provides a bounded precision audit, reference-solution validation, repository-context testing, and an implemented deployment demonstration. Defense experiments and reproducibility disclosures further improve assessability. Reporting ambiguities remain, including changed attack-length descriptions alongside unchanged original scores, and the deployment is not an end-to-end attack study; nevertheless, the added validation resolves important evidential gaps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe INSEC, despite the changed title and organization. Text, equations, figures, tables, and v2's appendices A–G support reliable comparison; v1 has no separate appendix.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original results on StarCoder2, attack composition and transfer, repository completion, evaluation validation, and defenses.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack evaluations on four completion engines, vulnerability and functional-correctness measurements, ablations, and case studies.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Machine learning plays an increasingly important role in computational
chemistry and materials science, complementing computationally intensive ab
initio and first-principles methods. Despite their utility, machine-learning
models often lack generalization capability and robustness during atomistic
simulations, yielding unphysical energy and force predictions that hinder their
real-world applications. We address this challenge by introducing a
physics-informed, weakly supervised approach for training machine-learned
interatomic potentials (MLIPs). We introduce two novel loss functions,
extrapolating the potential energy via a Taylor expansion and using the concept
of conservative forces. Our approach improves the accuracy of MLIPs applied to
training tasks with sparse training data sets and reduces the need for
pre-training computationally demanding models with large data sets.
Particularly, we perform extensive experiments demonstrating reduced energy and
force errors -- often lower by a factor of two -- for various baseline models
and benchmark data sets. Moreover, we demonstrate improved robustness during MD
simulations of the MLIP models trained with the proposed weakly supervised
loss. Finally, our approach improves the fine-tuning of foundation models on
sparse, highly accurate ab initio data. An implementation of our method and
scripts for executing experiments are available at
https://github.com/nec-research/PICPS-ML4Sci.

metadata.abstract: Machine learning is playing an increasingly important role in computational chemistry and materials science, complementing expensive ab initio and first-principles methods. However, machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) often struggle with generalization and robustness, leading to unphysical energy and force predictions in atomistic simulations. To address this, we propose a physics-informed, weakly supervised training framework for MLIPs. Our method introduces two novel loss functions: one based on Taylor expansions of the potential energy and another enforcing conservative force constraints. This approach enhances accuracy, particularly in low-data regimes, and reduces the reliance on large, expensive training datasets. Extensive experiments across benchmark datasets show up to 2× reductions in energy and force errors for multiple baseline models. Additionally, our method improves the stability of molecular dynamics simulations and facilitates effective fine-tuning of ML foundation models on sparse, high-accuracy ab initio data. An implementation of our method and scripts for executing experiments are available at \url{https://github.com/nec-research/PICPS-ML4Sci}.

Our method introduces two novel loss functions: one based on Taylor expansions of the potential energy and another enforcing conservative force constraints. This approach enhances accuracy, particularly in low-data regimes, and reduces the reliance on large, expensive training datasets. Extensive experiments across benchmark datasets show up to 2× reductions in energy and force errors for multiple baseline models. Additionally, our method improves the stability of molecular dynamics simulations and facilitates effective fine-tuning of ML foundation models on sparse, high-accuracy ab initio data. An implementation of our method and scripts for executing experiments are available at \url{https://github.com/nec-research/PICPS-ML4Sci}.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of when second-order terms matter, why thermostats affect stability comparisons, and why foundation-model selection matters. It also qualifies NoisyNode's applicability to non-equilibrium structures and discusses the memory obstacle to directly penalizing force curl. The earlier explanation of negligible benzene gains disappears with that benchmark.

D1.justification: V1's promise of code release upon publication becomes an explicit implementation-and-experiment-script repository link in v2. New reproducibility information includes MD integrators, thermostat parameters, stability thresholds, MACE configurations, fine-tuning splits, learning rates, loss weights, and training-time measurements. These are substantial additions to the documented setup; repository availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: V2 adds MD17(CCSD) aspirin energy-only fine-tuning, the 148-atom MD22 buckyball catcher, and actual aspirin MD simulations under NVE and NVT conditions. Conversely, v1's broad rMD17 benchmark covering benzene, naphthalene, and aspirin disappears; aspirin remains in the qualitative and simulation studies.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated MACE-from-scratch, MACE-OFF, and MACE-MP configurations, including comparisons between foundation-model fine-tuning and training from scratch (Tables 3–4). Its force-free WL comparison also substitutes predicted-force WL for reference-force WL (Table A24). That variant already appeared in v1 Table A17, but its participation in the corresponding comparison changes.

E3.justification: The larger TiO2 comparison changes from 1,000 to 2,000 training configurations in Table 2. ANI-1x training-size experiments extend to 100,000, one million, and five million samples with additional budgets. New protocols include MD stability measurements at 300 K with 0.5 fs steps, CCSD fine-tuning splits and budgets, and MAE evaluation on MD22.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct MD stability and energy-conservation analyses, including thermostat controls (Figure 3 and Figures A1–A2), and compares first- versus second-order PIWSL (Table A27). It also extends training-size sensitivity substantially. Most earlier loss, perturbation, training-duration, and curl analyses remain, although several move to Appendix F.

E5.justification: Retained results largely preserve their three-run averages and uncertainty reporting. V2 newly specifies fixed-seed MD hyperparameter selection followed by evaluation with three velocity seeds, and explicitly reports only one training run for the five-million-sample experiment (Table A5). These are experiment-specific reporting changes, not increased repetitions of the earlier benchmarks.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial fine-tuning, scaling, and MD results while removing the broad rMD17 result table. In the retained ANI-1x PaiNN-GF comparison, PIWSL energy/force RMSEs change from 20.23/11.13 to 18.62/10.94 (v1 Table A16; v2 Table A21). Table 2's replaced TiO2 scores use different training sizes. New MD results show NVE stability gains, while both methods reach 300 ps in the NVT plots.

M1.justification: V2 generalizes the first-order PITC objective to include displaced-configuration forces through a second-order coefficient, and extends PISC accordingly (Equations 2–4). Appendix E.3.2 also introduces two-point PISC variants, including one using reference energy, which is used in the new fine-tuning experiments. These change the training objectives rather than merely their explanation.

P1.justification: V1 Sections 5.4–5.5 are reorganized into Appendix F, while the main experimental narrative foregrounds MD stability and foundation-model fine-tuning. The impact statement moves from the final appendix to the first, and the experimental appendices gain new subdivisions. The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion are revised to reflect this restructuring.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. Earlier main-text tables move into the appendices, and v2 adds MD stability and energy-conservation plots plus new fine-tuning and second-order comparison tables. Figures 1–2 largely retain their original content, while the broad rMD17 table is removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted references concerning active learning, MD22, foundation-model training data, transferability, and non-equilibrium denoising. arxiv_record.abstract: Pre-trained models have become the preferred backbone due to the increasing complexity of model parameters. However, traditional pre-trained models often face deployment challenges due to their fixed sizes, and are prone to negative transfer when discrepancies arise between training tasks and target tasks. To address this, we propose KIND, a novel pre-training method designed to construct decomposable models. KIND integrates knowledge by incorporating Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) as a structural constraint, with each basic component represented as a combination of a column vector, singular value, and row vector from U, \Sigma, and V^\top matrices. These components are categorized into learngenes for encapsulating class-agnostic knowledge and tailors for capturing class-specific knowledge, with knowledge diversion facilitated by a class gate mechanism during training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that models pre-trained with KIND can be decomposed into learngenes and tailors, which can be adaptively recombined for diverse resource-constrained deployments. Moreover, for tasks with large domain shifts, transferring only learngenes with task-agnostic knowledge, when combined with randomly initialized tailors, effectively mitigates domain shifts. Code will be made available at https://github.com/Te4P0t/KIND.
