C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the central contribution from transferable learngenes for efficient diffusion-model adaptation to decomposable pre-trained models supporting resource-constrained deployment and large domain shifts. Adaptive recombination of pretrained components becomes a principal claim, while the novel-class performance claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly qualifies when pretrained tailors should transfer: related tasks can reuse them, whereas large domain shifts may make their knowledge harmful, motivating random tailors instead. It also interprets recombination as avoiding repeated compression costs. The original explanations of class-agnostic learngenes and the class gate remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies pseudocode, component counts, weight decay, DiT-block configuration, method/task-specific hyperparameters, downstream class assignments and superclass mappings. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing implementation changes. v2 also announces a future code release and provides its repository address; availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds generation experiments on CelebA-HQ, Hubble, MRI and Pokemon, substantially extending coverage beyond ImageNet to distinct visual domains. The ImageNet superclass construction, 150/461 class division and 18 downstream tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds Laptop-diff to the model-size comparison alongside traditional pre-training and existing learngene methods. The original novel-class comparison retains all its comparators in v2 Table 2; LoHa and DoRA were already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces model-size construction comparisons and FDD evaluation for domain-shift tasks. Main-text pre-training changes from 200K to 300K steps, although Appendix Table 6 still specifies 200K. Table 7 revises v1's blanket fine-tuning learning rate for several baselines, and the reused sample-grid caption changes guidance from 4.0 to 3.0. These reported revisions do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds explicit tests of transfer under large domain shifts across four domains, substantially extending distribution-shift evidence. The original component ablations, convergence snapshots, knowledge-distribution statistics and with/without-tailor visualizations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions specify two seeds for the with/without-tailor visualization. Neither supplies quantitative repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests, and v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds model-size results, four-domain FDD comparisons, per-task FIDs in Table 8 and supplementary generated samples. For example, Table 1 reports DiT-L KIND with 245.9M parameters and FID 9.33. v1 Tables 1–3 retain their numerical values as v2 Tables 2, 4 and 5, including KIND's novel-class DiT-L FID of 12.87.

M1.justification: The factorized training, class gate and frozen-learngene/random-tailor adaptation remain. Section 3.4 adds a deployment procedure that selects relevant pretrained tailors and discards unrelated ones, enabling smaller models without further training. This extends deployment while retaining the core algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 introduces a numbered section hierarchy, organizes results around deployment scenarios, removes the standalone baseline-description subsection and groups convergence with ablation analyses. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 3 are substantially redrawn, and Figure 2 clarifies pixel versus latent space. v2 adds comparison tables, a domain-shift image grid, appendix tables and sample galleries, while relocating retained displays and changing table highlighting. The retained tailor visualization's caption is corrected from 14 to 12 classes; its cases are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 substantially repositions KIND around variable-sized model initialization, pruning and distillation, adding discussion of methods including Laptop-diff and LD-Pruner. v1's biological Learngene discussion is reduced, and new domain-shift and evaluation references support the broadened positioning.

T1.justification: The denoising objective, factorized weight representation and class-based component partition retain their mathematical substance. v2 expands the product into component notation and supplies pseudocode, but introduces no substantive new theoretical assumptions, propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for transfer beyond ImageNet through four distinct domains and supports deployment claims with model-size comparisons. Its appendices supply important implementation and benchmark details missing from the supplied v1. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, particularly the conflicting 300K/200K pre-training budgets and changed guidance caption for identical samples, which still limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe KIND and retain matching methods, experiments and results despite the revised title. All supplied pages are readable. v1 mentions an appendix but contains none; v2 includes Appendices A–B. Supplementary additions are assessed as newly documented in the supplied PDFs.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and reports additional model-size comparisons, domain-shift experiments and per-task results in its appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet generation experiments, baseline comparisons, component ablations and analyses of learngenes, including Tables 1–3.

arxiv_record.abstract: Density-based mode-seeking methods generate a \emph{density-ascending dependency} from low-density points towards higher-density neighbors. Current mode-seeking methods identify modes by breaking some dependency connections, but relying heavily on local data characteristics, requiring case-by-case threshold settings or human intervention to be effective for different datasets. To address this issue, we introduce a novel concept called \emph{typicality}, by exploring the \emph{locally defined} dependency from a \emph{global} perspective, to quantify how confident a point would be a mode. We devise an algorithm that effectively and efficiently identifies modes with the help of the global-view typicality. To implement and validate our idea, we design a clustering method called TANGO, which not only leverages typicality to detect modes, but also utilizes graph-cut with an improved \emph{path-based similarity} to aggregate data into the final clusters. Moreover, this paper also provides some theoretical analysis on the proposed algorithm. Experimental results on several synthetic and extensive real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of TANGO. The code is available at https://github.com/SWJTU-ML/TANGO_code.

C1.justification: The central claims about global typicality, mode identification and graph-cut clustering remain. v2's introduction explicitly adds characterization of typicality's statistical properties to the contributions, extending the earlier claims about uniqueness and computational efficiency.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the Katz-centrality comparison with a PageRank/attraction-basin interpretation and expands explanations of mode selection, aggregation and stability as k increases. It adds substantive qualifications: segmentation results are preliminary and imperfect, and typicality can fail when sparse points surround a much denser core.

D1.justification: Compared with v1's references to unavailable supplementary settings, v2 supplies baseline search grids, manual-selection procedures and per-dataset parameter values in Appendix C and Table 2. It also adds code-access information and the segmentation hardware, software and 20-thread similarity-computation setting. These disclosures do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The original four synthetic and 16 real-world datasets remain. v2 adds pixel-level segmentation of six Berkeley benchmark images, extending coverage beyond clustering the existing feature datasets. Appendix C.7 also introduces highly noisy irregular-shape datasets and an extreme-density-contrast test scenario.

E2.justification: The corresponding original experiments retain their comparator sets: ten real-world baselines and Quick Shift/DPC for the synthetic examples. The added segmentation experiment reuses QKSPP, CPF, LDP-MST and LDP-SC; no new external comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: The original normalization, 64-dimensional image representations, metrics and TANGO parameter search remain. The added segmentation protocol uses 154,401 five-dimensional position/RGB vectors per image, fixed parameters and runtime measurements. Appendix C.6 also changes the TANGO-c control from replacing the similarity weighting to removing aggregation.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the original similarity-weighting ablation with an aggregation-removal ablation and corresponding results. It also adds a controlled illustration of typicality as points are added (Figure 3), noisy-data tests (Figure 11) and a concrete failure case (Figure 12). The original neighborhood-size sensitivity analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report Friedman testing followed by Nemenyi comparisons with CD = 2.30. v2 supplies the statistic, exact p-value and pairwise rank differences for these already reported tests, without introducing a new statistical procedure. Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The original benchmark scores are unchanged between v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 5. v2 adds segmentation outcomes and timings, noisy-data findings, detailed statistical outputs and replacement TANGO-c results. It also introduces an unresolved discrepancy: Table 2 gives TANGO banknote ARI/NMI/ACC as 96.53/93.59/99.13, while both benchmark figures report 96.24/93.17/99.05.

M1.justification: v2 Algorithm 3 revises the path-similarity computation to operate on modes and inter-subcluster edges, replacing the point-level connected-component processing in v1 Algorithm 2. This refines one computational component; the typicality equations, dependency-breaking rule, path-similarity definition and final spectral clustering remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, motivation, method explanations and conclusion are extensively rewritten around confidence in mode identification. v2 adds a preliminaries section and reorganizes detailed results, sensitivity analysis and ablations into Appendix C, substantially changing the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the opening illustration and adds a workflow diagram, typicality-evolution plot, detailed results/parameter table, statistical heatmap, segmentation grid, noise examples and failure visualization. Existing diagnostic plots are relocated and enlarged in the appendix. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical edits.

R1.justification: v2 adds a substantial spectral-clustering review covering guarantees, scalable methods and cluster-number selection. It removes the Katz-centrality positioning and introduces PageRank and power-law literature to motivate and analyze typicality, substantially expanding the work's connections to prior research.

T1.justification: The uniqueness and linear-time typicality theorems are retained and now have proofs in the supplied material. v2 adds Theorem 3 and Appendix A.2 claiming an O(nk log(nk)) path-similarity bound, replacing v1's O(n^2 log n) analysis. Appendix B additionally introduces a stochastic recurrence, independence and degree-distribution assumptions, and a power-law tail theorem.

improvement.justification: For the supplied PDFs, v2 substantially improves completeness and assessability: central proofs and experimental settings previously deferred to unavailable material are now inspectable, while clearer explanations and a concrete failure case improve understanding of the method's scope. Segmentation timings and noise tests extend its empirical support. The gains are tempered by inconsistent banknote scores and insufficient justification that Appendix B's distributional assumptions apply to the evaluated data.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TANGO, and their main methods, experiments, equations and figures can be reliably matched. However, v1 references supplementary proofs, baseline settings and statistical details that are absent from the supplied PDF; v2 includes Appendices A–C. Comparison of those earlier supplementary details is therefore limited.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and reports additional image-segmentation results, running times, noisy-data evaluations and a failure example.

before.justification: v1 reports original clustering experiments on four synthetic and 16 real-world datasets, parameter-sensitivity tests and component ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Encoding geospatial objects is fundamental for geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) applications, which leverage machine learning (ML) models to analyze spatial information. Common approaches transform each object into known formats, like image and text, for compatibility with ML models. However, this process often discards crucial spatial information, such as the object's position relative to the entire space, reducing downstream task effectiveness. Alternative encoding methods that preserve some spatial properties are often devised for specific data objects (e.g., point encoders), making them unsuitable for tasks that involve different data types (i.e., points, polylines, and polygons). To this end, we propose Poly2Vec, a polymorphic Fourier-based encoding approach that unifies the representation of geospatial objects, while preserving the essential spatial properties. Poly2Vec incorporates a learned fusion module that adaptively integrates the magnitude and phase of the Fourier transform for different tasks and geometries. We evaluate Poly2Vec on five diverse tasks, organized into two categories. The first empirically demonstrates that Poly2Vec consistently outperforms object-specific baselines in preserving three key spatial relationships: topology, direction, and distance. The second shows that integrating Poly2Vec into a state-of-the-art GeoAI workflow improves the performance in two popular tasks: population prediction and land use inference.

C1.justification: The unified encoding and learned-fusion contributions remain, but the headline claims expand substantially. v1 emphasizes consistent spatial-reasoning performance; v2 claims superiority across topology, direction and distance tasks and improved population prediction and land use inference through GeoAI integration. The abstract, introduction and conclusion now make practical workflow benefits a central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking directional errors to grid discretization, interprets the RegionDCL experiment as showing that encoded spatial information can replace distance bias, and argues that learned frequencies offer little benefit. It removes v1's discussion of global Fourier features limiting nearest-point distance estimation and its interpretation of transfer from complex to simpler geometries. These materially change the explanatory and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix A.4 adds dataset counts, OSM extraction tags and format, geographic boundary sources, land-use/population label sources, class aggregation and pair-generation instructions, alongside fuller baseline descriptions. Hardware, software and several training settings are retained and relocated. v1's explicit hidden-layer width and Douglas-Peucker tolerances are no longer documented. GeoAI training details are largely delegated to the cited RegionDCL work.

E1.justification: v1's synthetic geometries and California landmarks, roads, lakes and parks are replaced by Singapore/New York POIs, roads and buildings. v2 adds 16-direction classification, multiclass topology for polygon-involving pairs, population prediction and land use inference. Nearest-neighbor retrieval and the explicit cross-geometry transfer scenarios are removed. This substantially changes both represented populations and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated TILE, WRAP and GRID baselines, and T2VEC for polyline comparisons; v1 cited T2VEC but did not evaluate it. RegionDCL and its distance-bias removal control are new application comparators. Coord/DIRECT and NUFT/NUFTSPEC represent corresponding retained baselines rather than additions; THEORY and RESNET1D also remain.

E3.justification: v2 reports 5,000 topology pairs per class, versus 10,000 in v1 Section 4.2.1, and introduces position-adjusted pair generation and multiclass evaluation. Classification reporting changes from AUROC/weighted F1 to accuracy, precision, recall and F1. Distance evaluation changes from MSE to MAE, and point-polyline targets change from nearest-point distance to centroid distance. Maximum sampled frequency changes from 5.0 to 1.0. The 60:20:20 split and core spatial-task training budget remain.

E4.justification: v1's cross-geometry generalization study, including Appendix A.3, is removed. Its nearest-neighbor fusion ablation is replaced by fusion ablations across topology, direction and distance tasks in v2 Figures 4 and 6–9. v2 additionally tests learned versus fixed frequencies in Appendix A.3.2 and removes RegionDCL's distance bias as an application-level control. These substantially revise the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 Appendix A.4.3 newly specifies five runs for spatial-reasoning experiments, and its spatial and GeoAI result tables report means and standard deviations. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting; it does not establish that v1 used fewer runs.

E6.justification: The synthetic/California results are replaced by Singapore/New York results, with new directional and GeoAI outcomes and removal of retrieval/transfer results. For example, v2 Table 4 reports Singapore population MAE of 5807.54 for RegionDCL versus 4957.58 with Poly2Vec, and New York land-use L1 of 0.418 versus 0.397. These are new within-v2 comparisons, not performance gains over v1 under matched conditions.

M1.justification: The central Fourier encoding and magnitude/phase fusion remain. Polygon triangulation changes from ear clipping to constrained Delaunay. The topology predictor changes from sigmoid of an embedding dot product with binary cross-entropy to concatenated embeddings processed by an MLP with cross-entropy. These are limited procedural changes around the retained encoder; the new RegionDCL integration also replaces its original features and removes distance bias.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methods, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Evaluation is organized around four research questions and separated into spatial reasoning and GeoAI integration. Detailed derivations, normalization and experimental settings move into expanded appendices. These are substantial narrative and organizational changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts an ICML-style layout, redraws the Fourier illustration and workflow, and consolidates the affine-transformation diagrams into Figure 2. Result tables are extensively restructured, including uncertainty values. Distance scatter plots, directional/application tables and broader ablation figures replace or supplement v1's distance bars, retrieval tables and transfer plots, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands from mixed-geometry spatial reasoning to preserving coordinate information within GeoAI and future foundation models. v2 adds substantial literature on GeoAI applications, region representation, foundation models, point encoders and PolygonGNN. Some earlier interlinking, nearest-neighbor and polygon-coding references disappear, while the principal Fourier and polygon-encoding antecedents remain.

T1.justification: v2 adds explicit encoding properties, including monotonic distance preservation, and intermediate Fourier derivations while retaining most underlying mathematics. Some equations change non-equivalently: the final line-segment formula in Appendix A.2.2 uses inverse squared-length scaling, whereas v1 Equation 17 and v2 Equation 10 use squared-length scaling. Thus the mathematical revision includes a new internal inconsistency, not merely relocated notation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence of usefulness in complete GeoAI workflows: Section 4.2 and Table 4 provide controlled population and land-use comparisons, supported by broader baselines and newly reported uncertainty. The added data-construction details and targeted ablations also strengthen assessability. These gains outweigh the loss of cross-geometry transfer tests and the new main-text/appendix formula inconsistency, although those weaknesses limit confidence in generalization claims and mathematical reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Poly2Vec framework and authorship. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring and replacement of experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original Singapore and New York experiments on spatial relationships, population prediction and land use inference, plus frequency-sampling and fusion ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and California experiments on topology classification, distance estimation, nearest-neighbor search, cross-geometry generalization and fusion ablations, including appendix results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Advances in Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) bridged the performance
gap with Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) through sophisticated analysis of pre-trained
parameter spaces. Starting from drawing insights from Neural Engrams (NE) in
Biological Neural Networks (BNNs), we establish a connection between the
low-rank property observed during PEFT's parameter space shifting and
neurobiological mechanisms. This observation leads to our proposed method,
Synapse and Neuron (SAN), which decomposes and propagates scaling components
from anterior feature adjusting vectors towards posterior weight matrices. Our
approach is theoretically grounded in Long-Term Potentiation/Depression (LTP/D)
phenomena, which govern synapse development through neurotransmitter release
modulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness: on
\textbf{vision tasks} across VTAB, FGVC, and GIC (25 datasets) using ViT, SwinT
and ConvNeXt, SAN outperforms FFT up to 8.7% and LoRA by 3.2%; on language
tasks using Commonsense Reasoning (8 datasets) with LLaMA models (all
generations), surpassing ChatGPT up to 8.5% and LoRA by 4.7%; on
visual-language tasks using Mixed Visual Instruction (7 datasets) with LLaVA
models, it exceeds FFT up to 2.4% and LoRA by 1.9%. Our code and W&B log will
be released.

C1.justification: v1 presents SAN primarily as a biologically inspired PEFT method validated on vision tasks. v2 claims a general plug-and-play enhancement for existing PEFT methods across scalable vision, language and multimodal models, and elevates neural-engram-like task-specific adjustment patterns to a main contribution. This substantially broadens the claimed contribution and applicability.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting within-task similarity and between-task differences to neural engrams, random-propagation failures to layer proximity, and rank robustness to simplified adjustment requirements. Optimization-stability reasoning replaces v1's affine compensation rationale for nonlinearities. Some new interpretation overstates the evidence: Section 4.3 attributes 2.4–4.6-point gains to comparison with DoRA, whereas Table 2 shows those gains against LoRA.

D1.justification: Appendices A–B add dataset-specific learning rates and drop-path rates, model-specific batch sizes, search procedures, SSF/DoRA code-base pointers, and training hardware and budgets for new tasks. v1 provides mainly an optimizer, schedule and GPU description. v2 also revises the vision hardware description from RTX 3090 to RTX 3090 Ti. Its own code and W&B logs remain promised rather than released within the PDF.

E1.justification: The visual benchmark coverage is retained despite v2's inconsistent abstract count. v2 adds eight commonsense-reasoning datasets, seven visual-language benchmarks, and RoboVQA-based robotic video prediction using DynamiCrafter in Appendix G. These introduce substantially different domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: The main vision comparison adds NOAH, AdaptFormer and SPT-LoRA; new language comparisons include DoRA, P-Tuning v2, series/parallel adapters and ChatGPT with chain-of-thought. Conversely, the backbone radar drops Bitfit, LoRA, Adapter and VPT, retaining FFT, LP, SSF and SAN. Appendix Table 7 drops the earlier detailed Adapter results, although aggregate Adapter comparisons remain in Table 1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces multiple 7–13B language-model configurations, three-epoch language and one-epoch visual-language training, paired rank-8/16 vision settings, and rank-16/32 language controls. Appendix G introduces four criteria for evaluating generated robotic actions. The retained vision schedule remains 100 epochs with 10 warm-up epochs; newly disclosed vision hyperparameters alone do not establish changed experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds ordered-versus-random propagation tests, applied-layer and learning-rate comparisons, rank sensitivity, cross-layer distribution analyses, and robotic-generation case studies (Figure 5 and Appendices B–G). v1's dedicated component-separation ablation, including propagation-only results in Figure 3, is removed. The analysis now addresses substantially broader questions about propagation and compatibility.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's scaling-vector means, variances and histograms characterize learned parameter distributions rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial language, visual-language, ablation and video-generation results. Existing vision values also change: SAN's general CIFAR-100/ImageNet-1k accuracies move from 94.11/83.69 to 94.2/83.8. The reported VTAB mean changes from 75.00 to 77.7 despite largely retained per-dataset scores in Appendix Table 7, so this summary change does not establish a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: v2 extends the original SSF-style scaling procedure with a pooled adjusted/original-output ratio for LoRA integration and propagation to corresponding layers in subsequent blocks (Section 3.2 and Appendix C). arxiv_record.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale pre-trained models is prohibitively expensive in terms of computation and memory costs. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), a popular Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, offers an efficient solution by optimizing only low-rank matrices. Despite recent progress in improving LoRA's performance, the relationship between the LoRA optimization space and the full parameter space is often overlooked. A solution that appears flat in the loss landscape of the LoRA space may still exhibit sharp directions in the full parameter space, potentially compromising generalization. We introduce Flat-LoRA, which aims to identify a low-rank adaptation situated in a flat region of the full parameter space. Instead of adopting the well-established sharpness-aware minimization approach, which incurs significant computation and memory overheads, we employ a Bayesian expectation loss objective to preserve training efficiency. Further, we design a refined random perturbation generation strategy for improved performance and carefully manage memory overhead using random seeds. Experiments across diverse tasks-including mathematical reasoning, coding abilities, dialogue generation, instruction following, and text-to-image generation-demonstrate that Flat-LoRA improves both in-domain and out-of-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/nblt/Flat-LoRA.
arxiv_record.authors: Tao Li, Zhengbao He, Yujun Li, Yasheng Wang, Lifeng Shang, Xiaolin Huang
arxiv_record.title: Flat-LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation over a Flat Loss Landscape

arxiv_record.abstract:
Flow matching (FM) is a family of training algorithms for fitting continuous
normalizing flows (CNFs). Conditional flow matching (CFM) exploits the fact
that the marginal vector field of a CNF can be learned by fitting least-squares
regression to the conditional vector field specified given one or both ends of
the flow path. In this paper, we extend the CFM algorithm by defining
conditional probability paths along ``streams'', instances of latent stochastic
paths that connect data pairs of source and target, which are modeled with
Gaussian process (GP) distributions. The unique distributional properties of
GPs help preserve the ``simulation-free" nature of CFM training. We show that
this generalization of the CFM can effectively reduce the variance in the
estimated marginal vector field at a moderate computational cost, thereby
improving the quality of the generated samples under common metrics.
Additionally, adopting the GP on the streams allows for flexibly linking
multiple correlated training data points (e.g., time series). We empirically
validate our claim through both simulations and applications to image and
neural time series data.
arxiv_record.authors: Ganchao Wei, Li Ma
arxiv_record.title: Stream-level flow matching with Gaussian processes

The Bayesian perspective ceases to be a headline contribution but remains part of the paper.

C2.justification: v5 expands the mechanism account to suppression of spurious intermediate modes and easier numerical integration. It interprets CIFAR-10 results as suggesting limitations of high-dimensional minibatch OT and acknowledges that combining OT with GP streams need not improve performance. Conversely, v1's explicit complete-observation requirement and proposed latent-space remedy disappear, without a demonstrated missing-data solution. Appendix I adds a biological interpretation of the generated LFP trajectories.

D1.justification: v5 supplies hardware specifications and training timings for retained applications, plus CIFAR-10 optimizer, clipping, EMA, noise, solver and clean-fid details. It also documents LFP selection, temporal subsampling, rescaling and runtime. These substantially expand implementation and reproducibility information; the code-access link remains the same.

E1.justification: v5 adds unconditional CIFAR-10 natural-image generation and multiregion mouse-brain time-series generation using one LFP recording session. Appendix F also introduces a two-Gaussian-to-three-Gaussian transformation scenario. The original MNIST, HWD+ and toy-data coverage remains.

E2.justification: The existing standard-Gaussian-to-two-Gaussian comparison expands from I-CFM and GP-I-CFM in v1 Figure 1B to include OT-CFM and GP-OT-CFM in v5 Table 1. These methods already participated in the MNIST comparison, whose comparator membership remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce substantial protocols: CIFAR-10 uses a 128-channel U-Net, batch size 128, specified noise controls, DOPRI5 sampling, FID from 50,000 generated images and timed ten-image batches. The LFP application uses 214 trials, seven regions and five selected time points from 50, with rescaled time. These are new experimental settings; the retained MNIST/HWD+ architectures and HWD+ split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix F and Figure 7 add a focused comparison of intermediate distributions, testing whether GP streams suppress spurious modes during a two-to-three-Gaussian transformation. Appendix I also reports LFP runtime with five versus 50 time points. The existing variance-schedule and crossing-stream/covariate analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The existing 100-run experiments retain mean and standard-error reporting. v5 Table 4 adds a distinct repeated-evaluation procedure: each trained CIFAR-10 model undergoes 20 FID evaluations and 20 generation-timing measurements, summarized by means and standard errors. These are repeated evaluations of trained models, not 20 independent training runs.

E6.justification: For the retained Gaussian-mixture setting, I-CFM/GP-I-CFM Wasserstein means change from 1.51/1.27 in v1 Figure 1B to 1.54/1.51 in v5 Table 1. New CIFAR-10 FIDs are 3.75, 3.74, 3.62 and 3.75 for I-CFM, OT-CFM, GP-I-CFM and GP-OT-CFM, respectively, alongside timing results. Intermediate-mode and LFP findings are added, while MNIST means and variance-schedule scores are retained.

arxiv_record.abstract:
The minimax sample complexity of group distributionally robust optimization
(GDRO) has been determined up to a $\log(K)$ factor, where $K$ is the number of
groups. In this work, we venture beyond the minimax perspective via a novel
notion of sparsity that we dub $(\lambda, \beta)$-sparsity. In short, this
condition means that at any parameter $\theta$, there is a set of at most
$\beta$ groups whose risks at $\theta$ all are at least $\lambda$ larger than
the risks of the other groups. To find an $\epsilon$-optimal $\theta$, we show
via a novel algorithm and analysis that the $\epsilon$-dependent term in the

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add computationally efficient semi-adaptivity, a dimension-independent sample bound under a high-precision condition, and empirical claims of practicality and improved sample efficiency. v1's contributions were theoretical and left the computational expense of fully adaptive estimation unresolved.

C2.justification: v2 interprets convergence gains as overcoming initial estimation overhead by concentrating sampling on high-risk groups, and interprets disproportionate sampling of a small Adult subgroup as evidence of GDRO's robustness objective. It also explains the new method's high-precision restriction and explicitly qualifies suppression of log-log factors in Appendix B. The existing last-iterate-convergence limitation remains.

D1.justification: New Appendix F supplies substantial experimental reproduction information: synthetic loss scaling and parameters, Adult features and group composition, normalization by a common maximum feature norm, absence of batching, and the full-information reference-optimization procedure. These details accompany newly introduced experiments rather than disclose changed settings for an existing study.

E1.justification: v1 has no evaluated datasets or simulation scenarios. v2 adds actual simulation of the lower-bound construction and Adult income classification across ten race-by-gender groups. The theoretical construction already existed, but its empirical use is new.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an empirical baseline comparison against Zhang et al.'s Stochastic Mirror Descent for GDRO (SMD-GDRO), visibly reported against SB-GDRO-SA on Adult in Figure 3. v1 discusses prior algorithms theoretically but reports no evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The new experiments introduce protocols with 10^6 rounds, delta = 0.01, and target gaps of 0.005 for the synthetic instance and 0.001 for Adult. Section 5 and Appendix F specify normalized losses, single-sample updates, and a 10^7-round full-information procedure for estimating Adult's reference optimum.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses testing whether small dominant sets emerge during learning and how sampling concentrates across demographic groups. Figure 2 tracks dominant-set sizes and their running averages; Figure 4 examines Adult group-selection frequencies. v1 has no corresponding empirical diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports aggregation across five independent runs with seeds 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4. v1 has no empirical run information. The added reporting does not include confidence intervals, quantified dispersion, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first empirical findings. Figure 3 reports SB-GDRO-SA reaching an Adult optimality gap below 4 × 10^-5 before 400,000 samples, while SMD-GDRO remains near that gap around one million samples. Figures 2 and 4 additionally report small dominant sets and concentrated group sampling; these are new results, not improvements over measurements in v1.

M1.justification: v2 introduces SB-GDRO-SA (Algorithm 9), which estimates the sparsity gap during optimization, halves lambda when dominant sets exceed a threshold, and refreshes samples subject to a lower cutoff. This is distinct from the retained SB-GDRO-Full, renamed SB-GDRO-A, and the existing dimension-free method moved to Appendix C.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: the generic optimization discussion moves into Appendix B.1, Section 4 is recast around full and semi-adaptivity, and the former dimension-free Section 5 moves to Appendix C. The introduction and explanations are rewritten, algorithms are renamed, and experimental discussion becomes a main section.

P2.justification: v2 adds three empirical figures showing dominant-set trajectories, convergence with a zoomed inset, and group-selection counts. Table 1 gains the semi-adaptive bound, a new algorithm display is added, and MaxP moves into the main text. The original lower-bound illustration is retained as Figure 5.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 29 works. v2 makes limited positioning refinements, including distinguishing bounded-loss assumptions in prior work, revising its description of prior sleeping-bandit tuning requirements, and explaining the suitability of SMD-GDRO as an empirical baseline.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix B.3 add the semi-adaptive sample-complexity theorem, its more general formulation, and supporting proofs. Appendix D also changes the regret term from K^(1-alpha)/(eta_T(1-alpha)) to (K^(1-alpha)-1)/(eta_T(1-alpha)), repairing the stated alpha-to-one limit used to obtain the Shannon-entropy bound.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper by partly addressing v1's explicit computational-practicality limitation through SB-GDRO-SA, correcting the entropy-limit proof step, and adding the first empirical tests with documented settings. The new guarantee is conditional on high precision, and empirical support remains limited to two instances without uncertainty intervals. Nevertheless, the gains in theoretical support and demonstrated applicability are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GDRO research, with matching authors, foundational definitions, algorithms, and proofs. The main text and all appendices are readable, and renamed or relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 Section 5 reports original experiments on a synthetic lower-bound environment and Adult income classification, including dominant-set trajectories, convergence comparisons, and group-sampling counts. Appendix F documents the experiments.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results, proofs, and schematic illustrations, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes, including in its appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to complex reasoning tasks that require executing several complex steps before receiving any reward. Properly assigning credit to these steps is essential for enhancing model performance. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), a common reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm used for LLM finetuning, employs value networks to tackle credit assignment. However, recent approaches achieve strong results without it, raising questions about the efficacy of value networks in practice. In this work, we systematically evaluate the efficacy of value networks and reveal their significant shortcomings in reasoning-heavy LLM tasks, showing that they often produce poor estimate of expected return and barely outperform a random baseline when comparing alternative steps. This motivates our key question: Can improved credit assignment enhance RL training for LLMs? To address this, we propose VinePPO, a straightforward approach that leverages the flexibility of language environments to compute unbiased Monte Carlo-based estimates. Our method consistently outperforms PPO and other baselines across MATH and GSM8K datasets in less wall-clock time (up to 3.0x). Crucially, it achieves higher test accuracy for a given training accuracy, capturing more generalization signal per sample. These results emphasize the importance of accurate credit assignment in RL training of LLM.
arxiv_record.authors: Amirhossein Kazemnejad, Milad Aghajohari, Eva Portelance, Alessandro Sordoni, Siva Reddy, Aaron Courville, Nicolas Le Roux

C1.justification: The central claims about inaccurate PPO critics and effective Monte Carlo credit assignment remain. v2 extends superiority claims to RLOO/GRPO and newly claims to be the first RL post-training algorithm that scales generalization slope through additional compute. Higher test accuracy at comparable training accuracy was already claimed in v1 Appendix C.7; its promotion to the abstract is not an entirely new finding.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new critic diagnostics as evidence against undertraining and argues that already-capable LLMs justify spending more compute on accurate updates. Appendix E.27 adds a useful qualification: nonzero advantages need not correspond to logically incorrect or insightful steps. The earlier explanations concerning KL efficiency, temperature sensitivity, and errors later in reasoning chains remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds RLOO/GRPO hyperparameters and implementation information, identifies RhoMath across both datasets as the basis for PPO hyperparameter selection, and explains checkpoint loading and separate vLLM engines per GPU rank. Existing hardware, timing tables, software choices, and code/container access statements are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use MATH and GSM8K for mathematical reasoning. The added diagnostics and examples remain within this coverage; no additional dataset, domain, or distinct task scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: RLOO and GRPO, previously discussed but not experimentally compared, become evaluated baselines across both datasets and model sizes. v2 includes them in performance, generalization, and runtime comparisons in Figures 4–6, while retaining PPO, DPO+, and RestEM.

E3.justification: v2 adds explained variance as a critic diagnostic and specifies protocols for the new RLOO/GRPO experiments, including KL-coefficient tuning and a selected coefficient of 3e-3. Existing dataset splits, model sizes, Pass@1 evaluation settings, and PPO/VinePPO hyperparameters remain unchanged. Expanded descriptions of existing sampling budgets do not establish that those experiments changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds an analysis addressing critic undertraining through explained-variance and MAE trajectories (Appendix D.2), extends the existing rollout-count ablation to wall-clock efficiency (Figure 7b), and adds three credit-assignment case studies (Appendix E). Existing generalization, KL, temperature, and value-ranking analyses are retained or expanded rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 7 newly quantifies uncertainty in the 256-rollout reference values: their Bernoulli sample-mean variance is at most approximately 0.001. The reference sample count is unchanged, and both versions average accuracy over 16 evaluation rounds with different random seeds; no increase in repeated runs is established.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial comparator and diagnostic results. For DeepSeekMath on MATH, Figure 4 newly reports RLOO at 36.8% and GRPO at 36.4%, alongside unchanged PPO and VinePPO scores of 42.8% and 46.0%. It also adds rollout-count timing and case-study outcomes. Figure 5 revises the RhoMath/MATH train-versus-test trace from v1 Figure C.4 without explaining the revision; this should not be interpreted as a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Both versions replace PPO's critic with Monte Carlo value estimates, compute stepwise advantages, and assign each reasoning step's advantage to its tokens. Auxiliary rollouts remain excluded from direct policy training. Section 4 is clarified and rewritten without changing the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method explanation, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized around performance, efficiency, generalization, and rollout count; KL and temperature discussions move to the appendix, while the existing generalization analysis moves into the main text. An impact statement is added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, comparison plots gain additional methods, diagnostic panels are split or recombined, and numerous existing figures move between the main text and appendices. New diagnostic plots, a baseline hyperparameter table, and illustrated case studies further change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Chang et al., Chu et al., DeepSeek-R1, and Agent Q, while removing several earlier introductory and discussion references. It more explicitly positions the work against methods without stepwise credit assignment and adds the generalization-scaling novelty claim. The established relationships to Vine-TRPO, MCTS, and process supervision remain.

T1.justification: Appendix C.5 adds mathematical definitions of GRPO and RLOO advantages and reasoning about baseline dependence and gradient bias. Section 7 adds the Bernoulli variance calculation. The original MDP formulation, PPO/GAE equations, VinePPO estimator, and unbiasedness claim remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 discussed critic-free RL alternatives without testing them, leaving an important comparative gap. v2 directly evaluates RLOO and GRPO and adds critic-training diagnostics and rollout-count efficiency analysis, substantially strengthening the evidence for VinePPO's practical advantages. Additional implementation details improve reproducibility. The stronger claim about scaling generalization slope is less directly demonstrated than the accuracy and runtime findings, but the improved comparative evidence provides a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VinePPO research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and relocation of material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and reports additional RLOO/GRPO comparisons, critic diagnostics, rollout-count timing results, and credit-assignment examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original MATH and GSM8K experiments with RhoMath 1.1B and DeepSeekMath 7B, including benchmark results, ablations, timing measurements, and value-prediction analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are expected to be predictable and trustworthy
to support reliable decision-making systems. Yet current LLMs often show
inconsistencies in their judgments. In this work, we examine logical preference
consistency as a foundational requirement for building more dependable LLM
systems, ensuring stable and coherent decision-making while minimizing erratic
or contradictory outputs. To quantify the logical preference consistency, we
propose a universal evaluation framework based on three fundamental properties:
transitivity, commutativity and negation invariance. Through extensive
experimentation across diverse LLMs, we demonstrate that these properties serve
as strong indicators of judgment robustness. Furthermore, we introduce a data
refinement and augmentation technique, REPAIR, that enhances logical
consistency while maintaining alignment with human preferences. Finally, we
show that improving consistency leads to better performance in LLM-driven
logic-based algorithms, reinforcing stability and coherence in decision-making
systems.

Yinhong Liu, Zhijiang Guo, Tianya Liang, Ehsan Shareghi, Ivan Vuli\'c,
  Nigel Collier

Aligning with Logic: Measuring, Evaluating and Improving Logical
  Preference Consistency in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction refocus broad logical-consistency and overall-robustness claims on logical preference consistency and judgment robustness. The four principal contributions, alignment-preservation claim and downstream-performance claim remain; the conclusion still uses broader reliability language.

C2.justification: Appendices H, M and N add substantive guidance on choosing K, attribute alignment losses after downsampling to information loss, and discuss aggregation limitations involving indirect comparisons, ordering and ties. Section 3.3 also changes the interpretation of transitivity from a proxy for global reliability to one for local robustness.

D1.justification: Appendix G supplies previously missing NovelEval, CaTeRS and instruction-tuning prompt templates, plus explicit metric-computation instructions. Appendix B documents MS MARCO preparation and label provenance. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the existing LoRA settings, hardware description and ANONYMOUS code/data placeholder remain.

E1.justification: Appendices B and L add MS MARCO query–passage data for REPAIR training and evaluation, extending the intervention beyond summarization. Document reranking was already represented by NovelEval, and all original datasets and tasks remain.

E2.justification: v1 mentions Elo and Bradley-Terry as possible alternatives; v3 actually compares both against win-loss aggregation in Table 7. The original LLM comparator roster remains; Deepseek-chat-v2 clarifies the model already associated with the DeepSeek-v2 citation.

E3.justification: v3 adds training-data-size controls, a subgraph-size sweep and an MS MARCO protocol using 800 training and 200 test examples with ten retrieved candidates and GPT-3.5-derived rankings. Figure 7 also revises the existing SummEval prompt to require only A or B; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to subgraph size K (Appendix H), whether consistency gains persist after matching training-set sizes (Appendix M), and dependence on the ranking estimator (Appendix N). These address methodological questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Appendix I adds a binomial/normal-approximation sample-size argument at 95% confidence for the existing M=1000 sampling cap, although the numerical error margin is unspecified. The existing ten CoT samples, 100 PairS runs and correlation significance reporting remain unchanged; no new empirical uncertainty estimates are provided.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–5 retain their values. v3 adds substantial results in Tables 5–7 and Figure 9: for example, Table 5 reports MS MARCO transitivity of 86.7 versus 91.3 and PairS scores of 58.1 versus 61.0 for perturbed versus REPAIR training. v1's reported correlations below 0.05 between transitivity and human accuracy are removed.

M1.justification: The original win-loss aggregation, pairwise extrapolation and negated-relation augmentation pipeline remains, now named REPAIR. Appendix N adds evaluated variants substituting Elo or Bradley-Terry for win-loss aggregation, a limited adaptation of one component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion and several main-text passages are substantially condensed or rewritten, with revised preference-consistency terminology and REPAIR naming throughout. The original Section 4 motivation moves to Appendix K, the downstream subsection is consolidated, and the appendix organization expands considerably.

P2.justification: The main text and bibliography change from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Figure 7 expands into a three-task prompt grid, and v3 adds Figures 8–9 and Tables 5–7.

R1.justification: Appendix E adds a focused distinction from social-network clustering, triad census and E-I measures with supporting citations. Additional references support sampling theory, Elo and MS MARCO, while some instruction-tuning background references disappear. The main positioning against factual-knowledge and NLI consistency research remains.

T1.justification: v3 adds the sample-size reasoning in Equation 4, explicitly discusses the irreflexive assumption in Appendix J, and supplies analytical examples of ranking-rule limitations in Appendix N. The original consistency definitions and graph algorithms remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked a control for increased training-data volume and assessed downstream benefits by comparing different pretrained models. v3's size-matched ablation (Table 6) and training-to-downstream experiment (Table 5) address these important validation gaps, while sensitivity tests and fuller prompts strengthen assessment and reproducibility. The gains remain qualified by GPT-derived MS MARCO labels and unexplained baseline differences between Table 3 and Tables 6–7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same consistency metrics and ranking-based data refinement framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title and formatting.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds MS MARCO experiments, size-matched training comparisons, ranking-estimator comparisons and a subgraph-size sensitivity analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM evaluations, instruction-tuning experiments and downstream ranking results in Tables 1–4 and Figures 4–5.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can be misused to spread unwanted content at scale. Content watermarking deters misuse by hiding messages in content, enabling its detection using a secret watermarking key. Robustness is a core security property, stating that evading detection requires (significant) degradation of the content's quality. Many LLM watermarking methods have been proposed, but robustness is tested only against non-adaptive attackers who lack knowledge of the watermarking method and can find only suboptimal attacks. We formulate watermark robustness as an objective function and use preference-based optimization to tune adaptive attacks against the specific watermarking method. Our evaluation shows that (i) adaptive attacks evade detection against all surveyed watermarks, (ii) training against any watermark succeeds in evading unseen watermarks, and (iii) optimization-based attacks are cost-effective. Our findings underscore the need to test robustness against adaptively tuned attacks. We release our adaptively optimized paraphrasers at https://github.com/nilslukas/ada-wm-evasion.
arxiv_record.authors: Abdulrahman Diaa, Toluwani Aremu, Nils Lukas
arxiv_record.comments: To appear at the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML'25)

C1.justification: The central claim of inexpensive, transferable adaptive evasion remains. v2's contribution statement qualifies broad superiority as Pareto optimality above 90% evasion, explicitly acknowledging GPT-4o's quality advantage on some Pareto fronts. It also emphasizes success under the more restrictive no-box threat model and adds public paraphraser release as a contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving token-sequence avoidance, lexical substitutions, and learned edit distance, plus an interpretation of shorter outputs as a consequence of not penalizing brevity. It explicitly acknowledges imperfect alignment between LLM judges and human judgment and discusses restrictions of closed-model attacks. These substantially expand v1's mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 296-prompt evaluation set and its non-overlap with the retained 1,000-prompt training set, the MarkLLM implementation, and the GPT-4o version used. It changes a promised code/model release to a reported paraphraser release at a new repository location. The original hardware, prompting, optimizer, and LoRA details remain.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Exp, Dist-Shift, Binary, and Inverse. v2 adds SynthID, Unigram, and SIR evaluations, including training against Unigram, substantially expanding the watermark-generation conditions tested. KGW corresponds to the retained Dist-Shift scheme. The underlying task remains text generation and paraphrasing.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o as an evaluated paraphrasing comparator in Figure 7 and the subsequent text analyses; v1's closed-model comparator was GPT3.5. The original DIPPER, translation, word-perturbation, and open-model baseline families remain, so this is a limited extension of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The added appendix evaluation uses a 256-token limit and GPT-4o-mini as quality judge, while the original evaluation retains its existing settings and Llama3-8B judge. Appendix A.7 additionally evaluates n-gram overlap and normalized token edit distance. These are new evaluation protocols, not demonstrated changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices A.5–A.7 add distributions of text lengths, quality scores, and watermark scores, top-50-token comparisons, and n-gram/edit-distance analyses investigating attack behavior. The original model-size, adaptivity, FPR, watermark-bias, and example-based analyses remain; moving the FPR and bias studies into the appendix does not remove them.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 2 identifies its shaded bands as one standard deviation; v2 retains the bands but removes that explanation. The 95% confidence-interval description remains for the Qwen repetition experiment, moved from Figure 7 to Figure 6. No new repeated-run counts, seed reporting, or significance-testing procedures are documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Figures 7 and 9–15, including watermark-specific GPT-4o trade-offs and lower n-gram overlap after optimization. Figure 7 retains GPT-4o on the SIR and KGW Pareto fronts. Original results such as Figure 3 and the quality table remain numerically unchanged. However, v2 Table 4 retains v1 Table 3's values while reversing their quality/evasion labels, creating inconsistent metric assignments.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains surrogate-key generation, repeated paraphrasing, quality-and-detection filtering, preference pairing, and DPO optimization. The revised pseudocode is equivalent. Training a Qwen2.5-3b paraphraser against Unigram applies the existing procedure to another watermark without introducing a method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, threat model, and discussion are extensively revised. Related Work moves before the method, contributions become integrated introductory prose, and the FPR and bias discussions move into a substantially reorganized appendix. The title is shortened and terminology is standardized throughout.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column proceedings layout. v2 adds a workflow schematic and multiple analytical figures, resizes and relocates retained plots, changes Table 2 from stacked examples to three columns, and splits the bias table's paired values into labeled subcolumns. These are substantial visual and display changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantively positions the work against Jovanovic and Pang's sample-dependent attacks and Zhang's impossibility/random-walk setting, emphasizing inexpensive no-box optimization. It also adds references for SynthID, Unigram, SIR, MarkLLM, and AutoPrompt, while removing Nicks and Uchida citations. The revised distinctions materially expand the account of how this work differs from prior research.

T1.justification: Section 3 changes the stated attacker assumption from black-box API access to no-box access without provider watermarked training samples. Appendix A.7 introduces mathematical definitions for the newly evaluated overlap and edit-distance ratios. The original robustness inequality and optimization objective retain their substance, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's four-watermark evaluation through three additional watermark schemes, GPT-4o comparisons, a different quality judge, and direct textual analyses in Appendices A.4–A.7. Clearer training/evaluation documentation and explicit judge limitations also improve assessability. New reporting defects, including reversed Table 4 headings, conflicting overlap definitions in Equation 3 and Figure 15, and Figure 13's caption/legend mismatch, weaken specific details. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and deeper analysis provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-optimized watermark-evasion study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, and the original algorithm and experiments can be matched across the restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds watermark evaluations, GPT-4o comparisons, and analyses of paraphrased text in Appendices A.4–A.7.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-training experiments, evasion and text-quality measurements, ablations, and generated-text examples in Section 5 and the appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Customized Image Generation, generating customized images with user-specified concepts, has raised significant attention due to its creativity and novelty. With impressive progress achieved in subject customization, some pioneer works further explored the customization of action and interaction beyond entity (i.e., human, animal, and object) appearance. However, these approaches only focus on basic actions and interactions between two entities, and their effects are limited by insufficient ''exactly same'' reference images. To extend customized image generation to more complex scenes for general real-world applications, we propose a new task: event-customized image generation. Given a single reference image, we define the ''event'' as all specific actions, poses, relations, or interactions between different entities in the scene. This task aims at accurately capturing the complex event and generating customized images with various target entities. To solve this task, we proposed a novel training-free event customization method: FreeEvent. Specifically, FreeEvent introduces two extra paths alongside the general diffusion denoising process: 1) Entity switching path: it applies cross-attention guidance and regulation for target entity generation. 2) Event transferring path: it injects the spatial feature and self-attention maps from the reference image to the target image for event generation. To further facilitate this new task, we collected two evaluation benchmarks: SWiG-Event and Real-Event. Extensive experiments and ablations have demonstrated the effectiveness of FreeEvent.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhen Wang, Yilei Jiang, Dong Zheng, Jun Xiao, Long Chen
arxiv_record.title: Event-Customized Image Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: single-reference event customization, the training-free FreeEvent framework, compatibility with subject customization, two benchmarks and strong comparative performance. The added experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly explains how large reference-to-target shape differences create a trade-off between event fidelity and entity appearance, with a tuning remedy. Appendix E qualifies event-subject customization as a secondary capability and acknowledges differing comparison settings. The original limitations concerning small or numerous entities and Stable Diffusion capabilities are retained in Appendix G.

D1.justification: The default implementation settings in Appendix A remain unchanged. v2 additionally documents attribute-to-mask handling and an explicit alternative schedule in Figure 10: guidance increases from 10 to 15 steps, spatial injection decreases from 50 to 30, and self-attention injection decreases from 25 to 15. These are reproducible settings for the added case study, not revised defaults.

E1.justification: Both versions retain SWiG-Event with 5,000 samples and Real-Event with 30 reference images. v2 modestly extends generation requirements through explicit attribute-control tests, including color and material, and subject-customization examples using personalized background concepts. The increased user-study trial count does not establish a new dataset.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds MIGC alongside ControlNet and BoxDiff on SWiG-Event. Appendix E and Figure 9 introduce evaluated comparisons against AnyDoor, PhotoSwap and MS-Diffusion for event-subject customization, substantially broadening the comparison methods. The original six Real-Event baselines remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 expands retrieval evaluation with GSRTR verb-detection accuracy, CLIP-I, DreamSim, DINO, CLIP-T and FID. The user study changes from 30 trials requiring three selections to 50 trials allowing one to three selections. The subject-customization demonstration switches from DreamBooth to Break-A-Scene, and Appendix F introduces a separate experiment with altered guidance and injection schedules.

E4.justification: The original qualitative path and prompt ablations remain. v2 adds quantitative component-removal ablations on Real-Event in Table 3, attribute-control examples in Figure 8, expanded subject-customization investigations, and a shape-mismatch case study comparing guidance and injection schedules in Figure 10. These substantially broaden the analysis of component effectiveness and practical behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both present point scores and human-judgment counts; the revised number of user-study trials changes evaluation design rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 retrieval values are retained, including FreeEvent's 41.12/63.02/72.74. v2 adds MIGC results and additional metrics, including FreeEvent's 34.10 top-1 verb accuracy and 29.05 FID, plus quantitative ablations and new qualitative outcomes. Table 2 replaces the human-judgment counts under the revised protocol, including FreeEvent's 30 becoming 50; these counts have different trial denominators.

M1.justification: The core two-path FreeEvent procedure and Equations (1)–(6) remain unchanged. Appendix D adds a limited attribute-control adaptation: cross-attention guidance and regulation are applied to attribute words using the masks of their corresponding entities.

P1.justification: v2 shortens the abstract, revises the evaluation narrative and expands the appendix organization. Limitations move from the conclusion to Appendix G, the societal-impact paragraph becomes an Impact Statement, and acknowledgements are added. arxiv_record.abstract: LLM watermarks stand out as a promising way to attribute ownership of LLM-generated text. One threat to watermark credibility comes from spoofing attacks, where an unauthorized third party forges the watermark, enabling it to falsely attribute arbitrary texts to a particular LLM. Despite recent work demonstrating that state-of-the-art schemes are, in fact, vulnerable to spoofing, no prior work has focused on post-hoc methods to discover spoofing attempts. In this work, we for the first time propose a reliable statistical method to distinguish spoofed from genuinely watermarked text, suggesting that current spoofing attacks are less effective than previously thought. In particular, we show that regardless of their underlying approach, all current learning-based spoofing methods consistently leave observable artifacts in spoofed texts, indicative of watermark forgery. We build upon these findings to propose rigorous statistical tests that reliably reveal the presence of such artifacts and thus demonstrate that a watermark has been spoofed. Our experimental evaluation shows high test power across all learning-based spoofing methods, providing insights into their fundamental limitations and suggesting a way to mitigate this threat. We make all our code available at https://github.com/eth-sri/watermark-spoofing-detection .

arxiv_record.title: Discovering Spoofing Attempts on Language Model Watermarks

The abstract and conclusion also explicitly qualify the previously broader 'all current spoofing methods' language as learning-based attacks.

C2.justification: Appendices D–F add substantive interpretations of reference-data mismatch, attacker data scaling, and why reprompting is preferable to fixed calibration. v2 also acknowledges AAR false-positive inflation, explicitly identifies short input length as a limitation, and expands discussion of edited text, piggyback spoofing, and watermark security trade-offs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and specifies previously unstated attacker training-data sizes: 30,000 samples of 800 tokens for Stealing and 640,000 samples of 256 tokens for Distillation. New appendices document additional experimental parameters. The training-size disclosures do not establish changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds Wikipedia, Repliqa, and Math as reference corpora and OpenWebText for fixed-corpus calibration. It also evaluates new input scenarios involving AAR/KTH watermarks, insertion of human text, and DIPPER paraphrasing (Appendices D, F–H). C4 and Dolly coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Appendix F.2 newly evaluates a fixed-corpus correlation estimator as an alternative to Reprompting. The principal evaluated spoofing methods remain Stealing and Distillation; extending Distillation evaluation to AAR/KTH does not introduce another attack comparator.

E3.justification: The original Section 5 setup is retained, but substantial new protocols are added: LLAMA3-8B/QWEN2.5-7B model configurations, attacker training-size sweeps, perturbed reference counts, fixed-corpus calibration, and AAR/KTH settings. Edited-text experiments specify insertion proportions and separate sample counts for mixing and paraphrasing (Appendices A.5, D–H).

E4.justification: New analyses test sensitivity to reference-corpus mismatch and attacker training size, the effect of estimating prompts, and the necessity of reprompting versus fixed calibration. Additional robustness experiments examine another model pair and false positives after text insertion or paraphrasing. The original concatenation and context-dependence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.1 and Figure 2 supplement v1's visual normality assessment with Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Pearson normality tests, reporting p-values and rejection decisions. Figure 9 adds distributional boxplots with explicitly defined whiskers. Neither version reports repeated-seed uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–5 are retained in v2 Tables 1, 5, 2, 3, and 4, respectively. Substantial new results appear in Figures 6 and 9–15. For example, Appendix G reports about 90% AAR detection with 500 tokens at nominal 1% rejection, accompanied by approximately 2% empirical false positives. These results concern newly evaluated conditions.

M1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix G extend the detector beyond binary Red-Green colors. AAR uses negative-log watermark scores; KTH introduces Levenshtein alignment costs and a surrogate context of h = 5. These are substantive scheme-specific scoring adaptations, while the original Standard and Reprompting procedures remain.

P1.justification: v2 changes the title, rewrites substantial introductory material, combines background and related work in Section 2, and moves the spoofer-model study from Section 5.3 to Appendix A.4. The appendices are extensively reorganized, and impact and acknowledgment sections replace the earlier document's closing structure.

P2.justification: The main paper changes to a two-column layout with resized and relocated displays. The spoofer-model table and figure move to Appendix A, eight new figures are added, and Figure 2 gains p-values and colored normality-test indicators. The five original tables remain, with renumbering and layout adjustments.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and Appendix J substantially expand research positioning around learning-based, piggyback, and step-by-step spoofing, deployed watermarks, and cryptographic defenses. New citations include Aaronson, Dathathri et al., Christ and Gunn, and recent watermark-identification work. Existing publication-year and venue updates are separate from these substantive additions.

T1.justification: v2 adds a general mathematical representation of watermark transformations and nonbinary score definitions for AAR/KTH. Lemma 4.1, its assumptions, and its proof remain unchanged, moving from Appendix D to Appendix I. No corresponding generalized proof accompanies the new extensions.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens practical validation by testing assumptions that v1 left largely unchecked: reference-corpus mismatch, prompt estimation, fixed calibration, and modifications to genuine text. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, despite the changed title and publication format. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds experiments on reference-corpus mismatch, attacker training size, reprompting alternatives, additional watermark schemes, and modified watermarked text.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on generated and spoofed text, including false-positive rates, detection power, model comparisons, and validation analyses in Sections 5 and Appendices A–C.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is challenging because distribution shifts come in many forms. Numerous algorithms exist to address specific settings, but choosing the right training algorithm for the right dataset without trial and error is difficult. Indeed, real-world applications often involve multiple types and combinations of shifts that are hard to analyze theoretically.
  Method. This work explores the possibility of learning the selection of a training algorithm for OOD generalization. We propose a proof of concept (OOD-Chameleon) that formulates the selection as a multi-label classification over candidate algorithms, trained on a dataset of datasets representing a variety of shifts. We evaluate the ability of OOD-Chameleon to rank algorithms on unseen shifts and datasets based only on dataset characteristics, i.e., without training models first, unlike traditional model selection.
  Findings. Extensive experiments show that the learned selector identifies high-performing algorithms across synthetic, vision, and language tasks. Further inspection shows that it learns non-trivial decision rules, which provide new insights into the applicability of existing algorithms. Overall, this new approach opens the possibility of better exploiting and understanding the plethora of existing algorithms for OOD generalization.
arxiv_record.authors: Liangze Jiang, Damien Teney
arxiv_record.title: OOD-Chameleon: Is Algorithm Selection for OOD Generalization Learnable?
