C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from VIRT with cognitive-science-inspired RIP and robotic gaze to VIP pre-training using sparse flows and progressive masking. The vision-over-text claim remains but is framed around current robotic-data diversity. v1's abstract claim of improving success from nearly zero to over 65% is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations concerning reliance on privileged flow information, pre-training/inference mismatch and world-model prediction failure. It attributes harmful small-data pre-training to domain overfitting and identifies Gaussian noise as the strongest tested disturbance. Baseline explanations also change: Diffusion Policy's data demands and VIRT's encoder representation replace much of v1's feature-compression and ambiguity discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies 120K pre-training and 8K fine-tuning iterations, a 20-step horizon, 0.5 image-masking ratio, YOLOv10-small, and CoTracker sampling/filtering and masking procedures. Previously unstated budgets are disclosures, not established budget changes. Conversely, v1's stage-supervision, detector-freezing and appendix completion-step details are no longer provided.

E1.justification: Droid and the six real-robot/simulation tasks remain. v2 adds unseen brightness, Gaussian-noise and image-blur conditions on the simulated tasks (Section 4.3, Table 5), extending input-environment coverage without adding a dataset or core manipulation task.

E2.justification: ConvMLP, Diffusion Policy and ACT remain the external policy families. v2 Table 1 adds VIP-pretrained counterparts and no longer separately reports single-step ConvMLP. Table 2 also introduces a world-model-generated future-image instruction comparator. The evaluated alternatives change, but the main policy families remain stable.

E3.justification: v1 supplies CLIP-encoded text to comparison policies for instruction-following tasks; v2 supplies cropped-image instructions to every policy and evaluates each with and without VIP pre-training. Completion-score evaluation disappears. New protocols vary training-data fractions and introduce visual corruptions. Demonstration counts and 100 evaluation trials per policy/task remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's RG/enlargement/RIP/uncertainty ablation is replaced by instruction-source and backbone/uncertainty/image-mask studies on the three simulated tasks. v2 additionally studies data scaling, visual-corruption robustness, attention maps and world-model failures (Tables 2–5; Figures 1, 4 and 9). The original Open the Lid component ablation is absent.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 evaluation trials per policy/task without training-seed information, confidence intervals or significance tests. Predicted Laplacian uncertainty concerns the model's loss and outputs, not statistical uncertainty reporting for experimental performance.

E6.justification: VIRT's reported Transport/Stack success rates change from 0.69/0.65 in v1 Table 2 to 0.74/0.68 in v2 Table 1; its three real-task rates remain 0.42/0.71/0.37. Many baseline scores are replaced, completion-score entries disappear, and new instruction, scaling and robustness outcomes are reported. Changed methods and settings prevent interpreting these as controlled cross-version gains.

M1.justification: v1's RIP predicts trajectories from endpoint observations using L1 loss. v2's VIP adds CoTracker-derived sparse motion flows, an MLP flow encoder and progressive flow masking, and applies uncertainty-weighted supervision during pre-training. VIRT also gains random image masking. These change the procedure despite retaining the 12-encoder/3-decoder architecture and cropped-object instructions.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around VIP. Method subsections are reorganized, experimental setup becomes introductory paragraphs, and the evaluation narrative shifts toward pre-training effectiveness and instruction comparisons. Related work is condensed and the completion-score appendix is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts two columns, replaces the opening schematic with attention maps, redraws the pipeline and adds flow, world-model and disturbance figures. Existing platform/task figures are resized and rearranged. Real and simulated results are merged into a redesigned table, with additional analysis tables. An erroneous ICML formatting-instructions running header also appears.

R1.justification: v2 removes motor-imagery, gaze-anchoring and foveal-vision references supporting RIP/RG, while adding CoTracker, diffusion-image-generation and uncertainty references. The three related-work themes and principal positioning against text-conditioned robotic manipulation remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: v1's explicit MDP/demonstration-data formalization in Section 3.1 and completion-score definition i/k in Section 4.2 are removed. The Laplacian-loss formula is essentially retained, although its training role changes. Neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's main comparisons confound policy differences with different instruction modalities. v2 gives every policy cropped-image instructions and adds within-policy pre-training controls (Table 1), while Table 2 compares instruction choices within VIRT. This substantially strengthens evidence for the central claims; scaling and robustness studies also expose failure conditions. Partial-completion reporting is lost, and the DINOv2 ablation changes backbone architecture as well as initialization, but these limitations do not outweigh the improved experimental controls.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe successive versions of the same robotic-manipulation work. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. v1 includes Appendix A.1; v2 ends with references and contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 Tables 1–5 report original manipulation results, pre-training comparisons, instruction studies, ablations, data-scaling experiments and robustness tests.

before.justification: v1 Tables 1–3 report original real-robot and simulated manipulation results, including policy comparisons and component ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: The hierarchical structure inherent in many real-world datasets makes the modeling of such hierarchies a crucial objective in both unsupervised and supervised machine learning. While recent advancements have introduced deep architectures specifically designed for hierarchical clustering, we adopt a critical perspective on this line of research. Our findings reveal that these methods face significant limitations in scalability and performance when applied to realistic datasets. Given these findings, we present an alternative approach and introduce a lightweight method that builds on pre-trained non-hierarchical clustering models. Remarkably, our approach outperforms specialized deep models for hierarchical clustering, and it is broadly applicable to any pre-trained clustering model that outputs logits, without requiring any fine-tuning. To highlight the generality of our approach, we extend its application to a supervised setting, demonstrating its ability to recover meaningful hierarchies from a pre-trained ImageNet classifier. Our results establish a practical and effective alternative to existing deep hierarchical clustering methods, with significant advantages in efficiency, scalability and performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Emanuele Palumbo, Moritz Vandenhirtz, Alain Ryser, Imant Daunhawer, Julia E. Vogt
arxiv_record.title: From Logits to Hierarchies: Hierarchical Clustering made Simple

C1.justification: Both versions claim that logits-only L2H efficiently constructs hierarchies without fine-tuning, outperforms specialized hierarchical models, and supports interpretation of supervised classifiers. V2 foregrounds the critique more strongly but preserves these contributions. Its under-a-minute runtime wording was already stated in v1 Appendix A and supported by Table 2.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations concerning generality across backbones, robustness to misspecified K, normalized training loss as guidance for choosing K, and benefits of predicting at coarser taxonomy levels. The conclusion also introduces a concrete limitation: poorly calibrated logits may invalidate their use as a cluster-similarity proxy. These materially expand the applicability and limitations discussion beyond v1.

D1.justification: V2 documents the added taxonomy-level training and hierarchy-cutting procedure, the K sensitivity grid, and iTOL as the visualization tool. The existing implementation and baseline details remain largely unchanged. V1's separate statement advertising supplementary code disappears, although the complete Appendix A implementation is retained; this does not establish that external code availability changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds iNaturalist21, with 2.7 million natural-species images and evaluation across family, order, class, phylum, and kingdom labels. This substantially extends coverage to a taxonomy-based task testing predictions at multiple granularities. The four datasets used in v1 remain; ImageNet itself is not newly introduced.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparators remain. Appendix C adds the Lowe et al. (2024) UMAP-plus-Ward comparator, CLIP-based agglomerative and TreeVAE comparison variants, and separately trained flat TURTLE models for the taxonomy-level comparison (Tables 5, 6, and 8). These substantially broaden the alternatives evaluated against L2H.

E3.justification: The original benchmark splits and six evaluation metrics are retained. Added experimental designs include CLIP-input controls, fitting and evaluating the Lowe comparator on the test set, varying K from 85 to 115, and comparing a family-level hierarchy with separately trained models at coarser taxonomic levels. These are substantive new protocols, without evidence that the original experiments changed their settings.

E4.justification: V1's hierarchy visualizations and case studies are retained. V2 adds tests of dependence on foundation-model backbones using TCL, aggregation-function choice, sensitivity to over- and underestimated K, an alternative all-pairs merging strategy, and the benefit of hierarchical predictions over separately trained flat models (Tables 4 and 7-9; Figure 5). These address several previously untested assumptions and design choices.

E5.justification: V1 reports five-run comparison means and three-run runtime means without variability estimates. V2 adds runtime standard deviations over the same stated three runs, five-run standard-deviation bands in Figure 5, and statistical-indistinguishability markings in Table 8. However, Table 1 loses its five-run disclosure, and Table 8 specifies neither the statistical test nor its threshold. The change concerns reporting practices, not an established increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises values, including Food-101 leaf purity from 0.881 to 0.913 for L2H-TEMI and from 0.843 to 0.877 for L2H-TURTLE; Table 2 also revises runtimes. Tables 3-9 and Figure 5 add extensive results. The new iNaturalist findings are mixed: kingdom accuracy favors L2H-TURTLE, 0.734 versus 0.663, while class-level leaf purity favors standalone TURTLE, 0.827 versus 0.797.

M1.justification: The standard L2H procedure and Appendix A implementation remain unchanged. However, Appendix C introduces an alternative merging procedure that searches all group pairs instead of first selecting the lowest-scoring group (Table 9). This is a limited algorithmic variant evaluated as an ablation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting, with the critique of specialized models foregrounded and the contribution bullets reordered. Method explanations are repaired and clarified, and the end matter gains acknowledgements and an impact statement while losing the standalone reproducibility statement. These are broad language and narrative revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout, with reformatted tables and repositioned figures. V2 adds Tables 3-9 and the multipanel sensitivity plot, enlarges retained appendix hierarchies, and stacks the final ImageNet visualizations vertically. Existing tree results are retained under new numbering, and their ImageNet captions are corrected.

R1.justification: V2 adds relevant citations for unseen-dataset clustering, hierarchical and hyperbolic representations, TCL, iNaturalist21, and iTOL, including Lowe, Khrulkov, Linderman, and Sinha. The central positioning against specialized deep hierarchical clustering remains. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 corrects both pair-set definitions from the impossible condition x_j != x_j to x_i != x_j. This repairs a mathematical error in the written definitions underlying DP and LHD. The remaining mathematical formulation is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens weaknesses in v1's empirical support through CLIP-based comparison controls, a non-foundation-model backbone, and tests of aggregation, merging, and cluster-count choices. The iNaturalist experiment also directly examines the benefit of hierarchical predictions over separate flat models. Added variability reporting and the calibration limitation improve assessment of the evidence. Unspecified statistical tests in Table 8 and the lost Table 1 run-count disclosure are drawbacks, but the stronger controls and analyses provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same L2H research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A-C support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across layout changes and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds quantitative ImageNet results, iNaturalist21 experiments, additional comparisons, and ablations in Appendix C.

before.justification: V1 reports original clustering evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Food-101, runtime measurements, and an ImageNet hierarchy case study.

arxiv_record.abstract: DNA-Encoded Libraries (DELs) represent a transformative technology in drug discovery, facilitating the high-throughput exploration of vast chemical spaces. Despite their potential, the scarcity of publicly available DEL datasets presents a bottleneck for the advancement of machine learning methodologies in this domain. To address this gap, we introduce KinDEL, one of the largest publicly accessible DEL datasets and the first one that includes binding poses from molecular docking experiments. C1.justification: V2's abstract adds the claim that KinDEL is the first public DEL dataset containing molecular docking poses and frames its contribution as encompassing both 2D and 3D structures. This expands the central resource claim beyond v1. The conclusion also qualifies the earlier drug-like characterization to many molecules having properties within approved-drug ranges.

C2.justification: V2 interprets cluster splits as offering limited additional difficulty, tentatively associates MAPK14 disynthon degradation with overfitting, and explains objections to scaffold splitting. It adds qualifications about preselection-normalization errors and kinase-only coverage while retaining the principal denoising interpretation and existing applicability limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds Chemprop hyperparameters, clustering configuration and GPU/runtime information, BCA preparation and assay protocols, and detailed docking software, conformer, receptor and SDF specifications. It newly discloses sequencing depths and the cloning kit and corrects DDR1 gene labels. The existing repository link remains available in the text.

E1.justification: V2 extends experimental coverage beyond two kinases by adding Bovine Carbonic Anhydrase screening with replicate analysis (Section 4; Figure 7c). Appendix F also reports docking 234k ligand states against six kinase receptor models. The tabulated machine-learning affinity benchmarks still concern MAPK14 and DDR1.

E2.justification: Tables 1-2 newly evaluate Chemprop DMPNN against the existing methods, including within the retained random and disynthon comparisons. Counts, Poisson, RF, XGBoost, kNN, DNN, GIN and both DEL-Compose variants remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds a third evaluation split based on UMAP-reduced fingerprints, HDBSCAN clustering and whole-cluster assignment (Section 3.1; Appendix E). Appendix F introduces a specified multi-receptor docking protocol. The original top-1M training selection, random/disynthon protocols, affinity test-set sizes and Spearman metric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds cluster-split generalization comparisons and an empirical scaffold-frequency analysis assessing the suitability of scaffold splitting (Appendix E; Figure 9). It also adds held-out affinity distributions, BCA replicate diagnostics and qualitative docking cases (Figures 7-10), substantially extending v1's supplementary analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five training runs per splitting strategy, report performance with ± values, and use triplicate DEL measurements. V2 extends these practices to additional results without introducing a new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or changed run count for retained experiments.

E6.justification: All 28 pre-existing model/split rows in Tables 1-2 retain their numerical values. V2 adds Chemprop and cluster-split results, including MAPK14 cluster on-DNA correlation 0.713 ± 0.013 for Chemprop and off-DNA correlation 0.766 ± 0.012 for DEL-Compose(S). BCA replicate plots, scaffold statistics, affinity distributions and docking examples add further findings.

M1.justification: The retained predictive architectures, objectives and DEL-Compose variants remain unchanged in Section 3.2 and Appendix D. Chemprop is an added comparator; the new splitting and docking procedures extend evaluation and data generation without modifying these predictors.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract and expands selected dataset, evaluation and discussion passages while retaining the main section order and much existing prose. It updates authorship, adds an Impact Statement and Appendices E-F, and removes the standalone Reproducibility Statement while retaining the repository reference elsewhere.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column conference layout. V2 redraws synthesis/selection graphics, adds a data-schema panel, separates the UMAP and splitting diagrams, and expands the benchmark tables. New appendix displays include BCA replicates, affinity histograms, scaffold structures and docking poses.

R1.justification: Section 5.1 adds AIRCHECK (Wellnitz et al., 2024), contrasting its masked structures with KinDEL's representation. Additional citations support Chemprop, clustering and docking, and the abstract adds docking-related novelty positioning. The established related-work discussion remains largely intact.

T1.justification: No new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are introduced. The fluorescence-polarization and binding-curve equations in Appendix A remain mathematically equivalent; the new clustering and docking descriptions specify procedures rather than theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens KinDEL's usefulness and reproducibility through a non-kinase screen with replicate diagnostics, documented 3D pose generation, and explicit implementation details. arxiv_record.abstract: Evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) is very expensive, due to high computational cost and the wide variety of tasks. The good news is that if we already have some observed performance scores, we may be able to infer unknown ones. In this study, we propose a new framework for predicting unknown performance scores based on observed ones from other LVLMs or tasks. We first formulate the performance prediction as a matrix completion task. Specifically, we construct a sparse performance matrix $\boldsymbol{R}$, where each entry $R_{mn}$ represents the performance score of the $m$-th model on the $n$-th dataset. By applying probabilistic matrix factorization (PMF) with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we can complete the performance matrix, i.e., predict unknown scores. Additionally, we estimate the uncertainty of performance prediction based on MCMC. Practitioners can evaluate their models on untested tasks with higher uncertainty first, which quickly reduces the prediction errors. We further introduce several improvements to enhance PMF for scenarios with sparse observed performance scores. Our experiments demonstrate the accuracy of PMF in predicting unknown scores, the reliability of uncertainty estimates in ordering evaluations, and the effectiveness of our enhancements for handling sparse data.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—performance prediction through PMF, uncertainty-based active evaluation and sparse-data enhancements—are retained. v2's introduction additionally claims demonstrated generalization through expanding the matrix to new models and datasets, modestly broadening the stated contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations based on benchmark redundancy, shared architectures/training data, and differences between transfer to new models and new datasets. It interprets coreset and PMF predictions as complementary. The conclusion drops v1's cautions about uninformative high-uncertainty evaluations and identifying needed benchmarks; the existing zero-observation limitation is retained and promoted to the conclusion.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information with DMF/GCMC training configurations, exact prompts and decoding settings, coreset embedding/selection details, A100 timing measurements, additional model checkpoints, and new dataset counts and access links. These largely document added experiments rather than establish changes to existing implementations. The project's code-access information is retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark coverage and adds MathVision, EMMA, Video-MME and LongVideoBench, expanding mathematical/multimodal reasoning and video evaluation, including long-video understanding. Section 5.2 also introduces corrupted-image testing. These extend the represented tasks and input conditions beyond the original matrix.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's mean-based prediction baselines, v2 Table 10 evaluates Deep Matrix Factorization and Graph Convolutional Matrix Completion. Tables 4 and 14 additionally compare Random Selection, Herding and K-Center Greedy coreset predictors and their combinations with PMF. TinyBenchmarks' earlier citation alone did not constitute these comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 changes the reported active-evaluation design from initially masking 80% of scores to explicit 20% training, 60% acquisition-pool and 20% test partitions. Added protocols include observing 20% or 50% of new matrix blocks, ranking metrics, confidence-based prediction filtering, coreset sampling fractions and controlled prompt/decoding variations. The original NUTS sampling schedule is retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test Gaussian image noise, prompt changes, sampling temperatures and beam search; compare coreset fusion strategies and sampling fractions; and examine retaining only confident predictions. The earlier low-rank, profile, vision-encoder and zero-observation generalization analyses remain present, sometimes relocated to appendices.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 4 displays shaded ranges around its repeated-run curves, whereas v2 Figure 4 omits them. Their precise statistical meaning was not specified in v1. Both versions retain ten-seed averaging for active evaluation and enhancement experiments, and other error-bar displays remain.

E6.justification: v2 adds transfer, robustness, timing, ranking, neural-baseline and coreset results. For example, new Table 10 reports overall RMSE of 0.193 for PMF versus 0.225 for DMF at 20% masking. The original detailed PMF/PTF tables retain their numerical values. Figure 4 supplies replacement results under the revised protocol, while its MAE panel and Table 1's MAE entries are removed.

M1.justification: The Section 3 PMF/PTF framework remains unchanged. Sections 5.2–5.3 add bounded adaptations: representing evaluation settings through additional model rows or profiles, and combining PMF with coreset predictions through averaging or uncertainty-guided fusion. These change parts of the prediction procedure without replacing its core.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work prose are revised, and the discussion is reorganized around predictability, varying evaluation settings and coreset integration. The original low-rank discussion moves to Appendix B; the appendices are reorganized into A–C with five experimental subsections. Publication information and an impact statement are also added.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main document to a two-column conference layout, redraws Figure 1, and restructures Figure 4 from three panels into two with different axes. Table 1 drops its MAE columns, numerous experimental tables are added, and existing analyses and figures are redistributed between the main text and appendices. The original heatmaps are retained.

R1.justification: Focused additions distinguish the work from Zhang et al. (2024c)'s concurrent LLM performance-prediction study and explicitly position it as complementary to coreset methods. References also expand to neural matrix completion, newer models/benchmarks and benchmark redundancy. The central positioning around PMF for efficient LVLM evaluation remains.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds explicit top-K hit-rate definitions: Precision@K tests whether the predicted best model belongs to the true top K, while Recall@K tests whether the true best belongs to the predicted top K. The PMF/PTF likelihoods, priors, assumptions and profile equations remain mathematically unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps by explicitly separating acquisition from held-out testing and adding substantive matrix-completion comparisons. Transfer experiments and controlled setting perturbations substantially strengthen evidence about applicability beyond the original matrix. Reporting shortcomings remain: Figure 4 loses shaded ranges, and Table 13 leaves its two result blocks unlabeled. These limited drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger experimental validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PMF-based LVLM performance-prediction study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained content across substantial reformatting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations involving newer models and benchmarks, alternative predictors, evaluation-setting perturbations, coreset combinations, ranking metrics and computational costs.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 108 LVLMs across 176 datasets, performance-prediction experiments, active evaluation, ablations and appendix generalization results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of large language models is critical given their widespread applications. To achieve this, we aim to connect a formal mathematical framework - zigzag persistence from topological data analysis - with practical and easily applicable algorithms. Zigzag persistence is particularly effective for characterizing data as it dynamically transforms across model layers. Within this framework, we introduce topological descriptors that measure how topological features, $p$-dimensional holes, persist and evolve throughout the layers. Unlike methods that assess each layer individually and then aggregate the results, our approach directly tracks the full evolutionary path of these features. This offers a statistical perspective on how prompts are rearranged and their relative positions changed in the representation space, providing insights into the system's operation as an integrated whole. To demonstrate the expressivity and applicability of our framework, we highlight how sensitive these descriptors are to different models and a variety of datasets. As a showcase application to a downstream task, we use zigzag persistence to establish a criterion for layer pruning, achieving results comparable to state-of-the-art methods while preserving the system-level perspective.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds persistence similarity, pruning and consistent topology across models. v2 makes identification of four processing phases and quantitative discrimination between models and datasets central contributions, explicitly emphasizes the kNN-based zigzag framework, and recasts pruning as a showcase application.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 expands the mobile-versus-stationary interpretation into four phases linked to contextualization, stable relations, specialization and output preparation. It adds qualifications concerning last-token proxies and terminal-layer persistence, and discusses unexplained code and shuffling behavior. The earlier limitation concerning evaluation at only two pruning thresholds is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds the code-dataset source and execution details for the calendar example, including its prompt, token positions, k=2 and simplex dimension 3. Existing pseudocode, repository, computational libraries and hardware/runtime example are retained or relocated. The weighting exponent used for the pruning score remains unspecified.

E1.justification: Beyond retained SST and Pile coverage, v2 evaluates MATH and GitHub code, including five language subsets. It adds calendar-arithmetic prompts, shuffled SST inputs, and pruning evaluations on CMMLU, Commonsense-QA and WSC, substantially broadening domains and test scenarios.

E2.justification: The pruning comparators remain angular-distance pruning from Gromov et al. [6] and Block-Influence/ShortGPT from Men et al. [7], grouped as 'Other works.' The additional benchmarks use this same comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 specifies size-matched datasets of 8,000 prompts analyzed in 500-prompt subsets and changes the representative kNN setting from 5 to 4. It drops the aggressive condition selecting layers within 20% of peak similarity and the Llama2-13B pruning evaluation. New sliding-window experiments remove blocks of 5, 3 or 2 layers with corresponding strides of 2, 1 or 1; five-shot benchmark evaluation remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of weighting sensitivity, subset-size dependence, token-order disruption, code-language differences and calendar-token positions. Sliding-window layer ablations test the proposed connection between processing phases and performance. The existing kNN–Vietoris–Rips robustness analysis is retained in Appendix D, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1's descriptor curves lack sampling-variability bands. v2 reports means and standard deviations across 16 subsets of 500 prompts, or eight subsets of 1,000 for language-specific code analyses, and studies variance versus subset size. These quantify input-subset variability; pruning accuracies still lack reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: The surviving Table 1 scores exactly match v1's conservative-pruning results, while all aggressive-pruning entries and the Llama2-13B row disappear. New Table 3 adds benchmark scores, including Mistral CMMLU accuracy of 38.84 versus 29.68 for 'Other works.' New descriptor, calendar, shuffling and sliding-window findings substantially expand the results; revised topology plots should not be interpreted as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The kNN complexes, intersection filtration and FastZigZag pipeline remain. However, v2 Section 3.3 adds births' relative frequency and generalizes unweighted average persistence similarity to power-weighted inter-layer persistence. These expand the method's central analytical outputs beyond merely renaming the existing similarity measure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion are substantially rewritten around processing phases. Method and experiment sections are reorganized, both algorithms move to appendices, and a separate interpretation subsection is introduced. Terminology changes throughout from persistence similarity and p-cycles to inter-layer persistence and p-dimensional holes.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the main similarity heatmaps and kNN-sweep display with weighted-descriptor plots and sliding-window accuracy plots. It redraws persistence images, introduces uncertainty shading, converts the pruning schematic into Table 2, simplifies Table 1, and adds calendar barcodes, model-difference panels, supplementary analyses and Table 3.

R1.justification: A new 'Distinguishing Transformer Stages' discussion substantially expands positioning relative to research on processing phases. Sections 3.2–3.3 also distinguish the method from prior kNN filtrations, spatiotemporal persistence, persistent clustering and generalized rank invariants, with additional citations supporting these comparisons.

T1.justification: The zigzag-module formulation and interval decomposition in Appendix A are retained. v2 adds definitions for birth frequency and power weighting, specifies the zero-Betti case, corrects the persistence index endpoint to 2(Nlayers−1), and states a computational-complexity bound in Appendix B. These are limited mathematical extensions and corrections, without a new proof.

improvement.justification: The controlled layer removals, shuffled-input test and calendar example provide substantially stronger evidence about what the descriptors capture than v1's broad similarity patterns alone. Subset uncertainty and size-sensitivity analyses address an important reliability gap. Lost aggressive-pruning and 13B comparisons, unspecified pruning weights, and inconsistent variance-scaling descriptions in Appendix E.4/Figure 12 are drawbacks, but the net improvement in empirical grounding is substantial. The four-phase explanation remains interpretive.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same zigzag-persistence study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original representation and pruning results and adds calendar-token experiments, shuffled-input tests, subset analyses, sliding-window ablations and additional benchmark results.

before.justification: v1 reports original measurements of LLM representations on SST and Pile, topology sensitivity analyses, and comparative pruning accuracies in Table 1.

arxiv_record.abstract: Subspace optimization algorithms, such as GaLore (Zhao et al., 2024), have gained attention for pre-training and fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) due to their memory efficiency. However, their convergence guarantees remain unclear, particularly in stochastic settings. In this paper, we reveal that GaLore does not always converge to the optimal solution and provide an explicit counterexample to support this finding. We further explore the conditions under which GaLore achieves convergence, showing that it does so when either (i) a sufficiently large mini-batch size is used or (ii) the gradient noise is isotropic. More significantly, we introduce GoLore (Gradient random Low-rank projection), a novel variant of GaLore that provably converges in typical stochastic settings, even with standard batch sizes. Our convergence analysis extends naturally to other subspace optimization algorithms. Finally, we empirically validate our theoretical results and thoroughly test the proposed mechanisms. Codes are available at https://github.com/pkumelon/Golore.
arxiv_record.authors: Yutong He, Pengrui Li, Yipeng Hu, Chuyan Chen, Kun Yuan
arxiv_record.title: Subspace Optimization for Large Language Models with Convergence Guarantees

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions add an isotropic-noise convergence regime for GaLore beyond v1's deterministic and large-batch regimes, with additional conditions formalized in Appendix C. This materially expands the answer to a central research question. The principal GoLore convergence claim and sparse-extension contribution are retained.

C2.justification: v2 refines the failure explanation around anisotropic noise, adds task-dependent switching guidance, and attributes importance sampling's weaker performance to residual projection bias. It also explains equal WinoGrande test accuracy through overfitting and extends the stated theoretical limitation to variants such as Fira. v1 provided the simpler noise-dominance explanation and the MSGD-versus-Adam limitation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies quadratic-experiment batch sizes, FLORA's scaling factors, the OPT-13B training duration, and simulation/gradient-diagnostic details. Existing hardware disclosures, most retained hyperparameters, and the code link remain. OPT-13B's rank is ambiguous: Section 6 associates Table 2 with rank 4, while Appendix E describes reuse of a rank-1024 setup.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds a distinct synthetic scenario: Gaussian-noise matrix simulations assessing the leading property across three noise scales. C4, GLUE, WinoGrande, and BoolQ were already evaluated in v1. LLaMA-350M and OPT-13B extend model configurations on retained datasets rather than adding dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds FLORA to the GLUE comparison and evaluates importance sampling and Adam@40% against GoLore in the new LLaMA-350M comparison (Figure 12). These introduce substantive alternatives to the projection strategy. The full-parameter curve in v1's LLaMA-60M comparison is absent from v2 Figure 4, although the accompanying prose still lists full-parameter training.

E3.justification: LLaMA-60M pretraining changes from 10,000 to 30,000 iterations and from GoLore@20% to GoLore@50%. v2 adds LLaMA-350M and OPT-13B configurations, switching/frequency sweeps, and a gradient-error evaluation using 32 MRPC sequences; the 8-bit pretraining experiment is removed. The new WinoGrande accuracy column says 80 epochs while Appendix E specifies 30, leaving that evaluation budget unclear.

E4.justification: New Appendix F tests switching-point sensitivity, subspace-update frequency, singular-value-based importance sampling, and gradient approximation error on quadratic and MRPC tasks. Appendix C additionally tests the leading-property assumption under Gaussian noise. These substantially expand investigation of robustness and the proposed mechanism beyond v1's fixed-configuration demonstrations.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix C introduces Monte Carlo estimation of expected projection properties using 200,000 sampled matrices. This is a new statistical estimation procedure. LLM results remain without reported repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds FLORA's GLUE average of 84.72, OPT-13B BoolQ accuracies of 79.79 for GaLore and 81.96 for GoLore@30%, and WinoGrande accuracies of 68.51 for both GaLore and GoLore versus 69.85 for full-parameter training. It also adds simulation and ablation findings, replaces the C4 curves under changed settings, and removes the 8-bit results. Previously reported GLUE rows and LLaMA2-7B BoolQ scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: The core random projections, momentum transfer, hybrid training, and sparse variants are retained. Algorithm 1 changes Adam's bias-correction denominator from 1-beta_i^t to 1-(1-beta_i)^t. This is a local revision of the stated update; appendix Algorithms 2 and 6 retain the old expression, so a corresponding implementation change is not established.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: theoretical challenges move from Appendix A to Section 1.3, experiments precede algorithm connections, and the ReLoRA-like implementation moves from Appendix D to A. Main theorem statements are shortened by referring hyperparameter choices to the appendices. The introduction and related-work discussion are revised, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively rearranges displays. It adds a conceptual illustration, simulation and ablation figures, and an OPT-13B table; expands the GLUE and BoolQ tables; and removes the 8-bit figure. Figure 1 changes its vertical axis from loss to objective gap, while several retained displays are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through LDAdam, Fira, APOLLO, noise-geometry research, zeroth-order optimization, and gradient sketching. It explicitly contrasts GoLore's assumptions with LDAdam's error-feedback analysis and narrows the first discrete-time convergence positioning from memory-efficient LLM training generally to GaLore-like algorithms under standard assumptions.

T1.justification: New Appendix C introduces isotropic-noise and leading-property assumptions, projection and momentum lemmas, and Theorem 18/Corollary 19 establishing conditional small-batch GaLore convergence. Gaussian validity of the leading property is supported empirically rather than proved. Existing large-batch GaLore and GaSare bounds also revise constants, including doubling the lower bound on the subspace-update period.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the practical hybrid method: Appendix F tests previously unexamined switching and projection choices, measures gradient error directly, and complements new comparator evidence. The conditional isotropic-noise analysis also sharpens the convergence discussion. These gains outweigh the lost 8-bit and full-parameter C4 comparisons, although conflicting rank/epoch descriptions and the additional leading-property assumption limit the precision and scope of the new conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GaLore/GoLore research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds Gaussian-noise simulations, OPT-13B results, and sensitivity and gradient-error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original quadratic optimization experiments, C4 pretraining, and GLUE, WinoGrande, and BoolQ fine-tuning results, including appendix results.

arxiv_record.abstract:
External controls from historical trials or observational data can augment
randomized controlled trials when large-scale randomization is impractical or
unethical, such as in drug evaluation for rare diseases. However,
non-randomized external controls can introduce biases, and existing Bayesian
and frequentist methods may inflate the type I error rate, particularly in
small-sample trials where external data borrowing is most critical. To address
these challenges, we propose a randomization inference framework that ensures
finite-sample exact and model-free type I error rate control, adhering to the
"analyze as you randomize" principle to safeguard against hidden biases.
Recognizing that biased external controls reduce the power of randomization
tests, we leverage conformal inference to develop an individualized
test-then-pool procedure that selectively borrows comparable external controls
to improve power. Our approach incorporates selection uncertainty into
randomization tests, providing valid post-selection inference. Additionally, we
propose an adaptive procedure to optimize the selection threshold by minimizing
the mean squared error across a class of estimators encompassing both
no-borrowing and full-borrowing approaches. The proposed methods are supported
by non-asymptotic theoretical analysis, validated through simulations, and
applied to a randomized lung cancer trial that integrates external controls
from the National Cancer Database.
arxiv_record.authors: Ke Zhu, Shu Yang, Xiaofei Wang
arxiv_record.title:
Enhancing Statistical Validity and Power in Hybrid Controlled Trials: A
  Randomization Inference Approach with Conformal Selective Borrowing

C1.justification: The central claims of exact FRT type I error control and individualized conformal borrowing remain. V3 adds a prominent contribution claiming non-asymptotic guarantees for adaptive MSE-based threshold selection, while shifting emphasis away from presenting fixed and adaptive thresholds as parallel recommendations. Adaptive MSE selection itself was already proposed in v1.

C2.justification: V1 already explains power losses and borrowing trade-offs. V3 adds a rationale for optimizing MSE rather than family-wise error or false discovery rates, connects difficult-bias behavior to Hodges estimation and transferability detection, and explicitly discusses the absence of uniform improvement over RCT-only analysis. These refine existing interpretations rather than reverse them.

D1.justification: V1's clinical execution details—5,000 FRT iterations taking about 10 minutes on an eight-core MacBook—are omitted. The revised bootstrap algorithm specifies an input L without reporting its numerical value, whereas v1 specified 100 splitting repetitions. The intFRT repository disclosure and clinical preprocessing software information remain available; matching details move to Appendix D.

E1.justification: V3 changes the main simulated covariate population from two-dimensional normal covariates to uniform covariates on [-2, 2], and adds a five-dimensional correlated Gaussian scenario in Appendix C.6. The hybrid-trial task and CALGB 9633–NCDB clinical population remain unchanged.

E2.justification: The NB, FB, and ALSB point-estimator comparators are retained. ALSB newly participates in type I error and power comparisons using asymptotic inference, and v3 Figure 7 compares NB, ALSB, and CSB under asymptotic inference. V1 evaluated ALSB's estimation and selection performance but omitted its testing results. FB is also omitted from the corresponding fixed-threshold comparison plots in v3.

E3.justification: V3 adds an effect-size sweep for power curves at hidden-bias magnitudes 0 and 8 and introduces explicit asymptotic-versus-FRT evaluation protocols. The false-selection-rate metric reported in v1 is dropped. The principal sample sizes, 10-fold CV+, clinical preprocessing, and outcome definition remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds power-versus-effect-size curves, analyses comparing asymptotic inference with FRT, and robustness results for five dependent covariates. These substantially expand checks of power, calibration, and robustness. Conversely, v1's quantitative false-selection-rate analysis is removed, although selection scatterplots remain. Larger-EC-sample and fixed-threshold analyses were already present in v1.

E5.justification: V3 adds error bars to simulated type I error rates, including Figure 2 and appendix comparisons; v1 presents these rates without error bars. Their construction and coverage level are not explained. Both versions report 500 simulation replications and 5,000 FRT draws and provide asymptotic standard errors and confidence intervals for the clinical analysis.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes CSB's clinical estimate from 0.236 to 0.138, its confidence interval from (0.114, 0.359) to (0.024, 0.252), and its FRT p-value from 0.028 to 0.046. Selected controls change from 178 to 264 in the table, although v3's prose still says 178. Simulation results also change: the reported no-bias CSB power gain over NB rises from 38% to 45%, and new appendix results are added. Changed tuning and covariate generation prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The adaptive threshold algorithm changes substantially. V1 Section 3.2 estimates MSE through repeated two-fold splitting; v3 Section 3.3 and Algorithm 1 instead use the full-sample squared difference from the no-borrowing estimator, subtract its bootstrap-estimated variance, and add the borrowing estimator's bootstrap variance. The underlying FRT and four conformal variants remain; full conformal and jackknife+ move to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution narrative, method exposition, and discussion are extensively rewritten and compressed. Section 3 is reorganized around an estimator class and adaptive selection; full conformal and jackknife+ move to a new appendix section. Clinical matching details also move, and separate Software and Data and Impact Statement sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The manuscript changes from a spacious single-column format to a two-column conference main text. Figures are substantially recomposed: Figure 1 loses the CSB histogram row, performance and selection plots are merged, threshold boxplots are removed while histograms remain, and new comparison figures appear. Simulation axes and error-bar displays change, and the relocated clinical selection plot gains a shaded quantile-regression region.

R1.justification: V3 substantially expands the literature coverage and positioning around test-then-pool methods, Bayesian borrowing, control variates, and bias modeling. It adds connections to causal model selection, Hodges estimation, transferability costs, and regulatory guidance. Examples include Li et al. (2020), Schmidli et al. (2014), Rothenhäusler (2020), and Cai et al. (2024). The Gao ALSB citation's publication update is not a new comparator.

T1.justification: V3 adds Theorems 3.4 and 3.5, establishing uniform MSE-estimation error and oracle excess squared-error bounds under sub-Gaussian assumptions, with proofs in Appendices B.7–B.8. improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the previously unanalysed adaptive-selection component through an explicit revised criterion and non-asymptotic guarantees in Theorems 3.4–3.5. arxiv_record.abstract:
Methods for knowledge editing and unlearning in large language models seek to
edit or remove undesirable knowledge or capabilities without compromising
general language modeling performance. This work investigates how mechanistic
interpretability -- which, in part, aims to identify model components
(circuits) associated to specific interpretable mechanisms that make up a model
capability -- can improve the precision and effectiveness of editing and
unlearning. We find a stark difference in unlearning and edit robustness when
training components localized by different methods. We highlight an important
distinction between methods that localize components based primarily on
preserving outputs, and those finding high level mechanisms with predictable
intermediate states. In particular, localizing edits/unlearning to components
associated with the lookup-table mechanism for factual recall 1) leads to more
robust edits/unlearning across different input/output formats, and 2) resists
attempts to relearn the unwanted information, while also reducing unintended
side effects compared to baselines, on both a sports facts dataset and the
CounterFact dataset across multiple models. We also find that certain localized
edits disrupt the latent knowledge in the model more than any other baselines,
making unlearning more robust to various attacks.

C1.justification: The abstract and central claim that FLU improves robust editing/unlearning remain unchanged. The contribution summary shifts emphasis toward editing and explicitly claims that latent representations reflect the desired replacement answer, extending v1's claim that less original information remains recoverable.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies what its robustness tests establish: whole-sport relearning is described as invalid because facts are dependent, and held-out CounterFact relearning is too weak to distinguish methods reliably. It acknowledges difficulties averaging probes across unequal layer counts, discusses competitive Gemma-2 baselines and limited soft-prompt effectiveness, and interprets sequential editing as potentially beneficial. v1 presents its related relearning experiments primarily as positive robustness evidence.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix A.6 adds sweep ranges, a selection objective, hyperparameter-sharing rules, model/task-specific learning rates and loss coefficients, and an 8-bit optimizer disclosure. Appendix A.2 provides an explicit CounterFact localization threshold. However, v1's ordinary 80/20 split specification and detailed weight-masking optimizer, learning-rate, batching and regularization settings are omitted.

E1.justification: Sports Facts and CounterFact remain the datasets, but v2 adds sequential editing and adaptive soft-prompt recovery scenarios. It extends whole-sport replacement from basketball to baseball and football, while dropping v1's separate athlete-subset unlearning experiment (Table 5). Whole-sport editing itself already appeared in v1 Appendix A.1 and is not wholly new.

E2.justification: The six-localization comparison expands to nine with Causal Tracing MLPs, Attribution Patching MLPs and Random MLPs. These controls are actually evaluated in v2's appendix comparisons, substantially strengthening the comparison of mechanistic selection against simply restricting updates to MLPs. Manual interpretability is renamed FLU; the existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 evaluates three models across both datasets, adds 64-fact settings, changes athlete-edit targets from golf to randomly selected incorrect sports, and introduces hyperparameter tuning. Relearning changes from rank-64 LoRA on two athletes or all CounterFact forget facts to rank-512 LoRA with separate training and evaluation halves. Probe training and scoring change, edited-answer metrics are added, and sequential editing uses 100 total training steps versus 50 for batch editing.

E4.justification: v2 adds OT attribution profiles, learning-rate and loss-coefficient sensitivity analyses, adaptive soft-prompt attacks, and model-specific probes measuring both original and edited answers (Appendices A.3, A.6–A.8). The earlier sports attention-head ablation displays disappear. Much of v1's weight-masking analysis is retained in Appendix A.4 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A.8 newly states that soft-prompt evaluations are averaged over four prompts, adding limited information about evaluation repetition and aggregation. This does not establish independent seeded training runs. Neither version provides confidence intervals, error bars or formal significance tests for its main comparisons.

E6.justification: v2 adds or replaces extensive results for edited-answer accuracy, sequential editing, expanded models, probing and soft-prompt attacks. Under its revised relearning protocol, Figure 6 reports final forget accuracies of 0.199 for FLU, 0.469 for Causal Tracing and 0.631 for Causal Tracing MLPs; these are not same-setting comparisons with v1. Conversely, v1 Table 1 and mechanism-weight Tables 6–7 retain their numerical entries as v2 Tables 1–3.

M1.justification: The proposed editor still localizes fact-lookup MLPs and restricts fine-tuning to them using injection, retention and Pile losses. Unlearning and weight masking remain in the appendices. The expanded probe/path-patching explanation elaborates v1 Appendix A.2; sequential editing repeatedly applies the existing editor rather than introducing a new component.

P1.justification: The methods and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten around explicitly named editing tasks and revised metric terminology. Localization explanations expand, manual interpretability becomes FLU, and unlearning and the detailed weight-masking discussion move into a reorganized appendix. These changes substantially restructure the exposition despite the retained title and abstract.

P2.justification: Main results shift from accuracy tables and relearning trajectories to radar charts, grouped metric bars and before/after relearning bars. v2 adds multi-model probing and attribution panels, soft-prompt figures and tuning tables. Existing weight-masking displays move to Appendix A.4; Figure 1 and several tables and plots are retained despite renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of residual-knowledge tracing, representation engineering, circuit breakers and tamper-resistant safeguards, plus references for path patching and soft prompting. The book-unlearning and inserted-unlearning-layer discussion disappears. The central positioning against Hase et al.'s critique of localization remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The component-graph and importance-threshold formulation and the editing, unlearning and masking losses remain substantively equivalent. There are no added or removed theorems, proofs or substantive derivations. Expanded path-patching explanations and standard accuracy/error definitions concern exposition and evaluation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical case through MLP-only controls, evaluation across models, explicit measurement of successful replacement answers, and held-out relearning. These address important ambiguities in v1's evidence for robust editing. Tuning documentation and qualifications about weak robustness tests further improve assessability. Some earlier reproducibility details are lost, and sequential comparisons use unequal training budgets, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger validation of the central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The revisions can be matched reliably, including relocated unlearning and weight-masking results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Achieving both high safety and high usefulness simultaneously in large language models has become a critical challenge in recent years.Models often exhibit unsafe behavior or adopt an overly cautious approach leading to frequent overrefusal of benign prompts, which reduces their usefulness. A major factor underlying these behaviors is how the models are finetuned and aligned, particularly the nature and extent of the data used.In this work, we examine how overgenerating finetuning data with advanced teacher models (e.g., GPT-4o)-covering both general-purpose and toxic prompts-affects safety and usefulness in instruction-following language models.Additionally, we present POROver, an alignment strategy designed for models that are highly safe but prone to overrefusal. POROver employs preference optimization algorithms and leverages completions from an advanced teacher model to reduce overrefusals while maintaining safety.Our results show that overgenerating completions for general-purpose prompts significantly boosts safety with only a minimal impact on usefulness. Specifically, the F1 score calculated between safety and usefulness increases from 74.4% to 91.8% because of a substantial rise in safety. Moreover, overgeneration for toxic prompts raises usefulness from 11.1% to 57.6% while preserving safety. Finally, applying POROVer increases usefulness further-from 57.6% to 82.1%-while keeping safety at comparable levels. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/batuhankmkaraman/POROver.
arxiv_record.authors: Batuhan K. Karaman, Ishmam Zabir, Alon Benhaim, Vishrav Chaudhary, Mert R. Sabuncu, Xia Song

C1.justification: v2 explicitly frames POROver as targeting already highly safe but overrefusing models and claims that no existing post-training method specifically targets this setting. The three central contributions concerning general-purpose overgeneration, toxic-prompt overgeneration and preference optimization remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of unconditional compliance at zero toxic preference data, low usefulness at the opposite threshold extreme and diminishing returns from additional safety data. Limitations shift from a single student family/size to unresolved scaling near teacher size and language/domain transfer. It also newly interprets POROver as preserving adversarial robustness, although Table 6 shows increased GCG and PAIR attack success.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies ten epochs, 40 warm-up steps, checkpoint-selection rules, evaluation frequency and GPU hours; additional model-specific decoding and generation settings are documented. These disclosures do not establish changes to earlier runs. Conversely, v2 omits v1's selected threshold of 0.01, its 2,013-plus-166 preference-sample breakdown and several exact checkpoint links. The code/data access link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Section 3.3.4 adds JailBreakBench with 100 prompts evaluated under GCG, PAIR and hand-crafted JBC attacks, substantially extending coverage to adversarial input conditions. The original training datasets and capability, safety and overrefusal benchmarks remain represented.

E2.justification: The GPT-3/GPT-3.5 baselines and random, DeBERTa, ArmoRM and Llama Guard 2 selection comparisons remain. New experiments reuse these comparator sets. Llama-3-70B is an alternative teacher configuration, while GCG, PAIR and JBC are attack conditions; no new competing alignment method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The experimental design expands from Phi-3-7B to five students, adding Llama-3.1-8B, Falcon-3-7B and Llama-3.2-3B/11B, plus a Llama-3-70B teacher configuration. New protocols include transferred Vicuna attack artifacts, attack-success-rate evaluation and an ASD grid adding 5,000 and 10,000 examples. The retained Phi-3 decoding settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds adversarial robustness tests, student/teacher generalization checks, finer safety-data saturation analysis in Section 4.3 and qualitative threshold-sensitivity findings in Section 4.2. Figures 7–8 add teacher-response case comparisons. The original human-versus-automatic annotation analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means with standard errors and error bars. Neither specifies repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures. The expanded results do not establish a changed statistical estimation practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new students, the open-weight teacher and jailbreak attacks. Its headline OR-Bench F1 comparison changes from Phi-3's 70.81 to 88.33 to Llama-3.1-8B's 74.39 to 91.78, using different student and selection settings. Retained Phi-3 safety results match Table 7 and Figures 10–11, but its AlpacaEval results and additional-benchmark results from v1 Figure 4 are omitted.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning abilities, but they still struggle with faithful reasoning due to knowledge gaps and hallucinations. To address these issues, knowledge graphs (KGs) have been utilized to enhance LLM reasoning through their structured knowledge. However, existing KG-enhanced methods, either retrieval-based or agent-based, encounter difficulties in accurately retrieving knowledge and efficiently traversing KGs at scale. In this work, we introduce graph-constrained reasoning (GCR), a novel framework that bridges structured knowledge in KGs with unstructured reasoning in LLMs. To eliminate hallucinations, GCR ensures faithful KG-grounded reasoning by integrating KG structure into the LLM decoding process through KG-Trie, a trie-based index that encodes KG reasoning paths. KG-Trie constrains the decoding process, allowing LLMs to directly reason on graphs and generate faithful reasoning paths grounded in KGs. Additionally, GCR leverages a lightweight KG-specialized LLM for graph-constrained reasoning alongside a powerful general LLM for inductive reasoning over multiple reasoning paths, resulting in accurate reasoning with zero reasoning hallucination. Extensive experiments on several KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that GCR achieves state-of-the-art performance and exhibits strong zero-shot generalizability to unseen KGs without additional training.

C2.justification: New Appendices F.5 and G explicitly acknowledge that KG-valid paths can be irrelevant and that incomplete or incorrect KGs undermine answer correctness. They explain concrete failures and computational limits for longer paths. This substantially qualifies v1's predominantly successful-case discussion and brief medical-domain limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds CPU/memory specifications and construction-stack details, including Virtuoso SPARQL, Pickle, spaCy, ColBERTv2, the tokenizer and MARISA Trie. Figure 8 supplies the new coherence-evaluation prompt. Existing training hyperparameters and resource measurements are retained, although the coherence judge model and sample size remain unspecified.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 1–5 LLM scoring protocol for logical coherence and construction-efficiency evaluations across path lengths, pipeline stages and 1/4/10/20 processing threads. It also introduces answer-count and reasoning-hop breakdowns. The original QA splits, training recipe and main L=2, K=10 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, model, constraint and parameter studies, Appendices B and F.2–F.5 add construction-overhead and parallel-scaling analyses, multi-answer and multi-hop comparisons with RoG, logical-coherence evaluation and failure cases involving irrelevant paths and incomplete KGs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added mean timings and coherence score do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Main GCR benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds FreebaseQA scores, construction timings, stratified F1 results, failure examples and a mean coherence score of 3.9/5. P1.justification: Most original main-text prose and section order are retained. v2 adds localized clarifications, organizes the expanded appendix into lettered sections, and updates authorship, affiliations and acknowledgments while adding an Impact Statement. improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves assessment of the central efficiency and faithfulness claims. arxiv_record.abstract: Precipitation from tropical cyclones (TCs) can cause disasters such as flooding, mudslides, and landslides. Predicting such precipitation in advance is crucial, giving people time to prepare and defend against these precipitation-induced disasters. Developing deep learning (DL) rainfall prediction methods offers a new way to predict potential disasters. However, one problem is that most existing methods suffer from cumulative errors and lack physical consistency. Second, these methods overlook the importance of meteorological factors in TC rainfall and their integration with the numerical weather prediction (NWP) model. Therefore, we propose Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Diffusion (TCP-Diffusion), a multi-modal model for global tropical cyclone precipitation forecasting. It forecasts TC rainfall around the TC center for the next 12 hours at 3 hourly resolution based on past rainfall observations and multi-modal environmental variables. Adjacent residual prediction (ARP) changes the training target from the absolute rainfall value to the rainfall trend and gives our model the ability of rainfall change awareness, reducing cumulative errors and ensuring physical consistency. Considering the influence of TC-related meteorological factors and the useful information from NWP model forecasts, we propose a multi-model framework with specialized encoders to extract richer information from environmental variables and results provided by NWP models. The results of extensive experiments show that our method outperforms other DL methods and the NWP method from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).
arxiv_record.authors: Cheng Huang, Pan Mu, Cong Bai, Peter AG Watson
arxiv_record.comments: Camera-ready version. This paper has been accepted to ICML 2025

metadata.abstract: Deep learning methods have made significant progress in regular rainfall forecasting, yet the more hazardous tropical cyclone (TC) rainfall has not received the same attention. While regular rainfall models can offer valuable insights for designing TC rainfall forecasting models, most existing methods suffer from cumulative errors and lack physical consistency. Additionally, these methods overlook the importance of meteorological factors in TC rainfall and their integration with the numerical weather prediction (NWP) model. To address these issues, we propose Tropical Cyclone Precipitation Diffusion (TCP-Diffusion), a multi-modal model for forecasting of TC precipitation given an existing TC in any location globally. It forecasts rainfall around the TC center for the next 12 hours at 3 hourly resolution based on past rainfall observations and multi-modal environmental variables. Adjacent residual prediction (ARP) changes the training target from the absolute rainfall value to the rainfall trend and gives our model the capability of rainfall change awareness, reducing cumulative errors and ensuring physical consistency. Considering the influence of TC-related meteorological factors and the useful information from NWP model forecasts, we propose a multi-model framework with specialized encoders to extract richer information from environmental variables and results provided by NWP models. The results of extensive experiments show that our method outperforms other DL methods and the NWP method from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).

C1.justification: The principal contributions remain global TC rainfall forecasting, ARP-based change awareness, multimodal conditioning with NWP information, and claimed superiority over competing forecasts. v2 explicitly describes forecasting around an existing TC or given track location, consistent with v1's TC-centered task definition.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for Persistence's strength under a moving TC-centered window, interprets spectral agreement as capturing TC-scale structure, and attributes weaker phase/intensity performance to irregular cloud structures and rainfall-intensity variability. It also discusses stochastic samples as forecast uncertainty, hypothesizes why FuXi struggles, and qualifies usefulness when NWP forecast inputs are unavailable.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C supply detailed variable and pressure-level lists, split-selection information, denoising steps N=200, network depth K=4, noise settings, hardware/software versions, timing, and metric calculations. v2 states that code has been released at a repository, replacing v1's future-release promise; the earlier data-release commitment is absent. These are documentation and access-information changes, without evidence that existing training settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use MSWEP, ERA5, and IBTrACS data for the same global TC-centered, 10-degree rainfall forecasting task, covering 1980–2020 and predicting 12 hours at three-hour intervals. The new 2020 subset, phase/intensity breakdowns, and case visualizations remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains Persistence, U-Net, PreDiff, and NowcastNet. v2 adds ERA5-IFS alongside ECMWF-IFS in Table 2 and introduces FuXi in Appendix D.6/Table 6. These materially broaden comparisons to the input forecast system itself and a learned global weather model.

E3.justification: The reported main evaluation changes from repeated selections of half the test set to stochastic predictions across the full test set. Added evaluation protocols include RAPSD diagnostics, separate lead-time scores, timing comparisons, and a FuXi comparison using 349 samples from 2020 at 6–12-hour leads. The stated dataset split counts and six-hour NWP alignment remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component ablation remains, while v2 adds substantial analyses of spatial fidelity through RAPSD, lead-time-dependent skill and rainfall distributions, and errors across cyclone lifecycle phases and intensities. Figures 9 and 13 additionally examine eight stochastic predictions and an Olivia case against NWP forecasts.

E5.justification: v1 averages ten random half-test-set evaluations without reporting dispersion. v2 describes eight independent diffusion-noise predictions per test case and reports individual scores, means, and standard deviations in Table 5. This changes the estimation procedure and introduces explicit uncertainty reporting; the eight predictions are inference samples, not separate training runs.

E6.justification: Table 1's TCP-Diffusion ETS-6/24/60 and TPMAE values change from 0.43766/0.14971/0.00742/0.42582 to 0.43788/0.14703/0.00644/0.42344, while comparator values and rankings remain unchanged. Tables 2–3 also revise TCP-Diffusion scores. Numerous new runtime, FuXi, spectral, lead-time, stochastic-sample, and cyclone-stratified results substantially expand the evidence. Changed sampling limits direct performance comparisons between versions.

M1.justification: The ARP targets, rainfall reconstruction, conditional EA-3DUNet, historical encoders, ResNet-18 forecast encoder, and denoising objective remain unchanged. New pseudocode and expanded input and hyperparameter descriptions document the existing method; they do not establish an implemented algorithm or architecture change.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes existing material: model design precedes dataset discussion, detailed data descriptions and 3DUNet equations move into appendices, and evaluation methods and results receive separate sections. The abstract and introduction are revised, training/inference pseudocode is added, and structured appendices integrate technical explanations and extended analyses.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands into a fixed-versus-moving forecast-window explanation, and Figure 2 is redrawn with explicit denoising, network, and reconstruction panels. New input visualizations, spectral and lead-time plots, sample grids, case comparisons, and Tables 4–8 substantially expand the visual presentation. Table 2 gains an ERA5-IFS row, and the document adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds context from diffusion-based climate emulation, TC forecasting, FuXi, and residual prediction in global weather models, including Price, Nguyen, Oskarsson, and Hu. It removes the Hersbach ERA5 reference. These additions refine the surrounding literature while retaining the original central novelty positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies beta_s = 1 - cos(pi*s/(N-1)) and sigma_s = sqrt(beta_s), where v1 left these generic. This is a limited mathematical specification; as written, the schedule exceeds the stated beta_s range of (0,1). The principal equations remain unchanged, including Equations 12–14 moved to Appendix B.3. Appendix C explains existing metrics without adding theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses the supplied v1's limited implementation documentation, absent dispersion reporting, and narrow diagnostic analysis. Appendices A–D and the added comparisons make the method easier to assess and reveal performance weaknesses across cyclone phases and intensities. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including the newly specified noise schedule's conflict with the stated variance range, which limits direct reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TCP-Diffusion work, with readable text, equations, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–D. Supplementary material mentioned but not included in v1 cannot establish what was previously documented outside the supplied PDF.

after.justification: v2 retains original forecasting experiments and adds repeated stochastic predictions, runtime comparisons, spectral diagnostics, FuXi comparisons, and cyclone phase and intensity analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Many existing interpretation methods are based on Partial Dependence (PD) functions that, for a pre-trained machine learning model, capture how a subset of the features affects the predictions by averaging over the remaining features.
  Notable methods include Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) which computes feature contributions based on a game theoretical interpretation and PD plots (i.e., 1-dim PD functions) that capture average marginal main effects. Recent work has connected these approaches using a functional decomposition and argues that SHAP values can be misleading since they merge main and interaction effects into a single local effect. However, a major advantage of SHAP compared to other PD-based interpretations has been the availability of fast estimation techniques, such as \texttt{TreeSHAP}.
  In this paper, we propose a new tree-based estimator, \texttt{FastPD}, which efficiently estimates arbitrary PD functions.
  We show that \texttt{FastPD} consistently estimates the desired population quantity -- in contrast to path-dependent \texttt{TreeSHAP} which is inconsistent when features are correlated.
  For moderately deep trees, \texttt{FastPD} improves the complexity of existing methods from quadratic to linear in the number of observations.
  By estimating PD functions for arbitrary feature subsets, \texttt{FastPD} can be used to extract PD-based interpretations such as SHAP, PD plots and higher-order interaction effects.
arxiv_record.authors: Jinyang Liu, Tessa Steensgaard, Marvin N. Wright, Niklas Pfister, Munir Hiabu
arxiv_record.title: Fast Estimation of Partial Dependence Functions using Trees

Notable methods include Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) which computes feature contributions based on a game theoretical interpretation and PD plots (i.e., 1-dim PD functions) that capture average marginal main effects. Recent work has connected these approaches using a functional decomposition and argues that SHAP values can be misleading since they merge main and interaction effects into a single local effect. However, a major advantage of SHAP compared to other PD-based interpretations has been the availability of fast estimation techniques, such as `TreeSHAP`. In this paper, we propose a new tree-based estimator, `FastPD`, which efficiently estimates arbitrary PD functions. We show that `FastPD` consistently estimates the desired population quantity -- in contrast to path-dependent `TreeSHAP` which is inconsistent when features are correlated. For moderately deep trees, `FastPD` improves the complexity of existing methods from quadratic to linear in the number of observations. By estimating PD functions for arbitrary feature subsets, `FastPD` can be used to extract PD-based interpretations such as SHAP, PD plots and higher-order interaction effects.
