arxiv_record.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) is a powerful technique for discovering symbolic expressions that characterize nonlinear relationships in data, gaining increasing attention for its interpretability, compactness, and robustness. However, existing SR methods do not scale to datasets with a large number of input variables (referred to as extreme-scale SR), which is common in modern scientific applications. This ``large $p$'' setting, often accompanied by measurement error, leads to slow performance of SR methods and overly complex expressions that are difficult to interpret. To address this scalability challenge, we propose a method called PAN+SR, which combines a key idea of ab initio nonparametric variable selection with SR to efficiently pre-screen large input spaces and reduce search complexity while maintaining accuracy. The use of nonparametric methods eliminates model misspecification, supporting a strategy called parametric-assisted nonparametric (PAN). We also extend SRBench, an open-source benchmarking platform, by incorporating high-dimensional regression problems with various signal-to-noise ratios. Our results demonstrate that PAN+SR consistently enhances the performance of 19 contemporary SR methods, enabling several to achieve state-of-the-art performance on these challenging datasets.

arxiv_record.abstract: Modern physics simulation often involves multiple functions of interests, and traditional numerical approaches are known to be complex and computationally costly. While machine learning-based surrogate models can offer significant cost reductions, most focus on a single task, such as forward prediction, and typically lack uncertainty quantification -- an essential component in many applications. To overcome these limitations, we propose Arbitrarily-Conditioned Multi-Functional Diffusion (ACM-FD), a versatile probabilistic surrogate model for multi-physics emulation. ACM-FD can perform a wide range of tasks within a single framework, including forward prediction, various inverse problems, and simulating data for entire systems or subsets of quantities conditioned on others. Specifically, we extend the standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) for multi-functional generation by modeling noise as Gaussian processes (GP). We propose a random-mask based, zero-regularized denoising loss to achieve flexible and robust conditional generation. We induce a Kronecker product structure in the GP covariance matrix, substantially reducing the computational cost and enabling efficient training and sampling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ACM-FD across several fundamental multi-physics systems.

arxiv_record.abstract: Imitation learning (IL) enables agents to acquire skills directly from expert demonstrations, providing a compelling alternative to reinforcement learning. However, prior online IL approaches struggle with complex tasks characterized by high-dimensional inputs and complex dynamics. In this work, we propose a novel approach to online imitation learning that leverages reward-free world models. Our method learns environmental dynamics entirely in latent spaces without reconstruction, enabling efficient and accurate modeling. We adopt the inverse soft-Q learning objective, reformulating the optimization process in the Q-policy space to mitigate the instability associated with traditional optimization in the reward-policy space. By employing a learned latent dynamics model and planning for control, our approach consistently achieves stable, expert-level performance in tasks with high-dimensional observation or action spaces and intricate dynamics. We evaluate our method on a diverse set of benchmarks, including DMControl, MyoSuite, and ManiSkill2, demonstrating superior empirical performance compared to existing approaches.

arxiv_record.abstract: Markov processes serve as a universal model for many real-world random processes. This paper presents a data-driven approach for learning these models through the spectral decomposition of the infinitesimal generator (IG) of the Markov semigroup. The unbounded nature of IGs complicates traditional methods such as vector-valued regression and Hilbert-Schmidt operator analysis. Existing techniques, including physics-informed kernel regression, are computationally expensive and limited in scope, with no recovery guarantees for transfer operator methods when the time-lag is small. We propose a novel method that leverages the IG's resolvent, characterized by the Laplace transform of transfer operators. This approach is robust to time-lag variations, ensuring accurate eigenvalue learning even for small time-lags. Our statistical analysis applies to a broader class of Markov processes than current methods while reducing computational complexity from quadratic to linear in the state dimension. Finally, we illustrate the behaviour of our method in two experiments.
arxiv_record.authors: Vladimir R. Kostic, Karim Lounici, H\'el\`ene Halconruy, Timoth\'ee Devergne, Pietro Novelli, Massimiliano Pontil
arxiv_record.title: Laplace Transform Based Low-Complexity Learning of Continuous Markov Semigroups

arxiv_record.abstract: The high computational costs of large language models (LLMs) have led to a flurry of research on LLM compression, via methods such as quantization, sparsification, or structured pruning. A new frontier in this area is given by dynamic, non-uniform compression methods, which adjust the compression levels (e.g., sparsity) per-block or even per-layer in order to minimize accuracy loss, while guaranteeing a global compression threshold. Yet, current methods rely on estimating the importance of a given layer, implicitly assuming that layers contribute independently to the overall compression error. We begin from the motivating observation that this independence assumption does not generally hold for LLM compression: pruning a model further may even significantly recover performance. To address this, we propose EvoPress, a novel evolutionary framework for dynamic LLM compression. By formulating dynamic compression as a general optimization problem, EvoPress identifies optimal compression profiles in a highly efficient manner, and generalizes across diverse models and compression techniques. Via EvoPress, we achieve state-of-the-art performance for dynamic compression of Llama, Mistral, and Phi models, setting new benchmarks for structural pruning (block/layer dropping), unstructured sparsity, and quantization with dynamic bitwidths. Our code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/EvoPress}.
arxiv_record.authors: Oliver Sieberling, Denis Kuznedelev, Eldar Kurtic, Dan Alistarh
arxiv_record.title: EvoPress: Accurate Dynamic Model Compression via Evolutionary Search

A new frontier in this area is given by dynamic, non-uniform compression methods, which adjust the compression levels (e.g., sparsity) per-block or even per-layer in order to minimize accuracy loss, while guaranteeing a global compression threshold. Yet, current methods rely on estimating the "importance" of a given layer, implicitly assuming that layers contribute independently to the overall compression error. We begin from the motivating observation that this independence assumption does not generally hold for LLM compression: pruning a model further may even significantly recover performance.To address this, we propose EvoPress, a novel evolutionary framework for dynamic LLM compression. By formulating dynamic compression as a general optimization problem, EvoPress identifies optimal compression profiles in a highly efficient manner, and generalizes across diverse models and compression techniques. Via EvoPress, we achieve state-of-the-art performance for dynamic compression of Llama, Mistral, and Phi models, setting new benchmarks for structural pruning (block/layer dropping), unstructured sparsity, and quantization with dynamic bitwidths.

It also interprets seed consistency as evidence against problematic local optima and explains EvoPress–BESA complementarity. Appendix G adds qualifications about runtime/data tradeoffs, differing sparsity granularity, and incomplete tuning-cost accounting.

D1.justification: v2 adds RTX 4090 hardware information for Table 17, runtime-accounting exclusions for BESA, and vLLM precision/grouping requirements. Figure 3 newly clarifies minibatch fitness versus full-test-set perplexity measurement. The original hyperparameter table and code URL remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same calibration and evaluation corpora and the same language-model compression tasks, including the five zero-shot benchmarks. The added runtime studies, Wanda implementation, and vLLM precision restrictions change configurations and procedures within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix G adds evaluated comparisons against SLEB and BlockPruner for depth pruning and against layerwise and rowwise BESA for sparsity allocation. These substantially expand comparison with competing search procedures beyond v1's baseline set; the original comparisons remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: The original Table 8 settings remain, but substantial additional protocols appear: 1000-generation seed experiments, stopping after 20 generations without training-perplexity improvement, Wanda-based sparsity comparisons, and vLLM-compatible 4/8-bit search with coupled projection precisions. Table 17 adds runtime and forward-pass measurements on an RTX 4090. These are additional settings, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds seed sensitivity and configuration-consistency analyses in Appendix C.2, and tests layerwise perplexity prediction when removing 2, 4, or 6 blocks in Appendix D.4. This substantial addition is confined to the new robustness study; uncertainty is not added throughout the benchmark tables.

E6.justification: Most matched original scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Figures 4, 6, 7, and 10 and Tables 17–18. For example, Table 17 reports C4 perplexity/runtime of 19.87/53 minutes for EvoPress versus 20.91/159 minutes for SLEB at 37.5% depth pruning. Conversely, Tables 2–3 lose individual task scores for compressed models and the Llama-3.1 compressed-model rows, without restoring those scores in the appendices.

M1.justification: The level database, KL-divergence fitness, level-switch mutation, and multistage selection remain unchanged. Appendix G adds an early-stopping variant and a two-stage EvoPress+BESA procedure that refines EvoPress-derived block sparsities through rowwise allocation.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable progress on image-to-video (I2V) generation, while their noise-to-data generation process is inherently mismatched with this task, which may lead to suboptimal synthesis quality. In this work, we present FrameBridge. By modeling the frame-to-frames generation process with a bridge model based data-to-data generative process, we are able to fully exploit the information contained in the given image and improve the consistency between the generation process and I2V task. Moreover, we propose two novel techniques toward the two popular settings of training I2V models, respectively. Firstly, we propose SNR-Aligned Fine-tuning (SAF), making the first attempt to fine-tune a diffusion model to a bridge model and, therefore, allowing us to utilize the pre-trained diffusion-based text-to-video (T2V) models. Secondly, we propose neural prior, further improving the synthesis quality of FrameBridge when training from scratch. Experiments conducted on WebVid-2M and UCF-101 demonstrate the superior quality of FrameBridge in comparison with the diffusion counterpart (zero-shot FVD 95 vs. 192 on MSR-VTT and non-zero-shot FVD 122 vs. 171 on UCF-101), and the advantages of our proposed SAF and neural prior for bridge-based I2V models. The project page: https://framebridge-icml.github.io/.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a data-to-data bridge framework for I2V, effective diffusion-to-bridge transfer through SAF, and improved generation through neural priors. Updated headline scores and broader supporting experiments do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix C newly discusses the tradeoff between motion and consistency and the content bias of FVD. It also interprets the added curves as evidence of faster convergence and effective reduced-step sampling. The original explanation based on informative priors and frame-to-frames generation remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds training/sampling pseudocode, discrete-timestep SNR interpolation details and CogVideoX implementation sources, and updates the project-page address. Most existing hyperparameters remain documented. However, v1's explicit general specification of first-order, 250-step sampling is no longer retained as such.

E1.justification: V2 adds VBench-I2V evaluation inputs, including 50 sampled prompts used in the human study. WebVid-2M, UCF-101, MSR-VTT and the original class-conditional and text-conditional I2V tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 expands the zero-shot comparator set beyond DynamiCrafter and SEINE to include SVD, ConsistI2V, SparseCtrl and I2VGen-XL. The neural-prior ablation also adds a VDT-I2V baseline conditioned on the neural prior, providing an important additional control.

E3.justification: V2 adds 100k-step fine-tuning alongside 20k steps and evaluates a CogVideoX-2B backbone. The UCF-101 SAF ablation changes from uniformly 20k iterations to 5k/10k configurations. New protocols include VBench-I2V, CD-FVD, human rankings from 18 participants on 50 prompts, and sampling-step/runtime comparisons.

E4.justification: New analyses examine motion versus consistency using noisy image conditioning and increased frame stride, FVD content bias, training convergence and sampling efficiency. V2 also adds WebVid-2M SAF ablations for both backbones and the neural-prior-conditioned diffusion control; v1 mainly ablated SAF and prior choice.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed variability, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's user-ranking averages introduce a metric and study sample size, but no uncertainty analysis.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises multiple results: SEINE's MSR-VTT FVD changes from 176 to 245, and FrameBridge's SAF result changes from 83 to 99 for the reported 20k-step configuration. V2 separately adds a 100k-step result of 95, CogVideoX results and extensive new analyses. The neural-prior diffusion control scores 132 FVD; FrameBridge-NP's original 122 remains. These are revised and additional results, not uniform performance improvements.

M1.justification: Appendix A.3 extends SAF with output reparameterization for v-prediction models such as CogVideoX-2B, beyond v1's input and timestep alignment. The core bridge process, replicated prior and neural-prior construction remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial motivation/SAF passages are rewritten. Background and motivation are consolidated, the main experimental setup discussion is compressed, and the appendices are reorganized around new pseudocode and analysis sections, moving the original related-work appendix from B to E.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main layout, redesigns comparison tables with training-budget columns and ranking markers, and adds analytical plots, tables and algorithm boxes. Qualitative displays are reorganized: the rabbit example moves from Figure 5 to Figure 9, while v1 Figures 6–9 are retained as v2 Figures 12–15.

R1.justification: V2 expands discussion of coupled flow matching, noise calibration, newer bridge models and additional video-generation methods. It adds benchmark-related citations while retaining the central positioning against noise-to-data diffusion. Numerous venue/year updates refer to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds the mathematical construction of the aligned v-prediction output target. The bridge derivations and Propositions 1–3 with their proofs are otherwise retained. Removing the separately displayed neural-prior bridge loss from the main text is an equivalent restatement through prior substitution.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited empirical validation through broader baselines, explicit training-budget comparisons and the missing neural-prior-conditioned diffusion control. VBench-I2V, CD-FVD and human judgments better examine whether apparent gains reflect consistency at the expense of motion. Cross-backbone and efficiency analyses further support applicability. Uncertainty remains unreported and some sampling-plot labeling is inconsistent, but the added controls and complementary evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FrameBridge. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across restructuring and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark comparisons, efficiency analyses, further ablations and an 18-participant user study.

before.justification: V1 reports original image-to-video benchmark results, SAF and neural-prior ablations, and generated-video examples, including appendix results.

arxiv_record.abstract: A plethora of jailbreaking attacks have been proposed to obtain harmful responses from safety-tuned LLMs. These methods largely succeed in coercing the target output in their original settings, but their attacks vary substantially in fluency and computational effort. In this work, we propose a unified threat model for the principled comparison of these methods. Our threat model checks if a given jailbreak is likely to occur in the distribution of text. For this, we build an N-gram language model on 1T tokens, which, unlike model-based perplexity, allows for an LLM-agnostic, nonparametric, and inherently interpretable evaluation. We adapt popular attacks to this threat model, and, for the first time, benchmark these attacks on equal footing with it. After an extensive comparison, we find attack success rates against safety-tuned modern models to be lower than previously presented and that attacks based on discrete optimization significantly outperform recent LLM-based attacks. Being inherently interpretable, our threat model allows for a comprehensive analysis and comparison of jailbreak attacks. We find that effective attacks exploit and abuse infrequent bigrams, either selecting the ones absent from real-world text or rare ones, e.g., specific to Reddit or code datasets.
arxiv_record.authors: Valentyn Boreiko, Alexander Panfilov, Vaclav Voracek, Matthias Hein, Jonas Geiping
arxiv_record.title: An Interpretable N-gram Perplexity Threat Model for Large Language Model Jailbreaks

The central claims about interpretable benchmarking and the strength of discrete-optimization attacks remain.

C2.justification: v2 drops v1's interpretation that filtering can improve PRS success and revises the model-robustness conclusions. Transfer is reinterpreted relative to declining source-model ASR, rather than simply as an absolute decline under tighter constraints. New discussions address multilingual and tokenizer limitations, Gemma's refusals after the target token, and whether self-perplexity confounds attack cost with robustness.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit HarmBench judge templates, judge precision, PRS reimplementation/caching information, and self-perplexity thresholds and context-handling details in Appendices B, F, G, and I. The main code-repository link remains, while the standalone reproducibility statement and separate baseline-repository links disappear. These extend and revise existing documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds filter-rejection evaluation on translations of the 300 HarmBench queries into 12 languages, substantially extending the previously English-focused evaluation population (Section 5.3 and Table 2). The existing Dolma, Alpaca, and HarmBench coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated windowed and full-query self-perplexity comparators; the full-query result explicitly transfers the windowed attack (Table 3). P1.justification: Beyond retitling and widespread prose editing, v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative and experimental sections. Human evaluation moves from Appendix B to Section 5.6, filter-construction material moves into Appendix C, and related work and interpretation receive newly separated subsections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout, with extensive figure and table relocation and redesigned algorithms. v2 adds multilingual and self-perplexity tables and Figure 14, removes v1's attack-metric overview table, redraws transfer displays, and adds uncertainty bands to the PRS threshold plot.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations concerning circuit breakers and latent-space defenses, multilingual tokenization, N-gram modeling, and layered safety measures. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens scrutiny of the central threat model: it documents a more thorough PRS search, fills previously missing attack comparisons, and directly tests adaptive self-perplexity alternatives. arxiv_record.abstract: With large language models (LLMs) increasingly deployed as cognitive engines for AI agents, the reliability and effectiveness critically hinge on their intrinsic epistemic agency, which remains understudied. Epistemic agency, the ability to flexibly construct, adapt, and monitor beliefs about dynamic environments, represents a base-model-level capacity independent of specific tools, modules, or applications. We characterize the holistic process underlying epistemic agency, which unfolds in seven interrelated dimensions: prediction, decision-making, perception, memory, counterfactual thinking, belief updating, and meta-reflection. Correspondingly, we propose Reflection-Bench, a cognitive-psychology-inspired benchmark consisting of seven tasks with long-term relevance and minimization of data leakage. Through a comprehensive evaluation of 16 models using three prompting strategies, we identify a clear three-tier performance hierarchy and significant limitations of current LLMs, particularly in meta-reflection capabilities. While state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate rudimentary signs of epistemic agency, our findings suggest several promising research directions, including enhancing core cognitive functions, improving cross-functional coordination, and developing adaptive processing mechanisms. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/ReflectionBench.

C1.justification: V1 presents reflection as a criterion for AI intelligence and emphasizes shortcomings relative to human intelligence. V2 explicitly targets intrinsic epistemic agency, treats reflection as a process, and acknowledges rudimentary agency. It also adds central claims about contamination minimization and a three-tier performance hierarchy, substantially redefining the paper's contribution.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's cost-based criticism of CoT with task- and model-dependent interpretations supported by prompting comparisons. It expands discussion of local adaptation, global understanding and cognitive coordination. New applicability boundaries distinguish base LLMs from augmented or multi-LLM agents and address ecological validity, modalities and naturalistic interaction. It also interprets Centaur's results as evidence of contamination resistance.

D1.justification: V1's appendix supplies only Oddball prompts and annotation examples. V2 Appendix A documents system prompts and worked interactions across all seven tasks and gives the three strategy prompts; Appendix D explains the embedding scorer. Conversely, v1's explicit temperature-zero settings, API costs/counts and WPT last-20-of-100 estimation detail are omitted. These are substantial documentation changes, not proof that every underlying implementation changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same seven text-based cognitive tasks. V2's harder evaluations vary memory depth, reward probabilities and reversal intervals within those tasks; they do not introduce a new dataset domain, language or distinct task.

E2.justification: The main comparison changes from 13 to 16 models, adding models including DeepSeek-Reasoner/V3, QwQ, Grok-2 and Claude-Haiku while removing GPT-4, Gemini-1.5-pro and the Llama-3.1 variants from that comparison. Table 9 adds Centaur versus Llama-3.1-70B and chance baselines. The original 13 models remain represented in Appendix D's Oddball validation.

E3.justification: V1 generally restricts responses to choices; v2 evaluates direct generation, free output and zero-shot CoT, with only two strategies for reasoning models. Easy-setting WCST changes from 108 to 72 trials, PRLT probability from 0.9 to 0.8 and its smoothing window from 3 to 5, and MBT reversal interval from 3 to 2. V2 also adds hard configurations and automated Oddball scoring.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic prompting comparisons, difficulty sensitivity tests, a Centaur comparison intended to investigate contamination, and human-versus-automated Oddball scoring validation. Existing behavioral analyses are substantially extended, including five WPT response patterns and quantitative DC-IGT switching and earnings analyses (Appendices C–D).

E5.justification: Both versions describe two sessions for most tasks and three for Oddball; an increase in these counts is not reported. V2 adds one million random simulations per applicable task to estimate 95th-percentile chance thresholds, plus Pearson correlations, p-values and confidence intervals for Oddball scoring validation (Figures 18–19). These substantially expand statistical reporting beyond v1's averages.

E6.justification: V1 Table 2 ranks o1-preview first at 80.97; v2 Table 2 ranks Claude-3.5-Sonnet with CoT first at 68.78, ahead of o1-preview's direct-generation 66.57. These are revised-setting results, not a same-setting performance decline. V2 adds extensive strategy, difficulty and Centaur results. Some entries conflict internally: Grok-2's easy CoT PRLT score is 68.34 in Table 8 but 48.86 in Table 9.

M1.justification: The seven-task benchmark design is retained. V2 adds an automated Oddball scoring component: split responses into sentences, embed them and select the maximum cosine similarity to a reference surprise sentence (Appendix D). This changes one scoring procedure without redesigning the benchmark.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V2 adds a dedicated explanation of agency dimensions, reorders task descriptions, separates discussion from experiments and reorganizes the appendix into prompts, results, secondary analyses and scoring validation. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 and rearranges Figure 2. The original consolidated results table becomes an overall model-strategy table plus task-specific and easy/hard comparison tables. Behavioral plots are redesigned and moved to the appendix, alongside new interaction diagrams, switching analyses and correlation panels. The original Oddball MMN-style results plot is removed.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from emergent intelligence and first-principles accounts toward LLM agents, epistemic agency and cognitive-psychology evaluation. V2 adds substantial positioning around AgentBench, ReAct, MetaGPT, cognitive evaluation, philosophical agency and benchmark contamination, while retaining relevant cognitive-task foundations.

T1.justification: The weather transition matrices and MAE-based score normalization are retained. V2's expanded epistemic-agency framework is conceptual, while its new scoring and statistical procedures are empirical; no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged choice-only prompting limitation through direct strategy comparisons, replacing speculative CoT interpretation with experimental evidence. Full task prompts, harder-setting tests, chance thresholds and empirical validation of automated scoring improve the benchmark's interpretability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including conflicting PRLT entries in Tables 8–9, although the Centaur comparison supports a narrower conclusion than v2's strong contamination-resistance claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Reflection-Bench and its seven cognitive tasks. Their full text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes in framing and evaluation.

after.justification: V2 reports original model-by-prompting evaluations, harder-setting experiments, Centaur comparisons, random simulations and automated-scoring validation in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 13 LLMs across seven tasks, including numerical scores in Table 2 and behavioral analyses in Figures 3–7.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper investigates the use of transformers to approximate the mean-field dynamics of interacting particle systems exhibiting collective behavior. Such systems are fundamental in modeling phenomena across physics, biology, and engineering, including opinion formation, biological networks, and swarm robotics. The key characteristic of these systems is that the particles are indistinguishable, leading to permutation-equivariant dynamics. First, we empirically demonstrate that transformers are well-suited for approximating a variety of mean field models, including the Cucker-Smale model for flocking and milling, and the mean-field system for training two-layer neural networks. We validate our numerical experiments via mathematical theory. Specifically, we prove that if a finite-dimensional transformer effectively approximates the finite-dimensional vector field governing the particle system, then the $L_2$ distance between the \textit{expected transformer} and the infinite-dimensional mean-field vector field can be uniformly bounded by a function of the number of particles observed during training. Leveraging this result, we establish theoretical bounds on the distance between the true mean-field dynamics and those obtained using the transformer.
arxiv_record.authors: Shiba Biswal, Karthik Elamvazhuthi, and Rishi Sonthalia
arxiv_record.title: Universal Approximation of Mean-Field Models via Transformers

E3.justification: The added benchmark study introduces validation-selected comparisons and 3-/20-neighbor graph controls. Figure 4 adds Gibbs sampling over five fixed positions and an 11-by-11 velocity grid. v2 also reports 30 simulated Cucker-Smale particles instead of ten, although Figure 3 still captions ten; this inconsistency prevents establishing whether that experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 4 add a focused diagnostic comparing sampled expected-transformer errors with the theoretical bound across position/velocity settings. The trajectory and neural-network parameter-error analyses already present in Figures 1–3 are retained.

E5.justification: v2 specifies five trials per hyperparameter configuration and introduces plus/minus uncertainty entries in Table 1, without defining the uncertainty statistic. The existing 100-trial median and interquartile-range reporting in Figures 1–2 remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds substantial comparative results: the transformer has the lowest reported MSE on both Cucker-Smale (1.9e-6) and fish milling (2.2e-2). Figure 4 newly reports maximum sampled error 0.025 against a stated bound of at least 0.05. Figures 1–3 retain their earlier results.

M1.justification: The transformer architecture, expected-transformer construction, and mean-squared-error vector-field learning procedure are retained. The architecture definitions move from Section 3.1 to Appendix D; additional training specifications do not establish a changed proposed method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are extensively revised. Experiments move ahead of theory, notation becomes an introduction subsection, architecture definitions move to Appendix D, and related work becomes a dedicated later section. This is substantial restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 switches the main text to a two-column conference layout, adds Table 1 and the five-panel heatmap Figure 4, and substantially resizes and relocates Figures 1–3. The retained plots preserve their underlying results.

R1.justification: The broad neural-network/PDE approximation background is replaced by a focused Section 5 comparison of measure roles, architectures, and guarantees. v2 adds positioning against Kratsios and Furuya (2025), alongside new citations for probabilistic transformers, fish data, GNN baselines, and attention regularity, while removing much of the earlier general background.

T1.justification: v2 replaces Wp-based regularity with W1 regularity, removes the explicit smoothness assumption, and revises approximation bounds and their proofs. Theorem 4.12 and Appendix B add an existence-and-uniqueness argument using a cutoff, replacing v1's Assumption 2. The dynamics theorem is reformulated in W1, although inconsistent p/Wp expressions remain elsewhere.

improvement.justification: Table 1 supplies architectural comparisons and real-data validation absent from v1, while Appendix E substantially improves reproducibility information. These materially strengthen the paper's empirical support and auditability. The added existence-and-uniqueness argument also addresses a previously assumed condition, although theoretical consistency remains imperfect. The ambiguous '80-20-20' split, conflicting particle counts, and residual W1/Wp expressions limit confidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same expected-transformer approach to mean-field dynamics, despite the changed title. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: Section 3 retains the original simulations and adds comparative results on Cucker-Smale and real fish-milling data. Section 4.3 also reports a new approximation-error analysis.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–3 report original Cucker-Smale simulations and experiments approximating two-layer neural-network training dynamics.

arxiv_record.abstract: Foundation model-based agents are increasingly used to automate complex tasks, enhancing efficiency and productivity. However, their access to sensitive resources and autonomous decision-making also introduce significant security risks, where successful attacks could lead to severe consequences. To systematically uncover these vulnerabilities, we propose AdvAgent, a black-box red-teaming framework for attacking web agents. Unlike existing approaches, AdvAgent employs a reinforcement learning-based pipeline to train an adversarial prompter model that optimizes adversarial prompts using feedback from the black-box agent. With careful attack design, these prompts effectively exploit agent weaknesses while maintaining stealthiness and controllability. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that AdvAgent achieves high success rates against state-of-the-art GPT-4-based web agents across diverse web tasks. Furthermore, we find that existing prompt-based defenses provide only limited protection, leaving agents vulnerable to our framework. These findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in current web agents and emphasize the urgent need for stronger defense mechanisms. We release code at https://ai-secure.github.io/AdvAgent/.
arxiv_record.authors: Chejian Xu, Mintong Kang, Jiawei Zhang, Zeyi Liao, Lingbo Mo, Mengqi Yuan, Huan Sun, Bo Li
arxiv_record.title: AdvAgent: Controllable Blackbox Red-teaming on Web Agents

arxiv_record.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has become a widely used strategy for improving large language and multimodal model performance. However, it is still an open question under which settings CoT systematically reduces performance. In this paper, we seek to identify the characteristics of tasks where CoT reduces performance by drawing inspiration from cognitive psychology, focusing on six representative tasks from the psychological literature where deliberation hurts performance in humans. In three of these tasks, state-of-the-art models exhibit significant performance drop-offs with CoT (up to 36.3\% absolute accuracy for OpenAI o1-preview compared to GPT-4o), while in others, CoT effects are mixed, with positive, neutral, and negative changes. While models and humans do not exhibit perfectly parallel cognitive processes, considering cases where thinking has negative consequences for humans helps identify settings where it negatively impacts models. By connecting the literature on human verbal thinking and deliberation with evaluations of CoT, we offer a perspective for understanding the impact of inference-time reasoning.

C1.justification: v1 presents two conditions as predicting CoT failures and describes the three mismatch tasks as showing no negative effects. v4 explicitly acknowledges mixed positive, neutral and negative effects and frames the approach as an imperfect heuristic. It also claims statistically demonstrated enrichment of failure cases and introduces a released six-task benchmark.

C2.justification: The logical-inconsistency explanation shifts from low baseline performance toward differences in formal-logic knowledge. New controls support interpretations concerning image ordering and distracting features, while successful steering qualifies CoT failures as dependent on its default reasoning strategy. Appendix F.1 adds explicit discussion of the apartment implementation favoring models and possible memory restrictions.

D1.justification: v4 supplies decoding temperatures and output-token budgets throughout Appendices A–F, including the o1 temperature exception and an 8000-token apartment budget. It also provides a repository link for the six task datasets. These substantially extend v1's construction instructions and prompts; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E1.justification: The six task families remain, but v4 adds simpler grammar distributions, faces with differing descriptions, binary face matching and vehicle classification with a binary oracle feature. Appendix G additionally analyzes 378 published model-task comparisons as a new data source, without rerunning those benchmarks.

E2.justification: The model comparator sets in Tables 1–6 are unchanged, and tree-of-thought was already evaluated in v1. v4 adds comparisons involving bigram-guided CoT and progressively stronger license-plate steering alongside ordinary prompting conditions (A.7, C.6).

E3.justification: New protocols include temperature sweeps over 4400 grammar problems, a balanced 100-problem binary face test and a vehicle-oracle experiment capped at seven iterations. The bootstrap analysis uses vehicle classification accuracy instead of rounds to permit aggregation. These supplement the retained main experimental protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing tree-of-thought and learning-curve analyses, v4 tests grammar complexity, sampling temperature, face-task difficulty, image-ordering explanations, oracle features and steering strength. It also adds three failure examples and tests whether the task-selection heuristic disproportionately identifies CoT failures.

E5.justification: Section 4.5 and Appendix G add two bootstrap tests, each using 100000 resamples of size 50, assessing failure magnitude and frequency. Appendix C.6 also reports independent trial counts and an uncertainty interval for steering experiments. Existing main-table p-values and learning-curve error bars are retained.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 and the original tree-of-thought results retain their values. Substantial new results include direct/CoT accuracies of 61%/32% with differing face descriptions and 72%/62% for binary face matching; combined vehicle steering achieves perfect classification by iteration two in both conditions. These are newly evaluated conditions, not improvements to the original results.

M1.justification: Appendices A.7 and C.6 introduce task-specific inference instructions directing reasoning toward bigrams or retrieval of matching license plates. These modify prompting procedures in supplementary conditions; the underlying models and original direct/CoT procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, task discussions and concluding discussion are extensively rewritten. Task-specific Hypothesis paragraphs become Human failure descriptions, the numbered limitations/future-directions structure is consolidated, and a heuristic-effectiveness section is introduced. v4 also repairs malformed prose in v1.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one to two columns, with substantially resized tables and revised captions. The existing learning curve moves from appendix Figure 5 to main-text Figure 2. v4 adds two task-variation figures and three failure-example tables, while relocating many appendix tables to the document's end.

R1.justification: v4 adds relevant work on fragile mathematical reasoning, CoT-related bias/toxicity and long-context retrieval, including Mirzadeh, Shaikh and Liu. It also positions the heuristic empirically against Sprague's metastudy. The principal psychology-based research positioning remains intact; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: The finite-state grammar definitions, logical-consistency formulation, Gaussian distractor construction and additive apartment-utility assumption are retained. v4 adds empirical procedures and interpretations, without new theoretical propositions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the evidence through targeted robustness and steering tests and corrects the categorical no-harm claim that conflicted with v1's own tables. Dataset access and decoding details improve reproducibility. Appendix A.7 still mixes a stated subset experiment with full-dataset reference accuracies, limiting that comparison, but the broader gains in evidential support and calibration of claims are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same six-task study. Their main text, tables, figures, equations and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds controlled task variations, steering experiments, failure examples and an original bootstrap analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original model experiments on six tasks in Tables 1–6, plus tree-of-thought results and a vehicle-learning analysis in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract:
With the widespread deployment of long-context large language models (LLMs),
there has been a growing demand for efficient support of high-throughput
inference. However, as the key-value (KV) cache expands with the sequence
length, the increasing memory footprint and the need to access it for each
token generation both result in low throughput when serving long-context LLMs.
While various dynamic sparse attention methods have been proposed to speed up
inference while maintaining generation quality, they either fail to
sufficiently reduce GPU memory consumption or introduce significant decoding
latency by offloading the KV cache to the CPU. We present ShadowKV, a
high-throughput long-context LLM inference system that stores the low-rank key
cache and offloads the value cache to reduce the memory footprint for larger
batch sizes and longer sequences. To minimize decoding latency, ShadowKV
employs an accurate KV selection strategy that reconstructs minimal sparse KV
pairs on-the-fly. By evaluating ShadowKV on a broad range of benchmarks,
including RULER, LongBench, and Needle In A Haystack, and models like
Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3-8B-1M, GLM-4-9B-1M, Yi-9B-200K, Phi-3-Mini-128K, and
Qwen2-7B-128K, we demonstrate that it can support up to 6$\times$ larger batch
sizes and boost throughput by up to 3.04$\times$ on an A100 GPU without
sacrificing accuracy, even surpassing the performance achievable with infinite
batch size under the assumption of infinite GPU memory. The code is available
at https://github.com/bytedance/ShadowKV.

By evaluating ShadowKV on benchmarks like RULER, LongBench, and models such as Llama-3.1-8B and GLM-4-9B-1M, we demonstrate that it achieves up to 6$\times$ larger batch sizes and 3.04$\times$ higher throughput on an A100 GPU without sacrificing accuracy, even surpassing the performance achievable with infinite batch size under the assumption of infinite GPU memory.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have significantly enhanced the quality of image synthesis, yet they have also introduced serious safety concerns, particularly the generation of Not Safe for Work (NSFW) content. Previous research has demonstrated that adversarial prompts can be used to generate NSFW content. However, such adversarial text prompts are often easily detectable by text-based filters, limiting their efficacy. In this paper, we expose a previously overlooked vulnerability: adversarial image attacks targeting Image-to-Image (I2I) diffusion models. We propose AdvI2I, a novel framework that manipulates input images to induce diffusion models to generate NSFW content. By optimizing a generator to craft adversarial images, AdvI2I circumvents existing defense mechanisms, such as Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD), without altering the text prompts. Furthermore, we introduce AdvI2I-Adaptive, an enhanced version that adapts to potential countermeasures and minimizes the resemblance between adversarial images and NSFW concept embeddings, making the attack more resilient against defenses. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that both AdvI2I and AdvI2I-Adaptive can effectively bypass current safeguards, highlighting the urgent need for stronger security measures to address the misuse of I2I diffusion models.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) can handle many tasks within a
single model, yet the representations that enable this capability remain
opaque. We find that VLMs align conceptually equivalent inputs into a shared
task vector, which is invariant to modality (text, image) and format (examples,
instruction), and may simplify VLM processing. We measure this alignment via
cross-modal transfer -- the ability of a task vector derived in one modality to
trigger the correct generation in another -- on a range of tasks and model
architectures. Although the task vector is highly compressed, we find that this
single vector outperforms prompting the model with the full task information,
unique to this cross-modal case. Furthermore, we show that task vectors can be
transferred from a base language model to its fine-tuned vision-language
counterpart, and that they can be derived solely from instructions without the
need for examples. Taken together, our findings shed light on how VLMs
internally process task information, and how they map different modalities into
common semantic representations. Project page:
https://vlm-cross-modal-reps.github.io.

arxiv_record.title: Vision-Language Models Create Cross-Modal Task Representations

arxiv_record.abstract: To avoid myopic behavior, multi-step lookahead Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithms consider the sequential nature of BO and have demonstrated promising results in recent years. However, owing to the curse of dimensionality, most of these methods make significant approximations or suffer scalability issues. This paper presents a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework for multi-step lookahead BO in high-dimensional black-box optimization problems. The proposed method enhances the scalability and decision-making quality of multi-step lookahead BO by efficiently solving the sequential dynamic program of the BO process in a near-optimal manner using RL. We first introduce an Attention-DeepSets encoder to represent the state of knowledge to the RL agent and subsequently propose a multi-task, fine-tuning procedure based on end-to-end (encoder-RL) on-policy learning. We evaluate the proposed method, EARL-BO (Encoder Augmented RL for BO), on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter tuning problems, finding significantly improved performance compared to existing multi-step lookahead and high-dimensional BO methods.

arxiv_record.abstract: Abstract visual reasoning (AVR) involves discovering shared concepts across images through analogy, akin to solving IQ test problems. Bongard Problems (BPs) remain a key challenge in AVR, requiring both visual reasoning and verbal description. We investigate whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can solve BPs by formulating a set of diverse MLLM-suited solution strategies and testing $4$ proprietary and $4$ open-access models on $3$ BP datasets featuring synthetic (classic BPs) and real-world (Bongard HOI and Bongard-OpenWorld) images. Despite some successes on real-world datasets, MLLMs struggle with synthetic BPs. To explore this gap, we introduce Bongard-RWR, a dataset representing synthetic BP concepts using real-world images. Our findings suggest that weak MLLM performance on classical BPs is not due to the domain specificity, but rather comes from their general AVR limitations. Code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/pavonism/bongard-rwr

arxiv_record.abstract: Large-scale cell microscopy screens are used in drug discovery and molecular biology research to study the effects of millions of chemical and genetic perturbations on cells. To use these images in downstream analysis, we need models that can map each image into a feature space that represents diverse biological phenotypes consistently, in the sense that perturbations with similar biological effects have similar representations. In this work, we present the largest foundation model for cell microscopy data to date, a new 1.9 billion-parameter ViT-G/8 MAE trained on over 8 billion microscopy image crops. Compared to a previous published ViT-L/8 MAE, our new model achieves a 60% improvement in linear separability of genetic perturbations and obtains the best overall performance on whole-genome biological relationship recall and replicate consistency benchmarks. Beyond scaling, we developed two key methods that improve performance: (1) training on a curated and diverse dataset; and, (2) using biologically motivated linear probing tasks to search across each transformer block for the best candidate representation of whole-genome screens. We find that many self-supervised vision transformers, pretrained on either natural or microscopy images, yield significantly more biologically meaningful representations of microscopy images in their intermediate blocks than in their typically used final blocks. More broadly, our approach and results provide insights toward a general strategy for successfully building foundation models for large-scale biological data.

metadata.abstract: Deriving insights from experimentally generated datasets requires methods that can account for random and systematic measurement errors and remove them in order to accurately represent the underlying effects of the conditions being tested. Here we present a framework for pretraining on large-scale microscopy datasets that includes three steps: (1) curating a set of diverse and self-consistent training samples, (2) scaling training of an appropriate foundation model architecture on this dataset, (3) evaluating intermediate layers of the trained model to identify the best representation for downstream tasks. Using this strategy, we present the largest foundation model for cell microscopy data to our knowledge, a new 1.9 billion-parameter ViT-G/8 MAE trained on over 8 billion microscopy image crops. Compared to a previous published ViT-L/8 MAE, our new model achieves a 60\% improvement in linear separability of genetic perturbations and obtains the best overall performance on whole-genome relationship recall, batch correction replicate consistency, and compound-gene activity prediction benchmarks.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain curated training data, a scaled MAE-G/8, and intermediate-block selection through biological probes. v2 extends the abstract's best-performance claim to compound–gene activity prediction and emphasizes efficient use of experimental data, while preserving the original methodological contribution and scaling claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning unsuccessful DINO training, the resulting allocation of compute to MAEs, and the unresolved potential of other SSL and fine-tuning recipes. It attributes lower external-data recall to assay differences and variability, and interprets continued MAE reconstruction-loss improvement as suggesting further scaling potential. These materially expand the interpretation and qualification of the findings.

D1.justification: v2 announces inference, visualization and benchmarking code plus CA-MAE-S/16 weights, and supplies RxRx3-core access information. Appendices A.9 and A.11 add DINO hyperparameters and CellProfiler extraction, aggregation and missing-data details. Existing MAE hyperparameters are retained. Some disclosure remains inconsistent: Section 6 calls the baseline CellProfiler 4, whereas A.11 specifies version 2.2.0.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on external JUMP-CP images covering 7,976 gene knockouts and introduces compound–gene activity prediction on RxRx3-core, containing 735 genetic knockouts and 1,674 compounds across eight concentrations. These extend both acquisition conditions and task requirements beyond v1's genetic-perturbation evaluations. Existing RxRx1, RxRx3 and Anax coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds CellProfiler comparisons on JUMP-CP and RxRx3-core, a random baseline for compound–gene prediction, and microscopy-trained DINO models, including an MAE initialized variant in Appendix A.9. It removes the ImageNet WSL ViT-L/16 comparator from the original whole-genome comparison. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison approaches while changing membership in the retained benchmark.

E3.justification: Whole-genome recall changes from four database-specific columns to an aggregate over five databases, including Signor. New evaluations introduce PCA-based alignment, four-crop well averaging, concentration-dependent compound–gene ranking, and exclusion of 4,749 wells lacking CellProfiler features for all RxRx3-core models. Original MAE training budgets and probing settings remain unchanged. Appendix A.6 still lists only the original four relationship databases.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit generalization test across laboratories and assay protocols, examines trimming and compound concentration in the new prediction task, and diagnoses unsuccessful DINO training through loss curves and scratch-versus-fine-tuning results (Figure 7 and Table 6). The original Anax cell-condition checks and FLOP correlations are retained, with the latter moved from Appendix A.9 to A.10.

E5.justification: Beyond v1's existing permutation and replicate-consistency tests, v2 introduces mean and standard deviation over three null-sampling seeds for whole-genome recall, uncertainty reporting for JUMP-CP, and standard deviations and error bars over 100 benchmark seeds for RxRx3-core. It also reports improvement z-scores. These quantify benchmark sampling variability; they do not establish repeated model training.

E6.justification: v2 replaces database-specific whole-genome table entries with aggregate recall and adds substantial new results. JUMP-CP StringDB recall is 0.235 for trimmed MAE-G/8 versus 0.191 for CellProfiler; RxRx3-core mean average precision is 0.309 ± 0.015 for trimmed MAE-G/8 versus 0.290 ± 0.017 for the previous MAE-L/8. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over corresponding v1 experiments. The stated 42% gain concerns z-scores, 3.77 to 5.38. Original probing and KS/CVM results are largely retained.

M1.justification: The proposed Phenoprints-16M curation procedure, MAE architectures and losses, and linear-probe selection of intermediate blocks remain unchanged. The newly reported DINO training attempts are comparison experiments, rather than changes to the proposed MAE method.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around data efficiency, replacing the original contribution bullets with a developed narrative. Related-work topics are reordered, the discussion is expanded, and dedicated external-evaluation, compound–gene benchmarking, limitations/reproducibility and impact sections restructure the paper.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, moves the model inventory into the appendix, restructures the whole-genome table, and adds benchmark tables, a concentration plot and a DINO loss plot. The original replicate-similarity distribution figure is removed, while retained figures are resized or relocated. Figure 1's caption loses its detailed model-to-bar mapping and ends after introducing that mapping.

R1.justification: The principal positioning relative to Kraus, Celik and intermediate-layer research remains intact. v2 adds contextual references on language-model data curation, mechanistic interpretability, alternative SSL/fine-tuning approaches, CellProfiler and RxRx3-core, while removing some broad biological foundation-model background. This updates and extends the context without fundamentally redefining the claimed relationship to prior work.

T1.justification: The block-selection definition and perturbation-consistency, permutation-p-value, KS and CVM equations remain unchanged. v2 adds no original theorem, proof or substantive derivation; its discussion of MAE–contrastive relationships cites existing work.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's lack of validation on data from other laboratories and direct compound–gene prediction. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained material can be matched despite substantial reformatting and added evaluations in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds JUMP-CP evaluation, RxRx3-core compound–gene prediction, and microscopy DINO training experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original MAE training experiments, RxRx1 and Anax linear probes, whole-genome RxRx3 benchmarks, and supplementary cell-condition and scaling analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Transformers have had tremendous impact for several sequence related tasks, largely due to their ability to retrieve from any part of the sequence via softmax based dot-product attention. This mechanism plays a crucial role in Transformer's performance. We analyze the gradients backpropagated through the softmax operation in the attention mechanism and observe that these gradients can often be small. This poor gradient signal backpropagation can lead to inefficient learning of parameters preceeding the attention operations. To this end, we introduce a new attention mechanism called LASER, which we analytically show to admit a larger gradient signal. We show that LASER attention can be implemented by making small modifications to existing attention implementations. We conduct experiments on autoregressive large language models (LLMs) with upto 7.7 billion parameters with an average improvement of upto 1.44% over standard attention on downstream evaluations and 1.65% finetuning improvements. Additionally, LASER demonstrates generalization performance improvement across a variety of tasks (vision, text and speech):Vision Transformer (ViT) on Imagenet, Conformer on the Librispeech speech-to-text and BERT with 2.2 billion parameters.
arxiv_record.authors: Sai Surya Duvvuri, Inderjit S. Dhillon
arxiv_record.title: LASER: Attention with Exponential Transformation

C1.justification: The central gradient-bottleneck and LASER contribution claims remain. The abstract and introduction extend the reported scale from 2.2B to 7.7B parameters and add a fine-tuning benefit claim. The conclusion also moderates 'fix' to 'alleviate' when describing the gradient problem.

C2.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a substantive explanation linking fewer training spikes to reduced gradient saturation and conjectured residual-like behavior during strong self-attention. Section 4.3 newly interprets temperature and QK-normalization effects and attributes poorer per-dimension-temperature results to hyperparameters tuned without that component. These explanations extend the original gradient-magnitude interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 adds architecture and training-budget details for the larger and differential models, a per-dimension-scaling implementation reference, and reconstruction-test details: 4,800 cached tensors of shape (1024, 8, 256), four TPUv5 chips, and sixteen A100s. The core JAX implementation and original hyperparameter search tables are retained.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and tasks remain C4, the existing downstream language tasks, Wikipedia/MLPerf BERT, ImageNet, and LibriSpeech. SuperGLUE fine-tuning uses tasks already evaluated in v1. ARC Easy disappears from the 2.2B table but remains in v2 Tables 6–7; the new experiments principally change models and procedures within retained coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares LASER with standard attention. v2 adds evaluated temperature-tuned and per-dimension-temperature comparators in Table 2, QK-normalization and temperature variants in the vision/speech comparisons (Tables 4–5), and DiffTransformer against LASER+DiffTransformer in Table 7.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 7.7B models trained on 44B tokens, 2.2B DiffTransformer models trained on 24B tokens, ten-epoch SuperGLUE fine-tuning, and BF16 training and reconstruction tests. These are additional protocols, not replacements for the retained C4 setup. The OPTList evaluation protocol is removed, and vision/speech reporting expands beyond validation results to training and test results.

E4.justification: v2 adds temperature and normalization ablations, a parameter-versus-loss power-law fit, DiffTransformer compatibility tests, and Appendix A.5 analyses of early training spikes, BF16 training, and numerical reconstruction on TPUs and GPUs. The original depth/MLP and LAMB analyses remain, while the OPTList comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix A.4 and Table 10 newly report downstream means and standard deviations across five checkpoints. This is a focused uncertainty-reporting addition, not evidence of five independent training runs or increased seed counts. The primary vision/speech experiments retain their five-initialization reporting.

E6.justification: v2 revises the downstream and vision/speech results and removes OPTList scores. For example, ViT validation errors change from 0.2527/0.2412 in v1's text to 0.2532/0.2417 in v2 Table 4 for Standard/LASER. New LASER/comparator averages include 53.97/52.53 for 7.7B models and 51.52/50.59 for DiffTransformer variants; these use new experimental settings. Table 1 and BERT results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The central LASER formula, stabilization trick, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Section 4.4 adds LASER+DiffTransformer, applying the exponential/logarithmic transformation separately to two attention branches before their weighted subtraction. This is a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the introduction, method exposition, and original experimental prose remain. Targeted rewrites update the abstract, related work, and experiment summaries. New experimental and appendix subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement are added, while the standalone limitations section is removed.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Table 2 is reoriented and expanded, Figure 2's panels are stacked, and vision/speech curves are replaced by multi-metric tables. New scaling and stability figures appear. v1 Figure 4 is retained as v2 Figure 5 in Appendix A.3, rather than deleted.

R1.justification: Related work shifts substantially from efficient attention, sparse attention, and state-space models toward softmax sharpness, QK-normalization, and Lipschitz properties. v2 adds discussion of Veličković et al., Dehghani et al., and Kim et al., plus Differential Transformer elsewhere, while removing much of the Mamba, routing, Longformer, and context-parallelism discussion.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects causal masking from multiplying logits by a binary mask to adding a mask with zero for permitted positions and negative infinity otherwise. This changes the mathematical specification without establishing a code change. Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and the Appendix A.2 proof remain substantively unchanged; the new residual-connection explanation is conjectural.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's empirical support through temperature and normalization controls (Tables 2, 4–5) and direct precision and stability checks (Appendix A.5). These address important gaps in attributing benefits to LASER and assessing practical reliability. Removed OPTList evidence, checkpoint-only uncertainty, a conjectural stability explanation, and inconsistencies between some Table 2 summaries and entries limit the gains, but the stronger controlled evaluation provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LASER attention. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial layout changes and relocation of training curves.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, SuperGLUE fine-tuning, attention variants, and numerical-precision and training-stability experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results for C4 language models, BERT, ImageNet ViT, and LibriSpeech Conformer, including architecture and optimizer ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have improved significantly in their capabilities, but their complex architecture makes their safety alignment challenging. In this paper, we reveal an uneven distribution of harmful information across the intermediate layers of the image encoder and show that skipping a certain set of layers and exiting early can increase the chance of the VLM generating harmful responses. We call it as "Image enCoder Early-exiT" based vulnerability (ICET). Our experiments across three VLMs: LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Llama 3.2, show that performing early exits from the image encoder significantly increases the likelihood of generating harmful outputs. To tackle this, we propose a simple yet effective modification of the Clipped-Proximal Policy Optimization (Clip-PPO) algorithm for performing layer-wise multi-modal RLHF for VLMs. We term this as Layer-Wise PPO (L-PPO). We evaluate our L-PPO algorithm across three multimodal datasets and show that it consistently reduces the harmfulness caused by early exits.

C1.justification: The finding that intermediate encoder representations can compromise safety is retained. However, the abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution from diagnosing this vulnerability to proposing L-PPO and claiming effective mitigation, theoretical improvement guarantees and preserved utility. These are substantive new claims beyond renaming the vulnerability ICET.

C2.justification: Beyond the retained OOD explanation, v2 explains disagreements between binary safety judgments and reward scores, discusses incoherent early-layer outputs and evaluator errors, and explicitly limits L-PPO to per-layer alignment. It also distinguishes partial improvements from failures and frames ICET as an architectural safety blind spot rather than a new jailbreak attack (Section 4.2, Appendices E-G).

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation information absent from v1: LoRA rank 8, scaling 16 and dropout 0.05; Adam optimization; PPO epoch ranges; value-loss and adaptive-KL settings; PyTorch; and 2-4 NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs (Appendix F). It also supplies additional data-construction details and promises code, preprocessing scripts and aligned weights, without establishing their actual availability.

E1.justification: The original 100-pair dataset is retained as Custom Prompts (CP). v2 adds broader harmful-query categories and natural, generated and noisy image inputs through RedTeam/Jailbreak-V28K, plus AdvBench-COCO evaluation and HH-RLHF reward-model training. VQA-v2 and safe XSTest prompts introduce distinct utility and over-refusal tasks (Section 4.1, Appendices B-C and J-K).

E2.justification: v1 compares default inference with intermediate-layer inference without evaluating an alternative alignment method. v2 adds one explicit alignment comparator, supervised fine-tuning, against L-PPO and the original model using RedTeam-2K training and CP testing (Appendix L, Tables 21-22).

E3.justification: v2 adds alignment train/test protocols and LLaVA-NeXT experiments, supplements mean ASR and toxicity with reward scores, VQA accuracy and refusal metrics, and drops maximum-ASR/toxicity summaries. New procedures include blinded, shuffled human judging by three annotators assessing 200 outputs each, and string-matched refusal evaluation on 150 safe XSTest prompts (Appendices H and K).

E4.justification: v2 adds utility-preservation and over-refusal analyses, a reported value-loss-coefficient sensitivity search, and strong, partial and failed mitigation case studies (Table 3, Appendices F-G and J-K). Conversely, the separate Llama Guard 2 and 3 robustness checks in v1 Figures 4-5 are no longer reported.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports aggregation across three human annotators and inter-annotator agreement using Fleiss' kappa, 0.8916 (Appendix H). Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive mitigation, utility, refusal and human-rated results. For example, CP average ASR is 64.62% before alignment, 37.96% after L-PPO and 55.14% after SFT (Tables 2 and 21); human-rated CP ASR changes from 50.21% to 16.74% (Table 15). The reported original early-layer LLaVA-1.5 AASR also differs between versions: 49.995% in v1 Table 2 versus 75.38% in v2 Table 2. This unexplained baseline revision cannot establish a same-setting performance gain or loss.

M1.justification: The intermediate-layer projection procedure is retained and renamed ICET. The substantive addition is Layer-wise Clip-PPO: reward-guided optimization of the language backbone using a selected intermediate layer's embeddings, with clipped updates and KL regularization while freezing the image encoder and projector (Section 3.2, Algorithm 1).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around ICET and mitigation. Background becomes a broader related-work and research-gap section; methodology and experiments gain substantial internal structure; and a discussion section is introduced. The appendices are reorganized into dedicated datasets, metrics, limitations, implementation, analysis and theory sections.

P2.justification: The overview is redrawn to incorporate L-PPO (v1 Figure 1 becomes v2 Figure 2), and v2 adds a first-page demonstration and three-panel before/after results. v1 Table 1 becomes the expanded, color-coded v2 Table 4. New human-evaluation, utility and SFT tables substantially change the presentation, while retained examples and Llama 3.2 plots are relocated or regrouped.

R1.justification: The research positioning expands from cross-modal attacks and LLM layer analysis to dynamic early exiting, preference optimization and multimodal RLHF, with new discussions of works by Bakhtiarnia, Xu, Uzkent, Schulman, Rafailov and Sun. The new gap analysis and discussion also connect the vulnerability to multilayer feature fusion, including DenseConnector (Sections 1-2 and 5).

T1.justification: v1 provides forward-pass and metric equations without policy-improvement theory. v2 adds MDP definitions, a policy-improvement lemma, a cited performance bound and an argument extending it to L-PPO (Section 3.3), together with GAE derivations and a formal expected-regret interpretation of ICET (Appendices I and M).

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow 100-pair exploratory evidence through broader evaluation, an implemented mitigation, an SFT comparison and blinded human validation. Utility controls address an important alternative explanation: VQA accuracy changes only from 48.73 to 48.23, while average safe-prompt refusal falls from 0.047 to 0.040 (Tables 3 and 20). Unexplained baseline revisions and the unsupported leap from a conditional policy bound to guaranteed safety improvement remain weaknesses, but the expanded empirical validation and implementation disclosure provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same intermediate-image-encoder safety vulnerability. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, terminology and substantially expanded scope.

after.justification: Section 4 and the appendices report original vulnerability and alignment experiments, including LLaVA-NeXT results, human evaluations, visual-question-answering utility and over-refusal measurements.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix E report original layer-wise attack-success rates, toxicity scores and generated responses for LLaVA-1.5 and Llama 3.2.

arxiv_record.abstract:
The performance of embodied agents has been shown to improve by increasing
model parameters, dataset size, and compute. This has been demonstrated in
domains from robotics to video games, when generative learning objectives on
offline datasets (pre-training) are used to model an agent's behavior
(imitation learning) or their environment (world modeling). This paper
characterizes the role of scale in these tasks more precisely. Going beyond the
simple intuition that `bigger is better', we show that the same types of power
laws found in language modeling also arise in world modeling and imitation
learning (e.g. between loss and optimal model size). However, the coefficients
of these laws are heavily influenced by the tokenizer, task \& architecture --
this has important implications on the optimal sizing of models and data.
arxiv_record.authors:
Tim Pearce, Tabish Rashid, Dave Bignell, Raluca Georgescu, Sam Devlin,
  Katja Hofmann
arxiv_record.title: Scaling Laws for Pre-training Agents and World Models
