arxiv_record.abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions is fundamental in machine learning and statistics. As datasets grow larger, computational efficiency becomes increasingly important, particularly in reducing adaptive complexity, namely the number of sequential rounds required for sampling algorithms. While recent works have introduced several parallelizable techniques, they often exhibit suboptimal convergence rates and remain significantly weaker than the latest lower bounds for log-concave sampling. To address this, we propose a novel parallel sampling method that improves adaptive complexity dependence on dimension $d$ reducing it from $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log^2 d)$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log d)$. which is even optimal for log-concave sampling with some specific adaptive complexity. Our approach builds on parallel simulation techniques from scientific computing.
arxiv_record.authors: Huanjian Zhou and Masashi Sugiyama
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted to ICML2025 and this version corrects errors from the previous submission

metadata.abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional probability distributions is fundamental in machine learning and statistics. As datasets grow larger, computational efficiency becomes increasingly important, particularly in reducing *adaptive complexity*, namely the number of sequential rounds required for sampling algorithms. While recent works have introduced several parallelizable techniques, they often exhibit suboptimal convergence rates and remain significantly weaker than the latest lower bounds for log-concave sampling.To address this, we propose a novel parallel sampling method that improves adaptive complexity dependence on dimension $d$ reducing it from $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log^2 d)$ to $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log d)$.  Our approach builds on parallel simulation techniques from scientific computing.

C1.justification: v1 claims faster sampling under isoperimetry and matching a lower bound for exponentially small accuracy. v3 restricts the sampling contribution to strongly log-concave targets and removes the optimality/lower-bound-matching assertions. The logarithmic dimension dependence and diffusion-sampling contribution remain.

C2.justification: New Remarks 4.5–4.6 and 5.6–5.7 substantially qualify the efficiency claims: improving condition-number dependence remains open, limited processors can eliminate the advantage, and large score Lipschitz constants increase the required iteration depth. v3 also acknowledges that uniform Lipschitzness may fail near the data endpoint.

D1.justification: Appendix C.3.1 newly specifies log(1/η) ≲ T in the parameter prescription. Conversely, C.1 drops v1's explicit stopping relation t_N = T − η and its O(√η) Wasserstein-error guidance. These are changes to parameter documentation; neither version supplies implementation measurements or code/data access.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or empirical evaluation scenarios. Both study Langevin sampling and diffusion-model sampling theoretically; the stronger distributional assumption changes theoretical scope rather than evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. After matching updated citations, theoretical Tables 1–2 retain the same comparator membership.

E3.justification: Neither PDF reports experimental splits, training budgets, evaluation metrics, or testing procedures. Revised theoretical parameter conditions do not constitute changes to an experimental protocol.

E4.justification: Neither version contains original ablations, robustness tests, sensitivity experiments, or case studies. The new processor-count and Lipschitz discussions are theoretical qualifications rather than additional empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports empirical run counts, seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or related uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: No measured performance values or empirical findings are added, removed, or revised. Tables 1–2 retain the headline asymptotic rates for the same methods; changes concern theoretical assumptions and guarantees.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain diagonal updates across time slices, repeated inner Picard iterations for Langevin sampling, and the exponential integrator with early stopping for diffusion sampling. Pseudocode restructuring and expanded explanations do not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, 'iteration complexity' becomes 'adaptive complexity', and selected technical explanations are expanded. Appendix C consolidates existing material into revised subsections and gains a roadmap. The main section sequence and most proof text remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column conference layout. Tables 1–2 are reformatted with highlighted proposed-method rows and assumption markers. v1's lower-bound comparison Figure 1 is removed, while its algorithm schematic Figure 2 is retained as v3's Figure 1; both pseudocode displays are reformatted.

R1.justification: The comparison with Zhou, Wang and Sugiyama (2024), central to v1's optimality positioning, and its reference are removed. v3 instead emphasizes improved upper bounds under stronger assumptions and adds connections to finite-resource parallel MCMC, diffusion inference, and Lipschitz singularities in Remarks 4.5–5.7.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.2 replaces the log-Sobolev assumption with strong log-concavity, substantially restricting its guarantee. New remarks state finite-processor and Lipschitz-dependent complexity bounds, and Appendix C.3.1 adds log(1/η) ≲ T. Appendix A removes the f-divergence theorem and revises the Novikov-condition definition; C.2.1 replaces the detailed Girsanov application with a citation.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important mismatch: Theorem 4.2 now assumes strong log-concavity, consistent with the gradient-contraction argument already used in Appendix B.2, rather than claiming the guarantee under LSI alone. Removing optimality assertions and explaining processor and score-regularity limitations further improves reliability. The narrower scope and shortened appendix explanations are outweighed by this correction to a principal guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same parallel Picard algorithms and sampling problems. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C support comparison despite changes in title, theoretical scope, and layout.

after.justification: v3 likewise contains theoretical analysis and proofs, with no original experimental, simulation-run, user-study, or data-analysis results in the main text or appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports algorithms and theoretical convergence guarantees, including proof appendices. Its figures and tables present theoretical comparisons and an algorithm schematic, not original empirical outcomes.

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce ResGen, an efficient Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ)-based generative model for high-fidelity generation with fast sampling. RVQ improves data fidelity by increasing the number of quantization steps, referred to as depth, but deeper quantization typically increases inference steps in generative models. To address this, ResGen directly predicts the vector embedding of collective tokens rather than individual ones, ensuring that inference steps remain independent of RVQ depth. Additionally, we formulate token masking and multi-token prediction within a probabilistic framework using discrete diffusion and variational inference. We validate the efficacy and generalizability of the proposed method on two challenging tasks across different modalities: conditional image generation on ImageNet 256x256 and zero-shot text-to-speech synthesis. Experimental results demonstrate that ResGen outperforms autoregressive counterparts in both tasks, delivering superior performance without compromising sampling speed. Furthermore, as we scale the depth of RVQ, our generative models exhibit enhanced generation fidelity or faster sampling speeds compared to similarly sized baseline models.
arxiv_record.authors: Jaehyeon Kim, Taehong Moon, Keon Lee, Jaewoong Cho
arxiv_record.title: Efficient Generative Modeling with Residual Vector Quantization-Based Tokens

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central contributions: cumulative RVQ-embedding prediction, masking within a diffusion/variational framework, and efficient high-fidelity image and speech generation with inference steps decoupled from RVQ depth. The new experiments principally support these existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of depth-specific efficiency gains, MAR latency versus throughput, masking-schedule behavior, and architectural tradeoffs against VAR and LFQ-based models. It acknowledges MAGVIT-v2 and MaskBit's lower FID while arguing for representation flexibility. The original KV-caching, FSQ and missing low-step theoretical justification limitations are relocated unchanged to Appendix D.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the training masking function, codebook size, projection dimensions and detailed waveform-autoencoder architecture and losses. Table 4 supplies exact guidance schedules, top-p and temperatures. It also first specifies 50K samples for FID and A100 timing hardware, adds AI-Hub attribution and changes the project-page address. These substantially improve documentation without establishing that every newly disclosed setting changed.

E1.justification: The explicit evaluations remain ImageNet 256×256 and speech continuation/cross-sentence generation. However, v3 newly acknowledges using AI-Hub datasets, while v1 does not identify the speech corpora. The PDFs do not establish whether this represents additional data coverage or newly disclosed provenance.

E2.justification: The same-RVQ comparison expands from RQ-Transformer alone in v1 to include a depth-wise MaskGIT adaptation in v3 Table 1. Table 8 adds MAGVIT-v2 and MaskBit comparisons using their published scores. These materially broaden the relevant masked-generation comparisons; the external speech comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The depth-4 vision comparison is replaced by depth-16 comparisons with near-matched model sizes and a shared 2.8M-step training budget. Speech evaluation changes from 16 to 25 inference steps and includes 32- and 72-level codecs. New experiments vary MAR autoregressive/diffusion steps and cross-evaluate masking schedules using models trained for 400K iterations with EMA checkpoints.

E4.justification: The original sampling-step, top-p and temperature study is retained. v3 adds direct-token versus cumulative-embedding prediction, AR-ResGen controls isolating depth prediction, parameter scaling, reconstruction/generation quality versus RVQ depth, faster-MAR sweeps and training/sampling schedule sensitivity (Table 1, Figure 3 and Tables 5–7). These substantially expand the questions tested.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The main depth-16 guided image FID changes from 1.95 to 1.93. Table 3 replaces the original speech model's continuation/cross-sentence WER of 1.79/1.72 with Melvae-ResGen results of 1.94/1.75 and Rvqvae-ResGen results of 1.86/1.70. These speech results use changed models and inference settings, so they are not same-setting gains or losses. v3 also adds substantial architectural, reconstruction, MAR and masking-schedule results.

M1.justification: The core ResGen algorithm remains, but v3 adds substantial architectural variants. Rvqvae-ResGen uses a separately trained waveform/STFT autoencoder with ConvNeXt blocks and 72 RVQ levels alongside the existing 32-level MelVAE approach. AR-ResGen retains autoregressive spatial generation while replacing RQ-Transformer's depth transformer with a cumulative-embedding MLP; a direct-token prediction variant is also introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, related-work discussion and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Vision results are reorganized into ablation and benchmark subsections, training details are organized by modality, additional discussion forms Appendix C, and the former Section 7 becomes Appendix D. ResGen-d8/d16 terminology changes to ResGen-rvq8/rvq16.

P2.justification: The small original Table 2 is replaced by a two-part ablation table. v3 adds Tables 4–8 and the RVQ-depth reconstruction/generation plot, and expands the speech table. Figure 1's arrows and labels and Figure 2's curves/captions are revised. The original sampling plot and image galleries are retained with renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds substantive positioning against HART, MAGVIT-v2 and MaskBit while removing the opening VQ-GAN/DALL-E discussion. Appendix C develops extensive distinctions from VAR, MAR and LFQ-based masked models. ConvNeXt and Vocos references support the new audio architecture; publication updates to existing references are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds explicit asymptotic projection-cost estimates, including O(O*K*H) and the low-rank expression O(O*K*h + H*h). The existing discrete-diffusion formulation, variational bounds and Jensen-based objective derivation remain substantively unchanged; their notation and equation-number changes are presentational.

improvement.justification: v1's single same-token vision comparison did not isolate depth prediction from the generation framework. v3's controlled Table 1 comparisons and AR-ResGen directly address this weakness, while the additional sensitivity studies, faster-MAR comparisons and detailed settings substantially improve experimental rigor and reproducibility. Some new interpretations overgeneralize: Table 7's exponential-sampling advantage depends on classifier-free guidance. These limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ResGen work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 reports original image and speech results, architectural ablations, reconstruction measurements, faster-MAR comparisons and masking-schedule experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation and speech-synthesis results in Tables 1–3, plus sampling ablations in Appendix B.2.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are pivotal in graph-based learning, particularly excelling in node classification. However, their scalability is hindered by the need for multi-hop data during inference, limiting their application in latency-sensitive scenarios. Recent efforts to distill GNNs into multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) for faster inference often underutilize the layer-level insights of GNNs. In this paper, we present TINED, a novel approach that distills GNNs to MLPs on a layer-by-layer basis using Teacher Injection and Dirichlet Energy Distillation techniques. We focus on two key operations in GNN layers: feature transformation (FT) and graph propagation (GP). We recognize that FT is computationally equivalent to a fully-connected (FC) layer in MLPs. Thus, we propose directly transferring teacher parameters from an FT in a GNN to an FC layer in the student MLP, enhanced by fine-tuning. In TINED, the FC layers in an MLP replicate the sequence of FTs and GPs in the GNN. We also establish a theoretical bound for GP approximation. Furthermore, we note that FT and GP operations in GNN layers often exhibit opposing smoothing effects: GP is aggressive, while FT is conservative. Using Dirichlet energy, we develop a DE ratio to measure these effects and propose Dirichlet Energy Distillation to convey these characteristics from GNN layers to MLP layers. Extensive experiments show that TINED outperforms GNNs and leading distillation methods across various settings and seven datasets. Source code are available at https://github.com/scottjiao/TINED_ICML25/.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contributions: layer-wise distillation through teacher injection and DED, a GP approximation bound, and effective, fast MLP inference. They still summarize experiments as covering seven datasets despite v2's additional coverage.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations linking embedding similarity to knowledge transfer, deeper vanilla-MLP degradation to overfitting, and sensitivity results to tuning and sampling tradeoffs. It removes the description of the bound as demonstrating tightness and adds heterogeneous/dynamic graphs as future directions; the student-depth limitation remains.

D1.justification: The code-access statement changes from supplementary material to an explicit repository link. Appendix A.9 supplies VQGraph teacher and student hyperparameter search spaces. Existing TINED implementation details, hardware, training-time information and search spaces are retained after relocation.

E1.justification: V2 adds Squirrel and Amazon-ratings evaluations under the production setting (Table 6), extending coverage to explicitly heterophilic Wikipedia and product co-purchasing graphs. All seven original datasets remain.

E2.justification: KRD and FFG2M join Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–4; VQGraph is newly evaluated in Appendix A.9. Tables 8–9 introduce a four-layer vanilla MLP comparator. The standalone MLP comparison disappears from Figure 4 but remains elsewhere.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs include two-versus-four-layer MLP controls, eta/beta/zeta sweeps, embedding comparisons at epochs 0 and 500, and separately trained and tuned VQGraph teachers. The original dataset splits, production partition, accuracy metric and validation-based model selection remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds fine-tuning and DED-weight sensitivity tests, sampling-ratio analysis, MLP-depth controls and initialization/convergence t-SNE analyses (Tables 5, 7–9, 12; Figures 5 and 9). These substantially extend the retained component ablations, approximation-error analysis and DE-ratio studies.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten trials with distinct random seeds and report means and standard deviations; Figure 1 also averages ten repetitions. Added result tables follow the existing reporting practice, without new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Shared entries in Tables 1–2, ablations, approximation errors and retained Figure 4 bars are unchanged. Numerous results are added, including KRD exceeding TINED on Pubmed production accuracy (76.00 versus 75.79) and TINED achieving 41.95 on Squirrel production. New MLP-control tables report different two-layer MLP scores from the main tables without explaining the discrepancy.

M1.justification: Teacher injection, gradient-controlled fine-tuning, paired FC layers, the DED objective and adaptations to other GNN teachers are unchanged. Edge sampling and DE-ratio transformations already appear in v1 Appendix A.4; their subsequent evaluation does not introduce new method components.

P1.justification: V2 revises the title and abstract, edits selected related-work and results passages, shortens the Teacher Injection heading, and reorders appendix subsections. Acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. The main section sequence and most method exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain comparator columns, seven additional tables and two t-SNE figures are introduced, and existing displays are relocated or resized. Figure 4 is redrawn with additional baselines, a revised legend, removal of the standalone MLP bar and a narrower accuracy axis.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds explicit layer-wise distillation precedents, FreeKD, MLPInit and broader GNN application references, while removing some generic cross-domain references. V2 also distinguishes VQGraph's teacher retraining from fixed-teacher distillation. The central research positioning remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1, its assumptions and pseudoinverse proof, the Dirichlet-energy definitions and other-teacher derivations are retained. The proof moves from Appendix A.3 to A.2, with equation renumbering but no substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical validation by addressing important gaps in comparator coverage and testing heterophilic applicability, parameter sensitivity and model-depth alternatives. These additions make the retained method and results more thoroughly assessable. Unexplained MLP-score discrepancies and missing heterophilic split details limit reproducibility of some additions, but do not outweigh the broader comparative and diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TINED and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite retitling, renumbering and appendix reordering.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and reports additional baseline comparisons, heterophilic benchmarks, sensitivity analyses and embedding visualizations.

before.justification: V1 reports original node-classification experiments, inference-time measurements, ablations and approximation-error analyses across seven datasets.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Adaptive optimizers such as Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) have been central to the
success of large language models. However, they often require to maintain
optimizer states throughout training, which can result in memory requirements
several times greater than the model footprint. This overhead imposes
constraints on scalability and computational efficiency. Stochastic Gradient
Descent (SGD), in contrast, is a stateless optimizer, as it does not track
state variables during training. Consequently, it achieves optimal memory
efficiency. However, its capability in LLM training is limited (Zhao et al.,
2024b). In this work, we show that pre-processing SGD in a stateless manner can
achieve the same performance as the Adam optimizer for LLM training, while
drastically reducing the memory cost. Specifically, we propose to pre-process
the instantaneous stochastic gradients using normalization and whitening. We
show that normalization stabilizes gradient distributions, and whitening
counteracts the local curvature of the loss landscape. This results in SWAN
(SGD with Whitening And Normalization), a stochastic optimizer that eliminates
the need to store any optimizer states. Empirically, SWAN has the same memory
footprint as SGD, achieving $\approx 50\%$ reduction on total end-to-end memory
compared to Adam. In language modeling tasks, SWAN demonstrates comparable or
even better performance than Adam: when pre-training the LLaMA model with 350M
and 1.3B parameters, SWAN achieves a 2x speedup by reaching the same evaluation
perplexity using half as many tokens.
arxiv_record.authors: Chao Ma, Wenbo Gong, Meyer Scetbon, Edward Meeds
arxiv_record.comments:
In v2 we have revised the related work, added more comprehensive
  citations, and clarified our key contributions

C1.justification: The central stateless-training, Adam-level performance, and approximately 50% memory-saving claims remain. v3 adds fast whitening with Adam-like throughput without distributed gradient processing as a central contribution, and extends the memory claim through combination with LOMO. It also explicitly positions SWAN as a composition of established operators.

C2.justification: v3 adds a hypothesis connecting changed update directions to slower early but stronger late convergence, discusses noisier NSDS conditioning, and identifies operator composition and distributed scalability as unresolved issues. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit qualifications that shared Hessian diagonal blocks do not establish zero off-diagonal blocks and that practical normalization differs from the theoretical parameter grouping.

D1.justification: Appendix J substantially expands variant-specific learning rates, scaling factors, warmup, precision, and baseline tuning grids. It specifies NSDS's two iterations with beta 0.4 and distinguishes cited from reproduced comparisons. v1 already disclosed using Adam outside the selected projection weights and FP32 whitening of BF16 gradients; those are retained details, not new disclosures.

E1.justification: C4 pretraining, quadratic and Rastrigin optimization, and simplified-transformer simulations remain. The limited coverage addition is Appendix B.2's transformer-gradient diagnostic using randomly generated token sequences, introducing a synthetic input condition beyond the retained natural-language experiments.

E2.justification: v3 Table 2 adds Apollo, Apollo-mini, and Momentum+GradWhitening to the pretraining comparisons, retaining Adam, GaLore, Low-Rank, LoRA, and ReLoRA. Momentum+GradWhitening is explicitly described as Muon-like with Nesterov acceleration disabled. These substantially expand the relevant comparator set.

E3.justification: The added SWAN† and SWAN‡ experiments enable warmup and use a global learning rate of 0.02 with scaling factor 0.05, unlike v1's principal no-warmup setting. NSDS experiments use two BF16 iterations. Throughput testing changes from four to eight A100 GPUs and adds explicit controls with and without distributed whitening computation; memory testing adds per-layer training. Consequently, throughput values are not directly comparable across versions.

E4.justification: v3 Appendix B adds condition-number and update-direction diagnostics, NSDS iteration-count sensitivity, and BF16-versus-FP32 ablations. Earlier component, learning-rate, warmup, and initialization studies remain, with synthetic optimization studies moved to Appendix I. However, v1 Figure 4's value-projection KL panel and loss-comparison panel are omitted from the retained gradient-stability experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The gradient-distribution experiment retains estimation using 16 additional minibatches of size 64; its mean and standard-deviation calculations are not newly introduced statistical reporting.

E6.justification: v1's SWAN perplexities remain unchanged under SWAN-0 in v3 Table 2. Added SWAN‡ results are 30.59, 22.61, 16.63, and 13.56 across the four model sizes, under its new configuration. The reproduced 350M Adam value changes from 20.11 to 19.24. Main-table GaLore values switch to cited results, with larger-model reproductions retained in Table 6. Memory estimates also change, including 1.3B SWAN/SWAN-0 from 2.60G to 2.98G, and new throughput and NSDS-ablation outcomes are reported.

M1.justification: GradNorm changes from mean subtraction and standard-deviation normalization in v1 to uncentered RMS-style normalization in v3. Section 4.2 and Algorithm 2 also introduce Newton-Schulz with diagonal substitution (NSDS), used by SWAN‡, alongside the retained standard Newton-Schulz procedure. These alter the core gradient preprocessing.

P1.justification: The title and substantial portions of the abstract, introduction, method explanation, experimental narrative, and conclusion are rewritten. Related work moves from Section 6 to Section 2, theoretical-validation experiments move into Appendix I, appendices are reorganized, and a dedicated Open Questions and Extensions section is added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with additional memory and whitening-throughput comparisons, and the main results table gains multiple variants and baselines. New tables present memory/expressiveness, throughput, NSDS ablations, and reproduced results. Convergence and ablation plots are redesigned, while the relocated gradient-stability figure is reduced from four panels to two.

R1.justification: The expanded related-work discussion situates SWAN against Muon, Apollo, SGD-Sal, Adam-mini, PSGD, LAMB, and established gradient-orthogonalization and Kronecker-curvature methods. It more explicitly acknowledges prior uses of its components and introduces the relationship to the authors' subsequent multi-normalized gradient-descent framework.

T1.justification: The GradNorm definition and Theorem 1 proof are revised to remove centering. v1's separate structured-Hessian/Newton-equivalence theorem and derivation in Appendices B.2 and H are removed; its distinct quadratic contraction theorem survives as v3 Theorem 2. The later printed RMS denominator also omits the square required by its accompanying RMS description, leaving a mathematical inconsistency.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens assessment of SWAN's practical efficiency. Table 3 exposes standard whitening's throughput penalty without distributed processing and tests the NSDS remedy under controlled settings; Appendix B evaluates its numerical behavior, while broader comparisons and Appendix J improve reproducibility. These address important weaknesses in v1's broad low-overhead account and limited comparator coverage. Removed theoretical caveats and the inconsistent RMS formula are drawbacks, but the gains in experimental scrutiny, implementation guidance, and research positioning outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SWAN optimizer research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and reports additional SWAN variants, reproduced baseline results, and experiments evaluating its new whitening approximation.

before.justification: v1 reports original C4 pretraining results, optimizer ablations, gradient-distribution measurements, synthetic optimization experiments, and memory and throughput measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Leveraging long contexts is crucial for advanced AI systems, but attention computation poses a scalability challenge. While scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) exhibits token sparsity, i.e. only a few pivotal tokens significantly contribute to output, exploiting this sparsity remains challenging. Existing methods either suffer from quality degradation or require substantial additional resources. We show that identifying pivotal tokens is a Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) problem. However, existing MIPS solutions are not well-suited for SDPA, as they are not GPU-friendly and often underperform due to the separated query and key distributions. This paper introduces HashAttention, framing pivotal token identification as a recommendation problem. Given a query, HashAttention encodes keys and queries in Hamming space, capturing the required semantic similarity, using learned mapping functions. HashAttention efficiently identifies pivotal tokens for a given query using bitwise operations and computes attention using only these tokens, improving the overall attention efficiency. Trained on generic data, HashAttention reduces tokens used by up to $16\times$ with minimal quality loss, requiring only 32 bits of auxiliary memory per token. Sparsity can be further improved to $32\times$ through task-specific fine-tuning. On A100 GPU, at $32\times$ sparsity, incorporating HashAttention reduces attention latency by up to $4.3\times$ in GPT-FAST and $2.54\times$ in FlashDecode, and achieves up to $3.12\times$ higher throughput for GPT-FAST.
arxiv_record.authors: Aditya Desai, Shuo Yang, Alejandro Cuadron, Matei Zaharia, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica
arxiv_record.title: HashAttention: Semantic Sparsity for Faster Inference

C1.justification: v1's headline 32× sparsity with under 0.6-point quality loss becomes a distinction between 16× sparsity with generic training and 32× with task-specific tuning. v2 adds MIPS equivalence and end-to-end throughput as central claims and broadens validation across models and benchmarks. Its conclusion's within-one-point claim nevertheless exceeds some reported results.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving learned query/key alignment, distractor removal, token-level memory access and context-dependent latency bottlenecks. Its limitations discussion emphasizes per-model training requirements and evaluation restricted to GPU-resident KV caches, replacing much of v1's future-work discussion about training variants and end-to-end sparse models.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access link where v1 promised a future release, specifies the three-layer mapping dimensions, and describes page-size-one attention using indices without physically gathering tokens. It also documents fine-tuning splits and new system configurations. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing that newly disclosed architecture details represent architectural changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds RULER's needle-retrieval, tracking, frequency/counting and QA tasks, and expands LongBench evaluation beyond v1's selected datasets to the full benchmark (Tables 2–5). Chinese tasks now receive explicit results, although v1 already mentioned Chinese transfer, so a newly introduced language cannot be inferred.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the comparator set; Exact-Top becomes Oracle. v2 adds random-projection LSH comparisons in Table 8 and FlashDecode in Figure 4. LightLLM remains plotted in the latency comparison. MagicPig is discussed, but v2 explicitly distinguishes its LSH ablation from a direct MagicPig evaluation.

E3.justification: v2 reports a revised LongBench protocol using the first 175 examples for evaluation and the last 25 for training, excluding MFQA from training; v1 describes OpenWebText training and 200 RepoBench evaluation examples. v2 also adds Mistral-7B, a 32-token RULER prompt offset, A100 measurements and batch-one end-to-end throughput. The 128-token LongBench offset and 512-token Table 1 budget remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds learned-versus-LSH comparisons, bit-width versus prediction loss and scoring latency, query/key cosine-similarity analysis, and generic-versus-task-tuned comparisons. v1's runtime-component breakdown in Figure 6(b) is removed. The recall plots are identical images relocated to v2's Appendix C, not new analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper explores image modeling from the frequency space and introduces DCTdiff, an end-to-end diffusion generative paradigm that efficiently models images in the discrete cosine transform (DCT) space. We investigate the design space of DCTdiff and reveal the key design factors. Experiments on different frameworks (UViT, DiT), generation tasks, and various diffusion samplers demonstrate that DCTdiff outperforms pixel-based diffusion models regarding generative quality and training efficiency. Remarkably, DCTdiff can seamlessly scale up to 512$\times$512 resolution without using the latent diffusion paradigm and beats latent diffusion (using SD-VAE) with only 1/4 training cost. Finally, we illustrate several intriguing properties of DCT image modeling. For example, we provide a theoretical proof of why 'image diffusion can be seen as spectral autoregression', bridging the gap between diffusion and autoregressive models. The effectiveness of DCTdiff and the introduced properties suggest a promising direction for image modeling in the frequency space. The code is https://github.com/forever208/DCTdiff.

The introduction's contributions and conclusion extend the claimed advantage from pixel diffusion to latent diffusion. v1 instead described its FFHQ 256 latent comparison as competitive.

C2.justification: New discussion explains the balance between VAE overhead and DCTdiff's additional Transformer tokens, qualifies inference efficiency by sampling steps and generation quality, and identifies a block-size tradeoff between convergence speed and quality. These extend the interpretation locally; the spectral-autoregression explanation and limitations concerning 1024×1024 generation and frequency-specific architectures remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds 512×512 configurations, SD-VAE parameter counts, and parameter-selection guidance; the timing experiment specifies its A100 hardware and sample count. Code access is unchanged. Conversely, Appendix C.1 removes the explicit 16× VAE compression ratio for the unchanged reconstruction comparison. The new guidance also says τ=98 while the main text and tables specify 98.25.

E1.justification: v2 adds FFHQ 512×512 and AFHQ 512×512 generation and extends reconstruction-compression evaluation to FFHQ 512×512. This introduces higher-resolution generation requirements and an animal-image domain beyond the retained datasets. ImageNet 256 reconstruction examples already appeared in v1.

E2.justification: Pixel UViT, latent UViT, DiT, and the existing compression/upsampling comparators are retained. Latent UViT was already evaluated in v1 Table 3. The rows incorrectly labeled UViT in v1's DiT Table 5 become DiT in v2 Table 4, consistent with the original caption, surrounding text, and unchanged baseline scores.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: scaling percentile τ becomes 98.25 rather than 96.5, several SNR factors change, and FFHQ 256 DCTdiff training steps increase from 200k to 300k. New protocols vary model depth and size, evaluate IS/precision/recall/CMMD, and time 10k generated samples on one A100. These are reported setting changes; the PDFs do not establish the provenance of every revised result.

E4.justification: v2 adds model-capacity analyses on three datasets, a B=4 versus B=8 block-size ablation, and inference-time versus quality analyses. Appendix B also revises the coefficient-pruning controls: ECS variants with m=0, 7, and 8 precede frequency reweighting, replacing the earlier m=0, 8, and 9 study. The c=3 SNR ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability around benchmark scores. The existing 50,000-sample Monte Carlo procedures in Appendices A.1 and A.4 remain unchanged; additional metrics do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Many DCTdiff scores are revised alongside changed settings, including FFHQ 256 DPM-Solver FID at NFE=100 from 5.92 to 5.08. Newly reported NFE=100 results are 7.07 versus latent UViT's 10.89 on FFHQ 512 and 8.76 versus 10.86 on AFHQ 512. v2 also adds timing, scaling, additional-metric and ablation results, and revises reconstruction scores, including FFHQ 256 m=8 from 0.58 to 0.49.

M1.justification: The DCTdiff pipeline, frequency tokenization and pruning, entropy-consistent scaling, frequency-reweighted objective, SNR-scaling procedure, and inverse-DCT generation remain unchanged. P1.justification: v2 rewrites portions of related work and the scaling explanation, separates cost and scalability into Sections 6.3-6.4, adds Appendices A.7-A.9 and an Impact Statement, and reorders ablation and qualitative subsections. P2.justification: v2 adds a front-page AFHQ image panel, expands and replaces generated-sample grids, restructures the high-resolution and training-cost tables, and adds timing, scaling, metric and block-size displays. The earlier ablation tables are reorganized into Table 14. Existing pipeline, theoretical, compression and upsampling figures are largely retained or relocated, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Sections 2.2 and 5.3 add discussion of wavelet diffusion, DCT-based VampPrior, spectral tokenization, and recent frequency-autoregressive work, including Phung, Kuzina and Tomczak, Esteves, Yu, and Huang. Some attention/linear-layer references are removed, and dataset/metric citations are added. These refine the existing positioning without replacing its central distinction between frequency modules and full DCT-space modeling.

T1.justification: v2 removes Section 4.3's assertion that reconstruction FID determines a lower bound on generative FID. Theorems 5.1 and 5.2, their appendix proofs, and the SNR derivations otherwise retain their mathematical substance. Renaming reconstruction FID to rFID does not change its calculation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the scalability and efficiency case, which v1 supported mainly with experiments up to 256×256 and convergence iterations. arxiv_record.abstract: Shock waves caused by earthquakes can be devastating. Generating realistic earthquake-caused ground motion waveforms help reducing losses in lives and properties, yet generative models for the task tend to generate subpar waveforms. We present High-fidelity Earthquake Groundmotion Generation System (HEGGS) and demonstrate its superior performance using earthquakes from North American, East Asian, and European regions. HEGGS exploits the intrinsic characteristics of earthquake dataset and learns the waveforms using an end-to-end differentiable generator containing conditional latent diffusion model and hi-fidelity waveform construction model. We show the learning efficiency of HEGGS by training it on a single GPU machine and validate its performance using earthquake databases from North America, East Asia, and Europe, using diverse criteria from waveform generation tasks and seismology. Once trained, HEGGS can generate three dimensional E-N-Z seismic waveforms with accurate P/S phase arrivals, envelope correlation, signal-to-noise ratio, GMPE analysis, frequency content analysis, and section plot analysis.
arxiv_record.authors: Jaeheun Jung, Jaehyuk Lee, Changhae Jung, Hanyoung Kim, Bosung Jung, Donghun Lee
arxiv_record.title: Broadband Ground Motion Synthesis by Diffusion Model with Minimal Condition

C2.justification: v2 interprets ACM as enabling unnormalized conventional-LDM training and adds mechanism explanations concerning source noise and diffusion time in Appendix J. Discussion adds qualifications about missing geological information for fictitious events and consistency across regional models. It removes v1's specific discussion of failures above magnitude 5, high-frequency deficiencies above 10 Hz and distant-station artifacts.

D1.justification: v2 adds regional data-selection and normalization recipes, explicit GMPE coefficients and assumptions, similarity-normalization disclosures, and training/inference pseudocode specifying optional source-waveform initialization. Existing hardware, optimizer and training-budget details are retained. Conversely, v1's explicit detrending and unknown-instrument-response exclusion descriptions are no longer documented.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands from Southern California SCEDC data to South Korean KMA and Italian INSTANCE data. Section 4.2.4 also evaluates deliberately altered earthquake magnitudes without a source waveform, a fictitious-event scenario discussed but not experimentally demonstrated in v1.

E2.justification: The four SCEDC baseline families remain SeismoGen, ConSeisGen, BBGAN and LDM. v2 Table 2 adds a paired-input BBGAN attempt reported as diverged, while Table 3 adds LDM+ACM comparisons with and without paired training. E3.justification: v2 introduces dataset-specific filtering, splits, EQT fine-tuning, normalization and regional GMPE calculations, plus magnitude-manipulation and unnormalized-LDM control protocols. Existing SCEDC coordinate bounds also change: latitude normalization uses 32.024809-36.151200 in v1 Equation (12), versus 32.0-37.9 in v2 Table 5, with longitude bounds revised too. This establishes a reported setting change, not that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds controls testing whether ACM enables conventional LDM to handle unnormalized waveforms and how paired training contributes independently of end-to-end training. Figure 6 adds controlled magnitude manipulation and spectral-response analysis. Regional frequency and virtual-station analyses expand, while the appendix retains fewer SCEDC positive and negative ablation examples.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and retain the statement that SeismoGen and ConSeisGen results reflect the best performance across 30 iterations. Neither adds seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Existing SCEDC Table 2 scores, the original four Table 3 rows and VAE reconstruction scores remain unchanged. v2 adds regional results, two ablation rows, BBGAN divergence and magnitude-response findings. For example, HEGGS with source input reports P/S MAE of 0.2763/0.4644 seconds on KMA. These are new results, not improved SCEDC scores. Table 1 removes the earlier precision and recall entries.

P1.justification: The abstract and discussion are substantially rewritten, Problem Statement and Seismic Dataset are consolidated into Key Idea, and architecture details move into the appendices. Evaluation is organized around three generation scenarios, with expanded explanatory material in Appendix J and consistent HEGGS terminology.

P2.justification: Tables gain regional groupings, Figures 2-5 become regional comparisons, and magnitude-manipulation and algorithm displays are added. Appendix galleries are substantially reduced and reorganized. Spectrogram axes also change from approximately 0-60 seconds and 0-50 Hz to 0-6 seconds and 0-3000 Hz in Figure 4 and Appendix H, conflicting with the stated data duration and sampling.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for KMA and INSTANCE, regional magnitude/GMPE calculations and magnitude scaling, including Han, Michelini, Di Bona, Emolo, Lanzano, Sheen and Geller. Positioning relative to GAN synthesis, LDM, TANGO and MP-SeNet remains essentially unchanged.

arxiv_record.abstract: The rapidly increasing size of large language models (LLMs) presents significant challenges in memory usage and computational costs. Quantizing both weights and activations can address these issues, with hardware-supported fine-grained scaling emerging as a promising solution to mitigate outliers. However, existing methods struggle to capture nuanced block data distributions. We propose BlockDialect, a block-wise fine-grained mixed format technique that assigns a per-block optimal number format from a formatbook for better data representation. Additionally, we introduce DialectFP4, a formatbook of FP4 variants (akin to dialects) that adapt to diverse data distributions. To leverage this efficiently, we propose a two-stage approach for online DialectFP4 activation quantization. Importantly, DialectFP4 ensures energy efficiency by selecting representable values as scaled integers compatible with low-precision integer arithmetic. BlockDialect achieves 10.78% (7.48%) accuracy gain on the LLaMA3-8B (LLaMA2-7B) model compared to MXFP4 format with lower bit usage per data, while being only 5.45% (2.69%) below full precision even when quantizing full-path matrix multiplication. Focusing on how to represent over how to scale, our work presents a promising path for energy-efficient LLM inference.
arxiv_record.authors: Wonsuk Jang, Thierry Tambe
arxiv_record.title: BlockDialect: Block-wise Fine-grained Mixed Format Quantization for Energy-Efficient LLM Inference

arxiv_record.abstract: Merging multiple expert models offers a promising approach for performing multi-task learning without accessing their original data. Existing methods attempt to alleviate task conflicts by sparsifying task vectors or promoting orthogonality among them. However, they overlook the fundamental target of model merging: the merged model performs as closely as possible to task-specific models on respective tasks. We find these methods inevitably discard task-specific information that, while causing conflicts, is crucial for performance. Based on our findings, we frame model merging as a constrained optimization problem ($\textit{i.e.}$, minimizing the gap between the merged model and individual models, subject to the constraint of retaining shared knowledge) and solve it via adaptive projective gradient descent. Specifically, we align the merged model with individual models by decomposing and reconstituting the loss function, alleviating conflicts through $\textit{data-free}$ optimization of task vectors. To retain shared knowledge, we optimize this objective by projecting gradients within a $\textit{shared subspace}$ spanning all tasks. Moreover, we view merging coefficients as adaptive learning rates and propose a task-aware, training-free strategy. Experiments show that our plug-and-play approach consistently outperforms previous methods, achieving state-of-the-art results across diverse architectures and tasks in both vision and NLP domains.
arxiv_record.authors: Yongxian Wei, Anke Tang, Li Shen, Zixuan Hu, Chun Yuan, Xiaochun Cao

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: constrained model merging, a data-free objective, shared-subspace gradient projection, adaptive coefficients, and broad empirical effectiveness. Added evaluations support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v3 adds focused interpretations of coefficient stability and difficult unseen-task transfer, discusses storage, routing, and data tradeoffs against dynamic merging, and explicitly identifies heterogeneous model shapes or layer counts as an unaddressed limitation. The original conflict-resolution and shared-knowledge explanations remain.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies zero initialization of the modification vector, retention of the largest-magnitude 30% of parameters, and application only to linear layers. It also reports a 58-minute 13B merging run on one A100. Existing optimizer settings, software versions, and code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained eight vision datasets and eight GLUE tasks, v3 adds twelve vision datasets for 14- and 20-task merging, including CIFAR100, PCAM, and RenderedSST2. Table 10 adds instruction-following, mathematics, and code-generation evaluations on AlpacaEval, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP.

E2.justification: Original comparison sets are retained. v3 adds TA + DARE and TIES + DARE in Table 10, explicitly compares Consensus TIES and weight averaging in the vision scaling study, and adds quantitative resource/performance comparisons with EMR merging, Twin merging, and WEMoE in Table 15.

E3.justification: Added evaluations merge three 13B experts and report scores normalized to individual models, introduce a five-seen/three-unseen task design, and sweep eta from 0.01 to 0.09. Figure 3 switches the inspected MLP layer from the eleventh to the seventh. Existing benchmark training budgets and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds global-coefficient sensitivity analysis, transfer to three harder held-out tasks, scaling tests through 20 tasks, and analysis of static versus dynamic merging tradeoffs. These substantially extend the questions investigated. Original component, subspace-rank, corruption, and two-unseen-task analyses remain.

E5.justification: Figure 1 retains its 95% confidence intervals. Neither version specifies seeds or repeated-run counts, and the added evaluations introduce no uncertainty estimates or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in v1's ten tables are retained after matching relocated tables. Substantial new results appear: Table 10 reports a 90.0 normalized average versus 87.2 for TIES + DARE; Table 14 reports 20-task DOGE accuracies of 72.5 and 81.0. Table 12's unseen-task average is 51.5, below the pre-trained model's 55.6.

M1.justification: The loss-gap objective, modification vector, orthogonal gradient projection, and norm-based merging coefficients remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 now includes the second SVD already described in v1 Section 4.2. Newly stated pruning and linear-layer restrictions disclose implementation details without establishing a change to the underlying procedure.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and most prose remain. Changes include rewritten related-work paragraphs, expanded dataset descriptions, clearer methodological explanations, a revised conclusion, relocation of computational discussion into the main text, and updated author, affiliation, and acknowledgment information.

P2.justification: Five new tables substantially expand the experimental presentation. The original computational table moves from Appendix D to the main text, while existing tables are redistributed. Figure 2's projection legend is corrected, and Figure 3 is replaced with a larger seventh-layer distribution plot using a different vertical scale.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against MAP, MetaGPT, TATR, TSV, and KnOTS, discussing prior loss-gap formulations and subspace merging. Section 4.1 now explicitly attributes the objective to Zhou et al. rather than presenting it without that attribution. Dynamic merging receives a new substantive comparison.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 adds an explicit linear-regime/NTK assumption and derives the gradient proxy from accumulated fine-tuning updates, obtaining the initial gradient as the negative task vector divided by summed learning rates. v1 supplied only the accumulated-gradient intuition. The central optimization equations remain equivalent; no new theorem or appendix proof appears.

improvement.justification: The 13B instruction/math/code evaluations and 14-/20-task stress tests address important gaps in v1's evidence for scalability beyond eight-task vision and GLUE. Added sensitivity analysis, implementation disclosures, prior-work attribution, and an explicit architectural limitation improve support and assessability. Reporting remains imperfect—for example, Table 15's 81.0 with a +11.6 annotation is inconsistent with its 69.1 baseline—but these localized issues do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DOGE research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching of retained, relocated, and added material.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds generative-language evaluations, larger task collections, coefficient sensitivity results, and another unseen-task experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original vision and GLUE experiments, component ablations, unseen-task evaluations, corruption tests, and computational measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Subgraph GNNs have emerged as promising architectures that overcome the expressiveness limitations of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by processing bags of subgraphs. Despite their compelling empirical performance, these methods are afflicted by a high computational complexity: they process bags whose size grows linearly in the number of nodes, hindering their applicability to larger graphs. In this work, we propose an effective and easy-to-implement approach to dramatically alleviate the computational cost of Subgraph GNNs and unleash broader applications thereof. Our method, dubbed HyMN, leverages walk-based centrality measures to sample a small number of relevant subgraphs and drastically reduce the bag size. By drawing a connection to perturbation analysis, we highlight the strength of the proposed centrality-based subgraph sampling, and further prove that these walk-based centralities can be additionally used as Structural Encodings for improved discriminative power. A comprehensive set of experimental results demonstrates that HyMN provides an effective synthesis of expressiveness, efficiency, and downstream performance, unlocking the application of Subgraph GNNs to dramatically larger graphs. Not only does our method outperform more sophisticated subgraph sampling approaches, it is also competitive, and sometimes better, than other state-of-the-art approaches for a fraction of their runtime.

By drawing a connection to perturbation analysis, we highlight the strength of the proposed centrality-based subgraph sampling, and further prove that these walk-based centralities can be additionally used as Structural Encodings for improved discriminative power. A comprehensive set of experimental results demonstrates that HyMN provides an effective synthesis of expressiveness, efficiency, and downstream performance, unlocking the application of Subgraph GNNs to dramatically larger graphs. Not only does our method outperform more sophisticated subgraph sampling approaches, it is also competitive, and sometimes better, than other state-of-the-art approaches for a fraction of their runtime.

arxiv_record.abstract: We continue to study the learning-theoretic foundations of generation by extending the results from Kleinberg and Mullainathan [2024] and Li et al. [2024] to account for noisy example streams. In the noiseless setting of Kleinberg and Mullainathan [2024] and Li et al. [2024], an adversary picks a hypothesis from a binary hypothesis class and provides a generator with a sequence of its positive examples. The goal of the generator is to eventually output new, unseen positive examples. In the noisy setting, an adversary still picks a hypothesis and a sequence of its positive examples. But, before presenting the stream to the generator, the adversary inserts a finite number of negative examples. Unaware of which examples are noisy, the goal of the generator is to still eventually output new, unseen positive examples. In this paper, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for when a binary hypothesis class can be noisily generatable. We provide such conditions with respect to various constraints on the number of distinct examples that need to be seen before perfect generation of positive examples. Interestingly, for finite and countable classes we show that generatability is largely unaffected by the presence of a finite number of noisy examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Speculative sampling is a popular technique for accelerating inference in Large Language Models by generating candidate tokens using a fast draft model and accepting or rejecting them based on the target model's distribution. While speculative sampling was previously limited to discrete sequences, we extend it to diffusion models, which generate samples via continuous, vector-valued Markov chains. In this context, the target model is a high-quality but computationally expensive diffusion model. We propose various drafting strategies, including a simple and effective approach that does not require training a draft model and is applicable out of the box to any diffusion model. Our experiments demonstrate significant generation speedup on various diffusion models, halving the number of function evaluations, while generating exact samples from the target model.

arxiv_record.abstract: The notion of \emph{rank} of a Boolean function has been a cornerstone in PAC learning theory, enabling quasipolynomial-time learning algorithms for polynomial-size decision trees. We present a novel characterization of rank, grounded in the well-known Transformer architecture. We show that the rank of a function $f$ corresponds to the minimum number of \emph{Chain of Thought} (CoT) steps required by a single-layer Transformer with hard attention to compute $f$. Based on this characterization we establish tight bounds on the number of CoT steps required for specific problems, showing that \(\ell\)-fold function composition necessitates exactly \(\ell\) CoT steps. Furthermore, we analyze the problem of identifying the position of the \(k\)-th occurrence of 1 in a Boolean sequence, proving that it requires \(k\) CoT steps. C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add PAC learnability as a main contribution: proper learning for bounded single-head rank, improper learning for bounded multi-head rank, and conditional hardness of proper learning already for two-head rank one. Multi-head rank itself was already introduced in v1.

C2.justification: Section 6 explains why efficient learning through a larger single-head hypothesis class yields only improper learning of the multi-head class. New Section 7 qualifies comparisons with multilayer soft-attention results by explaining their different input encoding, with an entire function supplied in one token.

D1.justification: Neither version supplies implementation, hardware, training, or code/data-access information. The new constructive algorithm is described mathematically rather than accompanied by implementation details.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks for empirical training or evaluation. The new PAC-consistency problems are studied mathematically.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing methods. The added comparison with hardness results for 2-term DNFs concerns theoretical positioning, not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Neither version contains experimental evaluation protocols. Section 6's sample-access assumptions and accuracy parameters define a theoretical learning model.

E4.justification: Neither version reports empirical ablations, robustness tests, or supplementary experimental analyses. The new examples and gadgets support proofs.

E5.justification: Neither reports repeated experimental runs or statistical uncertainty estimates. v2's PAC confidence parameter is a formal guarantee, not uncertainty reporting from experiments.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance, empirical rankings, or observed qualitative outcomes. The added learnability and hardness results are mathematical contributions assessed under T1.

M1.justification: The decoder architecture and existing constructions remain unchanged, but Section 6.1 introduces a recursive consistency algorithm for fixed-rank functions over arbitrary fixed finite alphabets. It identifies lower-rank-consistent subsamples, recursively processes the remaining samples, and assembles a decision tree. v1 contains no corresponding learning procedure.

P1.justification: The earlier sections remain largely intact. v2 makes local language and notation edits, clarifies the Section 5.2 proof, moves Proposition 6's discussion after that proof, adopts author–year citations, and extends the abstract and roadmap for Sections 6–7.

P2.justification: v2 adds an unnumbered paired tabular display of positive and negative gadget samples in Section 6.2, page 23. Equation displays and bibliography formatting also change, while the overall single-column presentation is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Valiant, Kearns and Vazirani, Pitt and Valiant, Schaefer, and Chen et al. It positions its learning-hardness theorem as incomparable with 2-term-DNF hardness and distinguishes Chen et al.'s composition setting. The existing Transformer-expressivity positioning remains largely intact.

T1.justification: New Section 6 formalizes PAC learning and consistency, proves polynomial-time consistency for fixed single-head rank over finite alphabets (Theorem 4), and proves NP-completeness for Boolean two-head rank at most one (Theorem 5). Lemmas 3–6 provide the algorithmic argument and reduction machinery. The original rank/decoder equivalences and CoT bounds are retained.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates rank through PAC learning but does not examine learnability of its multi-head generalization. Section 6 of v2 addresses that substantive question with a constructive algorithm and detailed hardness reductions, distinguishing efficient improper learning from conditional proper-learning hardness. This substantially deepens the computational implications of the characterization while preserving the original CoT results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same rank/Chain-of-Thought research, with readable definitions, equations, constructions, and proofs. All 20 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2 support comparison. Neither contains a separate appendix.

after.justification: v2 adds theoretical learning algorithms and complexity proofs. Its labeled samples and sample matrices are mathematical constructions, not empirical study outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical characterizations and proofs of decoder-depth bounds, without original experiments, simulations, user studies, or empirical data analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Quantum control is concerned with the realisation of desired dynamics in quantum systems, serving as a linchpin for advancing quantum technologies and fundamental research. Analytic approaches and standard optimisation algorithms do not yield satisfactory solutions for more complex quantum systems, and especially not for real world quantum systems which are open and noisy. We devise a physics-constrained Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithm that restricts the space of possible solutions. We incorporate priors about the desired time scales of the quantum state dynamics - as well as realistic control signal limitations - as constraints to the RL algorithm. These constraints improve solution quality and enhance computational scaleability. We evaluate our method on three broadly relevant quantum systems and incorporate real-world complications, arising from dissipation and control signal perturbations. We achieve both higher fidelities - which exceed 0.999 across all systems - and better robustness to time-dependent perturbations and experimental imperfections than previous methods. Lastly, we demonstrate that incorporating multi-step feedback can yield solutions robust even to strong perturbations. Our implementation can be found at https://github.com/jan-o-e/RL4qcWpc.
arxiv_record.authors: Jan Ole Ernst, Aniket Chatterjee, Tim Franzmeyer, Axel Kuhn

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient constrained RL, fidelities above 0.999 across three systems, and noise robustness remain. V2 explicitly quantifies the Λ-system advantage as almost two orders of magnitude lower infidelity and extends the conclusion's applicability claim to noisy physical control more generally.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops practical applicability through measurement-budget estimates in Appendix F and hardware-bandwidth interpretations in Fig. 15. Appendix G.3 attributes much of the runtime advantage to compilation and automatic differentiation, qualifying the role of constraints. The conclusion adds error-correction relevance and cross-device policy generalization, while retaining the principal modelling and non-adiabatic limitations.

D1.justification: V1 promises future code and data release; v2 states that code is open source and supplies a repository address. V2 also adds a detailed PPO/DDPG/TD3 hyperparameter table, CleanRL implementation information, and hardware, batching, and timing details. These materially expand reproducibility documentation; repository contents were not independently checked.

E1.justification: The three quantum platforms and their control tasks remain. Noise-test coverage expands modestly: v2 Fig. 9 includes a Λ-system amplitude-noise level of 3 MHz alongside the 0.1 and 1 MHz levels shown in v1 Fig. 7. The new hardware-feasibility discussion does not introduce a physical-device study.

E2.justification: V2 adds Krotov to the Λ-system comparison and evaluates vanilla PPO plus constrained and vanilla DDPG/TD3 variants in the Λ and two-photon Rydberg environments. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set beyond v1. The retained 0.83 entry is relabeled PINN, rather than representing an additional baseline.

E3.justification: V2 introduces controlled RL comparisons with common batches and update budgets, CPU convergence-time benchmarking, and a 1 GSa/s waveform-analysis protocol. The reported Λ-system BFGS iteration limit also changes from 10,000 in v1 Table II to 1,000 in v2 Table 1 despite an unchanged score; this does not establish that the experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds constrained-versus-vanilla algorithm ablations in Figs. 2 and 12, an RL-versus-optimal-control state-evolution comparison in Fig. 10, and smoothing-dependent waveform analysis in Fig. 15. It revises the Λ noise study and omits v1 Fig. 10's quantitative single-photon Rydberg noise analysis. Existing pulse-area and smoothing ablations are retained.

E5.justification: The main comparison table retains its 32-seed reporting. New Fig. 2 explicitly reports two seeds and one-standard-deviation shading. For Λ noise robustness, v1 Fig. 7 reports min/max envelopes, whereas v2 Fig. 9 reports standard-deviation envelopes. These are reporting changes, not evidence of increased replication for existing results.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial numerical comparison and timing results, including Krotov fidelity 0.99 ± 0.001 and CPU convergence times of 239.1 seconds for PPO versus 3997 seconds for Krotov. The reported 0.25-microsecond Rydberg pulse fidelity changes from 0.9993 to 0.99958 alongside a revised waveform. Noise curves and the transmon solver-step curve also change; the principal Λ and transmon headline fidelities remain.

M1.justification: The constrained PPO framework, filtering, endpoint constraints, and multi-step feedback procedure remain. However, the stated low-pass smoothness penalty changes from an integrated signed residual in v1 Eq. E4 to an integrated absolute residual in v2 Eq. 23, altering the documented reward component. The PDFs do not establish whether this also changed the implementation.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method explanation undergo substantial rewriting. Quantum-control background moves from the main text to Appendix B, implementation material is reorganized into Appendix G, and experimental-feasibility and impact sections are added. Terminology and section conventions are revised throughout.

P2.justification: V2 adopts an ICML layout, expands and restructures the main comparison table, adds hyperparameter and timing tables, and introduces several analytical figures. V1's two-panel multi-step figure is redrawn as a combined main-text plot; noise and Rydberg plots are revised. The conceptual comparison table and single-photon noise plot are removed.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against Krotov, hybrid optimal control, logical-level quantum RL, error correction, compilation, and recent transmon-control work. It revises the discussion of model-based RL and replaces v1's categorical RL-versus-direct-differentiation table with more contextual comparisons. These changes extend beyond bibliographic formatting.

T1.justification: The absolute-value addition changes the mathematical smoothness definition, and v2 Fig. 15 introduces a sampled-waveform diagnostic. Most quantum and PPO equations are retained or relocated, without new proofs. The printed single-photon Hamiltonian summation limit also changes from 2 to 1 in Eq. 14 without explanation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central constrained-RL claim through vanilla-versus-constrained comparisons and broader baselines, addressing important gaps in v1. Hyperparameter disclosure, runtime benchmarks, and the code-access statement also materially improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed single-photon robustness evidence and localized equation/reporting inconsistencies. Physical-device feasibility remains an extrapolation rather than experimentally validated evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same constrained reinforcement-learning work for quantum control. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original simulation results and adds algorithm comparisons, runtime measurements, and analyses of learned control signals. These are simulation results, not new physical-device experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations of population transfer, Rydberg gates, and transmon reset, including fidelity, robustness, ablation, and computational timing results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Post-hoc calibration of pre-trained models is critical for ensuring reliable inference, especially in safety-critical domains such as healthcare. Conformal Prediction (CP) offers a robust post-hoc calibration framework, providing distribution-free statistical coverage guarantees for prediction sets by leveraging held-out datasets. In this work, we address a decentralized setting where each device has limited calibration data and can communicate only with its neighbors over an arbitrary graph topology. We propose two message-passing-based approaches for achieving reliable inference via CP: quantile-based distributed conformal prediction (Q-DCP) and histogram-based distributed conformal prediction (H-DCP). Q-DCP employs distributed quantile regression enhanced with tailored smoothing and regularization terms to accelerate convergence, while H-DCP uses a consensus-based histogram estimation approach. Through extensive experiments, we investigate the trade-offs between hyperparameter tuning requirements, communication overhead, coverage guarantees, and prediction set sizes across different network topologies. The code of our work is released on: https://github.com/HaifengWen/Distributed-Conformal-Prediction.
arxiv_record.authors: Haifeng Wen, Hong Xing, Osvaldo Simeone
arxiv_record.title: Distributed Conformal Prediction via Message Passing

arxiv_record.abstract: Test-time scaling, which is also often referred to as slow-thinking, has been demonstrated to enhance multi-step reasoning in large language models (LLMs). However, despite its widespread utilization, the mechanisms underlying slow-thinking methods remain poorly understood. This paper explores the mechanisms of external slow-thinking from a theoretical standpoint. We begin by examining the snowball error effect within the LLM reasoning process and connect it to the likelihood of correct reasoning using information theory. Building on this, we show that external slow-thinking methods can be interpreted as strategies to mitigate the error probability. We further provide a comparative analysis of popular external slow-thinking approaches, ranging from simple to complex, highlighting their differences and interrelationships. Our findings suggest that the efficacy of these methods is not primarily determined by the specific framework employed, and that expanding the search scope or the model's internal reasoning capacity may yield more sustained improvements in the long term. We open-source our code at https://github.com/ZyGan1999/Snowball-Errors-and-Probability.
