C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central claims: external search mitigates snowball errors, and reward-function reliability and reasoning resources matter more than the particular search framework. New supporting analyses do not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix D.2 interprets declining accuracy on easier problems as harm from overthinking and argues that length effects persist within difficulty groups. Appendix D.3 attributes faster PrOntoQA gains with increasing k to a more reliable value function. These extend interpretation without revising the central account.

D1.justification: v3 documents Game24 tree settings and cost-calibration quantities, names the larger evaluated models, and specifies the search-width sweep. Existing prompts, ten-answer MI sampling, HSIC bandwidth 50, reward-model information, and code-access statement are retained.

E1.justification: Appendices D.2 and D.4 add MATH-500 mathematics across five difficulty levels and Game24 arithmetic-puzzle planning. These substantially broaden coverage beyond the retained GSM8k word problems and PrOntoQA logical reasoning.

E2.justification: The corresponding GSM8k and PrOntoQA comparisons retain MCTS against BoN with Self-Consistency, ORM Vote, and ORM Max. Game24 evaluates existing MCTS and ORM-based BoN methods; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include Qwen2.5-14B/32B tests, difficulty-stratified MI and accuracy analyses, and an MCTS max-action sweep from k=1 to 8 with other hyperparameters held fixed. Game24 adds maximum tree width 20 and depth 4. The original GSM8k/PrOntoQA settings and MI workflow remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendices D.1–D.3 add targeted checks of whether snowball patterns persist at larger model sizes, whether length effects persist within difficulty groups, and how accuracy responds to search width. These substantially expand robustness and sensitivity analysis beyond v1's original experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports run-level uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-based variability. The new experiments continue to present point estimates and curves without adding statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original Figures 2–3 are retained, while Figures 4–6 add model-scale, difficulty, and search-width findings. New Table 3 reports Game24 MCTS accuracy of 64.80%, versus 66.85% for ORM-Vote and 67.13% for ORM-Max at N=18. These are newly reported results, not improvements over a corresponding v1 experiment.

M1.justification: The BoN, MCTS, and answer-selection procedures are retained. v3 introduces no new algorithm or architecture; its relaxed probability assumptions extend the theory, while additional model sizes extend evaluation.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. v3 adds brief explanations and cross-references, reorganizes the appendices around new theoretical and empirical sections, updates affiliations and publication information, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial visual material: larger-model curves, difficulty-stratified MI and accuracy panels, a search-width plot, and the Game24 results table. Table 2 gains a Game24 column. Figures 1–3 retain their displays, while Table 1 is relocated.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds Wu et al. (2024), Inference Scaling Laws, as empirical support for inference scaling. The remaining cited works and the paper's positioning relative to information theory and external search are retained.

T1.justification: New Appendix B replaces the specific exponential form, for its extended analysis, with a nonnegative function decreasing monotonically to zero. Proposition B.1 and bounds B.2–B.7 generalize the reasoning and search analyses. Existing main-text results and Appendix A proofs are retained; the lookahead derivation moves from Appendix C to E.

improvement.justification: v1 did not test length effects within difficulty groups or across larger models, and its probability analysis used a specific exponential form. Appendices B and D address these gaps and add search-width sensitivity and planning-task evidence, substantially strengthening the scope and support of the central account. The overthinking interpretation remains observational, and uncertainty estimates are still absent, but the targeted additions provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. The original experimental settings and lookahead analysis are retained as v3 Appendices C and E.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds larger-model evaluations, MATH-500 difficulty analyses, search-width experiments, and Game24 comparisons.

arxiv_record.abstract: We propose a new finetuning method to provide pre-trained large language models (LMs) the ability to scale test-time compute through the diffusion framework. By increasing the number of diffusion steps, we show our finetuned models achieve monotonically increasing accuracy, directly translating to improved performance across downstream tasks. Furthermore, our finetuned models can expertly answer questions on specific topics by integrating powerful guidance techniques, and autonomously determine the compute required for a given problem by leveraging adaptive ODE solvers. Our method is universally applicable to any foundation model pre-trained with a cross-entropy loss and does not modify any of its original weights, fully preserving its strong single-step generation capabilities. We show our method is more effective and fully compatible with traditional finetuning approaches, introducing an orthogonal new direction to unify the strengths of the autoregressive and diffusion frameworks.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains diffusion finetuning that preserves the original model while enabling additional inference computation. The abstract and introduction qualify superiority from 'is more effective' to 'can be more effective' and extend the claimed complementarity from traditional finetuning to search. These refine the scope without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D.6 newly acknowledge limitations in accessing confidence scores and directly controlling sampling through logits. V2 explains that relaxed GSM8K evaluation changes comparative advantages, that oracle verification can favor repeated sampling, and that R1-style reasoning introduces substantial costs and task tradeoffs. These materially qualify applicability and strengthen the interpretation of complementarity.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised code release with a repository link and a statement that code is provided, while removing Appendix B.1's separate data-release promise. It adds beam-search scoring and sampling details, clarifies the main evaluation's untempered generation, and describes new prompt-generation and parsing procedures. The existing hyperparameter table and dataset preparation recipe remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same curated SmolTalk training coverage and nine evaluation benchmarks, including the appendix tasks. V2's additional models, prompting variants, answer extraction, and pass@K evaluations change procedures within these retained tasks rather than adding datasets or domains.

E2.justification: V1 primarily compares against untuned models, LoRA, and full finetuning. V2 adds evaluated token-search and chain-of-thought comparators and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, together with combinations involving L2D (Tables 2 and 16–18). This substantially broadens comparison with alternative inference-scaling approaches.

E3.justification: The original training settings and main evaluation remain. New protocols include 15-hypothesis beam search, pass@5/10 evaluation for mathematics and knowledge, and a separate GSM8K setup using eight examples, greedy baseline decoding, and relaxed extraction. Appendix D.7 also introduces modified reasoning-model prompts and parsing, plus longer chain-of-thought demonstrations. These are additional settings, not evidence that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing learning-rate, noise-scale, initialization, velocity, and solver analyses are retained. V2 adds substantial analyses of oracle best-of-N scaling, sensitivity to GSM8K evaluation choices, and complementarity with search, chain-of-thought prompting, and an R1-distilled model. These test additional questions about when L2D helps and how its benefits combine with other approaches.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional pass@K evaluations concern sampling budgets and success metrics, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Matched original results are retained, including Table 1 and the existing appendix ablations. Substantial new results appear in Tables 13 and 15–17 and the search rows of Tables 2 and 18: token search scores 33.83 overall and its L2D combination 38.57. The new relaxed GSM8K evaluation gives Llama 1B full finetuning 46.36 versus L2D 43.41; the original setup's 33.48 versus 38.86 remains unchanged. These are additional conditions, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The core architecture, diffusion objective, conditioning, and training procedure remain unchanged. Section 4.3 adds an evaluated inference extension combining L2D with beam search, allocating half the original budget to each component. This extends decoding without redesigning L2D.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted wording corrections, clarifies method explanations, and revises the related-work and discussion prose. It inserts search and expanded appendix subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement. The main six-section organization and Appendices A–D remain recognizable; the revision is chiefly added scientific content rather than extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds four substantive comparison tables for best-of-N, relaxed GSM8K, R1-style reasoning, and chain-of-thought, and expands the extension tables with search rows. Existing plots retain their content but are resized or relocated, and Figure 5's reversed math/coding caption is corrected. The new Table 13 introduces a labeling error by placing MMLU columns under 'Coding'.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens positioning relative to search, repeated sampling, and contemporary reasoning approaches, adding discussion and citations for DeepSeek-R1, s1, inference-compute scaling, and diffusion alignment. Sections 6 and D.4–D.7 explicitly position L2D as complementary to these approaches. The earlier diffusion-model relationships remain, while the Lightman and Ye references are removed.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(8), the single-step diffusion interpretation, and the midpoint integration derivation are retained. V2 adds no substantive formal assumptions, theoretical results, or proofs; its beam-search scoring description supplies implementation information.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central test-time-scaling argument by adding direct comparisons with alternative scaling approaches, which v1 largely lacked. More importantly, Table 15 exposes evaluation-dependent rankings, while Section 6 and Appendix D.6 explain consequential sampling and confidence limitations. This improves the credibility and calibration of the conclusions. Differing comparison settings and the continued absence of uncertainty estimates still limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same L2D research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and renumbering in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds original search, best-of-N, evaluation-sensitivity, reasoning-model, and chain-of-thought comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original Llama and Qwen experiments on mathematics, coding, and knowledge tasks, with ablations and additional evaluations in Appendices C–D.

arxiv_record.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are emerging as a brain-inspired alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), prized for their potential energy efficiency on neuromorphic hardware. Despite this, SNNs often suffer from accuracy degradation compared to ANNs and face deployment challenges due to fixed inference timesteps, which require retraining for adjustments, limiting operational flexibility. To address these issues, our work considers the spatio-temporal property inherent in SNNs, and proposes a novel distillation framework for deep SNNs that optimizes performance across full-range timesteps without specific retraining, enhancing both efficacy and deployment adaptability. We provide both theoretical analysis and empirical validations to illustrate that training guarantees the convergence of all implicit models across full-range timesteps. Experimental results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and ImageNet demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among distillation-based SNNs training methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/Intelli-Chip-Lab/snn\_temporal\_decoupling\_distillation.
arxiv_record.authors: Chengting Yu, Xiaochen Zhao, Lei Liu, Shu Yang, Gaoang Wang, Erping Li, Aili Wang
arxiv_record.title: Efficient Logit-based Knowledge Distillation of Deep Spiking Neural Networks for Full-Range Timestep Deployment

arxiv_record.abstract:
Fine-grained steering of language model outputs is essential for safety and
reliability. Prompting and finetuning are widely used to achieve these goals,
but interpretability researchers have proposed a variety of
representation-based techniques as well, including sparse autoencoders (SAEs),
linear artificial tomography, supervised steering vectors, linear probes, and
representation finetuning. At present, there is no benchmark for making direct
comparisons between these proposals. Therefore, we introduce AxBench, a
large-scale benchmark for steering and concept detection, and report
experiments on Gemma-2-2B and 9B. For steering, we find that prompting
outperforms all existing methods, followed by finetuning. For concept
detection, representation-based methods such as difference-in-means, perform
the best. On both evaluations, SAEs are not competitive. We introduce a novel
weakly-supervised representational method (Rank-1 Representation Finetuning;
ReFT-r1), which is competitive on both tasks while providing the
interpretability advantages that prompting lacks. Along with AxBench, we train
and publicly release SAE-scale feature dictionaries for ReFT-r1 and DiffMean.

Conversely, generated-vector and affine-transfer comparisons shrink from broad baseline lists in v1 Tables 4–7 to ReFT-r1, DiffMean, and SAE in v3 Tables 4–5, removing prompting and finetuning comparators from those comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 divides the ten steering instructions per concept equally between steering-factor selection and held-out evaluation; v1 selects the factor maximizing the evaluation score without this separation. Prompting and finetuning also change from averaging factor-indexed generations to randomly scoring a generation on the testing instructions, equalizing sampling with steering methods. These substantially revise the central evaluation design.

E4.justification: BoW is added to the existing balanced-versus-imbalanced detection analysis. The data-scaling, generated-vector, affine-transfer, and SAE clamping studies remain, with revised steering outcomes rather than new analytical questions. The code-error clustering example also replaces one highlighted feature.

E5.justification: Both retain paired t-test reporting in Section 5.1, existing error-bar and distribution displays, and three data-scaling seeds, 42, 43, and 44. No new uncertainty estimator or increased replication count is reported. Condensed appendix tables omit duplicated significance markings that remain available in the main comparison.

E6.justification: Under the revised steering protocol, Table 2 replaces ReFT-r1's mean score of 0.735 with 0.543 and SAE's 0.315 with 0.165; ReFT-r1 moves from third to fifth. Table 3 changes ReFT-r1's mean win rate from 88.0% to 81.8%. v3 also adds BoW AUROC results, averaging 0.914, and 9B SAE-A entries, while updating generated-vector, transfer, scaling, and clamping results. These are not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The synthetic-data pipeline and core ReFT-r1 procedure remain: concept detection through a learned direction, top-k-dependent intervention training, and language-modeling loss with sparsity regularization. The equation corrections and newly documented optimization details do not establish an underlying algorithm change. Generated-vector and affine-transfer methods already appear in v1.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording and notation edits, moves the SAE concept-source footnote into Appendix B, consolidates the SAE ablation subsections, and adds an Impact Statements section. The main narrative, section order, and most appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The mean ROC plot moves from the main text to the appendix, comparison displays expand for BoW and 9B SAE-A, Figure 10 gains connecting lines, and Figure 11 is redesigned with a labeled cluster enlargement. Four large supplementary comparison tables become two compact paired tables, and hyperparameter tables gain BoW columns and rows. This substantially reorganizes the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 adds Bhalla et al. (2025) to the discussion of interpretability-based control and previous steering evaluations. The broader positioning and historical appendix remain substantially unchanged; other reference edits mainly concern bibliographic formatting.

T1.justification: Equation 9 corrects the ReFT-r1 intervention to add the mean top-k activation multiplied by the learned vector to each token representation. improvement.justification: The held-out steering-factor evaluation and matched generation sampling address an important source of optimistic and uneven comparisons in v1's central benchmark. Reporting remains imperfect: Section 5.2 still quotes win rates of 88.0% and 61.6%, although Table 3 now reports 81.8% and 58.7%, and retains optimistic ReFT-r1 comparison prose. These inconsistencies temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial evaluation improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AxBench study and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Appendix renumbering and reorganized displays can be matched reliably.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models, while powerful, can inadvertently generate harmful or undesirable content, raising significant ethical and safety concerns. Recent machine unlearning approaches offer potential solutions but often lack transparency, making it difficult to understand the changes they introduce to the base model. In this work, we introduce SAeUron, a novel method leveraging features learned by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to remove unwanted concepts in text-to-image diffusion models. First, we demonstrate that SAEs, trained in an unsupervised manner on activations from multiple denoising timesteps of the diffusion model, capture sparse and interpretable features corresponding to specific concepts. Building on this, we propose a feature selection method that enables precise interventions on model activations to block targeted content while preserving overall performance. Our evaluation shows that SAeUron outperforms existing approaches on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark for concepts and style unlearning, and effectively eliminates nudity when evaluated with I2P. Moreover, we show that with a single SAE, we can remove multiple concepts simultaneously and that in contrast to other methods, SAeUron mitigates the possibility of generating unwanted content under adversarial attack. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/cywinski/SAeUron.
arxiv_record.authors: Bartosz Cywi\'nski, Kamil Deja
arxiv_record.title: SAeUron: Interpretable Concept Unlearning in Diffusion Models with Sparse Autoencoders

E1.justification: V1 centers on UnlearnCanvas object and style unlearning. V3 adds COCO captions for training and quality evaluation, I2P nudity removal, the 143-prompt nudity attack benchmark, and broader inappropriate-content categories including hate, harassment, and violence.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original nine comparators. New safety comparisons introduce AdvUn, Receler, MACE, CPE, SLD-M, and separate ESD-x/ESD-u variants in Table 2, plus SAFREE and RECE in Table 7. Erasediff in Table 7 corresponds to the existing EDiff comparator.

E3.justification: Object-unlearning hyperparameters change substantially between v1 Table 4 and v3 Table 5, and the reported object-classification feature budget becomes 40 features, two per class. Added protocols include SD-v1.4 nudity evaluation with a 0.6 NudeNet threshold, Q16 evaluation, 49-of-50-style unlearning, and training-size sweeps.

E4.justification: V3 adds object and nudity attack analyses, training-data/time scaling, cat–dog feature-overlap failure studies, hyperparameter sweeps, classwise retention analysis, qualitative baseline comparisons, and automated feature annotations. E5.justification: Both versions report main UnlearnCanvas results averaged over five random seeds and retain the existing uncertainty presentation in sequential-unlearning plots. No changed repeated-run protocol, confidence-interval procedure, or significance-testing practice is documented.

E6.justification: Under revised selection and tuning, Table 1 replaces object UA/IRA/CRA of 84.23/90.05/76.78% with 78.82/95.47/95.58%; these are not same-setting gains. M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 replace percentile-threshold feature selection with explicit top-τ selection and add filtering of dead and excessively frequent features. These refine feature selection while retaining the SAE architecture, training objective, negative activation scaling, and inference intervention.

P1.justification: V3 edits the abstract and existing prose, converts several numbered subsections to paragraph headings, and reorders technical details. P2.justification: V3 adds safety-result tables, feature visualizations, efficiency plots, failure analyses, sensitivity heatmaps, comparative image grids, and annotated examples. arxiv_record.abstract: Many video-to-audio (VTA) methods have been proposed for dubbing silent AI-generated videos. An efficient quality assessment method for AI-generated audio-visual content (AGAV) is crucial for ensuring audio-visual quality. Existing audio-visual quality assessment methods struggle with unique distortions in AGAVs, such as unrealistic and inconsistent elements. To address this, we introduce AGAVQA-3k, the first large-scale AGAV quality assessment dataset, comprising $3,382$ AGAVs from $16$ VTA methods. AGAVQA-3k includes two subsets: AGAVQA-MOS, which provides multi-dimensional scores for audio quality, content consistency, and overall quality, and AGAVQA-Pair, designed for optimal AGAV pair selection. We further propose AGAV-Rater, a LMM-based model that can score AGAVs, as well as audio and music generated from text, across multiple dimensions, and selects the best AGAV generated by VTA methods to present to the user. AGAV-Rater achieves state-of-the-art performance on AGAVQA-3k, Text-to-Audio, and Text-to-Music datasets. Subjective tests also confirm that AGAV-Rater enhances VTA performance and user experience. The dataset and code is available at https://github.com/charlotte9524/AGAV-Rater.

C1.justification: Both versions claim the same dataset contribution, LMM-based multidimensional evaluator, leading benchmark performance, and improved user experience with 80% preference. The dataset rename and added Impact Statement do not materially alter these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for backbone performance and music pretraining, interpretations of rating variability, and the qualification that music aesthetics are not evaluated. Appendix B.5 also newly interprets SRCC 0.6860 as indicating independence between dimensions, an interpretation that the reported correlation does not establish.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed scoring rubrics, interface and equipment specifications, subject screening and fatigue controls, pretraining composition, loss formulas, audio preprocessing, training time, and direct code/dataset access information. These substantially improve documentation. However, the disclosed pretraining counts sum to 50,592, inconsistent with the stated 50,952 total.

E1.justification: The training sources, AGAVQA-MOS/Pair, TTA/TTM benchmarks, and 230-video ElevenLabs study remain the same. AGAVQA becomes AGAVQA-3k without expanding coverage. Figure 2 revises source counts and removes a duplicated Kling label; its represented source types remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Random and MOS-fine-tuned AVID-CMA, VALOR, and VAST to the selection comparison, which previously compared against unfine-tuned LMMs. These alignment methods previously appeared in scoring experiments, so their participation here is new. Table 5 additionally compares GroundingGPT and OneLLM backbones.

E3.justification: The new backbone experiments fine-tune default weights with three-score regression heads, and the selection evaluation gains a trained-comparator arm. Existing cross-validation and training budgets remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 introduces a 0–5 scoring description alongside retained 1–5 descriptions, leaving the annotation range inconsistent rather than establishing that ratings were recollected.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation with backbone ablations (Table 5), annotator agreement and relationships between scoring dimensions (Section 3.2 and Appendix B.5), and category-specific accuracy for the existing ElevenLabs study (Table 10). The original component ablations and MOS plots are retained.

E5.justification: v1 lacks quantitative annotator-reliability reporting. v2 adds Krippendorff's alpha, average correlations from ten random splits of subjects, and category-level inter-subject standard deviations (Section 3.2 and Table 7). The ten repetitions concern rating-consistency analysis, not additional model-training runs.

E6.justification: New results include selection accuracies of 0.52/0.55/0.64 for AVID-CMA/VALOR/VAST, backbone results, rating statistics, and category accuracies of 0.75–0.87. AGAV-Rater's selection accuracy remains 0.78, and all numerical cells in Tables 1, 2, and 4 are retained. Tables 1–2 correct the PLCC/KRCC headers, changing metric assignments rather than demonstrating performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Figure 3 retain the VideoLLaMA2 architecture, two-stage training, masking, and multidimensional score regression. The added loss and preprocessing descriptions document existing components. GroundingGPT and OneLLM are experimental alternatives, not replacements in the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes include the AGAVQA-3k name, localized wording edits, affiliation/publication information, an Impact Statement, and reorganized appendices separating human evaluation from dataset construction and experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds the scoring-interface figure and compact backbone, rating-variability, and category-accuracy tables. Table 3 gains rows and training-status headings; Tables 1–2 and Figure 2 receive label corrections. Existing MOS plots and instruction/latency tables are retained and relocated, with the overall visual format preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GroundingGPT, OneLLM, Krippendorff reliability, and three Sun et al. papers on visual attention/perception. The principal related-work discussion and positioning relative to existing audio-visual quality assessment remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 1 is retained. Appendix C.2 supplies standard formulas for the cross-entropy and PLCC objectives already specified in v1; it does not introduce new theoretical reasoning, assumptions, proofs, or substantively different mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps by reporting rating reliability and comparing selection against fine-tuned baselines, while substantially improving annotation and preprocessing documentation. Corrected metric headers also resolve inconsistencies between v1's benchmark and ablation tables. These gains strengthen the paper's evidential support and reproducibility despite conflicting scoring ranges, the pretraining-count mismatch, and the unsupported interpretation of correlation as independence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AGAV-Rater study. Their complete main texts, appendices, figures, tables, and equations support comparison, including matching renamed datasets and relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds backbone comparisons, annotator-reliability analyses, and category-specific selection results.

before.justification: v1 reports original subjective ratings, model comparisons on AGAVQA/TTA/TTM, ablations, cross-dataset selection results, and an ElevenLabs user-preference experiment.

arxiv_record.abstract: We demonstrate how neural networks can drive mathematical discovery through a case study of the Hadwiger-Nelson problem, a long-standing open problem at the intersection of discrete geometry and extremal combinatorics that is concerned with coloring the plane while avoiding monochromatic unit-distance pairs. Using neural networks as approximators, we reformulate this mixed discrete-continuous geometric coloring problem with hard constraints as an optimization task with a probabilistic, differentiable loss function. This enables gradient-based exploration of admissible configurations that most significantly led to the discovery of two novel six-colorings, providing the first improvement in thirty years to the off-diagonal variant of the original problem. Here, we establish the underlying machine learning approach used to obtain these results and demonstrate its broader applicability through additional numerical insights.

C1.justification: The introduction adds formal almost-colorings in two and three dimensions to the principal contributions, including the improved five-color bound. It also expands the claimed discovery process to include fully automated formalization in selected cases. v1 left these almost-coloring constructions tentative; the central off-diagonal six-coloring claim is retained.

C2.justification: v2 explains how freedom to enlarge the removed region enables automated formalization, discusses neural representations' advantages and tuning limitations, and identifies finer discretization as a possible improvement for the three-dimensional construction. It also qualifies the 15-color numerical solutions as near conflict-free. The existing interpretations concerning chromatic and polychromatic numbers remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link for reproduction code and formalized constructions. Appendix B supplies previously absent instructions for detecting periodicity through translated radial evaluations, constructing cell conflict masks, and repairing conflicts. Reported runtimes are also revised, including V100 runs from 5–20 to 2–20 minutes, without a controlled timing comparison.

E1.justification: v2 explicitly evaluates the almost-coloring objective in three dimensions, whereas v1 reports ordinary 14-color candidates and only proposes converting them into almost-colorings. Table 1 also extends planar almost-coloring coverage to one color. The existing four variants and alternative-norm examples remain.

E2.justification: Section 5 newly reports experiments with Fourier bases and Voronoi diagrams, stating that neural networks performed best. These are additional evaluated alternatives, although the comparison is qualitative and supplies no scores or matched experimental settings.

E3.justification: Table 1 replaces evaluation in a finite [-3,3]^2 box with evaluation on a parallelogram under periodic boundary conditions and adds formal verification through Algorithm 1. Reported hidden-layer widths change from 64–256 to 32–256, and the useful penalty range expands from 10^-3–10^-2 to 10^-3–10^-1. These are reported setting changes, without establishing that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: A new Section 3 footnote reports limited tests of Gaussian spatial sampling instead of uniform box sampling, finding no improved constructions. Section 5 adds qualitative sensitivity observations concerning architecture, penalty scale, and box size. The triangle conflict-threshold analysis in Appendix E was already present.

E5.justification: v1's Table 1 explicitly reports the best of 60 runs; v2 removes that run-count and selection disclosure. The general experimental description changes from hundreds to thousands of runs to thousands of runs, without establishing a specific increase. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces numerical entries and adds formalized results: the five-color entry changes from 4.01% in a finite box to 3.60% numerically under periodic evaluation and 3.74% formalized, specified as 3.7356% in the text. These are not same-setting performance comparisons. Section 4.3 newly reports 2.3% numerical conflicts and a formal almost-14-coloring excluding 3.4622% of space. The formal triangle-bound regions also change between v1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 4. Some prior-bound entries change beyond rounding, including 0.0143% to 0.02% for six colors.

M1.justification: v2 introduces Algorithm 1: extract periodicity, retrain with an exact periodic coordinate mapping, discretize the output, and repair conflicts through recoloring. It also applies this procedure in three dimensions. This substantially extends the procedure beyond v1's neural optimization and subsequent human formalization; the original losses remain.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution list are reorganized, the discussion is expanded, an Impact Statement is added, and terminology and prose receive local corrections. The section sequence, four-variant organization, and substantial portions of the narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 2 and an Algorithm 1 display, expands Table 1, and replaces Appendix B's numerical coloring displays with six formalized periodic constructions. It redraws the formal triangle-bound diagram, recolors other triangle plots, enlarges the three-dimensional visualization, and moves v1 Figure 7 into Appendix C as Figure 13. Together these substantially revise the presentation of constructions and verification.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to AlphaEvolve, Alfarano et al., Trinh et al., Gwyn and Stavrianos, and Croft, extending the discovery-method context and attribution of prior coloring bounds. The main positioning relative to combinatorial optimization and implicit neural representations remains. Several other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix B add a mathematical construction using periodic parallelogram cells and explain reducing continuous unit-distance avoidance to stricter discrete cell constraints. Proposition 3.1, its proof, and the existing loss formulations remain unchanged. No separate new theorem or complete construction proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v1 left the five-color and three-dimensional almost-colorings unformalized. v2 substantially addresses that gap through Algorithm 1, Appendix B's procedural explanation, separately reported numerical and formalized results, and code-access information. This strengthens the connection between neural exploration and checkable mathematical constructions. Full construction accounts remain deferred and Table 1 loses explicit run-count detail, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological completeness and evidential clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural approach to Hadwiger-Nelson coloring problems. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–F are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original numerical experiments and adds periodic almost-coloring evaluations and results from its automated formalization procedure.

before.justification: v1 reports original neural-network experiments, numerical conflict rates, and discovered colorings for planar, off-diagonal, three-dimensional, triangle-avoidance, and alternative-norm problems.

The goal of offline model-based optimization (MBO) is to propose new designs

Section 7 explicitly identifies untested noisy or sparse objectives, very high-dimensional spaces and small datasets as applicability limits. The median-quality tradeoff is foregrounded and elaborated, but its basic limitation was already acknowledged in v1 Appendix D.1.

D1.justification: The added experiments document synthetic dataset sizes, dimensions, oracle sources, objective negation and initialization choices. Existing architectures, hyperparameters, hardware and code/data access statements are retained. Algorithm 1 also omits the previously explicit initialization of the critic-loop convergence variable, without explaining an implementation change.

E1.justification: Appendix D.9 adds Vehicle Safety and Welded Beam evaluations, optimizing vehicle mass and beam manufacturing cost while assessing secondary safety and deflection objectives. It also evaluates GC content of candidates from the retained UTR task. The original six-task coverage remains.

E2.justification: The broader comparison adds Tri-Mentoring, ICT, PGS, Match-Opt and RGD, with results across the six original tasks and five quality/diversity metrics in v2 Tables A6–A8. These methods were absent from the corresponding v1 Tables A5–A6; existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix E.5 introduces controlled Sobol-versus-top-k initialization comparisons using 64 initial designs, with gradient ascent except Adam for RoMA. Appendix D.9 introduces 800-design synthetic datasets and evaluates secondary-objective dispersion among 128 candidates; Welded Beam is evaluated without its original constraints. These are added protocols, not demonstrated changes to the retained experiments. The dispersion metric is inconsistently called standard deviation in the prose and variance in Table A10.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.5 and Table A14 test whether initialization explains DynAMO's diversity advantage. New Appendix D.9 and Table A10 investigate whether candidate diversity accompanies broader secondary-objective values. E5.justification: Both versions report means and 95% confidence intervals over ten random seeds. Added tables follow that practice, and original uncertainty information remains in the relocated tables. Secondary-objective dispersion is an additional evaluation outcome, not a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

Existing per-task scores are retained, while ranks change with the expanded comparator set: DynAMO-BO-qUCB's Best@128 average rank changes from 4.8 in v1 Table A5 to 6.3 in v2 Table A6, with its optimality gap unchanged at 20.5. arxiv_record.abstract:
Conformal Prediction (CP) is a principled framework for quantifying
uncertainty in blackbox learning models, by constructing prediction sets with
finite-sample coverage guarantees. Traditional approaches rely on scalar
nonconformity scores, which fail to fully exploit the geometric structure of
multivariate outputs, such as in multi-output regression or multiclass
classification. Recent methods addressing this limitation impose predefined
convex shapes for the prediction sets, potentially misaligning with the
intrinsic data geometry. We introduce a novel CP procedure handling
multivariate score functions through the lens of optimal transport.
Specifically, we leverage Monge-Kantorovich vector ranks and quantiles to
construct prediction region with flexible, potentially non-convex shapes,
better suited to the complex uncertainty patterns encountered in multivariate
learning tasks. We prove that our approach ensures finite-sample,
distribution-free coverage properties, similar to typical CP methods. We then
adapt our method for multi-output regression and multiclass classification, and
also propose simple adjustments to generate adaptive prediction regions with
asymptotic conditional coverage guarantees. Finally, we evaluate our method on
practical regression and classification problems, illustrating its advantages
in terms of (conditional) coverage and efficiency.
arxiv_record.authors: Gauthier Thurin (CNRS), Kimia Nadjahi (CNRS), Claire Boyer (LMO)

C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain multivariate OT-based prediction regions, finite-sample marginal coverage, and asymptotic conditional coverage. The conclusion now explicitly qualifies the efficiency advantages by acknowledging potentially more conservative regression sets and greater computational cost, modestly narrowing the overall contribution narrative.

C2.justification: v2 explains why distribution-free fitted ranks alone do not justify the original coverage argument and motivates separate calibration. It adds substantive limitations concerning small-sample overcoverage, set-size and runtime costs, and opportunities for alternative reference distributions or entropic maps. Appendix D.4 also interprets classification benefits through label-confusion patterns.

D1.justification: Appendix D.1 newly identifies the network simplex solver in Python Optimal Transport; this is a disclosure, not evidence of a solver change. v2 adds neighborhood-size guidance and specifies the five-class MNIST labels. The CIFAR-10 neural-network architecture details disappear with that experiment.

E1.justification: v2 removes the five-class CIFAR-10 evaluation, eliminating the natural-image benchmark, and adds five-class MNIST and a synthetic classification scenario with less-confusable classes. The six regression datasets and full MNIST/Fashion-MNIST tasks remain. Thus represented image domains and classification scenarios change substantially.

E2.justification: Predictive baseline membership remains ELL/REC for synthetic regression, adaptive ELL for real regression, and IP/MS/APS for classification. Figure 12 newly compares OT-CP and OT-CP+ runtimes, adding a limited comparison between existing variants. Newly cited competing approaches are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: MNIST/Fashion-MNIST experiments change from 20,000 observations with a 10%/80%/10% train/calibration/test split to 25,000 with 10%/45%/45%. Calibration now includes D1/D2 splitting. Appendix D.2 additionally reports a square-root neighborhood rule for larger datasets, while new experiments vary calibration size and measure runtime, marginal coverage, and volume.

E4.justification: Appendix D.4 adds runtime scaling with calibration size and a controlled comparison of more versus less-confusable synthetic classes. These investigate computational scalability and when classification advantages arise, extending v1's existing five-versus-ten-class analysis. Figure 13 also exposes coverage, volume, and runtime tradeoffs in real regression.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten repeated random draws for the image-classification experiments and display error bars. v2 does not introduce a changed repetition policy, seed specification, confidence-interval definition, or significance-testing procedure. Changed error-bar magnitudes are result changes.

E6.justification: Numerous plotted results change. For example, Figure 4's low-data wq worst-set coverage for the adaptive method falls from approximately 0.92 to 0.79. New runtime, regression-efficiency, easier-classification, and five-class MNIST results appear, while CIFAR-10 results disappear. Given the method and protocol revisions, these are replaced or newly reported outcomes, not controlled same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces v1's fixed rank threshold with split calibration: D1 learns the transport map and D2 calibrates its threshold. OT-CP+ likewise replaces its fixed neighborhood-based threshold with a threshold calibrated across held-out conditional ranks. These change both procedures, rather than merely documenting them.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 expands procedural explanations, reorganizes the appendices into methodology, proofs, related work, and experiments, and adds an Impact Statement and affiliation edits. Much of the substantial rewriting accompanies scientific changes rather than an independent overhaul of the narrative.

P2.justification: Classification displays are reorganized into aggregated main-text metrics and paired label-wise coverage plots, with detailed results in the appendix. New runtime, regression-tradeoff, easier-classification, and MNIST-subset figures appear; CIFAR-10's figure disappears. Existing figures also receive layout, caption, and legend revisions, including identifying OT-CP+ correctly in Figure 4.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning across copula, multiple-testing, latent-space, density/sampling, and shape-optimization approaches. v2 discusses concurrent work by Klein, Dheur, Braun, and Luo and Zhou, including the relationship between OT-CP and entropic transport-based conformal prediction.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.4 changes its upper bound from alpha + 2/(n+1) to alpha + n_ties/(n2+1), with rewritten exchangeability arguments and a generalized tie lemma. Theorem 3.2 now specifies convergence in probability as both calibration subsets grow. Appendix B adds threshold-consistency Lemma B.2 and substantially replaces the conditional-coverage proof.

improvement.justification: The separate map-fitting and threshold-calibration stages address the exchangeability gap underlying v1's central coverage argument, substantially improving the paper's theoretical foundation. Added computational evidence, implementation details, and explicit limitations improve assessability. Removing CIFAR-10 narrows empirical breadth, and Section 3.2 still overstates Figure 4's worst-set coverage, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the repair of the main validity argument and fuller accounting of practical tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OT-CP research. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original regression and classification experiments, supplemented by runtime measurements and additional classification scenarios in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, regression evaluations on six real datasets, and classification results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, including appendix experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: This study considers multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) through the information gain of the Pareto-frontier. To calculate the information gain, a predictive distribution conditioned on the Pareto-frontier plays a key role, which is defined as a distribution truncated by the Pareto-frontier. However, it is usually impossible to obtain the entire Pareto-frontier in a continuous domain, and therefore, the complete truncation cannot be known. We consider an approximation of the truncate distribution by using a mixture distribution consisting of two possible approximate truncation obtainable from a subset of the Pareto-frontier, which we call over- and under-truncation. Since the optimal balance of the mixture is unknown beforehand, we propose optimizing the balancing coefficient through the variational lower bound maximization framework, by which the approximation error of the information gain can be minimized. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method particularly when the number of objective functions is large.
arxiv_record.authors: Masanori Ishikura and Masayuki Karasuyama
arxiv_record.title: Pareto-frontier Entropy Search with Variational Lower Bound Maximization

arxiv_record.abstract: Efficient sampling of unnormalized probability densities such as the Boltzmann distribution of molecular systems is a longstanding challenge. Next to conventional approaches like molecular dynamics or Markov chain Monte Carlo, variational approaches, such as training normalizing flows with the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence, have been introduced. However, such methods are prone to mode collapse and often do not learn to sample the full configurational space. Here, we present temperature-annealed Boltzmann generators (TA-BG) to address this challenge. First, we demonstrate that training a normalizing flow with the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence at high temperatures is possible without mode collapse. Furthermore, we introduce a reweighting-based training objective to anneal the distribution to lower target temperatures. We apply this methodology to three molecular systems of increasing complexity and, compared to the baseline, achieve better results in almost all metrics while requiring up to three times fewer target energy evaluations. For the largest system, our approach is the only method that accurately resolves the metastable states of the system.

C1.justification: The abstract, three introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: high-temperature reverse-KLD training avoids mode collapse, iterative reweighting anneals to the target temperature, and molecular experiments achieve strong accuracy with up to threefold fewer energy evaluations. Added appendix evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies efficiency and scalability. Appendix J explains that additional flow evaluations make TA-BG slower than FAB in the current setup, with anticipated benefits for expensive potentials. Appendix F.4 discusses high-dimensional importance-sampling failure. The discussion adds permutation-invariance limitations, while Appendix K explains the illustrative scope of GMM results and exclusion of symmetric-particle benchmarks.

D1.justification: The Software and Data statement changes from a promised release to concrete GitHub and Zenodo access locations. v2 also documents million-sample validation datasets, cosine scheduling for forward/reverse KLD, regularized-energy use in ESS, GMM implementation settings, and CPU/GPU hardware with timing details. These materially expand reproducibility information; newly disclosed details do not alone establish changed experiments.

E1.justification: The three peptide systems are retained, while v2 extends evaluation beyond molecular distributions with a 40-component two-dimensional Gaussian mixture (Appendix K) and a Gaussian IS/AIS scaling experiment reaching 500 dimensions (Appendix F.4). These add distinct synthetic sampling scenarios, without demonstrating coverage of larger molecular systems.

E2.justification: The molecular comparator set remains forward KLD, reverse KLD, and FAB. The new GMM comparison adds PIS, DDS, iDEM, and Real-NVP FAB alongside neural-spline FAB (Table 15), substantially broadening comparison methods. Appendix K explicitly attributes the diffusion and Real-NVP FAB scores to prior work; they are reported comparisons, not new runs by these authors.

E3.justification: v2 adds controlled annealing sweeps, Gaussian dimension-scaling protocols, and GMM-specific model configurations and evaluation using 1,000 samples per metric. It also revises molecular FAB's reported coordinate range from [-5,5] to [0,10] and initial HMC step size from 0.1 to 0.05 (v1 G.2; v2 G.1). These explicit setting revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained FAB ablations and qualitative workflow variations, v2 adds systematic TA-BG tests of direct reweighting, starting temperature, linear versus geometric schedules, final and intermediate fine-tuning, annealing count, and buffer size (F.3). Appendices F.4 and J additionally analyze dimensional scaling and computational cost.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains means and standard errors over four independent experiments. New Table 15 instead reports standard deviations, using four runs for the authors' GMM experiments and three for imported results. Appendix F.3 specifies single runs for most new ablations and four runs per starting temperature. No increase in the main experiments' run count is stated.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results change: Table 1's hexapeptide NLL becomes -501.511 instead of -501.523 for TA-BG, and -501.268 instead of -501.275 for FAB. Substantial new results include hexapeptide ESS of 15.38% versus 7.56% with versus without intermediate fine-tuning, GMM comparisons, and runtime measurements. Main molecular conclusions remain; revised settings prevent interpreting updated scores as demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The two-stage TA-BG algorithm and molecular flow architecture remain. Appendix C changes the specified regularized energy for E > E_max from E_max to log(E_max - E_high + 1) + E_high, a limited correction to the training loss definition. Whether implementation changed is unstated. The AIS extension in Appendix F.4 is proposed for future use.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v2 makes localized explanations of training, annealing, and metrics clearer, standardizes terminology, and reorganizes appendix hyperparameters by method. Acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. The retained narrative is refined rather than extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 5–11 and Tables 6–9, 14, and 15 for ablations, scaling, runtime, and GMM results. Earlier appendix Figures 5–11 correspond to Figures 12–18, with several heatmaps updated. The ICML format also changes typography, title and affiliation layout, headers, captions, reference columns, and table placement throughout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and context for diffusion samplers, transition-path sampling, adaptive AIS, and recent flow/protein-ensemble models. The central positioning against MD-dependent temperature-transfer approaches and FAB remains largely unchanged. Publication updates for existing works, such as TRADE, are not new research additions.

T1.justification: New Appendix F.4 introduces an independent-neighborhood clash model and derives expected normalized ESS = (1 - eta)^N, explaining exponential degradation with dimension. Appendix C also corrects the piecewise energy-regularization definition. These are limited mathematical additions and corrections; the main flow and reweighting derivations remain.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves important evidence and reporting gaps: Appendix F.3 tests design choices that v1 largely justified verbally, and Appendix J exposes the wall-time tradeoff behind energy-evaluation savings. Most new ablations remain single-run and the Gaussian tests are limited demonstrations, but the stronger empirical justification and more transparent costs substantially improve overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Temperature-Annealed Boltzmann Generators by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite formatting changes and substantial additions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advancements in data-driven weather forecasting models have delivered deterministic models that outperform the leading operational forecast systems based on traditional, physics-based models. However, these data-driven models are typically trained with a mean squared error loss function, which causes smoothing of fine scales through a "double penalty" effect. We develop a simple, parameter-free modification to this loss function that avoids this problem by separating the loss attributable to decorrelation from the loss attributable to spectral amplitude errors. Fine-tuning the GraphCast model with this new loss function results in sharp deterministic weather forecasts, an increase of the model's effective resolution from 1,250km to 160km, improvements to ensemble spread, and improvements to predictions of tropical cyclone strength and surface wind extremes.
arxiv_record.authors: Christopher Subich and Syed Zahid Husain and Leo Separovic and Jing Yang
arxiv_record.title: Fixing the Double Penalty in Data-Driven Weather Forecasting Through a Modified Spherical Harmonic Loss Function

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same central claims: a parameter-free loss modification produces sharper deterministic forecasts, improves effective resolution from 1,250 km to 160 km, and benefits ensemble spread, cyclone intensity and wind extremes. The added evidence supports these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds focused qualifications about the meaning of effective resolution, the untested use of AMSE throughout training, and possible regularization benefits of MSE. It also explains why multiscale separation is necessary to prevent coarse-scale variance from concealing missing fine-scale variability. Existing precipitation, lagged-ensemble and out-of-distribution limitations remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises training-code release upon publication. v2 instead reports access locations and licenses for the AMSE implementation, training code and fine-tuned checkpoints. It also documents the new loss-control configurations and filtering parameters. This substantially expands actionable reproducibility information, although external resource availability was not independently checked.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same HRES/ERA5 training coverage, 2022 weather evaluation, tropical-cyclone observations and North American station comparisons. The added controls reuse existing forecasting tasks, and the new filtered visualization examines the existing winter storm Eunice case.

E2.justification: Appendix B.5, Figure 14 and Table 2 add MSE AR12 and MAE AR12 as evaluated comparators. MSE AR12 is distinct from the retained, unmodified Control: it receives the fine-tuning curriculum, providing an important additional-training control. MAE AR12 adds a competing loss-function comparison.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the reported warm-up from 128 to 64 batches per stage. Appendix B.4 revises SER to form spatially aggregated variance/error ratios; B.4.1 adds bias-adjusted ensemble-error evaluation. The new visualization uses a fourth-order high-pass filter with cutoff wavenumber 50, while the new loss controls reuse the existing curriculum. These are localized protocol additions and revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AR1/AR12 and spectral analyses, v2 adds matched-curriculum loss ablations testing whether extra training explains improved sharpness (B.5), a high-pass analysis of Eunice forecast structures (B.1), and an analysis of finite-ensemble error bias (B.4.1). The new training control addresses a central attribution question absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds finite-ensemble bias estimation and a variance-subtraction correction for ensemble mean squared error, and explicitly uses unbiased ensemble variance in SER. The existing one-third-date bootstrap sampling and 90% significance threshold remain. No additional training seeds or repeated-run counts are reported.

E6.justification: New results establish that MSE/MAE fine-tuning retains fine-scale smoothing, although MAE improves intermediate-scale sharpness. Table 2 adds substantive comparisons: five-day z500 CRPS is 82.100 for MSE AR12, 80.621 for MAE AR12 and 80.469 for AMSE AR12; five-day q700 instead favors MAE, 0.499 versus AMSE's 0.510. Figure 13 adds results under the bias-adjusted metric, and some significance markers change in retained scorecards. The headline resolution and cyclone findings remain.

M1.justification: The proposed AMSE loss in Equation (6), variable/level weighting, GraphCast architecture and forecasting procedure are retained. The added MSE and MAE variants are comparison controls, rather than changes to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. Local changes expand the introduction and discussion, number the This Work subsection, rename Discussion as Discussion & Limitations, add appendix subsections, and update author, affiliation and acknowledgement text.

P2.justification: The main text and references are comprehensively reformatted from a single-column preprint into a two-column conference layout, with figures resized and relocated. v2 adds Figures 7, 13 and 14 and Table 2, adds a length-scale axis to the effective-resolution plot, and revises labels and captions in retained plots. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant antecedents and approaches, including Weyn, Keisler, Allen, Han and Lippe, and relates AMSE to Chakraborty's binned spectral power loss. Kent and Leutbecher–Palmer support the new resolution discussion and bias analysis. The central positioning relative to ensemble methods and NeuralGCM remains; publication updates to retained references are not new works.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4.1 adds a derivation of the finite-ensemble squared-error bias, including the variance divided by ensemble-size term, and defines its correction in Equation (18). The SER definition also changes its normalization and spatial aggregation. The central AMSE derivation and Appendix A's KL-divergence analysis are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 compares AMSE fine-tuning principally with an untouched checkpoint, leaving extra training as a confound, and only promises future code. v2's matched-curriculum MSE/MAE controls directly address that attribution gap, while its code/checkpoint access information substantially improves reproducibility documentation. The finite-ensemble analysis and clearer resolution qualifications further strengthen evaluation. A local mean/median inconsistency in the new MAE explanation does not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMSE loss and GraphCast fine-tuning study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds MSE/MAE fine-tuning comparisons, filtered forecast visualizations and a finite-ensemble bias analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original GraphCast fine-tuning results, including spectral resolution, lagged-ensemble verification, tropical-cyclone prediction and comparisons with station observations.

arxiv_record.abstract: In-Context Reinforcement Learning (ICRL) represents a promising paradigm for developing generalist agents that learn at inference time through trial-and-error interactions, analogous to how large language models adapt contextually, but with a focus on reward maximization. However, the scalability of ICRL beyond toy tasks and single-domain settings remains an open challenge. In this work, we present the first steps toward scaling ICRL by introducing a fixed, cross-domain model capable of learning behaviors through in-context reinforcement learning. Our results demonstrate that Algorithm Distillation, a framework designed to facilitate ICRL, offers a compelling and competitive alternative to expert distillation to construct versatile action models. These findings highlight the potential of ICRL as a scalable approach for generalist decision-making systems. Code released at https://github.com/dunnolab/vintix

native_events.abstract: In-Context Reinforcement Learning (ICRL) represents a promising paradigm for developing generalist agents that learn at inference time through trial-and-error interactions, analogous to how large language models adapt contextually, but with a focus on reward maximization. However, the scalability of ICRL beyond toy tasks and single-domain settings remains an open challenge. In this work, we present the first steps toward scaling ICRL by introducing a fixed, cross-domain model capable of learning behaviors through in-context reinforcement learning. Our results demonstrate that Algorithm Distillation, a framework designed to facilitate ICRL, offers a compelling and competitive alternative to expert distillation to construct versatile action models. These findings highlight the potential of ICRL as a scalable approach for generalist decision-making systems.

arxiv_record.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control often requires large amounts of online interaction data. Value-based RL methods can mitigate this burden by offering relatively high sample efficiency. Some studies further enhance sample efficiency by incorporating offline demonstration data to "kick-start" training, achieving promising results in continuous control. However, they typically compute the Q-function independently for each action dimension, neglecting interdependencies and making it harder to identify optimal actions when learning from suboptimal data, such as non-expert demonstration and online-collected data during the training process. To address these issues, we propose Auto-Regressive Soft Q-learning (ARSQ), a value-based RL algorithm that models Q-values in a coarse-to-fine, auto-regressive manner. First, ARSQ decomposes the continuous action space into discrete spaces in a coarse-to-fine hierarchy, enhancing sample efficiency for fine-grained continuous control tasks. Next, it auto-regressively predicts dimensional action advantages within each decision step, enabling more effective decision-making in continuous control tasks. We evaluate ARSQ on two continuous control benchmarks, RLBench and D4RL, integrating demonstration data into online training. On D4RL, which includes non-expert demonstrations, ARSQ achieves an average $1.62\times$ performance improvement over SOTA value-based baseline. On RLBench, which incorporates expert demonstrations, ARSQ surpasses various baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in learning from suboptimal online-collected data. Project page is at https://sites.google.com/view/ar-soft-q

arxiv_record.abstract: Asynchronous methods are fundamental for parallelizing computations in distributed machine learning. They aim to accelerate training by fully utilizing all available resources. However, their greedy approach can lead to inefficiencies using more computation than required, especially when computation times vary across devices. If the computation times were known in advance, training could be fast and resource-efficient by assigning more tasks to faster workers. The challenge lies in achieving this optimal allocation without prior knowledge of the computation time distributions. In this paper, we propose ATA (Adaptive Task Allocation), a method that adapts to heterogeneous and random distributions of worker computation times. Through rigorous theoretical analysis, we show that ATA identifies the optimal task allocation and performs comparably to methods with prior knowledge of computation times. Experimental results further demonstrate that ATA is resource-efficient, significantly reducing costs compared to the greedy approach, which can be arbitrarily expensive depending on the number of workers.

arxiv_record.abstract: Node classification is a fundamental task in graph analysis, with broad applications across various fields. Recent breakthroughs in Large Language Models (LLMs) have enabled LLM-based approaches for this task. Although many studies demonstrate the impressive performance of LLM-based methods, the lack of clear design guidelines may hinder their practical application. In this work, we aim to establish such guidelines through a fair and systematic comparison of these algorithms. As a first step, we developed LLMNodeBed, a comprehensive codebase and testbed for node classification using LLMs. It includes 10 homophilic datasets, 4 heterophilic datasets, 8 LLM-based algorithms, 8 classic baselines, and 3 learning paradigms. Subsequently, we conducted extensive experiments, training and evaluating over 2,700 models, to determine the key settings (e.g., learning paradigms and homophily) and components (e.g., model size and prompt) that affect performance. Our findings uncover 8 insights, e.g., (1) LLM-based methods can significantly outperform traditional methods in a semi-supervised setting, while the advantage is marginal in a supervised setting; (2) Graph Foundation Models can beat open-source LLMs but still fall short of strong LLMs like GPT-4o in a zero-shot setting. We hope that the release of LLMNodeBed, along with our insights, will facilitate reproducible research and inspire future studies in this field. Codes and datasets are released at \href{https://llmnodebed.github.io/}{\texttt{https://llmnodebed.github.io/}}.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, zeroth-order (ZO) optimization plays an essential role in scenarios where gradient information is inaccessible or unaffordable, such as black-box systems and resource-constrained environments. While existing adaptive methods such as ZO-AdaMM have shown promise, they are fundamentally limited by their underutilization of moment information during optimization, usually resulting in underperforming convergence. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces Refined Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (R-AdaZO). Specifically, we first show the untapped variance reduction effect of first moment estimate on ZO gradient estimation, which improves the accuracy and stability of ZO updates. We then refine the second moment estimate based on these variance-reduced gradient estimates to better capture the geometry of the optimization landscape, enabling a more effective scaling of ZO updates. We present rigorous theoretical analysis to show (a) the first analysis to the variance reduction of first moment estimate in ZO optimization, (b) the improved second moment estimates with a more accurate approximation of its variance-free ideal, (c) the first variance-aware convergence framework for adaptive ZO methods, which may be of independent interest, and (d) the faster convergence of R-AdaZO than existing baselines like ZO-AdaMM. Our extensive experiments, including synthetic problems, black-box adversarial attack, and memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), further verify the superior convergence of R-AdaZO, indicating that R-AdaZO offers an improved solution for real-world ZO optimization challenges.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present a novel generative approach based on Denoising Diffusion Models (DDMs), which produces high-quality image samples along with their losslessly compressed bit-stream representations. This is obtained by replacing the standard Gaussian noise sampling in the reverse diffusion with a selection of noise samples from pre-defined codebooks of fixed iid Gaussian vectors. Surprisingly, we find that our method, termed Denoising Diffusion Codebook Model (DDCM), retains sample quality and diversity of standard DDMs, even for extremely small codebooks. We leverage DDCM and pick the noises from the codebooks that best match a given image, converting our generative model into a highly effective lossy image codec achieving state-of-the-art perceptual image compression results. More generally, by setting other noise selections rules, we extend our compression method to any conditional image generation task (e.g., image restoration), where the generated images are produced jointly with their condensed bit-stream representations. Our work is accompanied by a mathematical interpretation of the proposed compressed conditional generation schemes, establishing a connection with score-based approximations of posterior samplers for the tasks considered.

We leverage DDCM and pick the noises from the codebooks that best match a given image, converting our generative model into a highly effective lossy image codec achieving state-of-the-art perceptual image compression results. More generally, by setting other noise selections rules, we extend our compression method to any conditional image generation task (e.g., image restoration), where the generated images are produced jointly with their condensed bit-stream representations. Our work is accompanied by a mathematical interpretation of the proposed compressed conditional generation schemes, establishing a connection with score-based approximations of posterior samplers for the tasks considered.
