C1.justification: The abstract and principal contributions retain the same claims: finite codebooks preserve generation quality, enable perceptual compression, and support compressed conditional generation with a posterior-sampling interpretation. Guidance and editing were already announced in v1. The new tokenization discussion is a perspective and future direction rather than a demonstrated core contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations concerning unreliable classifier gradients, random-subset selection for diversity, and the rate–perception–distortion interpretation of reduced prompt alignment. It discusses when editing's weaker structural preservation can be useful and interprets codebook indices as autoregressive image tokens. Existing limitations concerning the VAE, high bit rates, and incomplete theoretical understanding remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B and Table 1 disclose checkpoint identifiers, codebook sizes, timestep counts, matching-pursuit settings and normalization, and comparator configurations. Further additions specify caption generation and bit accounting, metric implementations, restoration sampler settings, and guidance/editing parameters. These substantially improve reproducibility; the project code/demo link was already present in v1.

E1.justification: v4 adds a concrete qualitative editing evaluation on modified-ImageNetR-TI2I (Appendix C.7, Figure 27), extending demonstrated coverage beyond v1's brief announcement of editing. The principal generation, compression, inverse-problem, and four face-restoration datasets were already specified in v1; additional face results and resolution settings do not constitute new datasets.

E2.justification: The main compression and restoration comparator sets are retained. The supplementary editing comparison adds DDPM inversion and full and mid-way DDIM inversion. Appendices C.5–C.6 also explicitly compare compressed guidance against standard CG and CFG, extending the reported comparisons without replacing the original baseline suite.

E3.justification: Newly reported evaluations introduce 768×768 compression, controlled timestep-selection comparisons, caption-conditioned compression at CFG scales 3 and 6, and compressed-guidance parameter sweeps. Generation evaluation expands to KID and DINOv2 distances, while text guidance adds CLIP alignment assessment. These substantially broaden evaluation design; newly disclosed configurations for retained experiments do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's codebook-size experiment and brief statement about prompts, v4 supplies direct analyses of ordinary versus adapted timestep reduction (B.4, Figure 15), caption conditioning (B.6, Figure 16), and guidance-strength/subset-size tradeoffs (C.5–C.6). These provide substantive evidence about design choices, sensitivity, and quality–fidelity tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly displays shaded ranges around KID and DINOv2 kernel-distance curves, whereas v1's generation plots show unbanded estimates. The text does not define these ranges or report repeated-run counts or seeds, so their confidence level and estimation procedure cannot be determined.

E6.justification: The main results are retained, while the appendices add substantial quantitative and qualitative evidence. Table 8 newly reports CCG FID 13.669 versus standard CG values 31.548, 14.481, and 14.921 under its stated setup; Figure 26 reports lower prompt alignment for CCFG. Additional results cover 768×768 compression and the other face datasets. Tables 2–5 tabulate existing Figure 5 results rather than demonstrating new performance gains.

M1.justification: The central sampler, compression rule, and restoration procedures in Eqs. (5)–(12) remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 adds an explicit adapted alternative to timestep skipping: retain 1000 denoising steps but use singleton codebooks outside steps 400–899. The detailed compressed-guidance and editing descriptions mostly elaborate applications already announced in v1.

P1.justification: The main section order, abstract, and much of the exposition are retained. v4 repairs unresolved appendix references, expands selected explanations, adds an impact statement and organized supplementary sections, and updates the publication footer. This is limited editorial revision of the existing narrative despite substantial added scientific material.

P2.justification: v4 adds extensive visual evidence and tabulation: Figures 8–27 and Tables 1–8 include metric plots, comparison grids, configurations, numerical results, and editing examples. Tables 2–5 redisplay existing compression results. Existing Figures 6–7 move, and Figure 5 refines its encoder-decoder-bound labeling and layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a focused comparison with Liu et al. (2021), distinguishing its entropy-constrained optimal-transport formulation from DDCM's cross-modal conditioning. The appendices add relevant editing, classifier-robustness, and evaluation references. The broader positioning around discrete diffusion generation and zero-shot compression remains stable.

T1.justification: v1 states Proposition 6.1 and mathematical connections without supplying the referenced proofs. v4 adds a general-SDE proof argument in C.1, derives the approximate compression connection using Gaussian norm concentration in C.2, and develops the MMSE-based restoration objective in C.4.1. The proposition's main-text statement remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially remedies v1's missing supporting material: the appendices provide implementable configurations, mathematical arguments, and actual evaluations for previously announced applications, including unfavorable tradeoffs. This materially improves reproducibility and critical assessment while retaining the original evidence. Limitations remain: Figure 8's bands are undefined, and C.1 does not establish why rescaling the diffusion coefficient preserves the claimed posterior.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DDCM work and are readable, including figures and equations. v1 ends after its references despite unresolved supplementary references; v4 supplies Appendices A–C. This is a difference in the supplied documents, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and supplies additional quantitative and qualitative results, including compressed guidance and image editing.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation, image-compression, inverse-problem, and face-restoration experiments in Figures 3–7.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper explores how theory can guide and enhance practical algorithms, using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022) in large language models as a case study. We rigorously prove that, under gradient descent, LoRA adapters align with specific singular subspaces of the one-step full fine-tuning gradient. This result suggests that, by properly initializing the adapters using the one-step full gradient, subspace alignment can be achieved immediately and applicable to both linear and nonlinear models. Building on our theory, we propose a theory-driven algorithm, LoRA-One, where the linear convergence (as well as generalization) is built and incorporating preconditioners theoretically helps mitigate the effects of ill-conditioning. Besides, our theory reveals connections between LoRA-One and other gradient-alignment-based methods, helping to clarify misconceptions in the design of such algorithms. LoRA-One achieves significant empirical improvements over LoRA and its variants across benchmarks in natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, and code generation. Code is available at: https://github.com/YuanheZ/LoRA-One.

C1.justification: The central claims about subspace alignment, spectral initialization, and convergence remain. v2 adds an explicit introductory claim of competitive performance at nearly LoRA's time and memory cost, centers the contribution on spectral initialization, and drops the introductory claim of stronger guarantees through a modified gradient update.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the explanation of competing methods' limitations: LoRA-GA's weight offset introduces a biased target, its approximation neglects a quadratic step-size term, and LoRA-SB restricts subspace adaptation. Practical preconditioning guidance shifts from the earlier emphasis on high ranks toward robustness to poorly chosen learning rates. New results also receive interpretations concerning reasoning, knowledge retention, and stability.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds method- and dataset-specific optimized learning rates, batch sizes, scaling parameters, prompting information, and settings for the added experiments. v2 also reports training time and memory. Conversely, the earlier spectral-initializer tuning tables and explicit gradient-averaging implementation description are removed. These materially change the available reproduction information.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST transfer from odd to even digits and Alpaca instruction fine-tuning evaluated on MMLU general knowledge. GLUE, MetaMathQA/GSM8K, and Code-Feedback/HumanEval remain. These additions extend the represented domains and tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds PiSSA and LoRA-Pro to the GLUE comparison and LoRA-SB to synthetic comparisons. Multi-step full fine-tuning disappears from the corresponding GLUE and LLM benchmark tables, although it appears in the new MNIST experiment. Table 2's v2 'Full' row represents a single gradient update, not the removed full-fine-tuning baseline.

E3.justification: v2 narrows the main benchmark comparisons to rank 8, revises learning-rate searches and method-specific settings, and adds 8-shot chain-of-thought evaluation and a separate 395K-sample, four-epoch MetaMathQA experiment. The synthetic comparator experiment changes sample size, rank configurations, and target spectrum. QNLI's one-step full-update learning rate changes from 0.02 to 0.05.

E4.justification: v2 adds T5/MRPC alignment measurements, MNIST optimization trajectories, rank-8 approximations of one-step updates, SST-2 learning-rate robustness tests, and a neuron-norm ratio histogram. The earlier CoLA/MRPC rank-by-initialization/preconditioning ablations are removed. The initialization-variance analysis and pretrained-versus-adapted singular-value plots are retained.

E5.justification: Mean/standard-deviation reporting remains, including three-run GLUE results. v2 adds five-seed, 95% confidence intervals for learning-rate robustness and two-run means for the full-data math experiment. Its NLG Table 3 changes the stated run count from three to five, but Appendix Table 6 still lists three, leaving the actual count unresolved.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced, added, or removed. One-step QNLI accuracy changes from 69.13 to 76.64 alongside the changed learning rate. New results include LoRA-One's 47.24 on MMLU and 63.80 after four epochs on full-data GSM8K, plus resource measurements. Higher-rank benchmark and ablation entries disappear. Revised LoRA-One scores are not same-setting gains because the procedure and tuning change.

M1.justification: v1's primary algorithm uses unweighted singular vectors, offsets the pretrained weights, and applies preconditioned AdamW. v2 replaces it with singular-value-weighted initialization without that offset and ordinary AdamW; this procedure already appeared as Spectral (-) in v1 Algorithm 2. Spectral preconditioning is separately implemented as LoRA-One-P. The former primary implementation and mask-free nonlinear update are removed, so this exceeds renaming.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, related work, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Algorithms/discussion and experiments become separate sections, linear convergence exposition moves into the appendix, and a new preconditioning appendix reorganizes the presentation. Proof sketches and the nonlinear exposition are substantially revised.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text and substantially redesigns its displays: a new three-panel overview, restructured benchmark tables, resource-cost reporting, epoch comparisons, confidence-band plots, and a histogram. Earlier rank-ablation displays disappear; the toy trajectories are reduced and relocated, while the singular-value plots move to Appendix G.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against recent LoRA theory, including Liu, Kim, and Xu et al., and connects the work to one-gradient-step feature-learning research. The previously acknowledged concurrent LoRA-SB work receives a substantive methodological critique and comparison. New analytical discussion also sharpens the distinction from LoRA-GA; these changes exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 replaces the nonlinear orthonormality/orthogonality and absolute-shift assumptions with neuron-balance and relative-shift conditions. Appendix D replaces Hermite-based population-gradient arguments with angular ReLU-gradient analysis, changing initialization scaling and convergence bounds. The smoothed-gradient theorem and proof are removed, and linear alignment analysis is specialized to equal step sizes. The linear convergence results are retained in Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between theory and practice: the primary implementation follows the spectral construction, alignment is tested on T5, and stronger comparator coverage, learning-rate robustness tests, and measured resource costs directly examine central claims. These gains outweigh the loss of rank ablations and full-fine-tuning benchmark controls. The conflicting NLG run counts remain a material reporting weakness, and revised scores should not be interpreted as controlled improvements over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoRA-One research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, alignment and transfer experiments, and learning-rate robustness analyses in Section 6 and Appendices B and G. Some comparator results are explicitly attributed to prior work.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments, T5 evaluations on GLUE, LLaMA 2-7B fine-tuning results, and initialization/preconditioning ablations in Section 5 and Appendix F.

arxiv_record.abstract: Heterogeneity in sensors and actuators across environments poses a significant challenge to building large-scale pre-trained world models on top of this low-dimensional sensor information. In this work, we explore pre-training world models for heterogeneous environments by addressing key transfer barriers in both data diversity and model flexibility. We introduce UniTraj, a unified dataset comprising over one million trajectories from 80 environments, designed to scale data while preserving critical diversity. Additionally, we propose TrajWorld, a novel architecture capable of flexibly handling varying sensor and actuator information and capturing environment dynamics in-context. Pre-training TrajWorld on UniTraj yields substantial gains in transition prediction, achieves a new state-of-the-art for off-policy evaluation, and also delivers superior online performance of model predictive control. To the best of our knowledge, this work, for the first time, demonstrates the transfer benefits of world models across heterogeneous and complex control environments. Code and data are available at https://github.com/thuml/TrajWorld.

native_events.abstract: Heterogeneity in sensors and actuators across environments poses a significant challenge to building large-scale pre-trained world models on top of this low-dimensional sensor information. In this work, we explore pre-training world models for heterogeneous environments by addressing key transfer barriers in both data diversity and model flexibility. We introduce UniTraj, a unified dataset comprising over one million trajectories from 80 environments, designed to scale data while preserving critical diversity. Additionally, we propose TrajWorld, a novel architecture capable of flexibly handling varying sensor and actuator information and capturing environment dynamics in-context. Pre-training TrajWorld on UniTraj yields substantial gains in transition prediction, achieves a new state-of-the-art for off-policy evaluation, and also delivers superior online performance of model predictive control. To the best of our knowledge, this work, for the first time, demonstrates the transfer benefits of world models across heterogeneous and complex control environments. Code and data are available at https://github.com/thuml/TrajWorld.

arxiv_record.abstract: Detailed image captioning is essential for tasks like data generation and aiding visually impaired individuals. High-quality captions require a balance between precision and recall, which remains challenging for current multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this work, we hypothesize that this limitation stems from weakening and increasingly noisy visual attention as responses lengthen. To address this issue, we propose SPARC (Selective Progressive Attention ReCalibration), a training-free method that enhances the contribution of visual tokens during decoding. SPARC is founded on three key observations: (1) increasing the influence of all visual tokens reduces recall; thus, SPARC selectively amplifies visual tokens; (2) as captions lengthen, visual attention becomes noisier, so SPARC identifies critical visual tokens by leveraging attention differences across time steps; (3) as visual attention gradually weakens, SPARC reinforces it to preserve its influence. Our experiments, incorporating both automated and human evaluations, demonstrate that existing methods improve the precision of MLLMs at the cost of recall. In contrast, our proposed method enhances both precision and recall with minimal computational overhead.

arxiv_record.abstract: Prediction-powered inference (PPI) enables valid statistical inference by combining experimental data with machine learning predictions. When a sufficient number of high-quality predictions is available, PPI results in more accurate estimates and tighter confidence intervals than traditional methods. In this paper, we propose to inform the PPI framework with prior knowledge on the quality of the predictions. The resulting method, which we call frequentist, assisted by Bayes, PPI (FAB-PPI), improves over PPI when the observed prediction quality is likely under the prior, while maintaining its frequentist guarantees. Furthermore, when using heavy-tailed priors, FAB-PPI adaptively reverts to standard PPI in low prior probability regions. We demonstrate the benefits of FAB-PPI in real and synthetic examples.

arxiv_record.title: FAB-PPI: Frequentist, Assisted by Bayes, Prediction-Powered Inference

arxiv_record.abstract: The Latent Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) is a powerful tool for time series and sequence modeling. E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same eight comparison methods. Adjoint sensitivity remains the competing training method in the added experiments. arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models generate high-quality synthetic data. They operate by defining a continuous-time forward process which gradually adds Gaussian noise to data until fully corrupted. The corresponding reverse process progressively "denoises" a Gaussian sample into a sample from the data distribution. However, generating high-quality outputs requires many discretization steps to obtain a faithful approximation of the reverse process. This is expensive and has motivated the development of many acceleration methods. We propose to accomplish sample generation by learning the posterior {\em distribution} of clean data samples given their noisy versions, instead of only the mean of this distribution. This allows us to sample from the probability transitions of the reverse process on a coarse time scale, significantly accelerating inference with minimal degradation of the quality of the output. This is accomplished by replacing the standard regression loss used to estimate conditional means with a scoring rule. We validate our method on image and robot trajectory generation, where we consistently outperform standard diffusion models at few discretization steps.
arxiv_record.authors: Valentin De Bortoli, Alexandre Galashov, J. Swaroop Guntupalli, Guangyao Zhou, Kevin Murphy, Arthur Gretton, Arnaud Doucet
arxiv_record.title: Distributional Diffusion Models with Scoring Rules

E4.justification: V3 adds population-size sensitivity tests: m=2 versus m=4 for images and m=2–64 at fixed beta=1 and lambda=0.5 for robotics. Appendix J additionally measures training-throughput scaling with m on three hardware platforms. Existing kernel, beta/lambda, and beta=2 robotics analyses are retained.

For example, Table 3 reports 10-evaluation CIFAR-10 FIDs of 3.19 for distributional diffusion, 3.55 for DPM++, and 2.99 for distillation. Figure 9 also changes values and rankings under the revised robotics setup, with the diffusion baseline becoming best at 50 steps.

P2.justification: V3 adds seven numbered result tables and a three-panel robotics figure, redraws Figure 9 and its appendix repeat with a different vertical scale, and revises captions and the notation-table formatting. arxiv_record.abstract: The discovery of new materials is essential for enabling technological advancements. Computational approaches for predicting novel materials must effectively learn the manifold of stable crystal structures within an infinite design space. We introduce Open Materials Generation (OMatG), a unifying framework for the generative design and discovery of inorganic crystalline materials. OMatG employs stochastic interpolants (SI) to bridge an arbitrary base distribution to the target distribution of inorganic crystals via a broad class of tunable stochastic processes, encompassing both diffusion models and flow matching as special cases. In this work, we adapt the SI framework by integrating an equivariant graph representation of crystal structures and extending it to account for periodic boundary conditions in unit cell representations. Additionally, we couple the SI flow over spatial coordinates and lattice vectors with discrete flow matching for atomic species. We benchmark OMatG's performance on two tasks: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) for specified compositions, and 'de novo' generation (DNG) aimed at discovering stable, novel, and unique structures. In our ground-up implementation of OMatG, we refine and extend both CSP and DNG metrics compared to previous works. OMatG establishes a new state of the art in generative modeling for materials discovery, outperforming purely flow-based and diffusion-based implementations. These results underscore the importance of designing flexible deep learning frameworks to accelerate progress in materials science. The OMatG code is available at https://github.com/FERMat-ML/OMatG.

E4.justification: v2 expands the selected-model comparisons into systematic studies of positional interpolants, ODE versus SDE sampling, and latent noise for perov-5 CSP, MP-20 CSP, and MP-20 DNG (Tables VI–XI). arxiv_record.abstract: Chest X-rays (CXRs) play an integral role in driving critical decisions in disease management and patient care. While recent innovations have led to specialized models for various CXR interpretation tasks, these solutions often operate in isolation, limiting their practical utility in clinical practice. We present MedRAX, the first versatile AI agent that seamlessly integrates state-of-the-art CXR analysis tools and multimodal large language models into a unified framework. MedRAX dynamically leverages these models to address complex medical queries without requiring additional training. To rigorously evaluate its capabilities, we introduce ChestAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark containing 2,500 complex medical queries across 7 diverse categories. Our experiments demonstrate that MedRAX achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to both open-source and proprietary models, representing a significant step toward the practical deployment of automated CXR interpretation systems. Data and code have been publicly available at https://github.com/bowang-lab/MedRAX

arxiv_record.abstract: Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks (SE-GNNs) are popular explainable-by-design GNNs, but their explanations' properties and limitations are not well understood. Our first contribution fills this gap by formalizing the explanations extracted by some popular SE-GNNs, referred to as Minimal Explanations (MEs), and comparing them to established notions of explanations, namely Prime Implicant (PI) and faithful explanations. Our analysis reveals that MEs match PI explanations for a restricted but significant family of tasks. In general, however, they can be less informative than PI explanations and are surprisingly misaligned with widely accepted notions of faithfulness. Although faithful and PI explanations are informative, they are intractable to find and we show that they can be prohibitively large. Given these observations, a natural choice is to augment SE-GNNs with alternative modalities of explanations taking care of SE-GNNs' limitations. To this end, we propose Dual-Channel GNNs that integrate a white-box rule extractor and a standard SE-GNN, adaptively combining both channels. Our experiments show that even a simple instantiation of Dual-Channel GNNs can recover succinct rules and perform on par or better than widely used SE-GNNs.
arxiv_record.authors: Steve Azzolin, Sagar Malhotra, Andrea Passerini, Stefano Teso
arxiv_record.title: Beyond Topological Self-Explainable GNNs: A Formal Explainability Perspective

arxiv_record.abstract: Selecting a layer normalization (LN) strategy that stabilizes training and speeds convergence in Transformers remains difficult, even for today's large language models (LLM). We present a comprehensive analytical foundation for understanding how different LN strategies influence training dynamics in large-scale Transformers. Until recently, Pre-LN and Post-LN have long dominated practices despite their limitations in large-scale training. However, several open-source models have recently begun silently adopting a third strategy without much explanation. This strategy places normalization layer peripherally around sublayers, a design we term Peri-LN. While Peri-LN has demonstrated promising performance, its precise mechanisms and benefits remain almost unexplored. Our in-depth analysis delineates the distinct behaviors of LN strategies, showing how each placement shapes activation variance and gradient propagation. To validate our theoretical insight, we conduct extensive experiments on Transformers up to $3.2$B parameters, showing that Peri-LN consistently achieves more balanced variance growth, steadier gradient flow, and convergence stability. Our results suggest that Peri-LN warrants broader consideration for large-scale Transformer architectures, providing renewed insights into the optimal placement of LN.

C1.justification: Both versions position Peri-LN as a unifying description of existing normalization layouts and claim improved activation control, gradient behavior, and training stability through 3.2B parameters. The revised abstract, shorter contribution bullets, and conclusion retain this central scientific contribution.

C2.justification: v3 develops a stronger variance-driven explanation of early instability and interprets weight decay and initialization as interventions on that mechanism. It adds implications for FP16/BF16, hardware, quantization, and OPT instability. Appendix B also replaces v1's huge-residual explanation of Post-LN suppression with an emphasis on depth and comparatively moderate activations.

D1.justification: v3 discloses the baseline initialization parameter of 0.02 in Table 2 and specifies 256 RedPajama samples for the retained representation analysis. It also supplies settings for the new ablations, including their forward-statistics sample count. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the original training setup.

E1.justification: Training, instruction-tuning, benchmark, C4, and Wikitext coverage is retained. v3 identifies RedPajama-Data-1T as the source for the existing representation analysis, whose plots are reused; this documents retained evidence rather than establishing new coverage. The added ablations vary model and training settings, not tasks or domains.

E2.justification: Appendix G.6 adds A+C and B-only normalization configurations to a comparison with Peri-LN and Post-LN; G.7 adds Peri-LN+QK-Norm. These are focused comparator additions. The original Pre-LN, Post-LN, and OLMo2-style comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The original benchmark protocol is retained, but v3 adds substantial experimental designs: controlled weight-decay and initialization sweeps, SGD learning-rate sweeps, and additional normalization configurations. Appendix G.8 specifies 400M models trained on 30B tokens and 100 samples for the new forward-statistics analyses. G.7 also changes the combined QK variant's normalizer to LayerNorm.

E4.justification: Sections 4.3–4.4, 6–7 and Appendices G/I add targeted instability diagnostics, final-layer gradient tracking, weight-decay and initialization interventions, alternative placements, QK augmentation, SGD checks, and an FP16-range analysis. These substantially extend tests of the proposed stability mechanism. The original representation and embedding-normalization analyses are retained, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report five pre-training seeds, benchmark means and standard deviations, individual-seed tables, and exclusion of diverged checkpoints. Additional individual-run plots and stronger wording about seed coverage do not establish increased repetitions or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2 and v3 Table 1 match numerically, as do all six detailed benchmark tables. v3 nevertheless adds substantial results: Table 5 reports losses of 3.01 for A+C, 3.05 for Post-LN, 2.91 for Peri-LN, and divergence for B-only; Tables 6–9 and the new SGD and precision figures add further findings under additional conditions.

M1.justification: The core Peri-LN residual update is unchanged. Appendix G.7 adds a combined Peri-LN+QK-Norm variant using LayerNorm, distinct from the OLMo2-style alternative already evaluated in v1. Calling embedding normalization optional reflects an option already tested in v1.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: v1's systematic-analysis subsection becomes a reordered standalone section, followed by separate Ablation Study and Implications sections. The abstract and contribution list are rewritten, theoretical exposition is expanded, and proofs, settings, and representation discussion are reorganized across appendices.

P2.justification: v3 adds new instability, intervention, SGD, and precision plots and several ablation tables, while removing v1's intuitive comparison table. The full representation figure moves to Appendix L with selected panels repeated in the main text; retained plots are resized and captions revised. Some new appendix plots are tightly packed, with overlaps on page 29.

R1.justification: Appendix A newly acknowledges Ding et al.'s Sandwich-LN precedent, and v3 adds Gemma 3 and supporting initialization, optimizer, and quantization literature. These refine prior-art attribution and broaden context while retaining the paper's positioning as an analytical and empirical study of existing normalization designs.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix C explicitly assumes a positive RMSNorm scale gamma, an assumption unstated in v1 Appendix D. The gradient formulas and proofs otherwise remain essentially unchanged. The Post-LN bound is relocated to Appendix B, and numbering the existing variance recurrence does not introduce new mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central stability argument through controlled weight-decay and initialization interventions absent from v1, complemented by placement and optimizer checks. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Peri-LN study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds normalization-placement, initialization, weight-decay, optimizer, and activation-range experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original Transformer pre-training, instruction-tuning, benchmark evaluations, and activation/gradient analyses, including per-seed results in Appendix H.

arxiv_record.abstract: Traditional robust methods in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often struggle against coordinated adversarial attacks in cooperative scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose the Wolfpack Adversarial Attack framework, inspired by wolf hunting strategies, which targets an initial agent and its assisting agents to disrupt cooperation. Additionally, we introduce the Wolfpack-Adversarial Learning for MARL (WALL) framework, which trains robust MARL policies to defend against the proposed Wolfpack attack by fostering systemwide collaboration. Experimental results underscore the devastating impact of the Wolfpack attack and the significant robustness improvements achieved by WALL. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunwoolee0504/WALL.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.4 compares computational costs, while E.5 tests whether robustness learned against action attacks transfers to observation noise and environment-parameter shifts. arxiv_record.abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) is a widely adopted visual imitation learning method in robot manipulation. Current BC approaches often enhance generalization by leveraging large datasets and incorporating additional visual and textual modalities to capture more diverse information. However, these methods overlook whether the learned representations contain redundant information and lack a solid theoretical foundation to guide the learning process. To address these limitations, we adopt an information-theoretic perspective and introduce mutual information to quantify and mitigate redundancy in latent representations. Building on this, we incorporate the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle into BC, which extends the idea of reducing redundancy by providing a structured framework for compressing irrelevant information while preserving task-relevant features. This work presents the first comprehensive study on redundancy in latent representations across various methods, backbones, and experimental settings, while extending the generalizability of the IB to BC. Extensive experiments and analyses on the CortexBench and LIBERO benchmarks demonstrate significant performance improvements with IB, underscoring the importance of reducing input data redundancy and highlighting its practical value for more practical applications. Project Page: https://baishuanghao.github.io/BC-IB.github.io.

Current BC approaches often enhance generalization by leveraging large datasets and incorporating additional visual and textual modalities to capture more diverse information. However, these methods overlook whether the learned representations contain redundant information and lack a solid theoretical foundation to guide the learning process. To address these limitations, we adopt an information-theoretic perspective and introduce mutual information to quantify and mitigate redundancy in latent representations. Building on this, we incorporate the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle into BC, which extends the idea of reducing redundancy by providing a structured framework for compressing irrelevant information while preserving task-relevant features. This work presents the first comprehensive study on redundancy in latent representations across various methods, backbones, and experimental settings, while extending the generalizability of the IB to BC. Extensive experiments and analyses on the CortexBench and LIBERO benchmarks show consistent performance improvements with IB across various settings, underscoring the importance of reducing input data redundancy and highlighting its practical value for real-world applications.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present the first gap-dependent analysis of regret and communication cost for on-policy federated $Q$-Learning in tabular episodic finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs). Existing FRL methods focus on worst-case scenarios, leading to $\sqrt{T}$-type regret bounds and communication cost bounds with a $\log T$ term scaling with the number of agents $M$, states $S$, and actions $A$, where $T$ is the average total number of steps per agent. In contrast, our novel framework leverages the benign structures of MDPs, such as a strictly positive suboptimality gap, to achieve a $\log T$-type regret bound and a refined communication cost bound that disentangles exploration and exploitation. Our gap-dependent regret bound reveals a distinct multi-agent speedup pattern, and our gap-dependent communication cost bound removes the dependence on $MSA$ from the $\log T$ term. Notably, our gap-dependent communication cost bound also yields a better global switching cost when $M=1$, removing $SA$ from the $\log T$ term.

arxiv_record.abstract: Reward design in reinforcement learning and optimal control is challenging. Preference-based alignment addresses this by enabling agents to learn rewards from ranked trajectory pairs provided by humans. However, existing methods often struggle from poor robustness to unknown false human preferences. In this work, we propose a robust and efficient reward alignment method based on a novel and geometrically interpretable perspective: hypothesis space batched cutting. Our method iteratively refines the reward hypothesis space through "cuts" based on batches of human preferences. Within each batch, human preferences, queried based on disagreement, are grouped using a voting function to determine the appropriate cut, ensuring a bounded human query complexity. To handle unknown erroneous preferences, we introduce a conservative cutting method within each batch, preventing erroneous human preferences from making overly aggressive cuts to the hypothesis space. This guarantees provable robustness against false preferences, while eliminating the need to explicitly identify them. We evaluate our method in a model predictive control setting across diverse tasks. The results demonstrate that our framework achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods in error-free settings while significantly outperforming existing methods when handling a high percentage of erroneous human preferences.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhixian Xie, Haode Zhang, Yizhe Feng, Wanxin Jin
arxiv_record.title: Robust Reward Alignment via Hypothesis Space Batch Cutting

arxiv_record.abstract: Feature learning in neural networks is crucial for their expressive power and inductive biases, motivating various theoretical approaches. Some approaches describe network behavior after training through a change in kernel scale from initialization, resulting in a generalization power comparable to a Gaussian process. Conversely, in other approaches training results in the adaptation of the kernel to the data, involving directional changes to the kernel. The relationship and respective strengths of these two views have so far remained unresolved. This work presents a theoretical framework of multi-scale adaptive feature learning bridging these two views. Using methods from statistical mechanics, we derive analytical expressions for network output statistics which are valid across scaling regimes and in the continuum between them. A systematic expansion of the network's probability distribution reveals that mean-field scaling requires only a saddle-point approximation, while standard scaling necessitates additional correction terms. Remarkably, we find across regimes that kernel adaptation can be reduced to an effective kernel rescaling when predicting the mean network output in the special case of a linear network. However, for linear and non-linear networks, the multi-scale adaptive approach captures directional feature learning effects, providing richer insights than what could be recovered from a rescaling of the kernel alone.

C1.justification: v1's demonstrated directional-learning contribution concerns output covariance in linear networks. v2 explicitly extends its contribution to nonlinear networks and claims differences in mean predictions and sample-complexity class, supported by the new nonlinear experiment. This substantially broadens the abstract, introduction, and discussion beyond the retained linear rescaling connection.

C2.justification: v2 explains cooperative amplification of coherent input and target structure and connects nonlinear directional learning to sample efficiency. It distinguishes rescaling equivalence under the cumulant approximation from its breakdown under finer approximations. The earlier linear-only limitation and nonlinear future-work statement are replaced by discussion of the remaining shallow-network scope.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access DOI and Appendix C.2/Algorithm 1 documenting solver initialization, annealing across scaling regimes, and stated O(P^3) computational cost. The existing Langevin training description and 10,000-step equilibration statement remain; the new solver documentation does not establish a change to the original experiments.

E1.justification: Coverage expands beyond the original Ising and linear teacher–student tasks to binary MNIST classification and nonlinear teacher–student regression with linear and cubic Hermite target components. Figure 11 also introduces structured and unstructured Ising input scenarios with varying signal strength.

E2.justification: Matched original experiments retain NNGP, Li–Sompolinsky rescaling, and the same approximation variants. New experiments reuse NNGP and scalar rescaling, using activation kernels for nonlinear networks. The change from 'One-Loop Rescaling' to 'One-Loop simpl.' does not introduce a different comparator.

E3.justification: v2 adds an erf-network sample-size sweep using component learnability, with N = 1,000, D = 30, and 4,000 test points, plus MNIST evaluation settings. E4.justification: New Figure 11 compares structured and unstructured kernels and varies the Ising signal parameter to test coherent amplification of input structure. E5.justification: Both versions report different initialization seeds, averaging 100 networks for Ising predictions and 5,000 for teacher–student output covariances. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or stated repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Figure 5 reports increasing cubic-component learnability captured by the adaptive approximation while NNGP and rescaling remain near zero. M1.justification: v1 develops the linear-network procedure and leaves nonlinear extensions to future work. v2 incorporates nonlinear activations and develops both cumulant-based and variational Gaussian approximation procedures for their prediction kernels and self-consistency equations (Appendices A.1.2 and A.2.3). R1.justification: Section 2 expands positioning through maximal-update scaling, representation-learning frameworks, and additional deep-linear results. This extends the theoretical positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds nonlinear-prior cumulant derivations, variational Gaussian self-consistency equations, an analytical argument for coherent kernel amplification, and Appendix B's derivation connecting another readout-weight scaling regime. arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models exhibit excellent sample quality, but existing guidance methods often require additional model training or are limited to specific tasks. We revisit guidance in diffusion models from the perspective of variational inference and control, introducing Diffusion Trajectory Matching (DTM) that enables guiding pretrained diffusion trajectories to satisfy a terminal cost. DTM unifies a broad class of guidance methods and enables novel instantiations. We introduce a new method within this framework that achieves state-of-the-art results on several linear, non-linear, and blind inverse problems without requiring additional model training or specificity to pixel or latent space diffusion models. Our code will be available at https://github.com/czi-ai/oc-guidance

arxiv_record.abstract: Do the rich representations of multi-modal diffusion transformers (DiTs) exhibit unique properties that enhance their interpretability? We introduce ConceptAttention, a novel method that leverages the expressive power of DiT attention layers to generate high-quality saliency maps that precisely locate textual concepts within images. Without requiring additional training, ConceptAttention repurposes the parameters of DiT attention layers to produce highly contextualized concept embeddings, contributing the major discovery that performing linear projections in the output space of DiT attention layers yields significantly sharper saliency maps compared to commonly used cross-attention maps. ConceptAttention even achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot image segmentation benchmarks, outperforming 15 other zero-shot interpretability methods on the ImageNet-Segmentation dataset. ConceptAttention works for popular image models and even seamlessly generalizes to video generation. Our work contributes the first evidence that the representations of multi-modal DiTs are highly transferable to vision tasks like segmentation.
arxiv_record.authors: Alec Helbling, Tuna Han Salih Meral, Ben Hoover, Pinar Yanardag, Duen Horng Chau
arxiv_record.comments: Oral Presentation at ICML 2025, Best Paper Award at CVPR Workshop on Visual Concepts

arxiv_record.abstract: Foundation models trained on patient electronic health records (EHRs) require tokenizing medical data into sequences of discrete vocabulary items. Existing tokenizers treat medical codes from EHRs as isolated textual tokens. However, each medical code is defined by its textual description, its position in ontological hierarchies, and its relationships to other codes, such as disease co-occurrences and drug-treatment associations. Medical vocabularies contain more than 600,000 codes with critical information for clinical reasoning. We introduce MedTok, a multimodal medical code tokenizer that uses the text descriptions and relational context of codes. MedTok processes text using a language model encoder and encodes the relational structure with a graph encoder. It then quantizes both modalities into a unified token space, preserving modality-specific and cross-modality information. We integrate MedTok into five EHR models and evaluate it on operational and clinical tasks across in-patient and out-patient datasets, including outcome prediction, diagnosis classification, drug recommendation, and risk stratification. Swapping standard EHR tokenizers with MedTok improves AUPRC across all EHR models, by 4.10% on MIMIC-III, 4.78% on MIMIC-IV, and 11.32% on EHRShot, with the largest gains in drug recommendation. Beyond EHR modeling, we demonstrate using MedTok tokenizer with medical QA systems. Our results demonstrate the potential of MedTok as a unified tokenizer for medical codes, improving tokenization for medical foundation models.
arxiv_record.authors: Xiaorui Su, Shvat Messica, Yepeng Huang, Ruth Johnson, Lukas Fesser, Shanghua Gao, Faryad Sahneh, Marinka Zitnik

The revised QA scores are not same-setting performance gains over v1.

Cross-attention projections become explicitly modality-specific. The dual encoders, partitioned codebook, top-K quantization and token-packing framework remain. These are localized changes to the specified computation; the PDFs do not establish corresponding implementation changes or reruns of retained experiments.

P1.justification: Editing concentrates on the method explanations, terminology, captions and appendix headings. Hyperparameter sensitivity receives a separate subsection, QA is renumbered, and an interpretability subsection is added. Publication metadata and a conflict-of-interest statement are updated. The overall narrative structure and most introductory, related-work and concluding text remain.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are substantially revised: v3 adds Table 5, rebuilds Figure 5 around loss-weight and codebook-size sensitivity, replaces the old QA panel with the three-panel Figure 6, and adds the token-frequency Figure 7. Figure 3 is relocated and reduced from full-width to a single-column display. The architecture figures and principal EHR tables are retained.

arxiv_record.abstract: Conformal prediction is a flexible framework for calibrating machine learning predictions, providing distribution-free statistical guarantees. In outlier detection, this calibration relies on a reference set of labeled inlier data to control the type-I error rate. However, obtaining a perfectly labeled inlier reference set is often unrealistic, and a more practical scenario involves access to a contaminated reference set containing a small fraction of outliers. This paper analyzes the impact of such contamination on the validity of conformal methods. We prove that under realistic, non-adversarial settings, calibration on contaminated data yields conservative type-I error control, shedding light on the inherent robustness of conformal methods. This conservativeness, however, typically results in a loss of power. To alleviate this limitation, we propose a novel, active data-cleaning framework that leverages a limited labeling budget and an outlier detection model to selectively annotate data points in the contaminated reference set that are suspected as outliers. By removing only the annotated outliers in this ``suspicious'' subset, we can effectively enhance power while mitigating the risk of inflating the type-I error rate, as supported by our theoretical analysis. Experiments on real datasets validate the conservative behavior of conformal methods under contamination and show that the proposed data-cleaning strategy improves power without sacrificing validity.

It also discusses label ambiguity, possible extensions using uncertainty information, and retaining uncertain points as inliers. These additions refine applicability and interpretation.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds implementation information for the new configurations, including the VGG-19 model source, SCALE’s activation-rescaling rule and 65% percentile setting, and the One-Class SVM RBF kernel. Existing split recipes, ReAct’s 90% threshold, and the method’s repository link remain.

E1.justification: The three tabular datasets and six visual-data pairings remain. However, v2 adds distinct scenarios with score-selected contaminants resembling inliers across the tabular datasets and changing test-time outlier populations on shuttle (Figures 16–20), substantially extending coverage beyond random contamination.

E2.justification: The comparison methods remain Standard, Oracle, Naive-Trim, and Small-Clean. LOF, One-Class SVM, ReAct/VGG-19, and SCALE/ResNet-18 are additional scoring configurations shared by Label-Trim and its comparators.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluations using LOF and One-Class SVM on tabular data and ReAct/VGG-19 and SCALE/ResNet-18 on visual data. New protocols include contamination rates up to 15%, percentile-based outlier selection, and shuttle tests varying outlier percentile ranges while training/calibration outliers come from the 30th–100th percentiles. These supplement the retained original protocols.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained contamination, labeling-budget, significance-level, and KDDCup99 variability analyses, v2 tests sensitivity to scoring models, heavier contamination, harder contaminants, and test-time outlier shifts. Figures 13–20 substantially expand robustness evidence and reveal settings with weak detection power.

E5.justification: Both versions generally use 100 random data splits, retain 400-split KDDCup99 labeling-budget analyses, and report standard errors in visual-data tables. The added results follow the existing reporting practices; no new statistical estimation procedure or increased repeat count is documented.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables are retained, including v1 Tables 4–9 as v2 Tables 6–11. Substantial new results appear in Figures 13–20 and Tables 4–5 and 12–23. For example, at alpha = 0.01 and 5% contamination, the new ReAct/VGG-19 and SCALE/ResNet-18 evaluations report Label-Trim relative powers of 1.606 and 1.627, respectively, both with type-I error 0.009.

M1.justification: Section 3.3, Equation (4), and Algorithms 1–2 retain the same procedure: annotate the highest-scoring calibration points, remove confirmed outliers, and calibrate using the retained set. Additional scoring models test the existing model-agnostic procedure.

P1.justification: Most original exposition is retained, with grammatical corrections, added pointers to experiments, and expanded discussion. The former tabular and visual appendices become subsections B.2.1 and B.2.2 under Additional Experiments. These are limited narrative and organizational changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and repositions figures, tables, and algorithms. It adds the method schematic in Figure 2, robustness Figures 13–20, and fourteen new tables. Existing graphics are retained and renumbered, while table captions more explicitly identify scoring configurations.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting LOF, One-Class SVM, SCALE, and the VGG-19 implementation. Section 5 also connects the work to ambiguous-ground-truth research by Stutz, Javanmardi, and Caprio and colleagues. The main related-work positioning in Section 1.3 remains stable.

T1.justification: Proposition 2.1, Lemma 2.2, Assumption 2.3, Theorem 3.1, and Appendix A’s auxiliary propositions, mixture-distribution corollary, and proofs are substantively unchanged. The labeling-budget condition m <= alpha(n + 1) is retained.

improvement.justification: v1’s empirical support relied on one scoring configuration per data modality and random contamination. v2 substantially strengthens that support by testing alternative scorers, harder contaminants, heavier contamination, and shifted test outliers, exposing low-power regimes alongside successes. These tests address important questions about robustness while preserving the original evidence. The schematic and clearer limitations further improve the paper, although the theoretical guarantees remain unchanged and require matching inlier distributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Label-Trim research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across the layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original outlier-detection experiments on three tabular datasets and six visual-data pairings in Section 4 and Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Model merging integrates the weights of multiple task-specific models into a single multi-task model. Despite recent interest in the problem, a significant performance gap between the combined and single-task models remains. In this paper, we investigate the key characteristics of task matrices -- weight update matrices applied to a pre-trained model -- that enable effective merging. We show that alignment between singular components of task-specific and merged matrices strongly correlates with performance improvement over the pre-trained model. Based on this, we propose an isotropic merging framework that flattens the singular value spectrum of task matrices, enhances alignment, and reduces the performance gap. Additionally, we incorporate both common and task-specific subspaces to further improve alignment and performance. Our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on vision and language tasks across various sets of tasks and model scales. This work advances the understanding of model merging dynamics, offering an effective methodology to merge models without requiring additional training. Code is available at https://github.com/danielm1405/iso-merging .

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly claims state-of-the-art performance on language as well as vision tasks. A new introduction contribution asserts versatility across vision/language benchmarks and fully fine-tuned/LoRA models. This materially broadens the claimed applicability beyond v1's vision-only evidence, while retaining the original alignment and isotropic-merging contributions.

C2.justification: V2 develops activation preservation as an explanation for reduced interference, interprets similar Iso-C/Iso-CTS NLP performance as evidence that the common subspace is sufficient there, and explains when isotropic scaling matters within Iso-CTS. The conclusion replaces v1's vision-only limitation with the limitation that low-rank structure is not fully exploited; the potentially suboptimal Task Arithmetic common subspace remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 supplies checkpoint sources, LoRA rank and reconstruction instructions, the language-model identity, and protocol references for the added evaluations. Existing vector-parameter averaging, the default common-subspace fraction, and the alpha table are retained. The same code URL remains, while v1's inconsistent statement promising a future release is removed; the PDFs do not establish a newly available resource.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates vision tasks only. V2 adds language-model merging on 7-task and 8-task subsets of the T0 mixture (Section 5.3, Table 3), substantially extending domain and task coverage. The original vision datasets are retained; the LoRA experiments reuse the existing eight vision tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains its comparator set. New comparisons evaluate DARE-TIES, KnOTS-TIES, and KnOTS-DARE-TIES for LoRA (Table 2); Fisher Merging, RegMean, and MaTS for language models (Table 3); and additional vision baselines including PCB and CART (Table 4). These are evaluated comparators, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: V2 introduces rank-16 LoRA evaluations using KnOTS ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 checkpoints, T5-Large-LM-Adapt language evaluations, and a separate vision comparison using Task Arithmetic checkpoints instead of the Consensus Merging checkpoints used in Table 1. Appendix D.2 also introduces mean L1 embedding distance as an interference measure. The retained Table 1 protocol and reported alpha choices are unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of embedding interference (Appendix D.2, Figure 7), the necessity of isotropic scaling within Iso-CTS (D.4, Figure 8), alignment across transformer layers (E.2, Figure 13), and whether the alignment–performance relationship persists on ViT-L/14 (E.3, Figure 9). The earlier interpolation, subspace-size, alpha-sensitivity, and single-task flattening analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or run-level uncertainty. The retained boxplots summarize variation across tasks rather than repeated runs. The revised Pearson correlation value changes a result, not the statistical reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 is numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results: Iso-CTS scores 75.0/89.6 normalized accuracy for LoRA ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 (Table 2), while Iso-C scores 75.6/83.3 absolute accuracy on the 8/7 NLP tasks (Table 3). Table 4 and the new analyses add further outcomes. Section 3.3 and Figure 3 revise the reported SAR–NAI correlation from 0.88 to 0.94. The added benchmark scores are not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the core spectral merging operations remain unchanged. Section 5.2 adds a limited input adaptation for LoRA: reconstruct each task update as Delta W_t = B_t A_t before applying the existing merging procedure. No substantial algorithm redesign or new training objective is introduced.

P1.justification: Most introductory and methodological prose is retained. Local rewrites clarify cosine similarity and alignment terminology; Section 5 is reorganized around fully fine-tuned vision, LoRA, language, and analyses; and existing appendix material is redistributed under experimental details, experiments, and visualizations. Affiliations, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated. These edits do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds dedicated tables for LoRA, NLP, and alternative-checkpoint vision comparisons, plus figures for interference, isotropic-scaling ablation, larger-model correlation, and per-layer alignment. Existing NAI plots have revised axes and Figure 3 has revised labeling. Earlier appendix plots and the alpha table are retained and relocated or renumbered, rather than removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantive distinction between static and dynamic merging, contrasting Twin-Merging and EMR-Merging and explicitly limiting its scope to static merging. References supporting the additional merging comparisons, language evaluations, interference analysis, and complexity analysis substantially expand the literature coverage. The updated publication details for TSV and KnOTS refer to works already cited in v1.

T1.justification: V2 adds theoretical appendices absent from v1: a spectral derivation of effective rank, a projection-based SAR monotonicity argument, an activation-interference decomposition, and a variance argument explaining underrepresented tasks (Appendix A). Appendix B adds an asymptotic SVD-cost comparison of Iso-C, Iso-CTS, and TSV-M. These additions go substantially beyond restating the existing method equations.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicit vision-only limitation with language experiments and adds LoRA evidence and broader baseline comparisons. The new Iso-CTS scaling ablation and interference measurements more directly test the proposed mechanism, while the theoretical appendices clarify its rationale and computational cost. These gains substantially strengthen generality and explanatory support while preserving the earlier evidence. The interference argument remains approximate and uncertainty reporting is still absent, but these limitations do not outweigh the improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Iso-C/Iso-CTS research, with readable text, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Shared content can be matched reliably despite the expanded experiments and reorganized appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds LoRA and language-model evaluations, additional vision comparisons, interference measurements, and component ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-merging results on 8, 14, and 20 vision tasks in Table 1, together with original alignment analyses and ablations in the main text and Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Accelerating the inference of large language models (LLMs) is a critical challenge in generative AI. Speculative decoding (SD) methods offer substantial efficiency gains by generating multiple tokens using a single target forward pass. However, existing SD approaches require the drafter and target models to share the same vocabulary, thus limiting the pool of possible drafters, often necessitating the training of a drafter from scratch. We present three new SD methods that remove this shared-vocabulary constraint. All three methods preserve the target distribution (i.e., they are lossless) and work with off-the-shelf models without requiring additional training or modifications. Empirically, on summarization, programming, and long-context tasks, our algorithms demonstrate significant speedups of up to 2.8x over standard autoregressive decoding. By enabling any off-the-shelf model to serve as a drafter and requiring no retraining, this work substantially broadens the applicability of the SD framework in practice.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains three lossless methods requiring no additional training. v2 specifies headline speedups of up to 2.8× for SLEM and 1.7× for TLI, and drops v1's claim that TLI outperforms SLEM on average. It also adds a claim that Hugging Face maintainers found both methods most effective among previously supported speculative-decoding algorithms.

C2.justification: The limitations discussion newly identifies architecture and training differences as factors affecting acceptance rates and points to benchmark failures with insufficiently fast or accurate drafters. It replaces v1's explicit qualification about optimized homogeneous SD potentially outperforming the proposals with greater emphasis on benefits even when homogeneous alternatives exist.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a benchmarking-repository address, identifies GPU types and counts for benchmark configurations, and states a generation range of 128–512 new tokens per prompt. It also reports completed TLI integration into Transformers, which was pending in v1. These substantially expand reproducibility and access information, although the repository itself was not inspected.

E1.justification: The Stack code-generation evaluation in v1 Table 7 is absent from v2. CNN-DailyMail, SCROLLS, and HumanEval remain, preserving summarization, long-context, and code-generation coverage. Added model families do not introduce new tasks or datasets.

E2.justification: Autoregressive decoding and Hugging Face's standard speculative decoding remain the comparison algorithms. Both are retained in the corresponding Gemma benchmarks, and the added DeepSeek benchmarks reuse these baselines. New target and drafter choices expand model configurations rather than introduce another competing decoding method.

E3.justification: v2 substantially revises the benchmark configuration matrix, adding DeepSeek distilled targets and drafters and comparisons across GPU setups, while removing standalone Llama throughput configurations. It drops the 1e-07 temperature condition, separates SLEM at temperature zero from TLI at temperature one, and adds explicit AR-relative speedups. The 30-prompt averaging protocol remains.

E4.justification: The task-conditioned vocabulary-overlap diagnostic expands from selected pair/task examples in v1 Table 6 to comparisons across datasets and additional model pairs in v2 Table 10. The token-decomposition complexity study, Figures 1–3, and tokenizer-injectivity experiment are retained. No new component-ablation study is introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions average benchmark results over 30 prompts without reporting repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The descriptive statistics and density estimation for token-decomposition counts are unchanged. Additional benchmark rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive DeepSeek results and replaces many existing benchmark values. For example, Mixtral/CNN-DailyMail at temperature zero reports AR/vicuna throughput of 10.2/9.9 tokens per second in v1 Table 7 versus 7.8/16.4 in v2 Table 1. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains, because v1 omits hardware details. Phi-4/SCROLLS values are retained, while task-specific overlap results are expanded.

M1.justification: Appendix B corrects Algorithm 5, which Algorithms 1 and 4 invoke: the final token uses the residual distribution only after rejection; otherwise it is sampled directly from the target. v1 always specified residual sampling. The core SLEM, SLRS, and TLI mechanisms remain unchanged; this establishes a pseudocode correction, not an implementation change.

P1.justification: v2 revises the contributions, empirical-results narrative, and limitations; standardizes algorithm terminology; and reorganizes appendices into separate speedup, vocabulary, and proof sections. It also changes the author list and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Most technical exposition and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The benchmark presentation is substantially redesigned into separate SLEM and TLI tables, with explicit method, hardware, and speedup columns and multipage appendix tables. arxiv_record.abstract: While there has been plenty of work on generating tests from existing code, there has been limited work on generating tests from issues. A correct test must validate the code patch that resolves the issue. This paper focuses on the scenario where that code patch does not yet exist. Doing so supports two major use-cases. First, it supports TDD (test-driven development), the discipline of "test first, write code later" that has well-documented benefits for human software engineers. Second, it also validates SWE (software engineering) agents, which generate code patches for resolving issues. This paper introduces TDD-Bench-Verified, a benchmark for generating tests from issues, and Otter, an LLM-based solution for this task. Otter augments LLMs with rule-based analysis to check and repair their outputs, and introduces a novel self-reflective action planner. Experiments show Otter outperforming state-of-the-art systems for generating tests from issues, in addition to enhancing systems that generate patches from issues. We hope that Otter helps make developers more productive at resolving issues and leads to more robust, well-tested code.

E2.justification: The six external comparison methods in Table 3 and the 22-system patch-filtering roster remain unchanged. E3.justification: V2 adds one-to-five-candidate scaling, temperature-1.0 sampling, mixed ten-candidate evaluation, and a one-attempt planner control. E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analysis beyond v1's component-removal and contamination studies. arxiv_record.abstract: We examine the problem of learning sequential tasks from a single visual demonstration. A key challenge arises when demonstrations are temporally misaligned due to variations in timing, differences in embodiment, or inconsistencies in execution. Existing approaches treat imitation as a distribution-matching problem, aligning individual frames between the agent and the demonstration. However, we show that such frame-level matching fails to enforce temporal ordering or ensure consistent progress. Our key insight is that matching should instead be defined at the level of sequences. We propose that perfect matching occurs when one sequence successfully covers all the subgoals in the same order as the other sequence. We present ORCA (ORdered Coverage Alignment), a dense per-timestep reward function that measures the probability of the agent covering demonstration frames in the correct order. On temporally misaligned demonstrations, we show that agents trained with the ORCA reward achieve $4.5$x improvement ($0.11 \rightarrow 0.50$ average normalized returns) for Meta-world tasks and $6.6$x improvement ($6.55 \rightarrow 43.3$ average returns) for Humanoid-v4 tasks compared to the best frame-level matching algorithms. We also provide empirical analysis showing that ORCA is robust to varying levels of temporal misalignment. Our code is available at https://github.com/portal-cornell/orca/
arxiv_record.authors: William Huey, Huaxiaoyue Wang, Anne Wu, Yoav Artzi, Sanjiban Choudhury
arxiv_record.title: Imitation Learning from a Single Temporally Misaligned Video

arxiv_record.abstract: The long-standing dominance of gradient-boosted decision trees on tabular data is currently challenged by tabular foundation models using In-Context Learning (ICL): setting the training data as context for the test data and predicting in a single forward pass without parameter updates. While TabPFNv2 foundation model excels on tables with up to 10K samples, its alternating column- and row-wise attentions make handling large training sets computationally prohibitive. So, can ICL be effectively scaled and deliver a benefit for larger tables? We introduce TabICL, a tabular foundation model for classification, pretrained on synthetic datasets with up to 60K samples and capable of handling 500K samples on affordable resources. This is enabled by a novel two-stage architecture: a column-then-row attention mechanism to build fixed-dimensional embeddings of rows, followed by a transformer for efficient ICL. Across 200 classification datasets from the TALENT benchmark, TabICL is on par with TabPFNv2 while being systematically faster (up to 10 times), and significantly outperforms all other approaches. On 53 datasets with over 10K samples, TabICL surpasses both TabPFNv2 and CatBoost, demonstrating the potential of ICL for large data. Pretraining code, inference code, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/soda-inria/tabicl.
arxiv_record.authors: Jingang Qu, David Holzm\"uller, Ga\"el Varoquaux, Marine Le Morvan
arxiv_record.title: TabICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for In-Context Learning on Large Data

On 53 datasets with over 10K samples, TabICL surpasses both TabPFNv2 and CatBoost, demonstrating the potential of ICL for large data. Pretraining code, inference code, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/soda-inria/tabicl.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a powerful class of generative models, capable of producing high-quality images by mapping noise to a data distribution. However, recent findings suggest that image likelihood does not align with perceptual quality: high-likelihood samples tend to be smooth, while lower-likelihood ones are more detailed. Controlling sample density is thus crucial for balancing realism and detail. In this paper, we analyze an existing technique, Prior Guidance, which scales the latent code to influence image detail. We introduce score alignment, a condition that explains why this method works and show that it can be tractably checked for any continuous normalizing flow model. We then propose Density Guidance, a principled modification of the generative ODE that enables exact log-density control during sampling. Finally, we extend Density Guidance to stochastic sampling, ensuring precise log-density control while allowing controlled variation in structure or fine details. Our experiments demonstrate that these techniques provide fine-grained control over image detail without compromising sample quality. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/density-guidance.
arxiv_record.authors: Rafa{\l} Karczewski, Markus Heinonen, Vikas Garg
arxiv_record.title: Devil is in the Details: Density Guidance for Detail-Aware Generation with Flow Models
