C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: explaining Prior Guidance through score alignment, controlling log-density through deterministic guidance, and extending control to stochastic sampling. New experiments support these claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 discusses finite-step accuracy and the additional sampling required under stronger stochastic noise. It also explains Prior Guidance's weakening control as noise reduces information from the initial latent, and notes that NIQE favors lower-detail images. These add practical qualifications to the retained interpretations.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link and documents implementation details for the new experiments, including Euler integration, moving-average finite-difference estimation of quantile derivatives, and early/late noise schedules. The existing JAX score-alignment listing is unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions cover CIFAR-10, ImageNet at 64 and 512 resolution, Stable Diffusion text-to-image generation, and synthetic Gaussian mixtures. The additions evaluate retained coverage; classifier-free guidance changes the model configuration rather than the dataset or task.

E2.justification: V2 adds Prior Guidance to the early/late stochastic-noise comparison in Figure 19 and regular samples as a reference in the NIQE comparison in Figure 20. The existing FLIPD comparison remains unchanged. LPIPS and SSIM are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include deterministic and stochastic sampling-step sweeps, quantile-estimation sample counts from 16 to 1024, noise strengths of 0.1, 0.5, and 0.9 times the diffusion strength, and a 1024-step reference likelihood estimate. V2 also adds classifier-free-guidance evaluation and NIQE scoring. These substantially expand evaluation without replacing the retained protocols.

E4.justification: Appendices E and H newly test whether requested likelihoods are reached and how discretization, quantile-estimation sample size, and stochastic noise affect accuracy. Appendices J–L add guidance-strength analyses, classifier-free-guidance compatibility, stochastic Prior Guidance comparisons, and perceptual-quality analysis.

E5.justification: Figure 19 newly specifies two starting seeds, four stochastic samples per seed, and shared inner-loop seeds across runs. New quantitative plots include error bars, although their statistical meaning is not defined. The retained normality tests and reported plus/minus values are unchanged.

E6.justification: V2 adds target-versus-obtained likelihood results, reporting correlations above 99% even with 32 deterministic Euler steps, and shows greater sampling requirements under stronger noise. Figures 16–20 add measured detail, likelihood, and NIQE trends. Existing results, including 97%/100% score alignment and 84% versus 29% detail correlations, are retained; these are additional results rather than same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Prior Guidance, score-alignment verification, deterministic Density Guidance, and the stochastic projection and drift corrections are retained. The new experiments apply existing procedures; the Rayleigh-quotient shorthand does not change the stochastic method.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order remain largely unchanged. V2 adds short experimental appendices and acknowledgements, updates cross-references, makes limited wording edits, and renames Appendix D from likelihood steering to Density Guidance.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the appendix displays with multi-panel convergence plots, paired image-and-metric comparisons, stochastic sampling grids, and NIQE plots and examples in Figures 12 and 15–20. Existing figures are largely retained, with some relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds Skreta et al. to the attribution of generalized density tracking and cites NIQE, LPIPS, SSIM, and a diffusion super-resolution application when motivating perceptual evaluation. The main research positioning is retained; the Karczewski citation's year update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the forward Gaussian kernel's covariance from sigma_t I to sigma_t^2 I. The score-alignment proofs, Gaussian-mixture theorem, and density-guidance derivations otherwise remain intact. Rewriting the stochastic derivation using the existing Rayleigh quotient introduces no new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: V1 supplied theoretical guarantees and qualitative detail control but lacked direct quantitative validation of reaching requested likelihoods. V2's Appendices E and H address that central evidence gap and expose discretization and noise dependence; additional detail and perceptual comparisons strengthen practical validation. Together with documented code access, this substantially improves the paper's empirical grounding. Undefined error bars and NIQE's preference for smoother images still limit statistical and perceptual conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Density Guidance work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds quantile-matching accuracy experiments, quantitative guidance comparisons, and NIQE evaluations.

before.justification: V1 reports original score-alignment measurements, image-detail correlations, generated-image comparisons, and Gaussian-mixture and image-data analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: A widespread strategy to obtain a language model that performs well on a target domain is to finetune a pretrained model to perform unsupervised next-token prediction on data from that target domain. Finetuning presents two challenges: (i) if the amount of target data is limited, as in most practical applications, the model will quickly overfit, and (ii) the model will drift away from the original model, forgetting the pretraining data and the generic knowledge that comes with it. We aim to derive scaling laws that quantify these two phenomena for various target domains, amounts of available target data, and model scales. We measure the efficiency of injecting pretraining data into the finetuning data mixture to avoid forgetting and mitigate overfitting. A key practical takeaway from our study is that injecting as little as 1% of pretraining data in the finetuning data mixture prevents the model from forgetting the pretraining set.
arxiv_record.authors: Louis Bethune, David Grangier, Dan Busbridge, Eleonora Gualdoni, Marco Cuturi, Pierre Ablin
arxiv_record.title: Scaling Laws for Forgetting during Finetuning with Pretraining Data Injection

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's central findings, and conclusion retain the same principal claims: finetuning and forgetting are predictable from model size, available target data, and injection fraction, and approximately 1% pretraining-data injection mitigates forgetting. The added experiments support these claims without redefining their central scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning corpus memorization, data diversity versus parameter proximity, and small models' suitability for sequential adaptation. It develops the rewarming explanation with measurements and discusses practical downstream effects, explicitly acknowledging near-chance MMLU performance. These extend v1's narrower capacity and regularization discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the existing training duration as 13–5200 epochs and adds instruction-tuning implementation details: mask storage in the sixteenth token-ID bit, bitwise extraction, and instruction delimiters. It also specifies anchored regularization strengths and discusses learning-rate-dependent weight decay. Core architecture, hardware, and training disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained language-modeling domains, v2 actually evaluates instruction finetuning on OpenHermes and downstream question answering on ARC-Easy and MMLU. These substantially extend both the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: Appendix A adds Anchored AdamW with regularization strengths 0.01, 0.10, and 1.00 to the Github comparison against Adam with and without data injection. A toy optimization example also compares Adam, AdamW, and Anchored AdamW. Existing scaling-law alternatives and the pretraining optimizer comparison are retained.

E3.justification: The original experimental grid is retained, but substantial new protocols are added: D = 10N pretraining on Freelaw, instruction-masked OpenHermes training with 189K–1,890K tokens, and zero-shot accuracy evaluation for Medium, Large, and XL models. Table 3 additionally measures baseline losses at the finetuning learning rate to account for rewarming.

E4.justification: v2 adds controls testing parameter anchoring as an explanation for data injection's benefits, robustness to a shorter pretraining budget, and explicit measurement of rewarming effects. These extend the original learning-rate, replay-data-size, and scaling-law analyses. The earlier extrapolation experiment is retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix B introduces z-score significance testing at the 99% threshold for ARC-Easy accuracy differences, marking nonsignificant comparisons. The existing practice of reporting scaling-law errors over 128 bootstrap repetitions remains unchanged; no increase in repeated training runs is reported.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises forgetting coefficients and average MRE from 0.49% to 0.40% under the revised predictor; finetuning and retained extrapolation results are unchanged. New results cover rewarming, Anchored AdamW, D = 10N, OpenHermes, and downstream accuracy. OpenHermes table MREs are 0.59% and 0.29%. The retained weight-decay plot also swaps Adam/AdamW labels, changing the attribution of its results.

M1.justification: The main data-injection procedure and model architectures remain unchanged. v2 refines the forgetting predictor by using a rewarmed baseline without the fitted offset E. Appendix A also introduces Anchored AdamW as an alternative and adapts finetuning to exclude instruction tokens from the loss.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and section organization are retained. v2 adds explanatory paragraphs, acknowledgments, and a practical-consequences appendix, moving coefficient estimation from Appendix B to C. arxiv_record.abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) have proven effective at enhancing mathematical reasoning for Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging increased inference-time computation. However, they are predominantly trained on mathematical data and their generalizability to non-mathematical domains has not been rigorously studied. In response, this work first shows that current PRMs have poor performance in other domains. To address this limitation, we introduce VersaPRM, a multi-domain PRM trained on synthetic reasoning data generated using our novel data generation and annotation method. VersaPRM achieves consistent performance gains across diverse domains. For instance, in the MMLU-Pro category of Law, VersaPRM via weighted majority voting, achieves a 7.9% performance gain over the majority voting baseline -- surpassing Qwen2.5-Math-PRM's gain of 1.3%. We further contribute to the community by open-sourcing all data, code and models for VersaPRM.

C1.justification: The abstract, five introduction contributions, and central conclusion retain the same claims: math PRMs generalize poorly beyond mathematics, and synthetic multi-domain supervision produces a broadly effective VersaPRM with released data, code, and models. The additions principally support and qualify these existing headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets held-out-domain performance as evidence beyond broader training coverage and acknowledges some benefit from learning the question format. Appendix F adds explanations of factual, arithmetic, and answer-consistency failures; Appendix G.2 proposes score-induced bias as an explanation for unsuccessful refinement. Section 7 also raises possible preference for Llama-family generators, substantially expanding applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 supplies prompts and operational details for rewriting, ablated labeling, open-ended generation and grading, and refinement, plus the 0.4 self-filtering threshold. It newly discloses AWS Bedrock batch inference and generation/labeling cost below $100. Original training hyperparameters and access information remain unchanged. Reproducibility is locally limited by Figure 15 listing a ground-truth answer despite describing its omission.

E1.justification: The original training sources and 14-domain MMLU-Pro coverage are retained. Appendix G.1 adds a limited but distinct task: answering 116 existing law questions with their answer choices removed. This extends evaluation beyond multiple choice, while the held-out-domain experiments change training splits within existing domain coverage.

E2.justification: The main math-PRM comparator suite is retained. Appendix B.5 newly evaluates Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct directly as a step judge, with reported comparisons in Figures 16–17. Those comparisons also include new self-filtered, rewrite-augmented, and prompt-ablated VersaPRM variants.

E3.justification: v2 enlarges the manual label audit from 30 to 64 questions and specifies a 30-question subset for the simplified-prompt audit. New evaluation designs include five domain-holdout controls, open-ended law questions graded by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and one-step refinement evaluated by average Pass@1 over 1,754 questions. The established main benchmark protocol remains intact.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's counterfactual, training-configuration, and aggregation analyses, v2 adds domain-holdout tests, rewrite augmentation, self-filtering, an end-to-end labeling-prompt ablation, manually analyzed successes and failures, and iterative refinement. These investigate transfer, supervision quality, robustness, and failure conditions. Counterfactual augmentation is retained and incorporated into expanded comparisons, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals for manual annotation agreement: 0.69–0.89 for CoTs labeled correct and 0.63–0.79 for those labeled incorrect. v1 reported point estimates alone. This is a localized addition to uncertainty reporting, concerning label quality rather than repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds extensive holdout, augmentation, judge-baseline, open-ended, failure-case, and DeepSeek-R1 Philosophy results. The enlarged audit reports 80%/71% agreement instead of 83%/70% on the smaller sample. The new refinement experiment reports Pass@1 of 51% without refinement, 45% with VersaPRM, and 44% with Qwen-2.5-Math-PRM.

M1.justification: The final VersaPRM architecture, loss, initialization, and fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds experimental procedural extensions: meaning-preserving rewrite augmentation, self-filtered retraining, and one-step refinement using PRM scores as feedback (Appendices B.2–B.3 and G.2). These supplement the existing method without replacing its central pipeline.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative and much existing prose remain intact. Revisions concentrate on related work, the DeepSeek discussion, future directions, and explanatory passages. Existing counterfactual material is regrouped into Appendix B, and an appendix roadmap is added; much remaining appendix movement is renumbering rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds held-out-domain plots, a Philosophy panel to the DeepSeek figure, expanded ablation grids, open-ended results, prompt displays, and highlighted error examples. Most existing plots are retained. Figure 2 removes the ground-truth input box despite its continued use in the text, and Figure 17's legend says Best of N although its caption identifies WMV.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through CoT's domain-dependent benefits, compute-optimal training, teacher–student distillation, and Constitutional AI, adding works by Sprague, Hoffmann, Hinton, Gu, Bai, and others. New appendices also connect filtering and refinement to relevant prior research. The original math-PRM literature remains represented.

T1.justification: The PRM definition, aggregation formulas, and inference equations in Section 3 are retained. Beam-search and MCTS pseudocode match across v1 Appendix B and v2 Appendix C. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central generalization claim through held-out-domain controls and comparison with the 70B labeler used directly as a judge. The larger audit with confidence intervals, downstream labeling ablation, and candid failure and negative-refinement results also improve assessment of reliability and applicability. Open-ended evidence remains preliminary and LLM-graded, and new prompt/legend inconsistencies are drawbacks, but these localized issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VersaPRM and retain the same core pipeline, datasets, and principal experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds held-out-domain evaluations, further ablations, open-ended questions, error examples, and iterative-refinement results.

before.justification: v1 reports original PRM training and evaluation results, reranking and search experiments, training ablations, and a manual audit of synthetic labels.

arxiv_record.abstract: The trade-off between accuracy and interpretability has long been a challenge in machine learning (ML). This tension is particularly significant for emerging interpretable-by-design methods, which aim to redesign ML algorithms for trustworthy interpretability but often sacrifice accuracy in the process. In this paper, we address this gap by investigating the impact of deviations in concept representations-an essential component of interpretable models-on prediction performance and propose a novel framework to mitigate these effects. The framework builds on the principle of optimizing concept embeddings under constraints that preserve interpretability. Using a generative model as a test-bed, we rigorously prove that our algorithm achieves zero loss while progressively enhancing the interpretability of the resulting model. Additionally, we evaluate the practical performance of our proposed framework in generating explainable predictions for image classification tasks across various benchmarks. Compared to existing explainable methods, our approach not only improves prediction accuracy while preserving model interpretability across various large-scale benchmarks but also achieves this with significantly lower computational cost.
arxiv_record.authors: Geyu Liang, Senne Michielssen and Salar Fattahi
arxiv_record.title: Enhancing Performance of Explainable AI Models with Constrained Concept Refinement

arxiv_record.abstract: Predictive tasks on relational databases are critical in real-world applications spanning e-commerce, healthcare, and social media. To address these tasks effectively, Relational Deep Learning (RDL) encodes relational data as graphs, enabling Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit relational structures for improved predictions. However, existing RDL methods often overlook the intrinsic structural properties of the graphs built from relational databases, leading to modeling inefficiencies, particularly in handling many-to-many relationships. Here we introduce RelGNN, a novel GNN framework specifically designed to leverage the unique structural characteristics of the graphs built from relational databases. At the core of our approach is the introduction of atomic routes, which are simple paths that enable direct single-hop interactions between the source and destination nodes. Building upon these atomic routes, RelGNN designs new composite message passing and graph attention mechanisms that reduce redundancy, highlight key signals, and enhance predictive accuracy. RelGNN is evaluated on 30 diverse real-world tasks from Relbench (Fey et al., 2024), and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the vast majority of tasks, with improvements of up to 25%. Code is available at https://github.com/snap-stanford/RelGNN.
arxiv_record.authors: Tianlang Chen, Charilaos Kanatsoulis, Jure Leskovec
arxiv_record.title: RelGNN: Composite Message Passing for Relational Deep Learning

native_events.abstract: Predictive tasks on relational databases are critical in real-world applications spanning e-commerce, healthcare, and social media. To address these tasks effectively, Relational Deep Learning (RDL) encodes relational data as graphs, enabling Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit relational structures for improved predictions. However, existing RDL methods often overlook the intrinsic structural properties of the graphs built from relational databases, leading to modeling inefficiencies, particularly in handling many-to-many relationships. Here we introduce RelGNN, a novel GNN framework specifically designed to leverage the unique structural characteristics of the graphs built from relational databases. At the core of our approach is the introduction of atomic routes, which are simple paths that enable direct single-hop interactions between the source and destination nodes. Building upon these atomic routes, RelGNN designs new composite message passing and graph attention mechanisms that reduce redundancy, highlight key signals, and enhance predictive accuracy. RelGNN is evaluated on 30 diverse real-world tasks from Relbench (Fey et al., 2024), and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the vast majority of tasks, with improvements of up to 25%.

arxiv_record.abstract: While self-attention has been instrumental in the success of Transformers, it can lead to over-concentration on a few tokens during training, resulting in suboptimal information flow. Enforcing doubly-stochastic constraints in attention matrices has been shown to improve structure and balance in attention distributions. However, existing methods rely on iterative Sinkhorn normalization, which is computationally costly. In this paper, we introduce a novel, fully parallelizable doubly-stochastic attention mechanism based on sliced optimal transport, leveraging Expected Sliced Transport Plans (ESP). Unlike prior approaches, our method enforces doubly stochasticity without iterative Sinkhorn normalization, significantly enhancing efficiency. To ensure differentiability, we incorporate a temperature-based soft sorting technique, enabling seamless integration into deep learning models. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets, including image classification, point cloud classification, sentiment analysis, and neural machine translation, demonstrate that our enhanced attention regularization consistently improves performance across diverse applications. Our implementation code can be found at https://github.com/dariansal/ESPFormer.

This extends the original efficiency contribution beyond parallel soft sorting; the other principal claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes approximate double stochasticity during soft-sort training from exact hard-sort inference. It adds limitations concerning strictly causal/autoregressive attention and memory growth with slice count, interprets the slicer ablation, and qualifies the soft-sort runtime advantage to Sinkformer with S>3. These materially clarify applicability and efficiency.

D1.justification: V1 promises code release upon acceptance; v2 supplies an implementation repository address. V2 documents the 40-epoch annealing schedule, decay factor 0.8, and TweetEval implementation and hyperparameters. Most previous implementation details and appendix hyperparameter tables are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds TweetEval sentiment classification, extending sentiment evaluation from movie reviews to tweets. All previous datasets and tasks remain; the MNIST patch-size experiment moves to Appendix A.2.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparators remain Transformer, DiffTransformer, and Sinkformer, including on TweetEval. Changed Sinkhorn iteration counts concern experimental settings, while sorting and slicer variants are internal ablations.

E3.justification: V2 adds a 40-epoch annealing protocol and separate sharpened-soft and hard-sort evaluations across the existing Cats and Dogs data fractions. It also introduces a slicer experiment varying L over 1, 8, 32, 64, and 128 and inverse temperature over 0.1, 1, and 10. Runtime comparisons replace Sinkformer S=50 with S=3. Existing task-training schedules remain documented unchanged.

E4.justification: New comparisons test the effects of annealing and hard-sort inference (Table 1), and whether learnable, frozen, or axis-aligned slicing performs better as slice count and inverse temperature vary (Table 6). These substantially expand evidence about core design choices. The previous data-scarcity and MNIST patch-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: Retained experiments preserve their run counts and reporting practices: three-run means and standard deviations for Cats and Dogs, four-run ModelNet40 and translation summaries, and ten-run runtime averages. New ablations extend the existing mean-and-standard-deviation practice without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or an explicit increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds TweetEval, slicer-grid, and hard-sort runtime results. Its expanded Cats and Dogs table reports 80.61% sharpened-soft and 81.23% hard-sort accuracy at full data after additional fine-tuning, alongside the retained 79.47% initial result; these are different training conditions. IMDb Sinkformer median accuracy changes from 85.40% to 85.39%, and Transformer worst accuracy from 85.30% to 85.20%. ModelNet40, translation, and MNIST results remain.

M1.justification: V2 adds temperature-annealed fine-tuning followed by replacement of soft sorting with hard sorting at inference (Section 4.4). This changes the training and inference procedure and introduces an exact-permutation variant; the original soft-sorting pipeline in Algorithm 1 remains.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition is retained, with localized wording and terminology clarifications. P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. V2 restructures the Cats and Dogs table into baseline and sorting-mode groups, adds TweetEval and slicer tables, revises runtime plots and legends, and relocates the MNIST figure. R1.justification: V2 adds references to TweetEval and Constrained Sliced Wasserstein Embedding, the latter supporting discussion of learned slicing. The broader positioning relative to Sinkformer, ESP, soft sorting, and differential attention remains substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central attention design through sorting-mode and slicer ablations, clarifies approximate versus exact double stochasticity, and documents important causal and memory limitations absent from v1. arxiv_record.abstract: We analyze nonlinearly preconditioned gradient methods for solving smooth minimization problems. We introduce a generalized smoothness property, based on the notion of abstract convexity, that is broader than Lipschitz smoothness and provide sufficient first- and second-order conditions. Notably, our framework encapsulates algorithms associated with the gradient clipping method and brings out novel insights for the class of $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions that has received widespread interest recently, thus allowing us to extend beyond already established methods. We investigate the convergence of the proposed method in both the convex and nonconvex setting.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is repairing a central theoretical gap: v1's Appendix B.4 infers monotonicity from eigenvalue bounds on generally nonsymmetric matrix products. Newly added Corollary 2.11 appears to reverse the required scaling, stating δL1 rather than L1/δ; this local defect remains, but does not outweigh the substantial repair to the main argument.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: self-supervised context-ablation rewards improve fine-grained citations through best-of-N sampling and preference optimization. The headline improvement of up to 5.3 citation-F1 points remains unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the interpretation that ContextCite SFT reduces answer correctness with one of approximately preserved correctness, following revised baseline scores. It adds substantive discussion of the mismatch between contributive training and corroborative evaluation, qualifies ALCE comparisons by training conditions, interprets latency tradeoffs, and explicitly limits applicability to models exposing output probabilities.

D1.justification: v2 adds a SelfCite source-code link, specifies NLTK segmentation of ContextCite responses, documents the NLI model and its capped sentence-ablation procedure, and supplies latency hardware settings. Appendix A's original training recipe is largely unchanged; these additions mainly expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds ALCE evaluation on ASQA and ELI5 (Appendix F, Table 8), extending sentence-level long-context evaluation to chunk-level citation tasks under a training-to-evaluation distribution and format mismatch. Existing LongBench-Cite coverage and training datasets are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds SimPO with NLI rewards, a controlled alternative initialized from LongCite-8B. The new ALCE comparison includes prompted Llama-2-13B-chat and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and reported results from Huang et al. (2024), with the latter explicitly distinguished by its in-distribution training. The Claude Citations comparison already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces zero-shot ALCE evaluation using NLI-based citation metrics, ASQA exact-match recall, and ELI5 correctness. It also adds a controlled reward comparison and a latency protocol using eight A100 GPUs, batch size one, and model parallelism. These are additional protocols; the original LongBench-Cite settings are largely retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether SelfCite's reward improves on an NLI reward with the training pipeline held fixed, whether sentence-level training transfers to chunk-level ALCE tasks, and how sampling versus reranking contributes to latency. Existing reward, length-balancing, training-size, iterative-training, and qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run performance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both retain the same candidate-diversity statistic: 4.8 unique candidates per statement on average, with standard deviation 3.2. The added experiments do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds NLI-baseline results (75.0 average citation F1), ALCE results, and latency measurements, while retaining the original SelfCite Table 1 scores. Table 2 changes Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct average correctness without citations from 60.2 to 68.9 and with citations from 71.7 to 63.3. Table 4 changes the 8K-training F1 from 64.4 to 65.9 and citation length from 195.2 to 158.1. These reported revisions do not establish across-version model improvements.

M1.justification: The context-ablation reward, citation-only best-of-N sampling, SimPO optimization, and length balancing remain unchanged. Expanded Algorithm 1 incorporates the 384-token filter already stated in v1's prose and clarifies candidate indexing; it does not establish a new procedure.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites clarify citation resampling, simplify the SimPO rationale, and revise results interpretation and limitations. v2 adds an Impact Statement, a latency subsection, and Appendices E–G, moving the existing qualitative appendix to H. The overall narrative and main section order remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column report to a two-column conference layout with different front matter, headers, and figure/table placement. v2 adds latency, ALCE, and prior-method comparison tables and expands Table 1. Existing figures and qualitative tables are retained but resized or relocated.

R1.justification: v2 adds Mudgal et al. (2024) to motivate best-of-N evaluation and expands positioning through Appendix G/Table 9, comparing citation granularity, generation passes, preference optimization, context capacity, and supervision. Most compared works and the central self-supervised positioning were already present in v1.

T1.justification: The necessity/sufficiency reward derivation and Appendix B's ContextCite surrogate-model and citation-extraction mathematics remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm clarification and explicit restatement of the reward sum introduce no new theoretical result or mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the reward's distinctive value: the controlled NLI comparison reports 75.0 versus SelfCite SimPO's 77.9 average F1, while ALCE transfer tests and latency measurements address generalization and practical cost absent from v1. Clearer applicability limits and code-access information also help. Some new prose overstates superiority: Appendix F's claim that LongCite beats prompting conflicts with the ELI5 citation scores in Table 8. This localized weakness does not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SelfCite. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial layout changes and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds an NLI-reward baseline, ALCE evaluations, and latency measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original SelfCite experiments on LongBench-Cite, including best-of-N sampling, SimPO training, ablations, iterative optimization, and a Claude Citations comparison.

arxiv_record.abstract: This work highlights a semantics misalignment in 3D human pose estimation. For the task of test-time adaptation, the misalignment manifests as overly smoothed and unguided predictions. The smoothing settles predictions towards some average pose. Furthermore, when there are occlusions or truncations, the adaptation becomes fully unguided. To this end, we pioneer the integration of a semantics-aware motion prior for the test-time adaptation of 3D pose estimation. We leverage video understanding and a well-structured motion-text space to adapt the model motion prediction to adhere to video semantics during test time. Additionally, we incorporate a missing 2D pose completion based on the motion-text similarity. The pose completion strengthens the motion prior's guidance for occlusions and truncations. Our method significantly improves state-of-the-art 3D human pose estimation TTA techniques, with more than 12% decrease in PA-MPJPE on 3DPW and 3DHP.
arxiv_record.authors: Qiuxia Lin, Rongyu Chen, Kerui Gu, Angela Yao
arxiv_record.title: Semantics-aware Test-time Adaptation for 3D Human Pose Estimation

Earlier limitations concerning motion timing and MotionCLIP generalization remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies substantial previously unavailable labeling details: GPT-4o identity, prompts, dictionary constraints, downsampling, CLIP consistency checking at 0.3 and manual correction. Section 5.2 also specifies the OpenPose confidence threshold of 0.3. Conversely, Section 4.1 drops v1's explicit stride-1 specification without stating a replacement.

E1.justification: Human3.6M training and 3DPW, 3DHP and EgoBody evaluation remain unchanged. Section 5.5 adds an explicit semantic-input failure scenario, evaluating pose adaptation with incorrect VLM labels versus correct oracle labels. No new dataset or domain is introduced.

E2.justification: The matched benchmark comparisons retain their baselines. The motion-discriminator and unpaired-local-pose alternatives in v1 Table 3 reappear in v2 Table 4 with clarified names and unchanged results. Added runtime and qualitative comparisons use existing comparators.

E3.justification: Existing backbones, pose metrics and training settings are retained. New analyses introduce a 5,000-frame labeling audit, incorrect-label/oracle/no-adaptation controls, per-frame runtime evaluation and an EMA grid from 0.75 to 0.95. The newly specified OpenPose threshold documents an existing setting rather than establishing changed preprocessing.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands analysis beyond the retained component and fill-in ablations. It adds VLM failure and oracle-label tests, EMA sensitivity, runtime analysis, CLIP-based label verification and qualitative case studies across all three evaluation datasets (Section 5.5 and Appendices A–C).

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The new labeling accuracy and audit sample size are point-result and evaluation-design information, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark, component-ablation and fill-in-threshold scores are unchanged. Substantial new results include 107.6 versus 74.1 ms runtime for the proposed method and CycleAdapt (Table 5), 96.4% labeling accuracy, and failure-case MPJPE of 213.8 initially, 92.2 with incorrect labels and 83.7 with oracle labels (Table 7). EMA, label-verification and qualitative results are also added.

M1.justification: The motion-text alignment, frozen encoders, global-rotation handling, EMA updates, missing-keypoint completion and overall objective remain the same. Appendix B documents the existing labeling and verification stage; it does not establish an algorithmic addition.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained. Changes include localized language and cross-reference corrections, a rewritten explanation of semantic comparison strategies, a clearer qualitative caption, a failure-case subsection, appendices and publication/acknowledgment text.

P2.justification: v2 adds runtime, label-failure and EMA tables; a fill-in quantity/PCK chart; labeling examples and a similarity heatmap; and extensive qualitative/failure panels. Existing ablation tables are reordered, while v1 Figure 4 becomes v2 Figure 5 with larger presentation, clearer highlights and an expanded caption.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to MHEntropy, ExtPose, pose-estimation calibration and blurry-image hand reconstruction. Section 5.4 narrows its statement about absent semantic approaches to TTA. The MotionDiffuse publication update is the same cited work, and the main research positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 corrects the smoothing-target definitions beneath Eq. 9: v1 assigns motion denoising to beta-bar and averaged shape to theta-bar; v2 assigns them to theta-bar and beta-bar, consistent with Section 3.1. This is a local definition correction; the loss sum remains equivalent and no proofs or theorems are added.

improvement.justification: v1 leaves its central semantic-labeling process largely undocumented in the supplied PDF and does not examine labeling failures or runtime. v2 makes prompts, verification and human correction inspectable, while adding targeted reliability, efficiency and sensitivity evidence. This substantially improves reproducibility and assessment of the method's central dependency without weakening the retained benchmark evidence. Manual correction still limits conclusions about fully automatic deployment, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but these residual limitations do not outweigh the gains.

arxiv_record.abstract: Text-to-song generation, the task of creating vocals and accompaniment from textual inputs, poses significant challenges due to domain complexity and data scarcity. Existing approaches often employ multi-stage generation procedures, leading to cumbersome training and inference pipelines, as well as suboptimal overall generation quality due to error accumulation across stages. In this paper, we propose SongGen, a fully open-source, single-stage auto-regressive transformer designed for controllable song generation. The proposed model facilitates fine-grained control over diverse musical attributes, including lyrics and textual descriptions of instrumentation, genre, mood, and timbre, while also offering an optional three-second reference clip for voice cloning. Within a unified auto-regressive framework, SongGen supports two output modes: mixed mode, which generates a mixture of vocals and accompaniment directly, and dual-track mode, which synthesizes them separately for greater flexibility in downstream applications. We explore diverse token pattern strategies for each mode, leading to notable improvements and valuable insights. Furthermore, we design an automated data preprocessing pipeline with effective quality control. To foster community engagement and future research, we will release our model weights, training code, annotated data, and preprocessing pipeline. The code is available at https://github.com/LiuZH-19/SongGen.

E1.justification: Both versions use approximately 540K English song clips from MSD, FMA and MTG-Jamendo and evaluate on the same 326 MusicCaps samples. E2.justification: v2 replaces Stable Audio Open and MusicGen in the main comparisons with a newly evaluated two-stage vocal-then-accompaniment baseline using SongGen's component architecture and training data. E4.justification: Appendix C adds qualitative codec failure analysis, reporting lyric-following failures, noise and silence for Encodec and DAC without quantifying their rates. The existing training-strategy, lyric-integration and codec ablations, attention visualizations and loss curves are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 2-3 add ± values to human ratings that v1 reported only as means. Five generation seeds and 36 samples evaluated by 20 listeners were already documented. v2 does not define the ± statistic or establish that additional runs were performed.

E6.justification: Retained scores are unchanged, but v2 adds multi-stage results, ground-truth automatic scores, CLaMP3/aesthetics results and latency measurements, while removing Stable Audio Open/MusicGen results. arxiv_record.abstract: Self-awareness, i.e., the ability to assess and correct one's own generation, is a fundamental aspect of human intelligence, making its replication in large language models (LLMs) an important yet challenging task. Previous works tackle this by employing extensive reinforcement learning or rather relying on large external verifiers. In this work, we propose Refine via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ReVISE), an efficient and effective framework that enables LLMs to self-correct their outputs through self-verification. The core idea of ReVISE is to enable LLMs to verify their reasoning processes and continually rethink reasoning trajectories based on its verification. We introduce a structured curriculum based upon online preference learning to implement this efficiently. Specifically, as ReVISE involves two challenging tasks (i.e., self-verification and reasoning correction), we tackle each task sequentially using curriculum learning, collecting both failed and successful reasoning paths to construct preference pairs for efficient training. During inference, our approach enjoys natural test-time scaling by integrating self-verification and correction capabilities, further enhanced by our proposed confidence-aware decoding mechanism. Our experiments on various reasoning tasks demonstrate that ReVISE achieves efficient self-correction and significantly improves reasoning performance.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about intrinsic verification, self-correction, two-stage preference training and efficient test-time scaling. Mathematical and coding applicability was already claimed in v1; the new coding experiment supplies evidence for that retained claim.

C2.justification: New discussion interprets transfer results as evidence of domain generalization and repeated-training results as demonstrating practical scalability. Appendix B.2 adds a claimed 30-fold training-cost advantage over SCoRe based on generation counts and acknowledges using published SCoRe results because code was unavailable. Existing mechanism explanations and limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, MBPP data-construction details specifying 16 valid GPT-4o reasoning/code paths per problem, and its prompt template and three demonstrations. Appendix B also documents DPO pair construction and generation counts for the new training comparison. Existing optimizer, hyperparameter and hardware disclosures are retained; most mathematics prompt material is reorganized.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual training and evaluation on MBPP Python programming problems, extending the demonstrated coverage beyond mathematics. It also introduces a distinct transfer scenario: training on MATH and evaluating on GSM8K (Table 4). These experiments were absent from v1, despite its introductory reference to coding.

E2.justification: v2 adds standalone DPO comparisons on GSM8K and MATH-500 (Table 5), a SCoRe comparison on Gemma-2-2B (Table 6), and comparison with the V-STaR verifier (Table 7). The SCoRe scores explicitly come from its original paper. Standalone DPO is distinct from v1’s existing ablation removing DPO loss.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce MBPP Pass@1 and three-shot prompting with supplied tests, Gemma-2-2B experiments, and Llama-3.1-8B evaluation on GSM8K. Appendix B extends sampling budgets from at most eight to 64 generations and evaluates additional training cycles with generation-budget comparisons. These are added protocols; the established mathematics training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of cross-dataset transfer, performance across repeated training cycles, and verifier discrimination relative to V-STaR, while extending sampling-budget sensitivity through 64 generations. Existing curriculum/loss ablations and qualitative examples are retained. Figure 8’s iterative-inference analysis moves from Appendix B.1 into Section 4.3 and is not new.

E5.justification: Unlike v1’s point estimates, v2 Table 8 reports ± quantities for the extended scaling results, such as 37.7% ± 0.5 at Maj@64. Their statistical meaning, run counts and seeds are unspecified, so this establishes additional uncertainty reporting but not an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 Maj@1/Maj@5 values remain unchanged, while substantial new results cover coding, transfer, additional model configurations and comparators. Examples include MBPP Pass@1 of 33.1% versus STaR+’s 30.7% (Table 2), Gemma accuracies of 23.2%, 24.2% and 25.8% across training cycles (Table 6), and 37.7% ± 0.5 at Maj@64 (Table 8). These are added evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds an iterative-training variant that resamples reasoning-path pairs from the current model and repeats preference optimization. The core two-stage training, losses, verification tokens and confidence-aware decoding remain unchanged. Iterative refinement during inference already appeared in v1.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 moves the iterative-inference discussion into Section 4.3, reorganizes Appendix B and the prompt documentation, removes a short related-work preamble, and adds acknowledgements, correspondence information and proceedings text. This is localized reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Table 1 is restructured to include 8B GSM8K results and omit its Maj@3 columns, and six new experimental tables are added. Figure 8 is relocated and resized. Appendix examples become captioned tables with integrated, colored verification tokens, while prompts are redesigned into separate template and demonstration tables. Existing plots retain their underlying results.

R1.justification: Austin et al. (2021) is newly cited for MBPP. Appendix B develops more explicit competitive positioning against already-cited DPO, SCoRe and V-STaR, particularly concerning training efficiency and intrinsic verification. The substantive related-work review otherwise remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical setup, preference-pair definitions, training losses and confidence-weighted aggregation rule in Section 3 are unchanged. Neither version supplies additional theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support: MBPP directly addresses v1’s unsupported coding claim, transfer testing probes generalization beyond the training dataset, and DPO/V-STaR comparisons better test the proposed training and intrinsic verification. Extended sampling and iterative-training experiments further substantiate scalability. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses, including undefined ± quantities, a DPO table/prose discrepancy, and SCoRe efficiency claims based on published scores and generation counts rather than matched runtime measurements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReVISE work. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–C, including equations, tables and figures, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds coding, transfer, baseline-comparison, iterative-training and extended-sampling results.

before.justification: v1 reports original GSM8K and MATH-500 experiments, curriculum and loss ablations, sampling analyses, and iterative-refinement results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Bayesian phylogenetics is vital for understanding evolutionary dynamics, and requires accurate and efficient approximation of posterior distributions over trees. In this work, we develop a variational Bayesian approach for ultrametric phylogenetic trees. We present a novel variational family based on coalescent times of a single-linkage clustering and derive a closed-form density for the resulting distribution over trees. Unlike existing methods for ultrametric trees, our method performs inference over all of tree space, it does not require any Markov chain Monte Carlo subroutines, and our variational family is differentiable. Through experiments on benchmark genomic datasets and an application to the viral RNA of SARS-CoV-2, we demonstrate that our method achieves competitive accuracy while requiring significantly fewer gradient evaluations than existing state-of-the-art techniques.
arxiv_record.authors: Evan Sidrow, Alexandre Bouchard-C\^ot\'e, Lloyd T. Elliott
arxiv_record.title: Variational phylogenetic inference with products over bipartitions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same central contributions: a differentiable variational family covering tree space, a closed-form density, no required MCMC subroutines, and competitive inference using fewer gradient evaluations. The added evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 identifies underestimation for tree lengths of eight or greater and suggests a mismatch between approximately exponential long-branch posteriors and log-normal pairwise distributions. The computational discussion newly attributes observed near-linear VIPR scaling to likelihood evaluation and explains VBPI's scaling through SBN normalization and parameter growth. These materially extend the earlier limitations and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds VIPR code and diagnostic-histogram access information, a more specific rooted-VBPI implementation reference, the MS simulation command, and runtime hardware details. It also explicitly discloses omission of VBPI's annealing schedule; v1 did not state this choice, so the disclosure alone does not establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: The original twelve genomic datasets are retained. Section 4.4 and Appendix B.3 add two synthetic evaluation regimes: neutral coalescent/infinite-sites MS datasets and Kingman/Jukes-Cantor datasets with known generating trees. This substantially extends evaluation beyond observed genomic data and their subsets.

E2.justification: Appendix B.1 adds a limited quantitative comparison with cubeVB's restricted tree-space coverage, previously discussed qualitatively. It does not add a fitted cubeVB likelihood benchmark. BEAST and VBPI10/VBPI20 remain in the existing comparisons; relocating VBPI20 table entries does not remove that comparator.

E3.justification: The runtime study replaces COVID-19 subsets containing 3–72 taxa with simulated datasets containing 8–512 taxa and 1,000 sites. It changes the stopping rule from 1,000 iterations to five minutes or 1,000 iterations, whichever occurs first. New protocols also specify MCC-based cube-space assessment and known-tree checks using ten eight-taxon simulations, 10,000 optimization iterations, and 10,000 posterior samples.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of posterior mass excluded by cube space, pairwise Hamming-distance characteristics, and recovery of known tree lengths and likelihoods. The revised scaling study also measures parameter counts. These investigate representation coverage, approximation failures, and computational bottlenecks beyond v1's posterior summaries and convergence plots.

E5.justification: Appendix B.4 newly identifies the parenthesized uncertainties as standard errors estimated using 100 bootstrap samples. The numerical uncertainties and existing chain/restart counts are retained, so this establishes improved reporting rather than additional experimental replications.

E6.justification: v1 Tables 1–2 are numerically preserved in v2 Tables 6–7, and all twelve appendix convergence traces are retained. Substantial new results include 15.2–99.9% of sampled trees lying outside the assessed cube space, parameter-count comparisons, and long-tree underestimation. The replacement runtime study reports approximately linear VIPR scaling instead of the earlier approximately quadratic behavior, under different experimental conditions.

M1.justification: The independent log-normal distance distributions, single-linkage tree construction, closed-form density, and LOOR, reparameterization, and VIMCO estimators remain unchanged. Algorithm input declarations and redistributed explanations clarify the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The six-section narrative remains recognizable. v2 copyedits prose, folds the notation subsection into Background, redistributes gradient explanations between Section 3.3 and Appendix C, reorganizes Appendix B into named subsections, and adds an Impact Statement.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny through controlled scaling experiments, quantitative support-coverage checks, and known-tree diagnostics exposing a concrete approximation failure. arxiv_record.abstract: Pre-trained vision language models still fall short of human visual cognition. In an effort to improve visual cognition and align models with human behavior, we introduce visual stimuli and human judgments on visual cognition tasks, allowing us to systematically evaluate performance across cognitive domains under a consistent environment. We fine-tune models on ground truth data for intuitive physics and causal reasoning and find that this improves model performance in the respective fine-tuning domain. Furthermore, it can improve model alignment with human behavior. However, we find that task-specific fine-tuning does not contribute to robust human-like generalization to data with other visual characteristics or to tasks in other cognitive domains.

arxiv_record.title: Testing the Limits of Fine-Tuning for Improving Visual Cognition in Vision Language Models

C1.justification: V2 explicitly narrows the abstract and concluding generalization claims to task-specific fine-tuning, with the conclusion specifying parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The central contributions and findings—within-task improvement, improved human alignment and limited transfer—remain.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the paired-image failure as evidence of task-specific shortcuts and adds binding-problem and supervised-memorization versus reinforcement-learning hypotheses. It explicitly acknowledges that joint models were not tested on a third cognitive task and that broader task distributions might help. Appendix D also adds an explanation for model–human agreement exceeding human–human agreement.

D1.justification: V2 documents the paired-image construction and removal prompt, but removes v1's Qwen architecture/pretraining description. Its alignment-figure caption also no longer identifies the joint model's exact training split. Core fine-tuning hyperparameters, hardware and analysis-software versions remain documented.

E1.justification: The existing Cubeworld tasks, Lerer naturalistic images and human datasets remain. V2 adds a restricted paired-pyramid scenario in which removing the red block creates a factual-stability test image corresponding to a causal-training image (Section 3.4, Figure 4). This extends input conditions within the existing cognitive domains.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 2 adds GPT-4o as an evaluated comparator, with reported accuracies across the three evaluation datasets. Base-model and human reference results, already represented elsewhere in v1, are also displayed alongside the fine-tuned models in the expanded heatmap.

E3.justification: The evaluated model set changes from Qwen2-VL 2B/7B to Qwen2-VL 7B and Llama 3.2 11B/90B. Main heatmap and alignment comparisons switch to 11B, while appendix learning trajectories switch to 90B. The new paired-image experiment tests transformed training configurations with an explicit red-block-removal prompt. Existing training budgets and core hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantial diagnostic control: causal-trained models must judge factual stability on corresponding pyramid images with the red block removed, alongside an unseen-causal-stimulus evaluation (Figure 4). This directly investigates whether cross-task failure persists when visual differences are minimized. Existing generalization and learning-trajectory analyses are also revised for the larger model set.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three seeds, Wilson score intervals for accuracy plots, and bootstrapped 95% intervals using 10,000 subsamples for agreement analyses. V2 reiterates the seed procedure and relocates the bootstrap description to Appendix D; it does not establish additional runs or a changed uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds Llama and GPT-4o results, removes 2B results, and replaces the main Qwen7B heatmap/alignment results and appendix learning trajectories with other models. For example, human-tuned agreement on Cubeworld/Lerer is 0.35/0.31 for Qwen7B in v1 versus 0.37/0.37 for Llama11B in v2; these are different-model results. New Figure 4 reports approximately 0.83–0.90 causal accuracy but roughly chance-level matched factual transfer.

M1.justification: The QLoRA intervention, cross-entropy objective, adapted vision/language layers and Yes/No scoring procedure are retained. Applying this procedure to Llama models expands the experimental model set; no new fine-tuning algorithm or architectural modification is introduced.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title to emphasize visual cognition, edits several paragraphs to lead with findings, condenses captions and adds an Impact Statement. Agreement-analysis details move to Appendix D, and the pretraining appendix is removed. The main section organization and much of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the four-panel paired-image Figure 4 and expands Figure 2 with comparator rows. Main and appendix plots revise model legends, visual encodings and some axis ranges for the expanded comparisons. Figure 1 is relocated and captions are revised; the appendix stimulus examples are retained with new numbering.

R1.justification: V2 substantially broadens the research context beyond the original neighboring fine-tuning studies. Section 1.1 adds neurosymbolic visual reasoning and mathematical/compositional generalization; the introduction and discussion add binding-problem research and supervised-versus-reinforcement-learning explanations. These additions introduce substantive relationships to alternative approaches and mechanisms.

T1.justification: The adapter mathematics, softmax formula and agreement definition are unchanged. The agreement equation moves from Section 3.5 to Appendix D. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new mechanism discussions do not introduce formal mathematical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central transfer evidence by testing a second model family up to 90B parameters and adding the paired-image control in Section 3.4. These changes address v1's reliance on small Qwen models and reduce visual differences that could explain cross-task failure. More explicit claim boundaries improve calibration. These gains outweigh the removal of 2B results and some model/split documentation, although the proposed mechanisms remain hypotheses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cubeworld fine-tuning study. Their complete main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison despite the changed title, model selection and figure numbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental and human-judgment results and reports additional Llama evaluations and the paired-pyramid transfer experiment in Section 3.4 and Figure 4.

before.justification: V1 reports original Qwen2-VL fine-tuning experiments, generalization evaluations and human-judgment studies, with results in Sections 3.1–3.6 and Appendices E–G.

arxiv_record.abstract: We present a Transformer-based framework for Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs). CSPs find use in many applications and thus accelerating their solution with machine learning is of wide interest. Most existing approaches rely on supervised learning from feasible solutions or reinforcement learning, paradigms that require either feasible solutions to these NP-Complete CSPs or large training budgets and a complex expert-designed reward signal. To address these challenges, we propose ConsFormer, a self-supervised framework that leverages a Transformer as a solution refiner. ConsFormer constructs a solution to a CSP iteratively in a process that mimics local search. Instead of using feasible solutions as labeled data, we devise differentiable approximations to the discrete constraints of a CSP to guide model training. Our model is trained to improve random assignments for a single step but is deployed iteratively at test time, circumventing the bottlenecks of supervised and reinforcement learning. Experiments on Sudoku, Graph Coloring, Nurse Rostering, and MAXCUT demonstrate that our method can tackle out-of-distribution CSPs simply through additional iterations.
arxiv_record.authors: Yudong W. Xu, Wenhao Li, Scott Sanner, Elias B. Khalil
arxiv_record.title: Self-Supervised Transformers as Iterative Solution Improvers for Constraint Satisfaction

C1.justification: The central claims remain self-supervised single-step learning, the importance of positional information, iterative OOD generalization, and leading neural performance on OOD Sudoku. The abstract names the expanded benchmark evidence, but the contribution statements and conclusion retain their scientific meaning.

C2.justification: New Section 5 explicitly states that parametric constraints, such as SAT clauses with variable negations, cannot be handled without richer constraint inputs. New discussions interpret Gumbel noise as aiding large-instance search, explain direct SGD failures through local optima and lack of transfer, and acknowledge ANYCSP's superior MAXCUT performance.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a GitHub implementation link and adds MAXCUT settings to Appendix D: four layers, three heads, embedding size 128, and selection probability 1.0. It also identifies implementations used for the added coloring baselines. Previously documented hardware, optimizer, training budget, and original model configurations remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds MAXCUT, extending evaluation from constraint feasibility to cut optimization. Training uses random 100-vertex graphs, while evaluation uses GSET graphs with 800–10000 vertices, including weighted graphs. The original Sudoku, coloring, and nurse-scheduling coverage is retained.

E2.justification: Appendix G adds evaluated Greedy Coloring, OR-Tools Feasibility Jump, and OR-Tools Random Search comparisons to the retained coloring baselines. The new MAXCUT comparison also includes SDP, RUNCSP, ECO-DQN, and ECORD, with reference scores drawn from prior work as identified in Section 4.3.

E3.justification: Original experimental settings are retained, but v2 adds substantially different evaluation designs: MAXCUT gap metrics and 180-second runs, Gumbel-Softmax versus softmax at temperatures 0.1 and 1, candidate-pool sweeps under a 10-second budget, and OR-Tools tests at 30 and 60 seconds. Appendix I adds 10000-step direct SGD tests measuring satisfied Sudoku constraints.

E4.justification: New analyses distinguish output sharpness from Gumbel noise (Appendix E), test multi-start pool size and iteration tradeoffs (F), examine sensitivity to comparator runtime (G), and test direct variable optimization as Sudoku difficulty increases (I). The original subset-selection and positional-encoding ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports averages across 10 runs for direct SGD in Appendix I and specifies 20 parallel MAXCUT runs in Appendix G. These disclosures concern added experiments; they do not establish additional repetitions of the retained results. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original Tables 2–3 and positional-encoding results are unchanged. New results include MAXCUT percentage gaps of 0.31, 0.34, 0.43, and 1.27 across size groups. New multi-start variants reach 55.67% and 15.00% on the two coloring OOD sets, compared with retained single-start results of 47.33% and 11.92%. Tables 9, 11, and 12 add further ablation and baseline outcomes.

M1.justification: Appendix F implements optional multi-start inference: several candidates are updated concurrently, and a solution is accepted when any candidate becomes feasible. v1 discussed pool-based extensions only as future work. The core Transformer architecture, single-step training, and constraint penalties remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section organization are retained. Changes include clarifying multi-head attention, separating limitations and future work from the conclusion, adding explanatory appendices, and inserting acknowledgments and an impact statement. The main narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with the MAXCUT table and Tables 9–12, including an expanded coloring comparison. It adds a MAXCUT hyperparameter column and redraws Figure 2 to show output distributions and selected updates more explicitly. Existing plots and tables are also reformatted or relocated; their renumbering alone is not counted.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly connects ConsFormer to constraint-based local search and adds references concerning learned SAT search, self-supervised constrained optimization, probabilistic relaxations, and set-function extensions. These broaden the existing positioning without replacing its organizing argument. Publication updates to already cited works are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: Appendix H adds a formal discrete ALLDIFFERENT violation-degree function and connects it to the existing penalty-design rationale. The original CSP formulations, continuous penalty equations, and zero-penalty feasibility condition are retained. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1 by testing output-function choices, direct optimization, competing heuristics, and runtime sensitivity, while examining scalability on much larger MAXCUT instances. The explicit limitation concerning parametric constraints materially improves the account of applicability, and the implementation link improves reproducibility information. These additions strengthen evidence and transparency, including unfavorable comparisons, although uncertainty reporting remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConsFormer research. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison; v2 retains Appendices A–D and adds E–I.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original MAXCUT, multi-start, output-function, baseline, and direct-gradient-descent experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original ConsFormer experiments on Sudoku, graph coloring, and nurse scheduling, including performance comparisons and ablations in Section 4.

arxiv_record.abstract: Multimodal representation learning is fundamentally about transforming incomparable modalities into comparable representations. While prior research primarily focused on explicitly aligning these representations through targeted learning objectives and model architectures, a recent line of work has found that independently trained unimodal models of increasing scale and performance can become implicitly aligned with each other. These findings raise fundamental questions regarding the emergence of aligned representations in multimodal learning. Specifically: (1) when and why does alignment emerge implicitly? and (2) is alignment a reliable indicator of performance? Through a comprehensive empirical investigation, we demonstrate that both the emergence of alignment and its relationship with task performance depend on several critical data characteristics. These include, but are not necessarily limited to, the degree of similarity between the modalities and the balance between redundant and unique information they provide for the task. Our findings suggest that alignment may not be universally beneficial; rather, its impact on performance varies depending on the dataset and task. These insights can help practitioners determine whether increasing alignment between modalities is advantageous or, in some cases, detrimental to achieving optimal performance. Code is released at https://github.com/MeganTj/multimodal_alignment.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings, and substantive conclusion retain the claims that heterogeneity and uniqueness constrain alignment and that alignment does not universally predict performance. The new experiments support the existing practitioner implications rather than redefine these central claims.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 replaces the interpretation that high corruption undermines the performance-capacity relationship with an account of flattening alignment-performance slopes while larger language models still perform better. Section 6.2 and Appendix D.7 add task-specific interpretations connecting alignment-performance slopes to the usefulness of explicit alignment.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 supplies the GPT-4o caption-generation prompt. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models have led to impressive progress in caption generation for images and short video clips. However, these models remain constrained by their limited temporal receptive fields, making it difficult to produce coherent and comprehensive captions for long videos. While several methods have been proposed to aggregate information across video segments, they often rely on supervised fine-tuning or incur significant computational overhead. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework for long video captioning based on graph consolidation. Our approach first generates segment-level captions, corresponding to individual frames or short video intervals, using off-the-shelf visual captioning models. These captions are then parsed into individual scene graphs, which are subsequently consolidated into a unified graph representation that preserves both holistic context and fine-grained details throughout the video. A lightweight graph-to-text decoder then produces the final video-level caption. This framework effectively extends the temporal understanding capabilities of existing models without requiring any additional fine-tuning on long video datasets. Experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms existing LLM-based consolidation approaches, achieving strong zero-shot performance while substantially reducing computational costs.

arxiv_record.abstract: Learned denoisers play a fundamental role in various signal generation (e.g., diffusion models) and reconstruction (e.g., compressed sensing) architectures, whose success derives from their ability to leverage low-dimensional structure in data. Existing denoising methods, however, either rely on local approximations that require a linear scan of the entire dataset or treat denoising as generic function approximation problems, often sacrificing efficiency and interpretability. We consider the problem of efficiently denoising a new noisy data point sampled from an unknown $d$-dimensional manifold $M \in \mathbb{R}^D$, using only noisy samples. This work proposes a framework for test-time efficient manifold denoising, by framing the concept of "learning-to-denoise" as "learning-to-optimize". We have two technical innovations: (i) online learning methods which learn to optimize over the manifold of clean signals using only noisy data, effectively "growing" an optimizer one sample at a time. (ii) mixed-order methods which guarantee that the learned optimizers achieve global optimality, ensuring both efficiency and near-optimal denoising performance. We corroborate these claims with theoretical analyses of both the complexity and denoising performance of mixed-order traversal. Our experiments on scientific manifolds demonstrate significantly improved complexity-performance tradeoffs compared to nearest neighbor search, which underpins existing provable denoising approaches based on exhaustive search.
arxiv_record.authors: Shiyu Wang, Mariam Avagyan, Yihan Shen, Arnaud Lamy, Tingran Wang, Szabolcs M\'arka, Zsuzsa M\'arka, John Wright

The conclusion retains the qualification that theoretical guarantees assume an ideal learned graph.

C2.justification: Appendix G adds substantive qualifications: tested autoencoders can achieve higher accuracy, image outputs exhibit pixelation and color artifacts, and radius tuning may extend the method's accuracy range. The new ablation also supports the proposed division of roles between first- and zero-order steps. Existing limitations concerning guarantees for learned landmarks remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, explicit streaming-average and affine-projection formulas in Appendix E, autoencoder architectures and Adam learning rate, and image preprocessing details. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Some ambiguity remains: G.1 describes a two-dimensional bottleneck, whereas Table 2 includes wider bottlenecks; code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic manifolds and generated gravitational waveforms. v2 retains this coverage and adds patch denoising using 300 ImageNet images and a single DIV2K image (Appendices G.2–G.3), substantially extending the domain and introducing a single-image learning scenario.

E2.justification: v1's quantitative comparison uses nearest-neighbor search. v2 retains it and adds 15 autoencoder configurations (Figure 13, Table 2), plus first-order-only traversal and zero-order search over all graph edges (Figure 18). These substantially broaden the evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: The gravitational-wave test set increases from 5,000 to 20,000 samples, while training remains at 100,000. New image protocols use 8 × 8 × 3 patches, Gaussian noise with sigma 0.1, and 890,000 or 170,000 training patches with strides 8 or 4. v2 also introduces autoencoder configurations and controlled component-ablation procedures. The retained hyperparameter table relabels the neighbor-radius entries from R_nbrs to R_nbrs squared.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained radius comparison and network visualizations, Appendix G.4 adds a controlled ablation testing why gradient steps and zero-order tunnels should be combined. Appendix B.2 adds a noisy-versus-denoised waveform case, and G.2–G.3 provide image and patch case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The larger test set changes evaluation size, while the theoretical probability bounds concern mathematical guarantees rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Figures 8–9 show revised gravitational-wave curves, with Figure 9 using the enlarged test set. v1 Table 1's exact landmark counts, computational costs, and MSEs are removed. v2 adds autoencoder outcomes, image-denoising curves and examples, and ablation findings showing low computational cost but high error for first-order-only traversal. These are added or replaced results; the revised curves do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the online graph-learning and mixed-order traversal framework. However, Appendix D revises the stated tangent-space update: Algorithms 4–5 replace inputs x_i with landmark-centered inputs x_i - q_M and formulate the update through eigenvalues of the second-moment matrix. This is a localized revision to the documented procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains intact, with mostly local condensation, terminology and notation edits, and revised explanations. Appendix D's exposition is reworked and Appendix E collects additional algorithm explanations. Author information, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated.
