arxiv_record.abstract: Significant efforts have been directed towards adapting self-supervised multimodal learning for Earth observation applications. However, most current methods produce coarse patch-sized embeddings, limiting their effectiveness and integration with other modalities like LiDAR. To close this gap, we present DUNIA, an approach to learn pixel-sized embeddings through cross-modal alignment between images and full-waveform LiDAR data. As the model is trained in a contrastive manner, the embeddings can be directly leveraged in the context of a variety of environmental monitoring tasks in a zero-shot setting. In our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the embeddings for seven such tasks: canopy height mapping, fractional canopy cover, land cover mapping, tree species identification, plant area index, crop type classification, and per-pixel waveform-based vertical structure mapping. The results show that the embeddings, along with zero-shot classifiers, often outperform specialized supervised models, even in low-data regimes. In the fine-tuning setting, we show strong performances near or better than the state-of-the-art on five out of six tasks.

C1.justification: Both versions claim pixel-level horizontal/vertical alignment, effective retrieval across seven tasks, competitive fine-tuning on five of six tasks and waveform generation from pixel embeddings. Rewording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 explicitly qualifies median composites as more informative than single-date images but less informative than full time series. H.10 attributes their advantage to more stable, representative reflectance patterns. These refine the temporal-information interpretation; the existing limitations concerning static inputs and geographic/year specificity remain.

D1.justification: Section 4 adds a code-repository link absent from v1, and Table G1 explicitly lists the selected neighbor count for each task. Most architecture, optimizer, hardware and diffusion settings are carried over from v1 Appendix D to v2 Appendix E.

E1.justification: The seven tasks and core French datasets are retained. Appendix H adds cross-year evaluation for 2019 and 2021, pooled 2019–2021 pretraining, single-sensor inputs and single-date imagery scenarios. These extend temporal and input-condition coverage within the existing domains.

E2.justification: Fine-tuning comparisons expand from AnySat and CROMA to include DOFA, DeCUR and SatMAE in Tables 2 and G2. Table 1 also adds canopy-height comparisons with Liu et al. (2023), Tolan et al. (2024) and Lang et al. (2023), alongside Schwartz et al. (2023). These are reported comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes comparator pretraining from 200K to 250K steps and DUNIA fine-tuning from the last two neighborhood-attention layers to the last layer. Added protocols vary input size, retrieval database size, neighbor count and temporal training/evaluation design. These reported revisions do not establish that retained results were rerun. Table G2 also changes the PASTIS sample count from 300 to 300K images, an unexplained inconsistency with the stated dataset size.

E4.justification: The five original ablations are retained as H.1–H.5. New sections H.6–H.10 examine retrieval overhead, input-size sensitivity, temporal stability, sensor contributions and median composites versus single-date inputs. Appendix D adds a t-SNE comparison of pixel and patch embeddings, and Appendix I expands qualitative map examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added evaluations continue to report point estimates without introducing uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial comparator and supplementary results. For example, Table H11 reports PASTIS wF1 of 42.3 with single-date inputs versus 77.0 with median composites; Table H6 reports DUNIA runtimes of 4.22/4.80 seconds versus 177.37 for AnySat. Existing principal DUNIA table values are retained or rounded, while smaller-data results move to Appendix G; these do not demonstrate new same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The dual-decoder architecture, waveform and multitemporal autoencoders, Zero-CL/VICReg alignment, reconstruction losses and diffusion generator remain unchanged. Matching the appendices confirms that expanded architectural explanations do not introduce new method components; the fine-tuning revisions concern evaluation settings.

P1.justification: Section 3 receives a rewritten, multi-paragraph architectural overview, and related work gains a dedicated EO subsection. Existing appendix material is substantially reorganized: objectives and waveform generation become separate sections, experimental settings move, and reduced-label evaluations receive their own section. Terminology and prose are also edited throughout.

P2.justification: Figure 2 becomes a simplified architecture diagram while the detailed diagram moves to Figure A1. v2 adds Figure D1 and Tables H6–H11, restructures Tables 1–2 with smaller-data results in G1–G2, and expands the original combined map figure into Figures I1–I3. The four waveform-example figures remain unchanged apart from presentation and numbering.

R1.justification: A dedicated Section 2.2 substantially expands domain-specific positioning by discussing masked-reconstruction and contrastive approaches for Earth observation, including SatMAE, SatMAE++, DOFA, CROMA, DeCUR and AnySat. Additional canopy-height literature also broadens the context beyond v1's primarily general contrastive and multimodal review.

T1.justification: The alignment losses, diffusion formulations and radar-normalization equation are retained after appendix relocation and equation renumbering. The decoder-channel index correction in Section 3.1 agrees with the formula already present in v1 Appendix A.1. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens comparative validation and the justification of practical design choices through broader baselines and targeted temporal, sensor, compositing and runtime tests. Clearer architectural diagrams and code-access information also improve usability. Table G2's inconsistent PASTIS count and unexplained setting revisions limit reproducibility, but these localized problems do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and explanation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DUNIA and provide readable main texts, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds comparator evaluations, runtime measurements, temporal tests and input-sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval, fine-tuning and waveform-generation results across seven Earth-observation tasks, alongside architectural ablations and qualitative examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Conformal prediction is a powerful distribution-free framework for constructing prediction sets with coverage guarantees. Classical methods, such as split conformal prediction, provide marginal coverage, ensuring that the prediction set contains the label of a random test point with a target probability. However, these guarantees may not hold uniformly across different subpopulations, leading to disparities in coverage. Prior work has explored coverage guarantees conditioned on events related to the covariates and label of the test point. We present Kandinsky conformal prediction, a framework that significantly expands the scope of conditional coverage guarantees. In contrast to Mondrian conformal prediction, which restricts its coverage guarantees to disjoint groups -- reminiscent of the rigid, structured grids of Piet Mondrian's art -- our framework flexibly handles overlapping and fractional group memberships defined jointly on covariates and labels, reflecting the layered, intersecting forms in Wassily Kandinsky's compositions. Our algorithm unifies and extends existing methods, encompassing covariate-based group conditional, class conditional, and Mondrian conformal prediction as special cases, while achieving a minimax-optimal high-probability conditional coverage bound. Finally, we demonstrate the practicality of our approach through empirical evaluation on real-world datasets.
arxiv_record.authors: Konstantina Bairaktari, Jiayun Wu, Zhiwei Steven Wu
arxiv_record.title: Kandinsky Conformal Prediction: Beyond Class- and Covariate-Conditional Coverage

C1.justification: The abstract and principal framework contributions remain unchanged. Introduction contribution 3 expands the empirical claim to multiple-choice question answering and explicitly claims best-calibrated coverage across boosting trees, neural networks, and LLMs.

C2.justification: Section 3 adds an explanation attributing the faster convergence analysis to concentration of weighted coverage rather than pinball loss. Section 5.3 interprets conservative conformal's comparable MCQA coverage deviation as requiring larger prediction sets. Existing experimental interpretations and computational limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 5.3 identifies the source and restricted availability of the logged model probabilities. Appendix C.3 lists the 16 subjects and their exact nine-basic/seven-advanced grouping. Existing implementation details in Appendix C are retained; MCQA calibration sample counts and splits remain unspecified.

E1.justification: Section 5.3 adds multiple-choice question answering on a 16-subject MMLU subset using LLaMA-13B predictions, with subjects grouped into basic and advanced categories. This substantially extends coverage beyond income regression and toxicity classification, which are retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding ACSIncome and CivilComments experiments retain their comparator sets. The new MCQA experiment reuses split and conservative conformal prediction; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: The added MCQA configuration uses logged four-choice probabilities from LLaMA-13B, APS scores, and a 40% subject-accuracy threshold for grouping. Existing experiments retain their stated splits, sample budgets, preprocessing, models, and evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: The analyses varying group counts on ACSIncome and calibration sample sizes on CivilComments are unchanged. The MCQA addition reports aggregate benchmark outcomes without introducing a separate ablation, robustness test, or error analysis.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly reports distributions across ten one-shot prompts for MCQA. The existing experiments retain their 100 reshuffled runs and associated distribution and standard-deviation reporting. This does not establish increased replication of the earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Figure 5 adds results for a new task: Kandinsky (FY) has lower group-average coverage deviation than split conformal and comparable deviation to conservative conformal, with smaller prediction sets. The six original ACSIncome and CivilComments plots and their findings are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same quantile-regression objectives, randomized scores, prediction-set construction, and test-time alternative. Explicit randomness notation and the MCQA application do not change the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 clarifies training-conditional versus marginal coverage, makes calibration conditioning and randomness explicit, adds a proof sketch and MCQA subsections, and updates an author affiliation. The overall section organization and most existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: v1's six-panel Figure 3 is split into four-panel Figure 3 and two-panel Figure 4, with revised captions and placement. v2 adds the two-panel MCQA Figure 5. The original plot contents and the two introductory artwork figures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused discussion of Blot et al. on joint covariate-label groups and Plassier et al. on joint distribution shifts, distinguishing its guarantees from theirs. A footnote distinguishes Brunekreef et al.'s same-named segmentation method. MMLU, MCQA, and LLaMA references are also added.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 replaces weight sup-norm scaling with coefficient L1-norm scaling under a normalized basis and changes log(4/delta) to log(4d/delta). Appendix A.1 separates a fixed-weight result into Lemma A.1 and adds a union-bound proof for the uniform guarantee. Corollaries 3.2–3.4 and their proofs are updated accordingly. Corollary 3.5 changes from a simultaneous guarantee over target distributions to a high-probability guarantee for each fixed target distribution.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is addressing the unsupported fixed-weight-to-uniform step in v1's central proof. Lemma A.1 and the new union-bound argument support appropriately revised guarantees, including corrected target-distribution quantifiers. Although the resulting bounds are weaker, their justification is materially stronger. The MCQA evaluation and more precise research positioning add useful support, despite sparse calibration details for the new experiment. Repairing the central theoretical argument constitutes a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Kandinsky Conformal Prediction. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, references, and appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original conformal-prediction evaluations using previously logged LLaMA-13B outputs on an MMLU subset in Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original conformal-prediction experiments on ACSIncome and CivilComments, including coverage and prediction-set-size results in Figure 3.

arxiv_record.abstract: We consider layerwise function-space learning rates, which measure the magnitude of the change in a neural network's output function in response to an update to a parameter tensor. This contrasts with traditional learning rates, which describe the magnitude of changes in parameter space. We develop efficient methods to measure and set function-space learning rates in arbitrary neural networks, requiring only minimal computational overhead through a few additional backward passes that can be performed at the start of, or periodically during, training. We demonstrate two key applications: (1) analysing the dynamics of standard neural network optimisers in function space, rather than parameter space, and (2) introducing FLeRM (Function-space Learning Rate Matching), a novel approach to hyperparameter transfer across model scales. FLeRM records function-space learning rates while training a small, cheap base model, then automatically adjusts parameter-space layerwise learning rates when training larger models to maintain consistent function-space updates. FLeRM gives hyperparameter transfer across model width, depth, initialisation scale, and LoRA rank in various architectures including MLPs with residual connections and transformers with different layer normalisation schemes.
arxiv_record.authors: Edward Milsom, Ben Anson, Laurence Aitchison
arxiv_record.comments: ICML 2025 Camera Ready Version, 27 pages, 26 figures

C.11 attributes noisy SGD curves to using SGD with transformers, supported by the smoother ResMLP experiment. These add specific interpretations without replacing the earlier conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses roughly 814M parameters for the retained widest transformer, explains cosine-schedule transfer through base-model learning-rate ratios, and supplies settings such as momentum 0.9 and AdamW weight decay 0.1. The original model/data details and code-access link remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use CIFAR-10, Wikitext-103, Cold French Law, and MathPile for the same classification and language-modeling tasks. The added test-loss evaluations and model/optimizer sweeps retain this data and task coverage.

E2.justification: The width-transfer comparisons expand beyond standard Adam to momentum SGD, SignSGD/Signum, AdamW, Adamax, and Adagrad, each compared with its FLeRM counterpart (Figures 20–25). Figure 15 also newly compares the Kronecker estimator against IID and no-assumption estimators.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings are retained, but Appendices C.7–C.11 introduce test-loss evaluation, cosine scheduling, affine layernorm parameters, simultaneous width/depth scaling, and alternative optimizer settings. E4.justification: v2 retains the periodic-update, equal-rate, and LoRA analyses and substantially expands diagnostics. New analyses examine covariance assumptions, generalization, sensitivity to schedules and layernorm configuration, joint scaling, optimizer robustness, and the effect of readout-specific variance reduction (C.6–C.11 and Appendix D).

E5.justification: Figure 15 newly reports empirical estimator bias and variance over 10,000 batches. This characterizes estimator variability rather than independent training-run uncertainty. The eight-seed base-model averaging and single-seed LoRA calibration remain unchanged, and the new performance plots do not add confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Figures 1–14 retain their results, while Figures 15–26 add substantial findings: the Kronecker estimator trades some bias for reduced variance, test-loss optima align more closely with FLeRM, additional optimizer/configuration comparisons support transfer, and readout-specific estimation reduces ResMLP curve noise. arxiv_record.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) can be circumvented through adversarially crafted inputs, yet the mechanisms by which these attacks bypass safety barriers remain poorly understood. Prior work suggests that a single refusal direction in the model's activation space determines whether an LLM refuses a request. In this study, we propose a novel gradient-based approach to representation engineering and use it to identify refusal directions. Contrary to prior work, we uncover multiple independent directions and even multi-dimensional concept cones that mediate refusal. Moreover, we show that orthogonality alone does not imply independence under intervention, motivating the notion of representational independence that accounts for both linear and non-linear effects. Using this framework, we identify mechanistically independent refusal directions. We show that refusal mechanisms in LLMs are governed by complex spatial structures and identify functionally independent directions, confirming that multiple distinct mechanisms drive refusal behavior. Our gradient-based approach uncovers these mechanisms and can further serve as a foundation for future work on understanding LLMs.

E2.justification: DIM remains the principal comparator. v2 adds no-intervention baselines to the JailbreakBench and RepInd comparisons, introduces DIM into the retain-loss trade-off plot, and reports a multiple-DIM-direction control for compositional ablation.

New protocols include an addition/ablation weight sweep with complementary weights, simultaneous top-k ablation, and an activation-strength sweep for safety versus over-refusal. The retain-loss analysis replaces validation-KL comparisons with average capability-score changes, and RepInd evaluation expands beyond Gemma 2 2B.

E4.justification: v2 adds component-loss ablations, compositional tests of independent directions, orthogonality analyses across models, and safety/over-refusal trade-offs. It substantially revises the retain-loss sensitivity analysis. Conversely, v1 Figure 12's experiment on cones with representationally independent basis vectors is removed.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 15 explicitly reports means and standard deviations over five runs per retain-loss weight. Its v2 replacement presents scatter points without the corresponding run-count or uncertainty explanation. The new loss-balance plot also leaves its error bars undefined; existing cone-sampling and RepInd candidate-count disclosures remain.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark and mechanistic results while retaining Table 1 and Figure 2's original results. Additional results appear in Tables 4–5 and the expanded appendices; the original RepInd-cone results disappear.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and the ablation, addition, retain, and RepInd objectives remain unchanged. Simultaneous ablation of multiple directions is introduced as a mechanistic experiment, without revising the proposed optimization algorithms.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose are preserved. v2 reorganizes the previously combined experimental appendix into topic-specific sections, expands selected related-work and RepInd explanations, and updates affiliation and publication text.

R1.justification: v2 adds an over-refusal literature paragraph and distinguishes its gradient-based discovery approach from concurrent independent-direction research by Pan et al. arxiv_record.abstract: Short-term memory is essential for cognitive processing, yet our understanding of its neural mechanisms remains unclear. Neuroscience has long focused on how sequential activity patterns, where neurons fire one after another within large networks, can explain how information is maintained. While recurrent connections were shown to drive sequential dynamics, a mechanistic understanding of this process still remains unknown. In this work, we introduce two unique mechanisms that can support this form of short-term memory: slow-point manifolds generating direct sequences or limit cycles providing temporally localized approximations. Using analytical models, we identify fundamental properties that govern the selection of each mechanism. Precisely, on short-term memory tasks (delayed cue-discrimination tasks), we derive theoretical scaling laws for critical learning rates as a function of the delay period length, beyond which no learning is possible. We empirically verify these results by training and evaluating approximately 80,000 recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which are publicly available for further analysis. Overall, our work provides new insights into short-term memory mechanisms and proposes experimentally testable predictions for systems neuroscience.

C1.justification: The two-mechanism, task-design and critical-learning-rate contributions remain. v2's introduction strengthens the empirical contribution from extracting scaling laws to explicitly claiming quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions within error bars. This refines the central validation claim without changing the research objective.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly cautions that the toy mechanisms are non-exhaustive and discusses transient, high-dimensional alternatives, refining v1's approximate-bound framing. It also drops v1's interpretation that adding a post-reaction period yields more efficient scaling, instead emphasizing agreement with theoretical ranges and changes in mechanism selection.

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive implementation and reproduction information: Euler updates, weighted MSE, optimizer settings, initialization, training schedules, parameter grids, hardware and figure-specific configurations (S3–S4). It states that code and model data are available through GitHub and Zenodo, replacing v1's release promise. Newly disclosed training details do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate delayed activation, delayed cue discrimination with and without post-reaction periods, and a no-delay cue-response control. v2's larger time constant and expanded parameter sweeps concern model configurations within these retained tasks, rather than new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates additional external baseline methods. Slow-point and limit-cycle mechanisms remain the principal comparisons; LSTMs, GRUs, Transformers and newly discussed alternative approaches are cited rather than experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: The empirical evaluation pipeline changes substantially. v2 normalizes reaction reliability by total output, revises success/failure criteria and training-window definitions, and replaces modified-ReLU cutoff estimation with exponential-saturation or sigmoid fits (v1 S2 versus v2 S3.4). It also extends the plotted rank-2 delay sweep and adds experiments with tau = 20 ms.

E4.justification: v2 adds a time-constant robustness study (Fig. S5), mechanism-discrimination diagnostics and a direct empirical test of slow-point scaling (Fig. S3), and representative successful and failed trajectories (Fig. S4). The existing no-delay ablation gains a quantitative scaling analysis in Fig. S6; it is not a newly introduced task.

E5.justification: Rank-2 repetitions increase from 10 to 100 networks per condition (v1 Fig. 4C; v2 Fig. 3C). v2 also tabulates seed counts and newly specifies covariance-based Monte Carlo estimation of 95% confidence intervals. v1 already reports regression uncertainties and Fisher tests with Bonferroni correction, so statistical reporting is expanded rather than introduced.

E6.justification: Without/with post-reaction periods, v1 Fig. 6 reports slopes of -2.40 ± 0.36 and -1.57 ± 0.18; v2 Fig. 4 reports decay-exponent magnitudes of 2.72 ± 0.07 and 2.65 ± 0.23. v2 additionally reports slow-point scaling of 4.05 ± 0.10 and no-delay scaling of 0.38 ± 0.02. These are revised or added results under changed analyses and expanded experiments, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The RNN architectures and ghost/limit-cycle toy models are retained. However, the auxiliary mechanism-classification procedure changes from firing-rate dispersion (OM, v1 S2.2) to a spectral-power ratio computed from correlations of principal components (MDI, v2 S3.4.1). This revises an analysis component without replacing the central models.

P1.justification: The introduction and discussion are extensively rewritten around three explicit research questions, with machine-learning motivation moved forward from the discussion. The separate conclusion is absorbed into concluding remarks, results gain explanatory subheadings, and the appendix is reorganized into background, theory, experimental methods and reproduction sections.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout and substantially restructures the figures. Fig. 1 combines revised mechanism diagrams with task illustrations; Fig. 2 contracts from five cases to three; v1 Fig. 3 moves to Fig. S1; theoretical and empirical phase diagrams are consolidated into Fig. 4. New diagnostic/control panels and Table S1 further expand the presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted literature on activity-silent and synaptic memory, reservoir/transient dynamics, universal approximation and low-dimensional computation. These additions broaden context and qualify applicability while retaining the principal connections to earlier ghost-model, low-rank RNN and sequential-memory research.

T1.justification: The central ghost and limit-cycle derivations and scaling exponents are retained, moving from v1 S1 to v2 S2. Limited mathematical changes include the revised reliability definition and replacement of OM with the formally defined MDI (v2 Eqs. S37–S38); no new central scaling theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between theory and evidence through direct slow-point scaling tests, mechanism diagnostics and a time-constant control. Its expanded methods and stated code/data access also address important reproducibility gaps in v1. Some inconsistent figure references and parameter descriptions in S4 limit reproducibility, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RNN short-term memory study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

arxiv_record.abstract: Synthetic data has the potential to improve the performance, training efficiency, and privacy of real training examples. Nevertheless, existing approaches for synthetic text generation are mostly heuristics and cannot generate human-readable text without compromising the privacy of real data, or provide performance guarantees for training Large Language Models (LLMs). In this work, we propose the first theoretically rigorous approach for generating synthetic human-readable text that provides convergence, performance, and privacy guarantees for fine-tuning LLMs on a target task. To do so, we leverage Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) that iteratively optimizes the embeddings of synthetic examples to match the noisy gradient of the target training or validation data, and maps them to a sequence of text tokens with low perplexity. In doing so, the generated synthetic text guarantees convergence of the model to a close neighborhood of the solution obtained by fine-tuning on real data and preserves their privacy. Experiments on various classification tasks confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/BigML-CS-UCLA/GRADMM.
arxiv_record.authors: Dang Nguyen, Zeman Li, Mohammadhossein Bateni, Vahab Mirrokni, Meisam Razaviyayn, Baharan Mirzasoleiman
arxiv_record.title: Synthetic Text Generation for Training Large Language Models via Gradient Matching

C1.justification: Although v1 already describes GRADMM as privacy-preserving, v2 strengthens this into an explicit differential-privacy contribution. Its abstract and introduction now claim privacy guarantees alongside convergence and performance guarantees, and its conclusion emphasizes matching noisy target gradients. Readability and transferability claims are retained.

C2.justification: v2 interprets gradient alignment and distribution similarity as explanations for performance, distance histograms as evidence against copying, and membership-inference results as privacy evidence even without DP. It newly qualifies effectiveness as dependent on real-example diversity and hypothesizes that privacy noise can improve generalization when only five real examples are available.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, documents privacy parameters and attack procedures, and explains that synthetic examples are generated independently. The independent-generation remark is additional documentation rather than an established procedural change. Existing optimization settings, hardware information and Appendix B prompts are retained; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs.

E1.justification: Appendix D and Figure 7 extend the existing data-scarce sentiment-classification evaluation to IMDB and a reported Sentence polarity benchmark. Section 5.3 also adds an SST-2 membership-inference test. The PDFs do not clarify whether Sentence polarity represents distinct data from the retained Rotten tomatoes benchmark.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain zero-shot generation, few-shot generation, Herding, K-center and Random comparisons. Added diagnostics reuse existing comparators or real data; different privacy settings are variants of GRADMM rather than newly introduced comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds privacy-controlled evaluations using epsilon values 0.05, 4 and infinity, delta 0.0001 and clipping threshold 1, plus normalized-gradient, FID and nearest-example-distance measurements. Its new membership-inference protocol selects a threshold on 100 members and 100 non-members, then evaluates another balanced group. Existing fine-tuning budgets and checkpoint-selection rules remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendix D add gradient-error trajectories, distribution matching measured by FID, nearest-training-example distance histograms, membership-inference attacks and privacy-budget sensitivity. These examine gradient alignment, representativeness, copying and privacy–utility tradeoffs. The original projection, last-layer and filtering ablations are retained.

E5.justification: v1 gives point accuracies without uncertainty or repeated-run information. v2 adds ± values throughout Table 1, shaded uncertainty bands in Figure 1, and membership-inference averages over 10 runs. Classification run counts and the meanings of the ± values and bands remain unspecified; an increase in runs for existing experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and Figure 1 contain revised results and new private-GRADMM results. For example, five-example SST-2 accuracy changes from 87.0 to 86.5±0.5 for non-private GRADMM, with 84.2±0.1 newly reported for epsilon 0.05. v2 also adds privacy, FID, gradient and benchmark outcomes. Table 2 and the original ablation values remain unchanged. The revised Table 1 supports the text's 13.1-point maximum advantage, although its caption retains 10.4%.

M1.justification: New Section 4.5 extends GRADMM with per-example gradient clipping and Gaussian noise added to the averaged target gradient. Algorithm 1 incorporates privacy parameters into optimization. This changes the gradient-matching procedure, while retaining the ADMM updates, top-k projection and filtering.

P1.justification: v2 makes targeted abstract, introduction and conclusion edits, inserts privacy and analysis subsections and Appendix D, and adds an impact statement and acknowledgements. It also updates affiliation and publication text and shortens some baseline explanations. Most existing prose and the overall narrative organization are retained.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains a privacy-setting column and uncertainty displays, and Figure 1 gains private-GRADMM curves and shaded bands. v2 adds the FID table and substantial new plots in Figures 2 and 7–10. Existing ablation tables, sample-text figures and prompt figures are retained with relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting differential privacy, noise calibration, membership inference, noise-related generalization and IMDB, while removing the Dubey et al. Llama reference. Section 2 also removes the blanket statement that dataset distillation preserves privacy. The broader positioning against existing text-distillation and generation approaches remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.5 extends the formal scope to differential privacy, specifying piecewise noise calibration in epsilon and delta and invoking composition to claim an (epsilon, delta)-DP guarantee. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's weakly supported privacy assurances by supplying an explicit clipping-and-noise mechanism, privacy settings and attack evaluations. arxiv_record.abstract: Transformers consist of diverse building blocks, such as embedding layers, normalization layers, self-attention mechanisms, and point-wise feedforward networks. Thus, understanding the differences and interactions among these blocks is important. In this paper, we uncover a clear Sharpness Disparity across these blocks, which emerges early in training and intriguingly persists throughout the training process. Motivated by this finding, we propose Blockwise Learning Rate (LR), a strategy that tailors the LR to each block's sharpness, accelerating large language model (LLM) pre-training. By integrating Blockwise LR into AdamW, we consistently achieve lower terminal loss and nearly $2\times$ speedup compared to vanilla AdamW. We demonstrate this acceleration across GPT-2 and LLaMA, with model sizes ranging from 0.12B to 2B and datasets of OpenWebText, MiniPile, and C4. Finally, we incorporate Blockwise LR into Adam-mini (Zhang et al., 2024), a recently proposed memory-efficient variant of Adam, achieving a combined $2\times$ speedup and $2\times$ memory saving. These results underscore the potential of exploiting the sharpness disparity to improve LLM training.
arxiv_record.authors: Jinbo Wang, Mingze Wang, Zhanpeng Zhou, Junchi Yan, Weinan E, Lei Wu
arxiv_record.title: The Sharpness Disparity Principle in Transformers for Accelerating Language Model Pre-Training

E3.justification: Existing OpenWebText/MiniPile protocols are retained. New settings include a 2B model, C4 training with sequence length 256, batch size 512 and approximately 20 training tokens per parameter, and zero-shot downstream evaluation using lm-evaluation-harness. E5.justification: v2 introduces no new seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures. Additional performance results retain the existing point-result reporting approach.

E6.justification: v2 adds 2B and C4 loss results, Lion/WSD outcomes, and seven downstream comparisons. The original ablation values remain unchanged in v2 Table 2.

arxiv_record.abstract: Many recent studies have found evidence for emergent reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs), but debate persists concerning the robustness of these capabilities, and the extent to which they depend on structured reasoning mechanisms. To shed light on these issues, we study the internal mechanisms that support abstract reasoning in LLMs. We identify an emergent symbolic architecture that implements abstract reasoning via a series of three computations. In early layers, symbol abstraction heads convert input tokens to abstract variables based on the relations between those tokens. In intermediate layers, symbolic induction heads perform sequence induction over these abstract variables. Finally, in later layers, retrieval heads predict the next token by retrieving the value associated with the predicted abstract variable. These results point toward a resolution of the longstanding debate between symbolic and neural network approaches, suggesting that emergent reasoning in neural networks depends on the emergence of symbolic mechanisms.

arxiv_record.abstract: We address the problem of code generation from multi-turn execution feedback. Existing methods either generate code without feedback or use complex, hierarchical reinforcement learning to optimize multi-turn rewards. We propose a simple yet scalable approach, $\mu$Code, that solves multi-turn code generation using only single-step rewards. Our key insight is that code generation is a one-step recoverable MDP, where the correct code can be recovered from any intermediate code state in a single turn. $\mu$Code iteratively trains both a generator to provide code solutions conditioned on multi-turn execution feedback and a verifier to score the newly generated code. Experimental evaluations show that our approach achieves significant improvements over the state-of-the-art baselines. We provide analysis of the design choices of the reward models and policy, and show the efficacy of $\mu$Code at utilizing the execution feedback. Our code is available at https://github.com/portal-cornell/muCode.

arxiv_record.abstract: Designing RNA molecules that interact with specific proteins is a critical challenge in experimental and computational biology. Existing computational approaches require a substantial amount of previously known interacting RNA sequences for each specific protein or a detailed knowledge of RNA structure, restricting their utility in practice. To address this limitation, we develop RNA-BAnG, a deep learning-based model designed to generate RNA sequences for protein interactions without these requirements. Central to our approach is a novel generative method, Bidirectional Anchored Generation (BAnG), which leverages the observation that protein-binding RNA sequences often contain functional binding motifs embedded within broader sequence contexts. We first validate our method on generic synthetic tasks involving similar localized motifs to those appearing in RNAs, demonstrating its benefits over existing generative approaches. We then evaluate our model on biological sequences, showing its effectiveness for conditional RNA sequence design given a binding protein.

arxiv_record.abstract: Diffusion policies are widely adopted in complex visuomotor tasks for their ability to capture multimodal action distributions. However, the multiple sampling steps required for action generation significantly harm real-time inference efficiency, which limits their applicability in real-time decision-making scenarios. Existing acceleration techniques either require retraining or degrade performance under low sampling steps. Here we propose Falcon, which mitigates this speed-performance trade-off and achieves further acceleration. The core insight is that visuomotor tasks exhibit sequential dependencies between actions. Falcon leverages this by reusing partially denoised actions from historical information rather than sampling from Gaussian noise at each step. By integrating current observations, Falcon reduces sampling steps while preserving performance. Importantly, Falcon is a training-free algorithm that can be applied as a plug-in to further improve decision efficiency on top of existing acceleration techniques. We validated Falcon in 48 simulated environments and 2 real-world robot experiments. demonstrating a 2-7x speedup with negligible performance degradation, offering a promising direction for efficient visuomotor policy design.

However, the multiple sampling steps required for action generation significantly harm real-time inference efficiency, which limits their applicability in real-time decision-making scenarios. Existing acceleration techniques either require retraining or degrade performance under low sampling steps. Here we propose Falcon, which mitigates this speed-performance trade-off and achieves further acceleration. The core insight is that visuomotor tasks exhibit sequential dependencies between actions. Falcon leverages this by reusing partially denoised actions from historical information rather than sampling from Gaussian noise at each step. By integrating current observations, Falcon reduces sampling steps while preserving performance. Importantly, Falcon is a training-free algorithm that can be applied as a plug-in to further improve decision efficiency on top of existing acceleration techniques. We validated Falcon in 48 simulated environments and 2 real-world robot experiments. demonstrating a 2-7x speedup with negligible performance degradation, offering a promising direction for efficient visuomotor policy design.

arxiv_record.abstract: Exploration is a cornerstone of reinforcement learning (RL). Intrinsic motivation attempts to decouple exploration from external, task-based rewards. However, established approaches to intrinsic motivation that follow general principles such as information gain, often only uncover low-level interactions. In contrast, children's play suggests that they engage in meaningful high-level behavior by imitating or interacting with their caregivers. Recent work has focused on using foundation models to inject these semantic biases into exploration. However, these methods often rely on unrealistic assumptions, such as language-embedded environments or access to high-level actions. We propose SEmaNtically Sensible ExploratIon (SENSEI), a framework to equip model-based RL agents with an intrinsic motivation for semantically meaningful behavior. SENSEI distills a reward signal of interestingness from Vision Language Model (VLM) annotations, enabling an agent to predict these rewards through a world model. Using model-based RL, SENSEI trains an exploration policy that jointly maximizes semantic rewards and uncertainty. We show that in both robotic and video game-like simulations SENSEI discovers a variety of meaningful behaviors from image observations and low-level actions. SENSEI provides a general tool for learning from foundation model feedback, a crucial research direction, as VLMs become more powerful.

C1.justification: The abstract and three introductory contributions retain their meaning. V2 extends the concluding account to Pokémon and changes iterative reward refinement from a future possibility into a claimed demonstrated reduction of out-of-distribution errors. It also removes the introduction's blanket assertion that prior approaches fail to transfer knowledge to novel states.

C2.justification: Beyond v1's occlusion and initial-data limitations, v2 explains how unseen regions undermine semantic rewards and leave exploration dependent on uncertainty. It interprets Pokémon behavior as influenced by the Brock-specific prompt, favoring Squirtle training over collection diversity, and explains refinement as correcting that distributional limitation. These materially expand the account of applicability and behavioral tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly provides a code-and-VLM-MOTIF-checkpoint link and documents Pokémon implementation details, including PokeGym version, observations, actions, frame skipping, reward modifications, starting checkpoint, hyperparameters, and annotation prompts. It also specifies the additional annotation data and continuation procedure. Most existing implementation and computational-cost disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: V2 adds Pokémon Red, covering navigation, battles, Pokémon collection, and progress toward the first Gym. It retains MiniHack and Robodesk and adds the half-open-drawer task used in Robodesk downstream evaluation. This substantially broadens the evaluated environments and task requirements.

E2.justification: The original comparison sets are retained. V2 adds a from-scratch DreamerV3 control for Robodesk block-pushing (Figure 22) and evaluates a task-reward-augmented Plan2Explore comparator in Pokémon Red. These are limited extensions of existing comparator families.

E3.justification: New protocols include 750k-step Pokémon comparisons with extrinsic rewards, a large RSSM, scheduled episode lengths, and map/battle metrics. Robodesk downstream evaluation uses models pretrained through 1M exploration steps. The refinement study adds 50k annotated pairs and 200 continuation episodes with original-reward and longer-running Plan2Explore controls. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: V2 retains the original ablations and adds substantial Pokémon analyses: exploration allocation across catching, leveling, and navigation (E.8), concrete reward failures in unseen locations, and a controlled continuation examining reward refinement versus longer training (E.9; Figures 26–27). These investigate additional mechanisms and failure conditions.

E5.justification: V2 adds explicit five-seed reporting for Pokémon and ten-seed reporting for Robodesk downstream learning. It also identifies the refinement demonstration as one continued SENSEI seed with a selected Plan2Explore seed, without aggregate uncertainty. Existing experiments retain their seed counts and standard-error or standard-deviation conventions; no increased replication of those experiments is established.

E6.justification: V2 adds Robodesk learning curves showing faster learning with SENSEI-pretrained models, with incomplete success on Lift-Ball (Figure 21). Pokémon results show stronger navigation and leveling, but greater catching diversity for Plan2Explore. The single-seed refinement study reports two Gym victories, first occurring around 1.8M steps. These are new results under added settings, not improvements to the retained MiniHack or Robodesk exploration scores.

M1.justification: V2 substantially extends the fixed, task-free pipeline with task-conditioned VLM comparisons and extrinsic-reward integration (Section 4.4; Appendices A.1 and D.4). It also implements a second annotation and distillation round using SENSEI-collected observations (E.9), which v1 only suggested as future work. The underlying RSSM, distillation architecture, and switching mechanism remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 locally condenses the introduction, related work, captions, and discussion while retaining most existing prose and the main section sequence. Prompting becomes Appendix D, extended results move to E, and computation becomes F. These are limited editorial and organizational changes alongside the added scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation with Pokémon maps, screenshots, progress plots, distributions, refinement comparisons, and Robodesk downstream curves. Figure 4 gains a Pokémon trajectory, Figure 7 becomes narrower, the hyperparameter table gains a Pokémon column, and the previously separate left-camera illustration is merged into Figure 9. Existing analyses are also relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds Pokémon-related references to Pleines et al., Suarez, and Whidden, and positions its screen-only observations against previous Pokémon agents (C.3). It narrows the introductory criticism of prior methods' transfer capabilities. The broader positioning relative to MOTIF, Plan2Explore, and RL-VLM-F remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 revises the mathematical reward definition in Equation 8 by adding an extrinsic-reward term controlled by chi, distinguishing task-free and task-based exploration. The existing dynamics and switching equations remain unchanged; neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important evidential gap: downstream usefulness, previously demonstrated only in MiniHack, is now tested across robotic tasks with ten-seed results (Figure 21). Pokémon evaluations and explicit reward-failure analyses further strengthen understanding of the method's capabilities and limits, alongside improved reproducibility documentation. The goal-specific Pokémon prompt and single-seed refinement success constrain generalization, but the broader controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SENSEI research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and reports additional Pokémon Red evaluations, Robodesk downstream learning, and second-generation reward-refinement results.

before.justification: V1 reports original MiniHack and Robodesk experiments, downstream task learning, and ablations of semantic rewards, annotation sources, and exploration weighting.

arxiv_record.abstract: Crystal symmetry plays a fundamental role in determining its physical, chemical, and electronic properties such as electrical and thermal conductivity, optical and polarization behavior, and mechanical strength. Almost all known crystalline materials have internal symmetry. However, this is often inadequately addressed by existing generative models, making the consistent generation of stable and symmetrically valid crystal structures a significant challenge. We introduce WyFormer, a generative model that directly tackles this by formally conditioning on space group symmetry. It achieves this by using Wyckoff positions as the basis for an elegant, compressed, and discrete structure representation. To model the distribution, we develop a permutation-invariant autoregressive model based on the Transformer encoder and an absence of positional encoding. Extensive experimentation demonstrates WyFormer's compelling combination of attributes: it achieves best-in-class symmetry-conditioned generation, incorporates a physics-motivated inductive bias, produces structures with competitive stability, predicts material properties with competitive accuracy even without atomic coordinates, and exhibits unparalleled inference speed.

arxiv_record.abstract: Calculating or accurately estimating log-determinants of large positive definite matrices is of fundamental importance in many machine learning tasks. While its cubic computational complexity can already be prohibitive, in modern applications, even storing the matrices themselves can pose a memory bottleneck. To address this, we derive a novel hierarchical algorithm based on block-wise computation of the LDL decomposition for large-scale log-determinant calculation in memory-constrained settings. In extreme cases where matrices are highly ill-conditioned, accurately computing the full matrix itself may be infeasible. This is particularly relevant when considering kernel matrices at scale, including the empirical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) of neural networks trained on large datasets. Under the assumption of neural scaling laws in the test error, we show that the ratio of pseudo-determinants satisfies a power-law relationship, allowing us to derive corresponding scaling laws. This enables accurate estimation of NTK log-determinants from a tiny fraction of the full dataset; in our experiments, this results in a $\sim$100,000$\times$ speedup with improved accuracy over competing approximations. Using these techniques, we successfully estimate log-determinants for dense matrices of extreme sizes, which were previously deemed intractable and inaccessible due to their enormous scale and computational demands.
arxiv_record.authors: Siavash Ameli, Chris van der Heide, Liam Hodgkinson, Fred Roosta, Michael W. Mahoney
arxiv_record.title: Determinant Estimation under Memory Constraints and Neural Scaling Laws

C1.justification: The abstract's opening problem statement narrows from positive semidefinite to positive definite matrices. The principal contributions—memory-constrained determinant computation, determinant scaling laws, FLODANCE extrapolation, and the approximately 100,000-fold speedup claim—remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: New discussion interprets numerical discrepancies as arising from input-matrix precision, explains the fitting-window cost/accuracy tradeoff, and discusses robustness and applicability beyond NTKs. The earlier assertion that large-scale double-precision computation is infeasible is replaced by a reported feasible computation. Existing burn-in and numerical-conditioning caveats remain.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 substantially clarifies the precision pipeline: 32-bit network training, separate NTK formation/storage precisions, and 64-bit determinant calculations across methods. v2 also documents the GH200 computation and its 244-hour duration, Matérn construction parameters, and how LDL permutations and diagonal outputs feed FLODANCE. Existing detkit and imate access information is retained.

E1.justification: Appendix G.2 adds one synthetic spatial Gaussian-process setting using a multi-output Matérn kernel: 10,000 two-dimensional locations with ten outputs each. Existing CIFAR-10 and MNIST coverage remains. This extends evaluation beyond neural kernels without changing the determinant-estimation task.

E2.justification: New Appendix E.5 explicitly evaluates MEMDET against NumPy's slogdet and eigh, including Table E.4 and Figure E.4. The main approximation comparator set—SLQ, block diagonal, pseudo-NTK, and direct computations at different precisions—is retained.

E3.justification: Section 4.2 replaces the stated 32-bit large-scale NTK reference with 64-bit matrices. Table 2 changes from normalized log-determinant estimates to percentage relative errors with unnormalized reference values. Added experiments introduce random-subsampling, fitting-window, block-count, and Matérn-kernel protocols; the newly disclosed precision pipeline is separately a documentation change.

E4.justification: v2 adds numerical agreement and block-count stability checks for MEMDET in Appendix E.5, plus FLODANCE sensitivity to random subsampling and fitting-window size in Figures G.2–G.3. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's runtime/memory analysis and global-fit demonstration. The latter is retained as Figure G.1 from v1 Figure H.1.

E5.justification: Figure G.2 introduces uncertainty analysis across 15 independent subsamples, reporting ensemble means, standard deviations, normalized standard deviations, and prediction-error variability. Existing reporting across five trained networks and ten profiling repetitions remains; these counts are not reported as increased.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces numerical results and changes rankings: pseudo-NTK is closest for ResNet18 in v1, whereas v2 reports 122.95% error for pseudo-NTK and 2.9% for the best FLODANCE configuration. Figure 5's ResNet9 endpoint error changes from 0.05% to 0.2% alongside the reference-precision change, so this is not a same-setting deterioration. Table 1 revises MEMDET from 8.8 days/$364 to 13.8 days/$601. Additional accuracy, sensitivity, Matérn, and runtime results are reported.

M1.justification: FLODANCE Algorithm 1 and MEMDET's LU, LDL, and Cholesky algorithms retain their computational steps; Algorithms C.1–C.3 become D.1–D.3. Expanded precision and permutation explanations and application to another kernel do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and argument remain intact, with targeted introductory, notation, derivation, and implementation rewrites. Appendices are consolidated: MEMDET implementation and ordering are grouped in D, and scaling-law background, proofs, and parameterization in F. A nomenclature section and expanded appendix roadmap improve navigation.

P2.justification: v2 adds notation, accuracy, complexity, and runtime tables, together with new numerical-stability, sensitivity, and Matérn figures. Table 2 is restructured around relative errors, and Figure 5 has revised curves, axes, and precision labeling. The earlier global-fit figure moves from H.1 to G.1 with updated plots; existing algorithm diagrams are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds NTK-related references including Hodgkinson et al. (2025) and Wilson et al. (2025), and spatial-statistics references supporting the Matérn experiment. The numerical-linear-algebra positioning remains largely unchanged. Publication updates for existing works, such as Bahri et al. and Barzilai and Shamir, are not new citations.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 corrects the covariance kernel's codomain from scalar to matrix-valued, and the Lemma 1 proof corrects the cross-covariance block dimension to (n−1)d by d. Table H.1 adds comparative complexity formulas. The central assumptions, lemma, LLN/CLT proposition, and substantive proof arguments remain.

improvement.justification: v1's flagship large-scale experiment used 32-bit matrices despite emphasizing precision problems. v2 supplies 64-bit references and independent numerical checks, addressing an important weakness in the accuracy evidence. Subsampling and fitting-window tests, non-neural kernel evaluation, and clearer precision documentation substantially strengthen reliability and applicability. Some new summaries overstate their evidence—for example, Appendix E.5's stated error range excludes the 1.7×10−6 MobileNet entry in Table E.4—but these reporting defects do not outweigh the validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MEMDET and FLODANCE research. All 30 pages of v1 and 38 pages of v2, including appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison. Relocated algorithms, proofs, and analyses can be matched.

after.justification: v2 retains original NTK experiments and adds numerical accuracy checks, subsampling and fitting-window analyses, Matérn-kernel experiments, and runtime comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original NTK determinant experiments on CIFAR-10 and MNIST, approximation comparisons, and empirical memory and runtime measurements in Appendix E.

arxiv_record.abstract: We perform Bayesian optimization using a Gaussian process perspective on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART). Our BART Kernel (BARK) uses tree agreement to define a posterior over piecewise-constant functions, and we explore the space of tree kernels using a Markov chain Monte Carlo approach. Where BART only samples functions, the resulting BARK model obtains samples of Gaussian processes defining distributions over functions, which allow us to build acquisition functions for Bayesian optimization. Our tree-based approach enables global optimization over the surrogate, even for mixed-feature spaces. Moreover, where many previous tree-based kernels provide uncertainty quantification over function values, our sampling scheme captures uncertainty over the tree structure itself. Our experiments show the strong performance of BARK on both synthetic and applied benchmarks, due to the combination of our fully Bayesian surrogate and the optimization procedure.
arxiv_record.authors: Toby Boyne, Jose Pablo Folch, Robert M Lee, Behrang Shafei, Ruth Misener
arxiv_record.comments: 9 main pages, 28 total pages, 14 figures, 9 tables

E2.justification: v2 adds GP-RBF to the retained four-dataset regression comparison through Table 7 and compares alternating and enumerated GP-RBF variants together on XGBoostMNIST in Figure 6. The other main BO comparator families remain.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds diagnostic experiments examining nonstationary function modeling and predictions for unseen categories. Section 7.4 and Appendix F.2 substantially extend the earlier posterior-sampling timing comparison to BO fitting and optimization costs across methods and benchmarks. P2.justification: v2 adds substantial displays: toy-regression and continuous-BO figures, runtime panels, a related-work matrix, a parameter-summary table and a GP-RBF regression table. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent research has shown an increasing interest in utilizing pre-trained large language models (LLMs) for a variety of time series applications. However, there are three main challenges when using LLMs as foundational models for time series forecasting: (1) Cross-domain generalization. (2) Cross-modality alignment. (3) Error accumulation in autoregressive frameworks. To address these challenges, we proposed LangTime, a language-guided unified model for time series forecasting that incorporates cross-domain pre-training with reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning. Specifically, LangTime constructs Temporal Comprehension Prompts (TCPs), which include dataset-wise and channel-wise instructions, to facilitate domain adaptation and condense time series into a single token, enabling LLMs to understand better and align temporal data. To improve autoregressive forecasting, we introduce TimePPO, a reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning algorithm. TimePPO mitigates error accumulation by leveraging a multidimensional rewards function tailored for time series and a repeat-based value estimation strategy. C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: language-guided cross-domain forecasting, TCP-based alignment, TimePPO mitigation of autoregressive error, and strong benchmark and zero-shot performance. Added evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation: it links final-step accuracy to sequence-wide return optimization, attributes GPT-2's shortfall to instruction following, and explains output-length and masking trade-offs. It also argues for applicability with limited fine-tuning data and TE-only updates. These mechanism and applicability discussions were absent from v1.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 supplies exact instruction and background paraphrases for the new prompt tests. Figure 8 newly discloses attention softmax renormalization after hiding system and special tokens, and Table 1 changes the source attribution for borrowed results from TimesNet to iTransformer. Existing hardware, optimizer, principal hyperparameters, and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: The same nine datasets remain represented. Appendix C.1 extends zero-shot evaluation beyond Traffic and Illness to held-out Weather, Electricity, and ETT targets. This broadens the tested domain-transfer scenarios without introducing a new dataset family.

E2.justification: v2 adds TimesFM as an evaluated external comparator in Table 14. The comparator sets in the original main benchmark and Traffic/Illness zero-shot comparison remain unchanged. iTransformer becomes a cited source of baseline results, rather than an additional evaluated method.

E3.justification: The original benchmark settings remain, but v2 adds restricted-source pre-training protocols, backbone and prompt controls, final-segment error metrics, 5–20% fine-tuning data conditions, component-freezing experiments, and mask-rate/output-length grids. These substantially extend evaluation design. One new transfer protocol is inconsistently documented: Appendix C.1 names ETTh2, whereas Table 13 labels ETTm2.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained TCP/reward ablations and alpha/tau analyses, v2 tests GPT-2 and linear backbones, prompt paraphrases, beta/eta sensitivity, and final-step error accumulation. Appendix C adds transfer analyses, fine-tuning data-volume and component controls, and joint masking/output-length sensitivity. These address several previously untested questions about mechanism, robustness, and adaptability.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty intervals. Reported averages aggregate forecasting horizons; the additional experiments do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical evidence in Tables 5–6, 8, and 13–17 and Figure 6. Original benchmark scores and retained appendix results are unchanged. Table 1 revises several win counts: fine-tuned LangTime changes from 49 in v1's table and 50 in its accompanying prose to 45 in both locations in v2.

M1.justification: The architecture, TCPs, and repeat-based TimePPO procedure remain. However, Equation (8) changes the maximized objective from adding a squared-error term to subtracting the Huber prediction loss. This substantively revises the stated alignment penalty, although the PDFs do not establish whether implementation or training runs changed.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the introduction and model-analysis explanations, expanded captions, and new acknowledgements and an impact statement. Appendix B gains ablation details, while new Appendix C subsections precede the retained full results and cases. The original narrative and main section order largely remain.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to separate temporal extraction, multitask pre-training, and TimePPO fine-tuning. v2 adds nine tables and a beta/eta sensitivity figure, expands explanatory captions, and rearranges the experimental displays. Existing detailed result tables and forecasting cases are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for TimesFM, Chronos, GPT-2, linear forecasting, iTransformer, and additional forecasting research. Appendix C.1 adds positioning against large-scale time-series foundation models. Section 2's central account of prior alignment methods and RLHF remains essentially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 corrects the small-error branches of both Huber definitions by restoring squared residuals in Equations (9)–(10). Equation (8) also corrects the penalty direction under maximization. These are limited mathematical corrections; no new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee appears.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the roles of the LLM backbone and TimePPO through backbone controls, final-step error evaluation, and additional transfer and fine-tuning studies absent from v1. These gains outweigh the new ETTh2/ETTm2 labeling inconsistency, although neither version quantifies run-to-run uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LangTime and TimePPO. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–C support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds backbone controls, prompt-variation experiments, error analyses, transfer comparisons, and fine-tuning sensitivity studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Multimodal data is a precious asset enabling a variety of downstream tasks in machine learning. However, real-world data collected across different modalities is often not paired, which is a significant challenge to learn a joint distribution. A prominent approach to address the modality coupling problem is Minimum Entropy Coupling (MEC), which seeks to minimize the joint Entropy, while satisfying constraints on the marginals. Existing approaches to the MEC problem focus on finite, discrete distributions, limiting their application for cases involving continuous data. In this work, we propose a novel method to solve the continuous MEC problem, using well-known generative diffusion models that learn to approximate and minimize the joint Entropy through a cooperative scheme, while satisfying a relaxed version of the marginal constraints. We empirically demonstrate that our method, DDMEC, is general and can be easily used to address challenging tasks, including unsupervised single-cell multi-omics data alignment and unpaired image translation, outperforming specialized methods.
arxiv_record.authors: Mustapha Bounoua, Giulio Franzese, Pietro Michiardi
arxiv_record.title: Learning to Match Unpaired Data with Minimum Entropy Coupling

arxiv_record.abstract: Cascade Ranking is a prevalent architecture in large-scale top-k selection systems like recommendation and advertising platforms. Traditional training methods focus on single-stage optimization, neglecting interactions between stages. Recent advances have introduced interaction-aware training paradigms, but still struggle to 1) align training objectives with the goal of the entire cascade ranking (i.e., end-to-end recall of ground-truth items) and 2) learn effective collaboration patterns for different stages. To address these challenges, we propose LCRON, which introduces a novel surrogate loss function derived from the lower bound probability that ground truth items are selected by cascade ranking, ensuring alignment with the overall objective of the system. According to the properties of the derived bound, we further design an auxiliary loss for each stage to drive the reduction of this bound, leading to a more robust and effective top-k selection. LCRON enables end-to-end training of the entire cascade ranking system as a unified network. Experimental results demonstrate that LCRON achieves significant improvement over existing methods on public benchmarks and industrial applications, addressing key limitations in cascade ranking training and significantly enhancing system performance.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a LCRON-specific source-code link, baseline implementation provenance, TF-Ranking adaptation details, explicit hyperparameter search grids, and A800 runtime and memory information. E1.justification: Both versions use RecFlow Period 1 and industrial advertising data. Appendix C.2 adds coverage of rerank_neg and rerank_pos samples, using rerank_pos as ground truth for three-stage evaluation. This extends the evaluated selection task within the existing dataset and domain.

E2.justification: Table 7 adds standalone NeuralSort and SoftSort training as evaluated comparators. The main and industrial comparator rosters remain unchanged. ARF-v2's documented definition also inherits the revised Lsingle objective.

E3.justification: V2 adds three-stage DSSM/MLP/DIN evaluation, sorting-operator controls, four learning-rate/batch-size configurations, and GPU profiling. E5.justification: V1 reports five-run means, standard deviations, and t-tests for the ablation table only. V2 extends this reporting to the main comparison and three-stage experiment, and reports five-run means and standard deviations for sorting comparisons. E6.justification: Table 2 updates baseline estimates, including FS-LambdaLoss joint Recall from 0.8674 to 0.8666, while LCRON's joint 0.8732 and industrial results remain. Single-stage metric assignments change: LCRON ranking Recall/NDCG becomes 0.8729/0.7291 instead of 0.7291/0.8729, so this is not evidence of performance improvement. New results include three-stage joint Recall of 0.7390, operator and training sensitivity, resource measurements, and quota-aligned Recall of 0.8714±0.0008.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused comparisons with FAA and SRCR, discusses optimal-transport sorting, revises ICC and ARF positioning, and connects future work to multi-task and meta-learning. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable advancements in enabling language agents to tackle simple tasks. However, applying them for complex, multi-step, long-horizon tasks remains a challenge. Recent work have found success by separating high-level planning from low-level execution, which enables the model to effectively balance high-level planning objectives and low-level execution details. However, generating accurate plans remains difficult since LLMs are not inherently trained for this task. To address this, we propose Plan-and-Act, a novel framework that incorporates explicit planning into LLM-based agents and introduces a scalable method to enhance plan generation through a novel synthetic data generation method. Plan-and-Act consists of a Planner model which generates structured, high-level plans to achieve user goals, and an Executor model that translates these plans into environment-specific actions. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce a synthetic data generation method that annotates ground-truth trajectories with feasible plans, augmented with diverse and extensive examples to enhance generalization. We evaluate Plan-and-Act using web navigation as a representative long-horizon planning environment, demonstrating a state-of-the-art 57.58% success rate on the WebArena-Lite benchmark as well as a text-only state-of-the-art 81.36% success rate on WebVoyager.
arxiv_record.authors: Lutfi Eren Erdogan, Nicholas Lee, Sehoon Kim, Suhong Moon, Hiroki Furuta, Gopala Anumanchipalli, Kurt Keutzer, Amir Gholami
