C1.justification: The abstract expands the headline empirical claim from approximately 54% success on WebArena-Lite to 57.58% there and a text-only state-of-the-art 81.36% on WebVoyager, extending claimed success to real-world web tasks. The architectural and synthetic-data contributions remain. The introduction's 53.94% contribution bullet and conclusion are not fully updated.

C2.justification: A new Limitations section identifies dependence on a capable trajectory-collection model when training data are unavailable and the efficiency cost of replanning after every action. Section 5.3.2 also interprets the smaller-model comparison as evidence for CoT's importance. Earlier interpretations concerning plan quality, overfitting and dynamic content remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.12/Figure 5 supplies previously absent training and inference specifications, including learning rate, optimizer, batch size, epochs, 8×A100 hardware, software frameworks and decoding limits. Section 5.1 identifies the CoT teacher and specifies five seed examples per ten generated examples; Section 5.5 documents WebVoyager collection and annotation models. These materially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only WebArena-Lite's simulated web tasks. v3 additionally trains and evaluates on WebVoyager's dynamic, real-world websites (Section 5.5), substantially extending the represented data and environmental conditions.

E2.justification: Within WebArena-Lite, Table 1 adds GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o, AWM + GPT-4-0613 and WebPilot + GPT-4o to the retained comparisons. Tables 3–4 additionally include NNetNav, AutoWebGLM, AgentOccam variants, OpenWebVoyager, WebVoyager variants, Wilbur and Agent-E. These are reported numerical comparisons, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: v3 adds full-WebArena evaluation and 8B/32B model configurations alongside the original 70B experiments. The new WebVoyager training setup uses 1,500 synthetic trajectories and 10,000 synthetic plans. Appendix A.11 adds step-count metrics separated by success/failure. The original WebArena-Lite settings remain; newly disclosed hyperparameters do not establish changes to those settings.

E4.justification: Tables 1–2 add a focused CoT comparison and examine whether smaller CoT models approach the non-CoT 70B model. Appendix A.11 adds website-level success rates and action-length analysis by outcome. The earlier augmentation ablations, replanning examples and failure classifications are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random-seed information, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3 continues point-estimate reporting; its additional average step counts do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All original Table 1 scores remain, including 53.94% for dynamic replanning. v3 adds 57.58% for the CoT variant, smaller-model results, and new benchmark results, including QWQ-32B's 48.15% on WebArena and 81.36% on WebVoyager. Appendix A.11 adds website and step-count results. Section 5.3.2's stated 4.36% CoT gain conflicts with Table 1's 3.64-percentage-point difference.

M1.justification: Sections 3.4 and 4.2.2 add a CoT training/inference extension, including teacher-generated action rationales and reasoning before plans/actions. The two-agent architecture, grounded-plan generation and dynamic replanning remain intact. v1 already included planner Reasoning fields in its appendix; the extension particularly changes executor reasoning and its supervision.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and Appendix A.1–A.10 remain unchanged. v3 inserts CoT subsections, additional benchmark sections, limitations and two appendix sections while preserving the original narrative sequence. Wording and cross-reference edits are limited rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds a first-page system overview, expands Table 1 with baseline and CoT rows, and introduces Tables 2–4. Appendix figures 4–5 present website statistics and training/inference settings as tables. The original two diagrams are retained as Figures 2–3. These additions substantially expand the visual presentation beyond renumbering and pagination.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 substantially expands positioning against hierarchical planning methods, including AgentOccam, WebPilot, AdaPlanner and ADaPT, and discusses complementary trajectory-generation approaches and robotic planners. It explicitly distinguishes the work through trainable models, architectural simplicity and synthetic planning data. Additional references support the CoT extension and new benchmarks.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical assumptions, theorems, proofs or mathematical derivations. The added CoT material concerns an empirical training and inference procedure.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation through full-WebArena and real-world WebVoyager experiments, while Appendix A.12 fills important reproducibility gaps. Expanded comparisons and explicit limitations also make the contribution easier to assess. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including the incorrect CoT-gain arithmetic and the conclusion's outdated treatment of executor CoT as future work. Sparse evaluation details for the new benchmarks and absent uncertainty estimates still limit confidence in the strongest performance claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same PLAN-AND-ACT study. Their text, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison. Appendix A.1–A.10 is retained unchanged; v3 adds A.11–A.12.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original CoT and model-size results, WebArena and WebVoyager evaluations, and website-level performance analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original WebArena-Lite experiments comparing planner/executor configurations, synthetic-data augmentation and dynamic replanning, particularly in Table 1.

arxiv_record.abstract: Current Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding multimodal data, but their potential remains underexplored for deepfake detection due to the misalignment of their knowledge and forensics patterns. To this end, we present a novel framework that unlocks LVLMs' potential capabilities for deepfake detection. Our framework includes a Knowledge-guided Forgery Detector (KFD), a Forgery Prompt Learner (FPL), and a Large Language Model (LLM). The KFD is used to calculate correlations between image features and pristine/deepfake image description embeddings, enabling forgery classification and localization. The outputs of the KFD are subsequently processed by the Forgery Prompt Learner to construct fine-grained forgery prompt embeddings. These embeddings, along with visual and question prompt embeddings, are fed into the LLM to generate textual detection responses. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks, including FF++, CDF2, DFD, DFDCP, DFDC, and DF40, demonstrate that our scheme surpasses state-of-the-art methods in generalization performance, while also supporting multi-turn dialogue capabilities.
arxiv_record.authors: Peipeng Yu, Jianwei Fei, Hui Gao, Xuan Feng, Zhihua Xia, Chip Hong Chang
arxiv_record.title: Unlocking the Capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models for Generalizable and Explainable Deepfake Detection

C1.justification: Both versions claim that knowledge-guided visual-text alignment and forgery prompts enable generalizable, explainable detection with multi-turn dialogue. The rewritten abstract and added DF40 evidence preserve these core contributions and the broad superiority claim.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 newly attributes detection failures to the mismatch between general VQA training and localized forgery reasoning, acknowledging that accurate localization can coexist with wrong textual judgments. Appendix A.3 also discusses increased inference cost relative to CADDM and FAK-Owl. These introduce substantive qualifications to v1's largely unqualified accuracy and explainability narrative.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 supplies description strings and their GPT-4/human-validation provenance, batch sizes, LoRA target modules, rank, alpha and dropout, plus frame sampling, response parsing and video-score aggregation. V2 also specifies the localization-loss weight and low-data training budget. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's backbone, optimizer, hardware and epoch details.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on 15 DF40 manipulation methods spanning face swapping, reenactment and entire-face synthesis, including GAN and diffusion generators. Appendix A.2 also introduces six corrupted FF++ input scenarios. These substantially extend the manipulation and input-condition coverage beyond v1's retained datasets.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CFM, ED, ProDet, RepDFD and UDD. The corresponding LVLM comparison also adds RepDFD and UDD, substantially broadening the competitive comparison. V1's P-Tuning row becomes Clipping with the same cited work and scores; this is a rename rather than an additional baseline.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs include controlled training with and without reference optimization, six FF++ perturbation conditions, and per-frame inference timing on one RTX 4090. Existing main training settings remain unchanged. The 500-step budget for low-data experiments and 32-frame LLM aggregation are newly specified; the PDFs do not establish that these disclosures represent changed earlier procedures.

E4.justification: V2 adds a direct test of reference optimization in Table 8, corruption robustness in Table 9, and failure cases where correct localization accompanies incorrect LLM judgments in Figure 6. It also supplies previously absent multi-turn conversation examples. The prompt-tuning, training-dataset and LLM-architecture ablations are retained, while the low-data analysis is revised.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains the original KFD scores, but added baselines change rankings: its DFDC AUC of 79.12 is now below UDD's 81.21. FAK-Owl's CDF2 AUC changes from 73.51 to 60.85 between v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3. The low-data table has replaced values and dataset columns, with a newly disclosed budget. DF40, robustness, reference-ablation, timing and qualitative results are also added.

M1.justification: Section 3.1 and Figure 3 revise the documented text-conditioning procedure: v1 places learnable context before the text encoder, whereas v2 concatenates learnable embeddings with encoded description features. The overall KFD–FPL–LLM pipeline and losses remain unchanged. LoRA was already used in v1's ablation experiments.

P1.justification: The abstract and introductory motivation are revised around LVLM–forensics misalignment, terminology and comparison prose are clarified, and publication details and acknowledgements are added. The placeholder appendix becomes organized subsections. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and analysis prose are retained.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the framework and KFD diagrams, removes the standalone FPL architecture diagram and detailed detector-branch schematics, enlarges the retained GradCAM display, and expands localization panels. It restructures the LVLM comparison into classifier/VQA blocks and adds experimental tables, failure illustrations and extensive dialogue screenshots.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for recent comparison methods, ImageBind, DF40 and GenFace, while removing several background citations with the revised introduction. The related-work discussion and positioning around external knowledge and fine-grained forgery prompts remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same similarity calculations, losses and image-blending formulation. Renaming consistency maps from C to rho does not change the mathematics. Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs, and v2 adds none.

improvement.justification: V2 resolves important deficiencies in v1's evidence and reproducibility: the placeholder appendix becomes substantive implementation documentation and actual dialogue examples, while new component and robustness tests strengthen validation. Explicit failure analysis also qualifies the explainability claim. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including Table 10's CDF2 label with CDF1-matching AUC values and superiority language broader than the expanded Table 1 supports.

arxiv_record.abstract: Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) has achieved notable success in continuous control tasks but struggles in sparse reward settings, where infrequent rewards make efficient exploration challenging. While novelty-based exploration methods address this issue by encouraging the agent to explore novel states, they are not trivial to apply to SAC. In particular, managing the interaction between novelty-based exploration and SAC's stochastic policy can lead to inefficient exploration and redundant sample collection. In this paper, we propose KEA (Keeping Exploration Alive) which tackles the inefficiencies in balancing exploration strategies when combining SAC with novelty-based exploration. KEA integrates a novelty-augmented SAC with a standard SAC agent, proactively coordinated via a switching mechanism. This coordination allows the agent to maintain stochasticity in high-novelty regions, enhancing exploration efficiency and reducing repeated sample collection. We first analyze this potential issue in a 2D navigation task, and then evaluate KEA on the DeepSea hard-exploration benchmark as well as sparse reward control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite. Compared to state-of-the-art novelty-based exploration baselines, our experiments show that KEA significantly improves learning efficiency and robustness in sparse reward setups.

C2.justification: V2 Appendix A interprets its derived revisit count as explaining delayed exploration and asserts relevance to longer-horizon tasks. Section 3.4 adds interpretation of performance as DeepSea depth increases. The existing explanation of effectiveness across SAC/SQL, DQN-P, and DQN, and the off-policy-only limitation, remain.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Appendix B newly document update sequencing, network architectures, optimizer settings, learning rates, replay buffers, reward processing, and task-specific hyperparameters. Appendix D supplies navigation grid dimensions, obstacle geometry, termination conditions, and episode limits. E1.justification: V2 adds DeepSea at sizes 10, 14, 20, 24, and 30, introducing sequential exploration with deceptive movement penalties and a sparse terminal reward. The existing 2D navigation task and three DeepMind Control Suite tasks remain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds comparisons against DeRL-A2C, DeRL-PPO, DeRL-DQN, SOFE-A2C, SOFE-PPO, and SOFE-DQN. These introduce two substantial baseline families. Comparator membership in the retained navigation, continuous-control, and DQN/SQL experiments is unchanged after matching renamed methods.

E3.justification: DeepSea introduces a protocol of 100,000 training episodes, evaluation every 1,000 episodes, and averaging across 100 test episodes. Separately, v1 Appendix A states 8/16/32/48 SAC updates per transition, whereas v2 Appendix C states per 32 transitions. This materially revises the reported update schedule without establishing that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The threshold sensitivity results, off-policy diagnostics, UTD analysis, and best/worst-seed exploration visualizations are retained in Table 2 and Figures 4, 7, and 8. The empirical appendix moves from A to C. DeepSea adds benchmark evidence; the UTD denominator correction changes the reported protocol rather than adding a new diagnostic analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report five random seeds and means with standard deviations, including shaded uncertainty bands. V2 applies the same reporting practice to DeepSea; it does not introduce additional seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: V2 adds the DeepSea result matrix. At size 30, KEA-RND-SAC reports 0.54 ± 0.32, versus 0.35 ± 0.44 for RND-SAC and 0.42 ± 0.33 for SOFE-DQN. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 under identical settings. Existing navigation, threshold, and continuous-control table values are unchanged.

M1.justification: The two-agent framework, shared replay buffer, reward objectives, and novelty-threshold switching rule are retained. A-SAC/A-B become A-N/A-S. arxiv_record.abstract: World models aim to learn action-controlled future prediction and have proven essential for the development of intelligent agents. However, most existing world models rely heavily on substantial action-labeled data and costly training, making it challenging to adapt to novel environments with heterogeneous actions through limited interactions. This limitation can hinder their applicability across broader domains. To overcome this limitation, we propose AdaWorld, an innovative world model learning approach that enables efficient adaptation. The key idea is to incorporate action information during the pretraining of world models. This is achieved by extracting latent actions from videos in a self-supervised manner, capturing the most critical transitions between frames. We then develop an autoregressive world model that conditions on these latent actions. This learning paradigm enables highly adaptable world models, facilitating efficient transfer and learning of new actions even with limited interactions and finetuning. Our comprehensive experiments across multiple environments demonstrate that AdaWorld achieves superior performance in both simulation quality and visual planning.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central claims: action-aware pretraining enables transferable latent actions, efficient adaptation, and improved simulation and planning. The added experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the iVideoGPT experiment as evidence of applicability across architectures and explains UMAP noise through actions that cannot execute in particular states. It also acknowledges that Flat block and Open drawer produce no meaningful scores under constrained adaptation and omits them from Table 4. The original limitations and failure-case discussion remain.

D1.justification: V2 discloses 300-sample validation sets, a two-layer continuous-action MLP trained for 3,000 steps, and its runtime. New Appendices B.5–B.6 document robot trajectory counts, adaptation hyperparameters, and iVideoGPT checkpoint and frozen-tokenizer choices. These targeted additions supplement unchanged core architecture, pretraining, sampling, and project-access information.

E1.justification: V2 adds nuScenes continuous-action driving simulation, VP2 robot planning with Robosuite and RoboDesk, and BAIR robot-pushing evaluation. These substantially broaden evaluation beyond the retained action-transfer, discrete-action simulation, and game-planning tasks. The original pretraining data mixture remains unchanged.

E2.justification: V2 Table 6 newly evaluates iVideoGPT against an action-aware iVideoGPT variant. The original action-agnostic, optical-flow, discrete-latent-action, and game-planning comparator sets remain intact; extending existing comparators to nuScenes does not itself change their membership.

E3.justification: New protocols include four volunteers judging 50 video pairs per action-transfer dataset, continuous-control adaptation, and MPPI robot planning using a low-resolution model with 1,000 adaptation steps. Appendix B.6 adds 27,000 continuation-pretraining steps, 1,000 BAIR finetuning steps, and evaluation on 256 videos. The existing discrete-simulation and Procgen protocols are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a backbone-generality test using iVideoGPT and a UMAP analysis comparing beta values of 0.0002 and 0.00002. It also extends initialization and adaptation-efficiency analyses to nuScenes. These address architecture dependence and latent-action disentanglement beyond the retained data-diversity, clustering, and failure-case analyses.

E5.justification: V2 newly specifies four runs per VP2 task with standard errors. Procgen retains the stated five-seed, standard-error reporting protocol. Its changed error values do not establish additional runs or a changed estimator and are assessed under E6.

E6.justification: V2 adds human transfer scores, nuScenes results, VP2 planning outcomes, and BAIR comparisons. Examples include AdaWorld's human success rates of 70.5% on LIBERO and 61.5% on SSv2, and BAIR PSNR/LPIPS of 17.40/0.204 for action-aware iVideoGPT versus 16.59/0.220 for iVideoGPT. Existing benchmark means remain unchanged, but Table 3 revises uncertainty values: finetuned AdaWorld's average changes from 56.67±0.44% to 56.67±2.16%.

M1.justification: V1 adapts discrete controls by averaging latent actions into action embeddings. V2 Section 2.3 adds an MLP mapping continuous raw actions into the latent-action interface, initialized using action–latent-action pairs. This extends the adaptation procedure while retaining the core autoencoder, diffusion model, and training objectives.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Section 4 to Appendix F, and the conclusion is renumbered. V2 separates game and robot planning, expands adaptation explanations, renames the ablation section, and makes localized wording and affiliation edits. Most existing prose and the overall narrative are retained.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the visual presentation: Figure 1 is redesigned with robot-planning results, Table 1 gains human-evaluation columns, and Table 2 and Figure 6 incorporate nuScenes. New robot-planning and iVideoGPT tables and a UMAP figure are added. Appendix displays are retained across renumbering, while the data-mixture table gains an automated-generation column.

R1.justification: The retained related-work discussion adds citations including DriveGAN, MotionClone, Space-Time Diffusion Features, and PreLAR. References supporting the new benchmarks, planning procedure, and UMAP analysis are also added. The positioning relative to passive-video pretraining and discrete latent actions remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The VAE, beta-VAE, and diffusion objectives in Equations 1–3 are unchanged. V2 adds empirical analysis and procedural explanations, without new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1's quantitative adaptation and planning evidence centered on discrete controls and games. V2 substantially strengthens the broad adaptability claim through continuous-control simulation, robot planning, and a second world-model architecture. Human judgments and the beta analysis also strengthen evaluation and design justification. Omitted low-scoring robot tasks and unexplained Procgen error revisions remain weaknesses, but the new controlled comparisons materially improve the paper's evidential foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same AdaWorld research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds human evaluations, continuous-action simulation, robot planning, and additional analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original action-transfer, simulation, visual-planning, ablation, and action-clustering results in the main text and appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: We propose a unified optimization framework for designing continuous and discrete noise distributions that ensure differential privacy (DP) by minimizing R\'enyi DP, a variant of DP, under a cost constraint. R\'enyi DP has the advantage that by considering different values of the R\'enyi parameter $\alpha$, we can tailor our optimization for any number of compositions. To solve the optimization problem, we reduce it to a finite-dimensional convex formulation and perform preconditioned gradient descent. The resulting noise distributions are then compared to their Gaussian and Laplace counterparts. Numerical results demonstrate that our optimized distributions are consistently better, with significant improvements in $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP guarantees in the moderate composition regimes, compared to Gaussian and Laplace distributions with the same variance.

C1.justification: The abstract, conclusion, and central framework and endpoint-recovery claims remain unchanged. The introductory performance illustration broadens its lower-epsilon claim from Gaussian and Laplace to the enlarged comparator set including Cactus and Staircase.

C2.justification: V2 expands the mechanism-selection interpretation, presenting optimized noise as a reliable default when the best conventional mechanism is unclear. Appendix D explains how noise scale shifts the improvement region and explicitly limits the dataset comparison to noise addition, excluding the shared quantile-release privacy cost.

D1.justification: V2 adds an implementation repository reference and substantial experimental documentation in Appendix D: dataset sizes and features, query descriptions, percentile rescaling, clipping, and sampling procedures. New distribution examples also specify their numerical parameters. These additions improve documentation without changing the core algorithm.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates noise distributions without real-data query experiments. V2 adds private statistical queries on Breast Cancer Wisconsin Diagnostic, Diabetes, and UCI Heart Disease Cleveland data, covering feature averages and subgroup-specific clinical statistics.

E2.justification: Cactus and Staircase were discussed but not evaluated as comparators in v1. V2 adds them to the privacy curves and composition grid, including discrete counterparts in Figures 5 and 7, and directly compares distribution shapes in Figure 2. The new dataset table reports comparisons against Gaussian.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a dataset protocol using percentile normalization, clipping, ten queries, and 100,000 noisy outputs per query, measuring MSE at fixed privacy budgets. Figure 1 changes its standard deviation from 5 to 8. The earlier standard-deviation-5 pointwise comparison remains in Appendix D, alongside additional parameter settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct numerical checks of Cactus recovery at 50,000 compositions and Staircase recovery at one composition in Figure 2. It also expands distribution-shape examples and adds a delta = 10^-9 composition grid in Appendix D, substantially extending the earlier parameter and regime analyses.

E5.justification: V2 introduces mean and standard deviation reporting across 20 random seeds for the new MSE experiments in Table 1. V1 contains no comparable uncertainty reporting. This addition does not establish any increase in runs for the retained numerical evaluations.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds mean MSE reductions of 8.11–11.48% against Gaussian, alongside new distribution-recovery results and broader comparator rankings. Figure 1 changes the reported optimized epsilon from 2.66 to 1.62, but also changes standard deviation from 5 to 8; these are different-setting results.

M1.justification: The distribution families, geometric tails, RDP optimization objective, initialization, preconditioned gradient descent, and alpha updates remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–3 specify the same procedures.

P1.justification: The title changes to 'Optimizing Noise Distributions for Differential Privacy.' V2 rewrites and expands the numerical discussion and adds Appendix D, acknowledgements, and an impact statement. The main section sequence, methodological exposition, and proof text remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: The visual presentation is extensively revised: comparison plots gain curves and legends, the composition grid gains additional mechanism categories, and new paired distribution plots and an MSE table appear. V1's Figure 3 comparison is retained and expanded as v2's appendix Figure 7; the original single-distribution illustration is replaced by other examples.

R1.justification: The existing methodological references are retained, while dataset sources and an implementation reference are added. Cactus and Staircase receive more explicit positioning as practical alternatives, although their previously stated optimality regimes and the paper's methodological novelty remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical framework, Theorems 3.1 and 3.6, Proposition 3.5, and proofs in Appendices A–C are unchanged. Equation 1 merely abbreviates the expectation notation; the added experiments do not introduce new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation by addressing v1's omission of Cactus and Staircase from evaluated baselines and directly testing the claimed recovery of these mechanisms. It also adds dataset utility experiments with uncertainty reporting and reproduction details while preserving the theory. The dataset results exclude quantile-release privacy costs, limiting their interpretation to relative noise-mechanism utility, but the broader comparative evidence provides a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-optimization framework despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original numerical evaluations, including additional mechanism comparisons and repeated-seed MSE experiments on three datasets.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–4 report original numerical evaluations of optimized noise distributions and their privacy guarantees.

arxiv_record.abstract: Deep neural networks often degrade under distribution shifts. Although domain adaptation offers a solution, privacy constraints often prevent access to source data, making Test-Time Adaptation (TTA, which adapts using only unlabeled test data) increasingly attractive. However, current TTA methods still face practical challenges: (1) a primary focus on instance-wise alignment, overlooking CORrelation ALignment (CORAL) due to missing source correlations; (2) complex backpropagation operations for model updating, resulting in overhead computation and (3) domain forgetting. To address these challenges, we provide a theoretical analysis to investigate the feasibility of Test-time Correlation Alignment (TCA), demonstrating that correlation alignment between high-certainty instances and test instances can enhance test performances with a theoretical guarantee. Based on this, we propose two simple yet effective algorithms: LinearTCA and LinearTCA+. LinearTCA applies a simple linear transformation to achieve both instance and correlation alignment without additional model updates, while LinearTCA+ serves as a plug-and-play module that can easily boost existing TTA methods. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical insights and show that TCA methods significantly outperforms baselines across various tasks, benchmarks and backbones. Notably, LinearTCA achieves higher accuracy with only 4% GPU memory and 0.6% computation time compared to the best TTA baseline. It also outperforms existing methods on CLIP over 1.86%.

C1.justification: The abstract removes v1's specific claim of a 5.88% LinearTCA improvement on OfficeHome and adds a headline CLIP performance claim. The central contributions—source-free correlation alignment, theoretical support, efficient LinearTCA, and plug-and-play LinearTCA+—remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting CLIP performance to image-text embedding alignment and small-batch robustness to incremental covariance estimation. It also interprets true-source controls as evidence of the importance of approximating source distributions. The existing limitations concerning imperfect pseudo-sources, weak feature extractors, and nonlinear shifts remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies a fixed 1e-3 transformation-optimization learning rate, AdaNPC tuning information, and TorchVision initialization for ImageNet-C. The code link and core implementation description remain unchanged. Conversely, the explicit continual-corruption order and associated caption wording are removed, reducing protocol documentation without establishing that the underlying procedure changed.

E1.justification: v2 adds DomainNet's six-domain, 345-class evaluation, ImageNet-C's 1,000-class corruption evaluation, and VLCS classification within the CLIP experiments. The original PACS, OfficeHome, CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, and synthetic-shift coverage is retained.

E2.justification: T3A, AdaNPC, and PLC are added to the existing accuracy, efficiency, and forgetting comparisons and corresponding appendix tables. The new CLIP comparison also includes TPT, CLIPArTT, WATT-P, and WATT-S, with their baseline values explicitly attributed to WATT. Existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include CLIP-ViT-B/16 comparisons following WATT, target-domain fine-tuning and true-source-distribution controls, and OfficeHome testing across batch sizes 1–1024. DomainNet adds clipart-based hyperparameter selection. The existing default ResNet and ViT batch sizes remain 128 and 64.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of nonlinear transformation depth, performance with true source distributions or target-domain fine-tuning, and batch-size sensitivity of accuracy and pseudo-source estimation error (Tables 6–8). These address questions beyond v1's retained pseudo-source-size, test-sample-size, and synthetic linear/nonlinear-shift analyses.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without empirical uncertainty intervals. v2 Table 5 introduces ± values for the work's LinearTCA+ CLIP results and reproduces uncertainty values for borrowed baselines. The meaning of ± and the run or seed counts remain unspecified.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for the new benchmarks, CLIP comparisons, and Tables 6–8 analyses. On CIFAR-10-C with ViT-B/16, LinearTCA+ remains at 79.55%, but the strongest baseline changes from EATA at 73.67% to AdaNPC at 74.60%, reducing its margin from 5.88 to 4.95 points. Some retained baseline scores and runtime/memory measurements also change; these do not establish same-setting efficiency gains.

M1.justification: v2 adds two- and three-layer MLP transformation variants of LinearTCA and LinearTCA+ in Section 5.5 and Table 6. These extend the original linear alignment procedure, while the principal algorithms in Section 4 and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, parts of the introduction, and efficiency, forgetting, and ablation discussions receive localized rewrites. A foundation-model subsection is inserted before the expanded analysis section, while the overall narrative and Appendix A–E organization remain stable.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially reorganized into separate domain and corruption blocks with method categories; Table 2 combines its memory and runtime displays. Figure 1 adds comparator traces, Tables 5–8 introduce new main-text displays, and the appendix gains benchmark tables and comparator rows. The original pipeline and diagnostic figures are retained rather than replaced.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting T3A, PLC, WATT, CLIP, DomainNet, and probabilistic contrastive TTA, and expands Appendix A's descriptions of selected comparators. The CORAL positioning and distinction between backpropagation-free and backpropagation-based methods were already present in v1 and remain intact.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.5 and Appendix B.1 substantially revise the probability bound and its Chernoff derivation, introducing source-sample-size dependence and explicitly sampling source instances from Ds intersect Omega. The covariance concentration argument is rewritten to distinguish sampled, true-source, and pseudo-source matrices and specifies a unit-range assumption. Theorem 3.6 and Corollary 3.7 are substantively retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central efficiency and applicability claims by adding directly relevant backpropagation-free comparators, larger-scale and CLIP evaluations, and tests of nonlinear alignment and small-batch behavior. These address important evidential gaps in v1. The gains outweigh reporting problems: Section 5.3 overstates LinearTCA's DomainNet ranking relative to Table 1, and Table 7 uses unexplained OfficeHome reference scores that differ from the main comparison.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Test-time Correlation Alignment with the same authors and core framework. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E are accessible and matchable despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds DomainNet, ImageNet-C, CLIP, nonlinear-transformation, source-access, and batch-size results. Table 5 explicitly distinguishes borrowed baseline results from the work's TCA results.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark, efficiency, forgetting, theoretical-validation, and synthetic-shift experiments in Sections 5 and Appendix E.

arxiv_record.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with delays is challenging as sensory perceptions lag behind the actual events: the RL agent needs to estimate the real state of its environment based on past observations. State-of-the-art (SOTA) methods typically employ recursive, step-by-step forecasting of states. This can cause the accumulation of compounding errors. To tackle this problem, our novel belief estimation method, named Directly Forecasting Belief Transformer (DFBT), directly forecasts states from observations without incrementally estimating intermediate states step-by-step. We theoretically demonstrate that DFBT greatly reduces compounding errors of existing recursively forecasting methods, yielding stronger performance guarantees. In experiments with D4RL offline datasets, DFBT reduces compounding errors with remarkable prediction accuracy. DFBT's capability to forecast state sequences also facilitates multi-step bootstrapping, thus greatly improving learning efficiency. On the MuJoCo benchmark, our DFBT-based method substantially outperforms SOTA baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/QingyuanWuNothing/DFBT.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: direct belief forecasting reduces compounding errors, supports stronger performance guarantees, and enables efficient multi-step SAC learning. The additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: Section 6.2.5 newly argues that frozen beliefs can miss task-specific information and that fine-tuning can address this, while explaining why the main approach separates belief learning from online RL. Existing limitations concerning offline-data dependence and unresolved sample complexity remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository address in the abstract, supplementing the existing supplementary-material code pointer. It also discloses SAC-based collection of 500k-sample datasets and approximate training durations. Appendix A's implementation framework and hyperparameter tables remain unchanged; detailed fine-tuning and timing configurations are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 expands beyond HalfCheetah, Hopper, and Walker2d to Pusher-v2, Reacher-v2, and Swimmer-v2, adding manipulation, reaching, and swimming tasks. It also evaluates noisy versions of the original environments, a distinct scenario from the stochastic observation delays already tested in v1.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparator set remains A-SAC, BPQL, ADRL, DATS, D-Dreamer, and D-SAC, including the added task and noisy-environment comparisons. The timing experiment uses the same belief-based comparators already evaluated for prediction accuracy; no new baseline method is introduced.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce online/offline/fine-tuning controls at 32 delays, SAC-collected datasets of 500k samples for additional tasks, noise occurring with probability 0.001 at 128 deterministic delays, and inference-latency measurements across 8, 32, and 128 delays. Existing evaluation metrics and Appendix A hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained bootstrapping ablation and qualitative comparisons, v2 tests dependence on belief-training strategy, robustness to environmental noise, and computational scaling with delay. Tables 4, 6, and 7 provide substantial new evidence about practical limitations previously untested.

E5.justification: Both versions state evaluation across five random seeds and report tabulated ± quantities and shaded learning curves. v2 extends this reporting style to new results without introducing new run-count disclosures, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3, matched appendix scores, and plotted results are unchanged. New Tables 4–7 add task, noise, training-strategy, and timing results; DFBT-SAC scores 1.04, 0.93, and 1.01 on Pusher, Reacher, and Swimmer. Fine-tuning improves Hopper and Walker2d but lowers HalfCheetah's mean. Table 4 also reports HalfCheetah's offline result as 0.42 ± 0.12, versus 0.42 ± 0.03 in retained Table 1, without explaining the discrepancy.

M1.justification: Section 6.2.5 introduces an evaluated adaptation that fine-tunes the pretrained belief during online RL, extending v1's offline-trained, frozen-belief procedure. This is an experimental variant: the main transformer architecture, losses, SAC updates, and default Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes scattered wording, spelling, and punctuation edits, expands the opening related-work paragraph, and adds four experimental subsections, acknowledgements, and an impact statement. Correspondence and publication information change, but the main narrative and Appendix A–E organization remain intact.

P2.justification: New Tables 4–7 substantially expand the displayed evidence to cover training strategies, additional tasks, noisy environments, and timing. Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 relocate, Figure 3 becomes more compact, and qualitative-panel captions are reformatted. Existing figure content is retained, while appendix tables are renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a paragraph positioning delayed RL against classical delay-differential-equation methods, with five additional control references. The introduction also adds Wei et al. (2017) on HVAC control. Existing delayed-RL and sequence-modeling positioning is retained; the VDPO publication update is bibliographic.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Lipschitz assumptions, recursive and direct forecasting bounds, and comparison propositions in Section 5 are retained. Appendix B contains the same proofs; notation and wording edits do not change the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical validation beyond v1's three locomotion tasks: Tables 4–7 examine broader tasks, environmental noise, reliance on pretrained beliefs, and computational cost. The training-strategy ablation replaces an untested limitation with informative, mixed outcomes, and the repository pointer improves access information. These gains preserve the original evidence, although sparse new-protocol details and Table 4's unexplained uncertainty discrepancy limit reproducibility and precision.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DFBT/DFBT-SAC research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–E are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on further MuJoCo tasks, noisy environments, belief-training strategies, and computational efficiency in Sections 6.2.4–6.2.7.

arxiv_record.abstract: The rise of LLMs has increased concerns over source tracing and copyright protection for AIGC, highlighting the need for advanced detection technologies. Passive detection methods usually face high false positives, while active watermarking techniques using logits or sampling manipulation offer more effective protection. Existing LLM watermarking methods, though effective on unaltered content, suffer significant performance drops when the text is modified and could introduce biases that degrade LLM performance in downstream tasks. These methods fail to achieve an optimal tradeoff between text quality and robustness, particularly due to the lack of end-to-end optimization of the encoder and decoder. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end logits perturbation method for watermarking LLM-generated text. By jointly optimization, our approach achieves a better balance between quality and robustness. To address non-differentiable operations in the end-to-end training pipeline, we introduce an online prompting technique that leverages the on-the-fly LLM as a differentiable surrogate. Our method achieves superior robustness, outperforming distortion-free methods by 37-39% under paraphrasing and 17.2% on average, while maintaining text quality on par with these distortion-free methods in terms of text perplexity and downstream tasks. Our method can be easily generalized to different LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/KahimWong/E2E-LLM-Watermark.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: joint encoder-decoder optimization, differentiable online prompting, a robustness-quality advantage and cross-LLM transfer without additional training. The new appendix evidence does not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands explanations of robustness through neural decoding and adaptive context dependence, and explains temperature effects through top-logit selection. It newly discusses watermark-theft vulnerability, mitigation costs and the tradeoff between token-distribution bias and robustness. These materially qualify the method's practical behavior beyond v1's discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit code-repository link and documents a consequential three-stage curriculum: detection alone before 10k steps, joint objectives during 10k-20k, and online paraphrasing after 20k. It also revises the batch-size disclosure and specifies keyed fine-tuning details. The curriculum is newly documented; the PDFs do not establish that it replaced a different earlier schedule.

E1.justification: v3 adds watermark-theft evaluation on Dolly CW and MMW BookReports, extending evaluation beyond ordinary text modifications. Table 14 also adds green-list-ratio measurements on five corpora: xsum, StackOverflow-QA-C-Language-40k, ML-ArXiv-Papers, mimic-cxr-dataset and finance-alpaca. The original training and downstream-task datasets are retained.

E2.justification: The existing accuracy-comparison baseline sets are retained. The efficiency study expands from measurements of the proposed method alone to a direct comparison with KGW, Unbiased and EXP-Edit in v3 Table 19; EXP-Edit was previously discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include 2,000-query spoofing attacks, TPR at a fixed 1% FPR, context-size comparisons and evaluation of a variant fine-tuned for 5,000 steps. The stated training batch size also changes from 16 in v1 Table 8 to 8 in v3 Table 15. This reporting change does not establish that the retained benchmarks were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices B.2-B.5 and C.2 substantially expand analysis through edited-text neural-versus-statistical decoder comparisons, context-size ablations, watermark-theft and mitigation tests, green-list statistics, token-distribution bias and training stability. Existing length, temperature, sampling and component ablations remain.

E5.justification: v3 adds three from-scratch training runs of 5,000 steps with seeds 63, 64 and 65, plus mean and standard deviation reporting for corpus-level green-list ratios. The five generation trials, shared-seed practice, paired t-tests and uncertainty values from v1 Appendix I are retained in v3 Appendix A.6.

E6.justification: The original benchmark tables retain their numerical results, while v3 adds substantial security, decoder, bias, stability and timing results. Its new fine-tuning comparison reports PPL of 7.28 versus 7.73, but paraphrasing TPR of 0.53 versus 0.75 at 1% FPR (Table 13). These compare variants within v3, not improved performance of the unchanged method across versions. Some summary percentages also change, including 17.2% to 17.3% in Section 4.2.

M1.justification: The core encoder-decoder architecture, losses, online prompting and cross-LLM converter remain unchanged. Appendix B.3 adds a limited extension using a key-driven binary logit bias on top-k candidates and fine-tuning to obtain distinct watermarks.

P1.justification: The appendix is substantially reorganized from separate A-K sections into thematic A-E groups with nested subsections and a contents page. Existing significance tests, training details and editing examples are regrouped. Main-text copyediting, revised cross-references, acknowledgements and an impact statement accompany this structural revision.

P2.justification: v3 adds seven tables and two figures presenting the new analyses. Figures 1-10 are retained with layout adjustments, while existing tables receive clearer metric and task labels. Figure 8's incorrect ROC-curve caption is corrected to describe sentence-length detection performance.

R1.justification: v3 adds Bengio et al. on curriculum learning and Jovanovic et al. on watermark stealing to support the new training discussion and security evaluation. The main related-work section and positioning against existing watermarking approaches remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds a conditional mathematical argument for distinct keyed watermarks: independent uniform binary assumptions produce a Bin(k, 0.5) mismatch model and an identical-watermark probability of 2^-20 for k=20. The original method equations and tokenizer-alignment calculation remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves scrutiny of the robustness claims through fixed-FPR decoder comparisons, mechanism analyses and explicit watermark-theft testing that v1 lacked. The security extension's reduced paraphrasing TPR is reported, making its practical tradeoff visible. Documenting the training curriculum and code access also improves reproducibility information. These gains materially strengthen the paper despite unchanged main benchmark results and the limited 5,000-step scope of the new training-stability study.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same end-to-end LLM watermarking work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds original watermark-theft experiments, decoder comparisons, corpus statistics and training-stability analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original watermark detection, text-quality, translation, code-generation, ablation and efficiency results, including repeated-trial significance tests in Appendix I.

arxiv_record.abstract: While several feature embedding models have been developed in the literature, comparisons of these embeddings have largely focused on their numerical performance in classification-related downstream applications. However, an interpretable comparison of different embeddings requires identifying and analyzing mismatches between sample groups clustered within the embedding spaces. In this work, we propose the \emph{Spectral Pairwise Embedding Comparison (SPEC)} framework to compare embeddings and identify their differences in clustering a reference dataset. Our approach examines the kernel matrices derived from two embeddings and leverages the eigendecomposition of the difference kernel matrix to detect sample clusters that are captured differently by the two embeddings. We present a scalable implementation of this kernel-based approach, with computational complexity that grows linearly with the sample size. Furthermore, we introduce an optimization problem using this framework to align two embeddings, ensuring that clusters identified in one embedding are also captured in the other model. We provide numerical results demonstrating the SPEC's application to compare and align embeddings on large-scale datasets such as ImageNet and MS-COCO. The project page is available at https://mjalali.github.io/SPEC/.
arxiv_record.authors: Mohammad Jalali, Bahar Dibaei Nia, Farzan Farnia
arxiv_record.title: Towards an Explainable Comparison and Alignment of Feature Embeddings

C1.justification: The central contributions of interpretable embedding comparison, scalable computation, and alignment remain. The introduction refines the scalability claim from O(max{d^3,n}) to O(d^2 n+d^3), preserving linear dependence on sample size for bounded feature dimension.

C2.justification: v3 adds practical qualifications concerning low-feature-budget cluster inconsistencies and the scaling limits of direct eigendecomposition (Appendix B.1). Remark 2 explains the minibatch-optimization advantage of Frobenius alignment. Existing interpretations of embedding semantics and the limitation to spectrally detectable clusters largely remain.

D1.justification: v3 identifies PyTorch eig as the direct implementation used in the runtime comparison and replaces the abstract's direct code-repository pointer with a project-page pointer. Existing hardware information, synthetic-data prompt, and fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions cover AFHQ, FFHQ, ImageNet-1K including ImageWoof and text-overlaid subsets, MS-COCO images and captions, GPT-4o-generated text, and WikiText-2. The new experiments vary computation and alignment within existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 introduces a runtime comparison between direct Algorithm 1/PyTorch eig and the Cholesky alternative. Existing embedding-model and classification comparators remain. The K-means agreement comparison on text-overlaid ImageNet disappears with Figure 3's diagnostic panels.

E3.justification: New experiments in v3 Appendix B.1 measure runtime across dimensions from 1,000 to 10,000 and sweep random Fourier features from 1,000 to 6,000, including paired visualizations at 2,000 and 6,000. Retained experiments preserve the default 2,000 features, bandwidth-selection rule, and fine-tuning configuration.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of eigensolver scalability, cluster sensitivity to the random-feature budget, and convergence under the alternative alignment loss (Appendices B.1 and B.6). Conversely, Figure 3 loses its UMAP, within-cluster-distance, and K-means agreement diagnostics. Earlier visualization-method ablations and similarity-ranking sanity checks remain.

E5.justification: Both versions disclose 50 K-means runs, retain the same AMI/NMI uncertainty-reporting practice, and specify training seed 0. v3 introduces no new repeated-run, uncertainty-estimation, or significance-testing procedure. The deleted Figure 3 statistics are removed results rather than a revised reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 Table 1 adds runtimes, including 72 seconds for direct computation versus 33 for Cholesky at d=4,000, and 85 seconds for Cholesky at d=10,000. Figures 6-9 add feature-budget-dependent cluster findings, and Figure 22 adds l2-alignment convergence results. Figure 3 loses four AMI results and associated diagnostics. Matched ImageNet accuracies remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v3 adds a Cholesky-based reduction to a symmetric eigenproblem (Remark 1 and Appendix A.3) and an eigenvalue-l2/Frobenius alignment objective with minibatch computation (Remark 2). These extend the computational procedure and alignment loss beyond v1. Algorithm 1 also corrects its symmetric-factorization expression and eigenpair indexing.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify terminology, complexity, and matrix asymmetry. Remarks 1-2 and new appendix subsections expand the exposition, while the main section order and most existing experimental and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands visual presentation with feature-budget image grids, paired t-SNE/UMAP displays, an alignment-kernel and convergence figure, and a runtime table. Figure 3 is shortened by removing diagnostic panels. Existing configuration and accuracy tables move from v1 page 28 to v3 page 38; most other figures are retained with new numbering.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly positions SPEC as a kernel-PCA extension, contrasts it with Vargas et al. (2024), and acknowledges concurrent Frobenius alignment by Gong et al. (2025). It adds selected random-feature and generative-evaluation references while removing citations including Boggust et al. (2022) and Ng et al. (2001). The overall related-work scope remains similar.

T1.justification: v3 adds the Cholesky spectral-equivalence derivation and Frobenius-distance identity. It restores feature-dimension factors in the complexity analysis and changes Theorem 2's bound from 128 log(2/delta)/m to 128 log(3/delta)/m, correcting the exponential factor in its appendix proof. These are substantive mathematical additions and corrections.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens technical reliability by correcting Algorithm 1's treatment of the nonsymmetric matrix, restoring feature-dimension factors in the scalability analysis, and repairing Theorem 2's bound. The Cholesky derivation, runtime measurements, and feature-budget sensitivity tests give the central scalability argument stronger practical support. These gains and the evaluated alignment alternative outweigh the loss of Figure 3's diagnostic evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPEC/SPEC-align work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds eigensolver timings, random Fourier feature sensitivity results, and an alternative alignment experiment.

before.justification: v1 Section 6 and Appendix B report original embedding comparisons, clustering diagnostics, alignment experiments, and ImageNet classification results.
